01. Bitly (URL Shortener) (Easy)

Bitly takes a long web address, like a 300-character product link, and gives back a tiny one, like short.ly/aZ3k9. When anyone clicks the tiny link, they land on the original page. The interviewer is really testing three things: can you generate short codes that never collide, can you make a read-heavy system fast with caching, and can you scale writes without breaking uniqueness.

1. Functional requirements

Core (must have):

  1. Users can submit a long URL and get back a short URL.
  2. Users can optionally pick a custom alias (for example short.ly/my-sale).
  3. Users can optionally set an expiration date for the link.
  4. Anyone who opens a short URL is redirected to the original long URL.

Below the line (out of scope):

  1. Click analytics (counts per country, per device). Useful, but it is a separate pipeline and does not change the core design.
  2. User accounts and link management dashboards. We assume an API key is enough.
  3. Spam and malware scanning of target URLs. Real systems do it, but it is a side service.

2. Non-functional requirements

  1. Uniqueness: every short code maps to exactly one long URL. A collision is a correctness bug, not a performance bug.
  2. Low latency: p99 redirect latency under 100 ms, measured at the server. Creating a link can be slower, p99 under 500 ms.
  3. High availability for reads: 99.99% for redirects (about 52 minutes of downtime per year). A broken redirect breaks every page that embedded the link.
  4. Scale: 1 billion stored links, 100 million daily active users, 10k redirects per second at peak.
  5. Consistency: eventual consistency is fine for reads. If a new link takes a second to appear in every cache, nobody notices. Strong consistency is needed only for the uniqueness check when writing.
  6. CAP choice: we pick availability over consistency (AP) for redirects. During a network partition we would rather serve a slightly stale mapping than fail the redirect. Writes rely on a database UNIQUE constraint, which is a local, consistent check.

3. Back-of-the-envelope estimates

Assumption Number
Daily active users 100M
New links per day 1M
Read to write ratio 1000 : 1
Average row size (code + URL + metadata) 500 bytes
Retention 5 years
Average redirect response size 500 bytes 
Writes:  1M links/day / 86,400 s     ~= 12 writes/sec  (peak x5 = 60/s)
Reads:   12 x 1000                   ~= 12k reads/sec  (avg)
         Design target: 10k-20k redirects/sec, peak 50k/s

Storage: 1M/day x 365 x 500 B        ~= 182 GB/year
         5 years                     ~= 0.9 TB  (fits one Postgres box)

Bandwidth (reads): 12k/s x 500 B     ~= 6 MB/s  (tiny)

Cache: 20% of links get 80% of traffic.
       Hot set = 20% of 1M daily new x 500 B = 100 MB/day, a few GB total.

The key takeaway: storage and bandwidth are small. The hard part is read QPS and unique code generation.

4. Core entities

  • URL mapping: the record that ties a short code to a long URL. Fields: short_code, long_url, created_at, expires_at, user_id.
  • User: who created the link. Fields: user_id, api_key_hash, created_at.
  • Counter: a single global number used to generate unique codes. Fields: name, value.
  • Custom alias: not a separate table, just a URL mapping whose short_code was chosen by the user.
CREATE TABLE url_mapping (
  short_code  VARCHAR(16) PRIMARY KEY,   -- PRIMARY KEY gives a B-tree index
  long_url    TEXT        NOT NULL,
  user_id     BIGINT,
  created_at  TIMESTAMP   NOT NULL DEFAULT now(),
  expires_at  TIMESTAMP,
  is_custom   BOOLEAN     NOT NULL DEFAULT false
);

CREATE TABLE users (
  user_id       BIGSERIAL PRIMARY KEY,
  api_key_hash  TEXT NOT NULL,
  created_at    TIMESTAMP NOT NULL DEFAULT now()
);

5. API design

POST /urls – create a short URL.

// request (Authorization: Bearer <api key>)
{
  "long_url": "https://shop.example.com/product/12345?ref=summer",
  "custom_alias": "summer-sale",
  "expires_at": "2027-01-01T00:00:00Z"
}
// response 201 Created
{
  "short_url": "https://short.ly/summer-sale",
  "short_code": "summer-sale",
  "expires_at": "2027-01-01T00:00:00Z"
}

Status codes: 201 created, 400 invalid URL, 409 alias already taken, 401 bad API key, 429 rate limited.

GET /{short_code} – redirect to the long URL. No auth, this is public.

HTTP/1.1 302 Found
Location: https://shop.example.com/product/12345?ref=summer
Cache-Control: private, max-age=0

Status codes: 302 redirect, 404 unknown code, 410 Gone expired.

We start with one stateless server and one database. Deep dives add the cache, the counter, and split services.

How will users shorten a URL?

  1. Client sends POST /urls with the long URL, optional alias, optional expiry.
  2. Server checks the API key, then validates the URL (scheme is http/https, length under 2,048 chars, host is not our own domain to avoid redirect loops).
  3. If a custom alias was given, the server checks it only contains [A-Za-z0-9-] and is not reserved (like api or login).
  4. Otherwise the server generates a short code (deep dive below).
  5. Server inserts the row. The PRIMARY KEY on short_code rejects duplicates. For a custom alias, a duplicate returns 409.
  6. Server returns 201 with the short URL.
sequenceDiagram
    participant C as Client
    participant L as Load balancer
    participant S as Server
    participant G as Code generator
    participant D as Postgres
    C->>L: POST /urls with long URL
    L->>S: forward request
    S->>S: check API key and validate URL
    alt custom alias given
        S->>S: check alias characters and reserved words
    else no alias
        S->>G: request next short code
        G-->>S: short code
    end
    S->>D: INSERT row
    D-->>S: ok or duplicate key
    S-->>L: 201 short URL or 409
    L-->>C: response

We do not deduplicate long URLs by default. Two users shortening the same link may want different expirations, so each gets its own code.

How will users be redirected from a short URL to the original long URL?

  1. Browser requests GET https://short.ly/aZ3k9. Our domain points at our load balancer.
  2. Server looks up aZ3k9 in the database by primary key.
  3. If missing, return 404. If expires_at is in the past, return 410 Gone.
  4. Otherwise return 302 Found with Location: <long_url>.
  5. The browser follows the Location header automatically.

Why 302 and not 301? A 301 means “moved permanently”, and browsers cache it forever. After the first click, the browser would skip our server, so we could never expire or edit the link, and we lose click counts. A 302 means “temporary”, so every click comes back to us.

Code Browser caches? Can we expire/edit? Server load
301 Moved Permanently Yes, aggressively No, not reliably Lower
302 Found No Yes Higher

7. Deep dives

How can we ensure that each shortened URL is short and unique?

The problem: we need codes that are short (6-8 chars), never collide, and are cheap to generate.

First, how short can we go? We use Base62, which means the 62 characters 0-9, a-z, A-Z. Each character holds 62 possibilities.

62^6 = 56.8 billion codes
62^7 = 3.5 trillion codes
We need 1B links -> 6 characters is already enough, 7 gives headroom.
Option How it works Pros Cons
Random string Pick 7 random Base62 chars, retry on conflict Simple, unpredictable Collisions grow as table fills; needs a DB check every time
Hash + truncate base62(md5(long_url))[:7] Same URL gives same code Collisions still possible; must handle them
Counter + Base62 Global counter increments, encode number in Base62 Zero collisions by construction, very short codes Needs a shared counter; codes are predictable

Recommended: counter + Base62, with a Redis counter shared by all write servers. Uniqueness is guaranteed because each number is handed out once. If predictability matters (people guessing other links), we can run the number through a reversible scramble, like a Feistel cipher or a fixed bijective shuffle, before encoding. The DB PRIMARY KEY is the final safety net.

ALPHABET = "0123456789abcdefghijklmnopqrstuvwxyzABCDEFGHIJKLMNOPQRSTUVWXYZ"

def base62_encode(n: int) -> str:
    """Turn a non-negative integer into a Base62 string."""
    if n == 0:
        return ALPHABET[0]
    out = []
    while n > 0:
        n, rem = divmod(n, 62)
        out.append(ALPHABET[rem])
    return "".join(reversed(out))

# Example: counter value 1,000,000,000 -> "15ftgG" (6 chars)

To keep custom aliases from clashing with future generated codes, we can require custom aliases to contain a hyphen or be at least 8 characters, so the two namespaces never overlap.

How can we ensure that redirects are fast?

The problem: a redirect is on the critical path of every click. A DB round trip is 5-10 ms when warm, but under 10k QPS a single DB becomes the bottleneck.

Step one is the index. Because short_code is the primary key, Postgres uses a B-tree index, so lookups are O(log n), not a full table scan. For 1B rows that is about 30 comparisons.

Step two is caching. The access pattern is extremely skewed: a viral link gets millions of clicks.

Option Latency Hit rate Notes
DB only with index 5-10 ms n/a Fine at low QPS, falls over at peak
In-memory cache (Redis) in front of DB under 1 ms 90%+ Cache-aside, LRU eviction
CDN / edge redirect under 20 ms end to end for the user Very high for hot links Short TTL needed so expiry still works

Recommended: Redis cache-aside, plus optional CDN edge caching for very hot links with a short TTL (for example 60 s).

def resolve(code: str) -> str | None:
    long_url = redis.get(f"url:{code}")
    if long_url:
        return long_url                      # cache hit, < 1 ms
    row = db.fetch_one(
        "SELECT long_url, expires_at FROM url_mapping WHERE short_code = %s",
        (code,))
    if row is None or (row.expires_at and row.expires_at < now()):
        redis.set(f"url:{code}", "__none__", ex=60)  # negative cache
        return None
    ttl = 86400
    if row.expires_at:
        ttl = min(ttl, int((row.expires_at - now()).total_seconds()))
    redis.set(f"url:{code}", row.long_url, ex=ttl)
    return row.long_url

Notice two details. The cache TTL never outlives the link’s expiry, so expired links stop working on time. And we cache “not found” briefly, so a bot hammering random codes does not hit the database every time.

How can your system scale to support 10k redirects (reads) per second?

The problem: one server and one DB will not survive 10k reads per second plus spikes, and we want the read path to survive failures.

Per-instance capacity (rough): a stateless redirect server ~2-5k RPS
10k RPS / 2k per box = 5 boxes, run 8 for headroom and AZ loss.
Redis single node: ~100k ops/sec, so one primary + replica is plenty.
Expected DB load after a 95% cache hit rate: 10k x 5% = 500 QPS.
Option What it fixes Trade-off
Split Read Service and Write Service Scale redirects independently of creates Two deployables
Horizontal scaling behind a load balancer More RPS, survives a box dying Needs stateless servers
DB read replicas Absorb cache misses Replication lag of ~ms
Shard DB by short_code hash Past 10 TB or very high write QPS Not needed at 1 TB

Recommended: split read and write services, run the read service on 6-10 stateless instances across availability zones, put Redis in front, and add 1-2 Postgres read replicas. Sharding is not needed at this size; say so in the interview and explain when you would add it.

The write side has one catch. If several write servers each keep their own counter, they will hand out the same number. So we keep one counter in Redis and use counter batching:

BATCH = 1000

class CodeAllocator:
    def __init__(self):
        self.next = 0
        self.end = 0

    def next_code(self) -> str:
        if self.next >= self.end:
            # INCRBY is atomic in Redis, so two servers never get
            # overlapping ranges.
            self.end = redis.incrby("global_url_counter", BATCH)
            self.next = self.end - BATCH
        n = self.next
        self.next += 1
        return base62_encode(n)

Each write server talks to Redis once per 1,000 links instead of once per link. If a server crashes, it wastes up to 999 numbers, which is fine: we need uniqueness, not a gap-free sequence.

What happens when something fails?

Failure Effect Mitigation
Redis cache node dies Cache misses spike to DB Replica promotion; DB replicas absorb ~10k QPS briefly
Redis counter loses last writes on failover A few numbers might be reissued DB PRIMARY KEY rejects duplicate, writer retries with next number
Primary DB dies Writes fail, reads keep working from cache and replicas Automatic failover (for example RDS Multi-AZ, ~60 s)
One region down Users in that region fail Multi-region read path, each region gets a disjoint counter range

9. Common mistakes and interviewer follow-ups

  • Using a 301 redirect. It hurts because browsers cache it and you lose control of expiry and analytics. Say: “I’ll use 302 so every click hits us; I can add a short CDN TTL if load is an issue.”
  • Hashing the long URL and ignoring collisions. Truncated hashes do collide. Say how you detect and retry, or switch to a counter.
  • Keeping a counter in each server’s memory. Two servers produce the same code. Say: “One atomic counter in Redis, with batching.”
  • Jumping to sharding. 1 TB fits on one machine. Say: “We don’t need to shard yet; here is the size where I would.”
  • Forgetting expiry in the cache. A cached entry with a 24 h TTL keeps an expired link alive. Cap the TTL at expires_at.
  • Predictable codes. Sequential codes let people enumerate links. Mention a reversible scramble if privacy matters.
  • Follow-up: “How do you add analytics?” Answer: the read service emits a click event to Kafka asynchronously, so the redirect is not slowed down.

10. One-page cheat sheet

Topic Key point
Scale 1B links, ~12 writes/s, 10k-50k reads/s, ~1 TB over 5 years
Code format Base62, 7 chars = 3.5 trillion codes
Uniqueness Redis INCRBY counter with batches of 1,000 + DB primary key
Redirect 302 Found, 410 for expired, 404 for unknown
Fast reads B-tree primary key, Redis cache-aside, negative caching, CDN for hot links
Scaling Separate read/write services, 8 stateless read nodes, read replicas
CAP AP for redirects, uniqueness enforced by DB constraint
Failure Cache dies: DB replicas; counter loses data: PK catches dupes

02. Dropbox (File Storage and Sync) (Easy)

Dropbox lets you drop a file into a folder on your laptop and see it appear on your phone and your other computers a few seconds later. You can also share files with other people and download them from anywhere. The interviewer is really testing how you move big files (up to 50 GB) reliably over flaky networks, how you keep many devices in sync, and whether you keep your servers out of the heavy data path.

1. Functional requirements

Core (must have):

  1. Users can upload a file from any device.
  2. Users can download a file from any device.
  3. Users can share a file with other users and see files shared with them.
  4. Files sync automatically across all of a user’s devices.

Below the line (out of scope):

  1. Full version history and restore. We keep a simple version number, but a full timeline is a separate feature.
  2. Real-time collaborative editing (like Google Docs). That needs operational transforms, a different problem.
  3. Search inside file contents. It needs a text index and is not core to storage.

2. Non-functional requirements

  1. Large files: support files up to 50 GB.
  2. Reliability and durability: no uploaded file is ever lost. Target 11 nines (99.999999999%) durability, which is what S3 advertises.
  3. Resumable transfers: a dropped connection should not restart a 50 GB upload from zero.
  4. Low sync latency: a change on one device shows on others within about 5 seconds when online.
  5. Availability over consistency: 99.99% availability for upload and download. It is fine if a user in another country sees the new file a few seconds late. We choose AP because nothing breaks when sync is briefly stale, unlike a bank balance.
  6. Security: only owners and people a file was shared with can read it. Encryption in transit (TLS) and at rest.

3. Back-of-the-envelope estimates

Assumption Number
Total users 500M
Daily active users 100M
Files uploaded per DAU per day 2
Average file size 1 MB (most are small; a few are huge)
Chunk size 5 MB
Downloads per upload 3
Metadata per file 1 KB 
Uploads:   100M x 2 / 86,400 s        ~= 2,300 uploads/sec  (peak ~7k/s)
Downloads: 2,300 x 3                  ~= 7,000 downloads/sec

New data/day:  200M files x 1 MB      = 200 TB/day
Per year:      200 TB x 365           ~= 73 PB/year (before dedup)
With ~30% dedup savings               ~= 50 PB/year

Metadata/year: 200M x 365 x 1 KB      ~= 73 TB/year (DB, shardable)

Upload bandwidth: 200 TB / 86,400 s   ~= 2.3 GB/s (straight into S3)

One 50 GB upload at 100 Mbps:
  50 GB x 8 bits / 100 Mbps = 4,000 s ~= 1.1 hours

The 1.1 hour number is the whole point: you cannot do that in a single HTTP request.

4. Core entities

  • File: the raw bytes. Stored in blob storage (S3), not in a database.
  • FileMetadata: name, size, MIME type, owner, status, content fingerprint, list of chunks.
  • Chunk: a 5 MB slice of a file. Fields: index, SHA-256 fingerprint, upload status, ETag.
  • User: the account. Fields: user_id, email.
  • SharedFile: who can access which file. Fields: file_id, user_id, permission.
  • Device: a client that syncs. Fields: device_id, user_id, last_sync_cursor.

A fingerprint is a hash, like SHA-256, of the bytes. Same bytes always give the same fingerprint, so it is a way to recognize content without comparing whole files.

// FileMetadata (stored in DynamoDB or Postgres)
{
  "file_id": "f_8f2c",
  "owner_id": "u_42",
  "name": "trip.mov",
  "size": 734003200,
  "mime_type": "video/quicktime",
  "fingerprint": "sha256:9b1e...",
  "status": "uploading",
  "version": 3,
  "s3_key": "blobs/9b1e...",
  "chunks": [
    {"index": 0, "fp": "sha256:aa01...", "status": "uploaded", "etag": "\"e1\""},
    {"index": 1, "fp": "sha256:bb02...", "status": "not_uploaded"}
  ],
  "updated_at": "2026-11-03T10:00:00Z"
}
CREATE TABLE shared_files (
  file_id    TEXT NOT NULL,
  user_id    TEXT NOT NULL,
  permission TEXT NOT NULL CHECK (permission IN ('read', 'write')),
  PRIMARY KEY (user_id, file_id)       -- "files shared with me" is one scan
);

5. API design

All endpoints require a session token or JWT in the Authorization header. The user id comes from the token, never from the request body, because a client can forge the body.

POST /files – start an upload. Returns presigned URLs for each chunk.

// request
{"name": "trip.mov", "size": 734003200, "fingerprint": "sha256:9b1e...",
 "chunk_fingerprints": ["sha256:aa01...", "sha256:bb02..."]}
// response 201
{"file_id": "f_8f2c", "upload_id": "s3-mpu-123",
 "parts": [{"index": 1, "url": "https://s3.../part1?X-Amz-Signature=..."}],
 "already_uploaded": [0]}

PATCH /files/{file_id}/chunks/{index} – report a finished chunk. Body {"etag": "\"e1\""}. Response 200. When all chunks are done, the server completes the upload.

GET /files/{file_id} – get metadata plus a short-lived signed download URL. Response 200 {"metadata": {...}, "download_url": "https://cdn.../f_8f2c?Expires=..."}. 403 if no access, 404 if missing.

POST /files/{file_id}/share – share. Body {"emails": ["bob@example.com"], "permission": "read"}. Response 204.

GET /files/changes?since={cursor} – list changes since the last sync. Response 200 {"changes": [{"file_id": "f_8f2c", "type": "updated", "version": 3}], "next_cursor": "c_9912"}.

6. High-level design

The key idea: the File Service is a control plane. It handles metadata and signs URLs. File bytes go straight from the client to S3 and from the CDN to the client. Our servers never touch a 50 GB stream.

How will users upload a file?

  1. The client splits the file into 5 MB chunks and computes a SHA-256 for each chunk and for the whole file.
  2. Client calls POST /files. The File Service starts an S3 multipart upload, writes metadata with status = uploading, and returns one presigned URL per chunk.
  3. A presigned URL is a normal S3 URL with a signature and expiry baked in. Anyone holding it can do exactly one action (PUT this part) for a short time.
  4. The client uploads chunks in parallel (for example 4 at a time) directly to S3.
  5. After each chunk, the client sends PATCH .../chunks/{i} with the ETag S3 returned.
  6. When all chunks are uploaded, the service calls S3 CompleteMultipartUpload and sets status = uploaded.
sequenceDiagram
    participant C as Client
    participant F as File service
    participant M as Metadata DB
    participant S as S3
    C->>C: split into 5 MB chunks and hash
    C->>F: POST /files with fingerprints
    F->>S: start multipart upload
    S-->>F: upload id
    F->>M: write metadata status uploading
    F-->>C: presigned URL per chunk
    loop each chunk in parallel
        C->>S: PUT chunk via presigned URL
        S-->>C: ETag
        C->>F: PATCH chunk done with ETag
    end
    F->>S: CompleteMultipartUpload
    F->>M: set status uploaded

How will users download a file?

  1. Client calls GET /files/{id}. The service checks ownership or the share table.
  2. The service returns a CDN signed URL valid for 5 minutes.
  3. The client downloads from the nearest CDN edge. On a miss, the CDN pulls from S3 once and caches it.

How will users share a file?

  1. Owner calls POST /files/{id}/share with emails.
  2. The service resolves emails to user ids and inserts rows into shared_files.
  3. Bob’s “shared with me” list is a single query on user_id = bob, which the primary key covers.

How will files sync across devices?

  1. Local to remote: a sync agent watches the folder using OS events (FSEvents on macOS, inotify on Linux, ReadDirectoryChangesW on Windows), queues changed files, and uploads them with the flow above.
  2. Remote to local: each device holds one WebSocket connection. When a file changes, the server pushes a small “file f_8f2c is now version 3” message.
  3. The device then calls GET /files/changes?since=<cursor> and downloads only what changed.
  4. As a safety net, the device also polls /files/changes every few minutes in case a push was missed.

7. Deep dives

How do we upload a 50 GB file reliably? (chunking)

The problem: a single 50 GB POST would take over an hour, hit gateway limits (Amazon API Gateway caps payloads at 10 MB), and restart from zero on any network blip.

Option How it works Pros Cons
Single POST to our server Stream whole file through app servers Simple Timeouts, payload limits, servers burn bandwidth
Single presigned PUT to S3 Client sends whole file to S3 Servers out of data path S3 caps one PUT at 5 GB; no resume
Client-side chunking + multipart upload 5-10 MB parts, each its own PUT Parallel, resumable, progress bar More client logic, more metadata

Recommended: client-side chunking with S3 multipart upload. Chunking must happen on the client. Chunking on the server is a classic mistake, because the whole file still has to cross the network in one piece first.

import hashlib

CHUNK = 5 * 1024 * 1024  # 5 MB

def chunk_file(path):
    """Yield (index, sha256, bytes) for each 5 MB slice."""
    with open(path, "rb") as f:
        i = 0
        while True:
            data = f.read(CHUNK)
            if not data:
                break
            yield i, hashlib.sha256(data).hexdigest(), data
            i += 1

# 50 GB / 5 MB = 10,240 parts (S3 allows up to 10,000, so use ~6 MB
# for files this big; S3 parts must be 5 MB to 5 GB each).

How do we make uploads resumable?

The problem: if the laptop closes at 49 GB, the user should only send the last 1 GB.

Option Source of truth for “which chunks are done” Risk
Client remembers locally Local file Lost if client reinstalls or switches device
Client reports each chunk, server trusts it Metadata DB Client could lie or a PATCH could be lost
Client reports, server verifies with S3 ListParts S3 + Metadata DB Small extra call

Recommended: the third option. On resume, the client sends the whole-file fingerprint. The server finds the matching uploading record, calls S3 ListParts, and returns which part numbers exist. The client uploads only the rest.

def resume(user_id, file_fp):
    meta = db.find_one(owner_id=user_id, fingerprint=file_fp,
                       status="uploading")
    if not meta:
        return None
    done = {p["PartNumber"] for p in
            s3.list_parts(Bucket=B, Key=meta.s3_key,
                          UploadId=meta.upload_id)["Parts"]}
    missing = [c.index for c in meta.chunks if c.index + 1 not in done]
    return {"upload_id": meta.upload_id,
            "urls": [presign_part(meta, i + 1) for i in missing]}

Unfinished multipart uploads cost storage, so add an S3 lifecycle rule that aborts them after 7 days.

How do we sync fast and handle conflicts?

The problem: a 1 GB file where the user changed one paragraph should not re-upload 1 GB. And two devices may edit the same file while offline.

For delta sync, fixed 5 MB chunks have a flaw. Insert one byte at the start and every boundary shifts, so every chunk hash changes. Content-defined chunking (CDC) fixes this. A rolling hash (like Rabin fingerprinting) slides over the bytes and cuts a chunk wherever the hash hits a pattern, for example its low 22 bits are zero. Because boundaries depend on content, an edit only changes the one or two chunks around it.

Conflict strategy Behavior Good for
Last write wins Latest timestamp overwrites Simple, but silently loses edits
Version check + conflicted copy Upload says “I edited version 3”; if server is at 4, save as a copy What Dropbox actually does
Merge (OT/CRDT) Combine edits Docs editors, out of scope

Recommended: optimistic version check. Each upload carries the base_version it edited. The server only commits if the current version still matches.

UPDATE file_metadata
SET version = version + 1, chunks = :new_chunks, updated_at = now()
WHERE file_id = :id AND version = :base_version;
-- 0 rows updated -> someone else won. Save ours as
-- "trip (Alice's MacBook conflicted copy).mov" and notify the user.

Nobody loses work, and the user decides which copy to keep.

How do we save storage with deduplication?

The problem: 50 PB a year is expensive, and many users upload the same files (the same PDF, the same installer).

Option Scope Savings Trade-off
No dedup n/a 0% Simple
File-level dedup Same whole-file hash Medium Misses near-identical files
Chunk-level dedup Same chunk hash Highest Need a chunk index and reference counts

Recommended: chunk-level dedup, keyed by the chunk’s SHA-256. Store each unique chunk once at chunks/<sha256>. When a client starts an upload, the server checks which chunk hashes already exist and tells the client to skip them. A reference count per chunk tells a cleanup job when nothing uses a chunk anymore. One security note: cross-user dedup can leak whether a file exists (“does anyone have this leaked PDF?”). A safe default is to dedup within one user or team, or always require the upload to finish before showing the skip.

How do we make downloads fast with a CDN, and what if something fails?

The problem: a user in Sydney pulling from a US bucket gets 200 ms+ per round trip and slow throughput.

A CDN (content delivery network) caches files at edge servers around the world. We hand out a CDN signed URL that expires in 5 minutes, so a leaked link stops working quickly. For big files the client uses HTTP Range requests (Range: bytes=0-10485759) to download several byte ranges in parallel and resume a broken download.

Failure Mitigation
Client disconnects mid-upload Resume via ListParts
PATCH for a chunk is lost Server verifies against S3, not just DB
WebSocket drops Periodic poll of /files/changes
Metadata DB node dies DynamoDB replicates across 3 AZs automatically
S3 region outage Cross-region replication for paid tiers

9. Common mistakes and interviewer follow-ups

  • Sending file bytes through your app servers. It wastes bandwidth and hits payload limits. Say: “Servers sign URLs; bytes go client to S3.”
  • Chunking on the server. The file still crosses the network in one piece. Chunk on the client.
  • Identifying a file by its name for resume or dedup. Names collide. Use a content fingerprint plus a UUID file_id.
  • Trusting the client’s chunk status. Verify with S3 ListParts before marking parts done.
  • Last write wins with no warning. It silently destroys edits. Use a version check and a conflicted copy.
  • Fixed-size chunks for delta sync. One inserted byte changes every chunk. Mention content-defined chunking.
  • Follow-up: “Polling or push?” Answer: push over one WebSocket per device, plus slow polling as a safety net.

10. One-page cheat sheet

Topic Key point
Scale 100M DAU, ~2.3k uploads/s, ~200 TB/day new data
Big files 50 GB at 100 Mbps = 1.1 h, so chunk on client (5-10 MB)
Upload path Presigned URLs, S3 multipart, servers out of data path
Resume Whole-file fingerprint finds record, ListParts finds done parts
Sync Fs watcher up, WebSocket push down, poll as backup, cursors
Delta Content-defined chunking, re-upload only changed chunks
Conflicts base_version check, conflicted copy on mismatch
Dedup Chunk-level by SHA-256, ref counts, beware cross-user leaks
Download CDN signed URL (5 min), HTTP Range for parallel/resume
CAP AP: availability first, sync is eventually consistent

03. Yelp (Business Reviews with Geo Search) (Easy)

Yelp lets you search for local businesses, like “pizza near me”, look at a business page with its reviews, and leave your own 1 to 5 star review. The interviewer is really testing three things: how you search by location quickly (a geospatial index), how you keep the average rating cheap to read at huge read volume, and how you enforce a simple business rule, one review per user per business, correctly.

1. Functional requirements

Core (must have):

  1. Users can search businesses by name or keyword, by location (latitude and longitude plus a radius), and by category.
  2. Users can view a business and its reviews.
  3. Users can leave a review: a required 1-5 star rating and optional text. One review per user per business.

Below the line (out of scope):

  1. Admin tools to add or edit businesses. We assume businesses are loaded by another system.
  2. Map view with pins. It reuses the same search API, so it adds no new backend design.
  3. Personalized recommendations. That needs an ML pipeline, a separate problem.

2. Non-functional requirements

  1. Low latency: p99 search latency under 500 ms; business page under 200 ms.
  2. High availability: 99.99% for search and viewing. Reviews can tolerate brief write failures with a retry.
  3. Scale: 100M daily users, 10M businesses, about 1B reviews total.
  4. Consistency: eventual consistency for search results and the average rating. If a new review shows up in the average 30 seconds later, that is fine.
  5. Correctness: the one-review-per-user rule must be strongly enforced. A user must never end up with two reviews on one business.
  6. CAP choice: AP for reads (search and view), because showing a slightly stale rating is better than failing. The uniqueness rule is enforced inside a single database with a constraint, which gives us a consistent check where we need it.

3. Back-of-the-envelope estimates

Assumption Number
Daily active users 100M
Searches per user per day 5
Business page views per user per day 3
Reviews written per day 1M
Businesses 10M
Business row size 1 KB
Review size (with text) 1 KB 
Search QPS:  100M x 5 / 86,400       ~= 5,800/s  (peak x3 ~= 17k/s)
View QPS:    100M x 3 / 86,400       ~= 3,500/s
Review QPS:  1M / 86,400             ~= 12 writes/s

Read : write ratio                   ~= 800 : 1

Business data:  10M x 1 KB           = 10 GB  (fits in memory)
Reviews total:  1B x 1 KB            = 1 TB
New reviews:    1M x 365 x 1 KB      ~= 365 GB/year

Two takeaways. The business table is small enough to fit in RAM on one machine. Reviews are bigger but writes are tiny, so this is a read-heavy system.

4. Core entities

  • Business: a place. Fields: id, name, category, lat, lng, address, avg_rating, num_ratings.
  • Review: one user’s opinion of one business. Fields: id, business_id, user_id, rating, text, created_at.
  • User: the person. Fields: id, name.
  • Location: a named area, like “Brooklyn” or “San Francisco”. Fields: id, name, polygon.
CREATE EXTENSION IF NOT EXISTS postgis;

CREATE TABLE businesses (
  id           BIGSERIAL PRIMARY KEY,
  name         TEXT NOT NULL,
  category     TEXT NOT NULL,
  location     GEOGRAPHY(Point, 4326) NOT NULL,  -- lat/lng on Earth
  avg_rating   NUMERIC(2,1) NOT NULL DEFAULT 0,
  num_ratings  INT NOT NULL DEFAULT 0
);

CREATE TABLE reviews (
  id           BIGSERIAL PRIMARY KEY,
  business_id  BIGINT NOT NULL REFERENCES businesses(id),
  user_id      BIGINT NOT NULL,
  rating       SMALLINT NOT NULL CHECK (rating BETWEEN 1 AND 5),
  text         TEXT,
  created_at   TIMESTAMP NOT NULL DEFAULT now(),
  UNIQUE (user_id, business_id)       -- one review per user per business
);

5. API design

GET /businesses?query=pizza&lat=40.71&lng=-74.00&radius_m=2000&category=restaurant&cursor=abc&limit=20 – search. Public, no auth needed.

// response 200
{
  "results": [
    {"id": 101, "name": "Joe's Pizza", "category": "restaurant",
     "avg_rating": 4.5, "num_ratings": 2381, "distance_m": 420}
  ],
  "next_cursor": "def"
}

GET /businesses/{id} – business details. Response 200 with business fields, 404 if missing.

GET /businesses/{id}/reviews?cursor=xyz&limit=10 – paginated reviews, newest first. Response 200 {"reviews": [...], "next_cursor": "..."}.

POST /businesses/{id}/reviews – leave a review. Requires a logged-in user (JWT). The user id comes from the token.

// request
{"rating": 5, "text": "Best slice in town."}
// response 201
{"id": 99012, "business_id": 101, "rating": 5, "created_at": "2026-11-03T12:00:00Z"}

Status codes: 201 created, 400 rating not 1-5, 401 not logged in, 409 already reviewed this business.

6. High-level design

We split reads (Business Service) from writes (Review Service) because reads are 800 times more frequent. Both talk to one Postgres database with the PostGIS extension for location queries.

How will users search for businesses?

  1. Client sends GET /businesses with keyword, lat/lng, radius, and category.
  2. The gateway routes it to the Business Service.
  3. The Business Service runs one query that filters by distance, category, and name, then sorts.
  4. It returns the first 20 results and a cursor for the next page.
sequenceDiagram
    participant C as Client
    participant G as API gateway
    participant B as Business service
    participant P as Postgres PostGIS
    C->>G: GET /businesses with keyword lat lng radius
    G->>G: rate limit check
    G->>B: route search request
    B->>P: ST_DWithin plus category and name filter
    P-->>B: matching rows sorted by distance
    B->>B: take first 20 and build cursor
    B-->>G: results and next cursor
    G-->>C: 200 results
SELECT id, name, avg_rating, num_ratings,
       ST_Distance(location, ST_MakePoint(-74.00, 40.71)::geography) AS d
FROM businesses
WHERE ST_DWithin(location, ST_MakePoint(-74.00, 40.71)::geography, 2000)
  AND category = 'restaurant'
  AND name ILIKE '%pizza%'
ORDER BY d
LIMIT 20;

Without the right indexes this scans all 10M rows. The deep dive fixes that.

How will users view a business and its reviews?

  1. Client calls GET /businesses/101. The service reads one row by primary key (fast).
  2. Client calls GET /businesses/101/reviews. The service reads from an index on (business_id, created_at DESC) and returns 10 at a time.
  3. We never load all 2,381 reviews at once. Cursor pagination keeps each page a cheap index range scan.

How will users leave a review?

  1. Client sends POST /businesses/101/reviews with a JWT.
  2. Review Service validates the rating is 1-5 and inserts the row.
  3. If the UNIQUE (user_id, business_id) constraint fires, return 409 Conflict.
  4. The service updates the business’s average rating (see deep dive).

7. Deep dives

How do we search by location efficiently? (geospatial index)

The problem: “find businesses within 2 km” on a normal B-tree index does not work well. A B-tree sorts one dimension. You can index latitude or longitude, but a range on both still scans a wide strip of rows. We need an index that understands 2D space.

Option How it works Pros Cons
Geohash Encode lat/lng into a string; nearby points share a prefix Works on any B-tree or key-value store; easy to shard Edge cases at cell borders; must query neighbor cells
Quadtree Split the map into 4 squares, recursively, until each holds at most N businesses Adapts to density (Manhattan gets tiny cells, Nevada big ones) Custom in-memory structure; rebuild on changes
PostGIS / R-tree (GiST index) Database indexes bounding boxes of shapes Built in, exact distance, handles polygons Ties you to Postgres; heavy queries at very high QPS
Elasticsearch geo_point Search engine with geo plus full-text Combines location, text, filters in one query Another system to sync and operate

A geohash turns a location into a short string. Each extra character makes the cell smaller. For example a 6-character geohash is a cell about 1.2 km by 0.6 km. Two points with the same 6-character prefix are in the same cell.

# pip install pygeohash
import pygeohash as pgh

def candidate_cells(lat, lng, precision=6):
    """The user's cell plus its 8 neighbors, so we don't miss
    businesses just across a cell border."""
    center = pgh.encode(lat, lng, precision=precision)
    return [center] + pgh.neighbors(center)   # 9 cells

# Query: WHERE geohash6 IN (...9 cells...) then filter exact distance.

Recommended: for 10M businesses, PostGIS with a GiST index is enough and simplest. The whole table is 10 GB, so it lives in memory. If search QPS or text-search needs grow, move search to Elasticsearch with geo_point and full-text in one index (next deep dive).

CREATE INDEX idx_biz_location ON businesses USING GIST (location);

How do we search by name and location together at scale?

The problem: name ILIKE '%pizza%' cannot use a normal index because of the leading %. So the database scans every row in the radius and string-matches each one. Real search also wants typo tolerance (“piza”) and relevance ranking.

Option Text search Geo Ranking Ops cost
Postgres ILIKE Full scan PostGIS Manual Low
Postgres full-text (tsvector + GIN) + PostGIS Inverted index PostGIS Basic Low
Elasticsearch Inverted index, fuzzy geo_point, geo_distance BM25 + boosts Medium

An inverted index is a map from each word to the list of documents that contain it, like the index at the back of a book. It makes word lookup fast.

Recommended: Elasticsearch as the search index, fed from Postgres by change data capture (CDC). CDC means reading the database’s change log (for example with Debezium) and streaming every insert or update to another system. Postgres stays the source of truth.

{
  "query": {
    "bool": {
      "must":   [{"match": {"name": {"query": "piza", "fuzziness": "AUTO"}}}],
      "filter": [
        {"term": {"category": "restaurant"}},
        {"geo_distance": {"distance": "2km",
                          "location": {"lat": 40.71, "lon": -74.00}}}
      ]
    }
  },
  "sort": [{"_score": "desc"}, {"avg_rating": "desc"}],
  "size": 20
}

For named places like “Brooklyn”, store each area’s boundary polygon in a locations table. Resolve “Brooklyn” to its polygon, then use a geo_shape filter (Elasticsearch) or ST_Within (PostGIS) instead of a circle.

How do we keep the average rating fast to read at scale?

The problem: search results show the average rating of every business. Computing AVG(rating) over 2,381 reviews for each of 20 results on every search, at 17k searches per second, is far too expensive.

Option How Read cost Write cost Freshness
Compute on read SELECT AVG(rating) ... GROUP BY High None Exact
Store running totals, update in the same transaction Keep avg_rating and num_ratings on the business row One column read One row update Exact
Async aggregation Queue the event, a worker updates the average One column read Tiny Seconds stale

Recommended: store the running average on the business row and update it in the same transaction as the review insert. At about 12 reviews per second overall, row contention is not a real issue. Use the incremental formula so you never re-scan reviews.

BEGIN;
INSERT INTO reviews (business_id, user_id, rating, text)
VALUES (101, 42, 5, 'Best slice in town.');

-- new_avg = (old_avg * n + new_rating) / (n + 1)
UPDATE businesses
SET avg_rating  = (avg_rating * num_ratings + 5) / (num_ratings + 1),
    num_ratings = num_ratings + 1
WHERE id = 101;
COMMIT;

The single UPDATE statement takes a row lock, so two concurrent reviews on the same business apply one after the other and neither is lost. If a single business ever got thousands of reviews per second, switch to the async option: push events to a queue and let one worker per business batch the updates.

How do we ensure a user can only leave one review per business?

The problem: a check like “select first, insert if none” has a race. Two requests from the same user (a double click) can both see “no review” and both insert.

Option Correct under races? Notes
Check in app code before insert No Race window between SELECT and INSERT
Database UNIQUE (user_id, business_id) Yes The database rejects the second insert atomically
Distributed lock per (user, business) Yes Overkill and adds a failure point

Recommended: the database unique constraint. It is the simplest correct answer. The second insert fails with a unique violation, and the service returns 409 Conflict. If reviews are later sharded, shard by business_id so that the (user_id, business_id) pair always lands on one shard and the constraint still works locally.

from psycopg2 import errors

def create_review(user_id, business_id, rating, text):
    try:
        with db.transaction():
            insert_review_and_update_avg(user_id, business_id, rating, text)
        return 201
    except errors.UniqueViolation:
        return 409   # already reviewed; client can offer "edit your review"

Failure handling: if the database primary fails, reviews fail for about 30-60 seconds during failover. The client retries with the same request, and the unique constraint makes the retry safe, it can never create a duplicate. Reads keep working from replicas and Elasticsearch.

9. Common mistakes and interviewer follow-ups

  • Using a B-tree on lat and lng for “nearby”. It still scans a large strip. Say: “I need a 2D index: geohash, quadtree, or PostGIS GiST.”
  • Forgetting neighbor cells with geohash. A business 10 m away across a border gets missed. Always query the 8 neighbors too.
  • Computing AVG() on every search. Too slow at 17k QPS. Store avg_rating and num_ratings on the business.
  • Enforcing one review per user in app code only. Races create duplicates. Use a UNIQUE constraint.
  • ILIKE '%term%' for search. Full scan. Use an inverted index (Postgres full-text or Elasticsearch).
  • Making Elasticsearch the source of truth. It is a derived index. Keep Postgres as truth and rebuild ES from it.
  • Follow-up: “How do you search by city name?” Answer: store area polygons, resolve the name, filter with ST_Within or geo_shape.

10. One-page cheat sheet

Topic Key point
Scale 100M DAU, ~6k search/s (peak 17k), ~12 review writes/s
Data 10M businesses = 10 GB, 1B reviews = 1 TB
Geo index PostGIS GiST at this size; geohash/quadtree to explain the idea
Text search Elasticsearch fed by CDC; fuzzy match, geo_distance filter
Avg rating Running avg_rating, num_ratings updated in same transaction
One review UNIQUE (user_id, business_id), return 409
Named areas Polygons + ST_Within / geo_shape
CAP AP for reads, consistent constraint for writes

04. Local Delivery Service (Gopuff) (Easy)

A local delivery service like Gopuff stocks snacks, drinks, and household items in hundreds of small warehouses called distribution centers (DCs), also known as micro-fulfillment centers. A customer opens the app, sees what can reach them within 1 hour, and places an order. The interviewer is really testing two things: can you answer “what is available near me?” in under 100 ms by combining many nearby warehouses, and can you take an order without ever selling the same physical item twice.

1. Functional requirements

Core (must have):

  1. Customers can see which items are available to them for delivery within 1 hour, based on their location. Availability is the sum of stock across all DCs that can reach them in time.
  2. Customers can order several items in one order.

Below the line (out of scope):

  1. Payments. A payment provider handles it; it does not change inventory design.
  2. Driver dispatch and routing. A separate logistics system.
  3. Catalog search and browsing pages. We focus on availability and ordering.
  4. Cancellations and returns. They add a “put stock back” flow but no new concepts.

2. Non-functional requirements

  1. Fast availability: p99 under 100 ms. It is called on every page and search, so it must feel instant.
  2. Strong consistency for orders: two customers must never buy the same physical unit. Overselling means a driver shows up with half an order.
  3. Scale: 10k DCs, 100k catalog items, 10M orders per day.
  4. Availability: 99.9% for ordering, 99.99% for availability reads.
  5. CAP choice: split by path. Availability reads are AP: a count that is a few seconds stale is fine, since the order step re-checks. Ordering is CP: if we cannot confirm stock consistently, we reject the order rather than oversell.

3. Back-of-the-envelope estimates

Assumption Number
Orders per day 10M
Items per order 5
Availability calls per order (browse, search, cart) 20
DCs 10,000
Items stocked per DC 5,000 (of 100k catalog)
Inventory row size 50 bytes 
Order QPS:        10M / 86,400            ~= 115 orders/s  (peak x5 ~= 600/s)
Inventory decrements: 115 x 5             ~= 600 row updates/s (peak 3k/s)
Availability QPS: 10M x 20 / 86,400       ~= 2,300/s  (peak ~= 12k/s)

Inventory rows:   10k DCs x 5k items      = 50M rows
Inventory size:   50M x 50 B              = 2.5 GB  (fits in memory)
Orders/year:      10M x 365 x 1 KB        ~= 3.6 TB/year

Inventory is small, only 2.5 GB. The hard parts are latency of the availability query and correctness of the order write.

4. Core entities

  • Item: a product type, like “Cheetos 8 oz”. Fields: item_id, name, price. Think of it as a class.
  • Inventory: how many units of an item sit in one DC. Fields: dc_id, item_id, quantity. Think of it as instances at a place.
  • Distribution Center (DC): a warehouse. Fields: dc_id, lat, lng, region.
  • Order: a customer’s purchase. Fields: order_id, user_id, status, delivery_lat, delivery_lng.
  • OrderItem: one line of an order. Fields: order_id, item_id, dc_id, quantity.
CREATE TABLE inventory (
  dc_id     INT    NOT NULL,
  item_id   INT    NOT NULL,
  quantity  INT    NOT NULL CHECK (quantity >= 0),  -- can never go negative
  PRIMARY KEY (dc_id, item_id)
);

CREATE TABLE orders (
  order_id      UUID PRIMARY KEY,
  user_id       BIGINT NOT NULL,
  status        TEXT NOT NULL,          -- 'placed', 'packed', 'delivered'
  created_at    TIMESTAMP NOT NULL DEFAULT now()
);

CREATE TABLE order_items (
  order_id  UUID NOT NULL REFERENCES orders(order_id),
  item_id   INT  NOT NULL,
  dc_id     INT  NOT NULL,
  quantity  INT  NOT NULL,
  PRIMARY KEY (order_id, item_id, dc_id)
);

5. API design

GET /availability?lat=40.71&lng=-74.00&item_ids=11,12,13 – quantities deliverable within 1 hour. Or ?lat=..&lng=..&cursor=..&limit=50 to page through everything available. Auth optional.

// response 200
{"items": [{"item_id": 11, "name": "Cheetos 8 oz", "available": 37},
           {"item_id": 12, "name": "Sparkling Water 12pk", "available": 0}],
 "next_cursor": null}

POST /orders – place an order. Requires a logged-in user. Includes an idempotency key so a retry does not create two orders.

// request  (Idempotency-Key: 6f1c-...)
{"lat": 40.71, "lng": -74.00,
 "items": [{"item_id": 11, "quantity": 2}, {"item_id": 13, "quantity": 1}]}
// response 201
{"order_id": "9b2e...", "status": "placed", "eta_minutes": 34}

Status codes: 201 placed, 409 an item is out of stock (body lists which), 400 invalid request, 401 not logged in.

How will customers see what is available near them?

  1. Client calls GET /availability with its location.
  2. The Availability Service asks the Nearby Service: “which DCs can deliver here within 1 hour?”
  3. The Nearby Service returns a short list, typically 1-5 DC ids.
  4. The Availability Service queries inventory for those DCs and sums quantity per item.
  5. It returns the totals.
sequenceDiagram
    participant C as Client
    participant G as API gateway
    participant A as Availability service
    participant N as Nearby service
    participant I as Inventory replica
    C->>G: GET /availability with location
    G->>A: forward request
    A->>N: which DCs reach here in 1 hour
    N-->>A: list of 1 to 5 DC ids
    A->>I: SUM quantity per item for those DCs
    I-->>A: totals per item
    A-->>G: item totals
    G-->>C: 200 available counts
SELECT i.item_id, it.name, SUM(i.quantity) AS available
FROM inventory i
JOIN items it ON it.item_id = i.item_id
WHERE i.dc_id = ANY(:nearby_dc_ids)
  AND i.item_id = ANY(:item_ids)
GROUP BY i.item_id, it.name;

How will customers place an order?

  1. Client calls POST /orders with location, items, and an idempotency key.
  2. The Order Service gets the nearby DCs again (the customer may have moved).
  3. In one database transaction it checks stock, decrements it, and writes the order.
  4. If any item is short, the whole transaction rolls back and the client gets 409 with the missing items.
  5. On success the client gets 201 and the order id.

7. Deep dives

How do we find nearby DCs that can deliver within 1 hour?

The problem: “within 1 hour” is about driving time, not straight-line distance. A DC 3 km away across a river with one bridge might take 50 minutes. But calling a maps API for all 10k DCs on every request is too slow and too expensive.

Option How Accuracy Latency Cost
Straight-line distance (Haversine) Math on lat/lng Poor near rivers, highways under 1 ms Free
Travel-time API for every DC Ask maps for 10k routes Exact Seconds Very high
Filter by distance, then travel-time API on the few left Haversine to get top ~10 within 30 km, then route those Good 20-50 ms Low
Precomputed delivery zones (isochrones) Each DC stores a polygon reachable in 1 hour; point-in-polygon test Good, refresh hourly for traffic under 5 ms Low

An isochrone is a map shape covering every point reachable within a set time from a location, like a 60-minute “blob” around each DC.

Recommended: precomputed isochrone polygons per DC, refreshed every 15-60 minutes from the travel-time service, with a fast point-in-polygon check. Because there are only 10k DCs, the whole set fits in memory on each Nearby Service instance. Fall back to “Haversine filter, then route the top 10” if a polygon is stale.

import math
from shapely.geometry import Point

def haversine_km(lat1, lng1, lat2, lng2):
    """Great-circle distance on a sphere of radius 6371 km."""
    p1, p2 = math.radians(lat1), math.radians(lat2)
    dp, dl = p2 - p1, math.radians(lng2 - lng1)
    a = math.sin(dp/2)**2 + math.cos(p1)*math.cos(p2)*math.sin(dl/2)**2
    return 2 * 6371 * math.asin(math.sqrt(a))

def nearby_dcs(lat, lng, dcs):
    # Step 1: cheap prefilter, nothing beyond 40 km reaches us in 1 hour
    close = [d for d in dcs if haversine_km(lat, lng, d.lat, d.lng) < 40]
    # Step 2: exact-ish check against the 60-min isochrone polygon
    p = Point(lng, lat)
    return [d.id for d in close if d.isochrone_60min.contains(p)]

We must also leave time to pack and hand off. If packing takes 10 minutes, use the 50-minute isochrone, not the 60-minute one.

How do we keep inventory consistent when orders are placed?

The problem: two customers both see “1 left” and both tap Order at the same moment. Without care, both succeed and we oversell. An order also spans several items, and we want all or nothing.

Option How Correct? Notes
Read, check in app, then write SELECT then UPDATE in two steps No Race between read and write
Distributed lock (Redis) per item Lock, check, decrement, unlock Yes if done right Extra system; lock and DB can disagree on failure
Single ACID transaction with conditional update UPDATE ... SET q = q - n WHERE q >= n Yes Simple; DB serializes per row

Recommended: one Postgres transaction with conditional decrements. The WHERE quantity >= n clause makes each decrement atomic. If it updates 0 rows, there was not enough stock. The CHECK (quantity >= 0) constraint is a second safety net.

def place_order(user_id, idem_key, lines, nearby_dc_ids):
    with db.transaction():              # BEGIN ... COMMIT or ROLLBACK
        if db.exists("SELECT 1 FROM orders WHERE order_id = %s", idem_key):
            return get_order(idem_key)  # retry of a past request
        db.execute("INSERT INTO orders (order_id, user_id, status) "
                   "VALUES (%s, %s, 'placed')", (idem_key, user_id))
        for line in lines:
            # Pick the DC with most stock among nearby ones, lock its row.
            row = db.fetch_one("""
                SELECT dc_id FROM inventory
                WHERE item_id = %s AND dc_id = ANY(%s) AND quantity >= %s
                ORDER BY quantity DESC LIMIT 1
                FOR UPDATE""", (line.item_id, nearby_dc_ids, line.qty))
            if row is None:
                raise OutOfStock(line.item_id)     # whole tx rolls back
            db.execute("""UPDATE inventory SET quantity = quantity - %s
                          WHERE dc_id = %s AND item_id = %s""",
                       (line.qty, row.dc_id, line.item_id))
            db.execute("INSERT INTO order_items VALUES (%s,%s,%s,%s)",
                       (idem_key, line.item_id, row.dc_id, line.qty))
    return {"order_id": idem_key, "status": "placed"}

FOR UPDATE takes a row lock, so a second order for the same row waits until the first commits, then sees the new quantity. At a peak of ~3k row updates per second, one well-sized Postgres primary handles this. If it ever does not, shard inventory by region, since an order only touches DCs near one customer.

Failure handling: the idempotency key (used as order_id) means a client retry after a timeout returns the original order instead of charging twice. If the primary fails mid-transaction, the transaction rolls back, nothing is half-written, and the client retries.

How do we make the availability query fast (under 100 ms)?

The problem: every browse and search page calls availability, up to 12k QPS at peak. Each call needs a nearby-DC lookup plus a sum over inventory rows. Sending all of that to the order primary would slow down orders.

Option Latency Freshness Load on primary
Query primary directly 10-30 ms, worse under load Exact High
Read replicas 5-20 ms ~100 ms lag None
Redis cache of per-DC inventory, short TTL 1-3 ms A few seconds None

Recommended: read from Postgres read replicas, plus a Redis cache keyed by DC with a short TTL (for example 5 s). Because many customers in the same neighborhood share the same 2-3 DCs, the cache hit rate is high. Staleness is safe because the order transaction re-checks real stock.

Latency budget for GET /availability (target p99 < 100 ms):
  Gateway + auth                  5 ms
  Nearby DCs (in-memory polygons) 2 ms
  Redis MGET inv:{dc} for 3 DCs   3 ms  (on miss: replica query 15 ms)
  Sum + JSON                      2 ms
  Network to client              30 ms
  Total                         ~42 ms  (miss path ~55 ms)
def availability(dc_ids, item_ids):
    keys = [f"inv:{dc}" for dc in dc_ids]
    totals = defaultdict(int)
    for dc, blob in zip(dc_ids, redis.mget(keys)):
        stock = json.loads(blob) if blob else load_and_cache(dc)  # replica
        for item in item_ids:
            totals[item] += stock.get(str(item), 0)
    return totals

A nice extra: when a cached count is 0, the UI greys the item out, so most customers never even try to order out-of-stock items.

How do we estimate travel time, and what if the maps service fails?

The problem: isochrones and ETAs depend on an external travel-time service (Google Maps, Mapbox, or OSRM, an open-source routing engine). It can be slow, rate limited, or down.

Failure Mitigation
Travel-time API slow or down Keep using last good isochrones (they change slowly); refresh later
Traffic spike makes ETA wrong Refresh isochrones every 15 min at rush hour; add a safety buffer
A DC goes offline (power cut) Mark DC inactive; Nearby Service drops it, its stock vanishes from totals
Postgres primary fails Orders return 503 for ~30-60 s during failover; reads keep working from replicas and cache

The availability, nearby and order services plus the isochrone refresh job run in the service subnet, Redis and Postgres sit in the data subnet, and the travel time provider is the only third party.

9. Common mistakes and interviewer follow-ups

  • Using straight-line distance for “within 1 hour”. Rivers and highways make it wrong. Say: “Distance to prefilter, travel time or isochrones to decide.”
  • Mixing up Item and Inventory. An item is a product type; inventory is units at a DC. Availability is a sum of inventory across DCs.
  • Check-then-write in app code. Two orders both pass the check. Use a conditional UPDATE ... WHERE quantity >= n in a transaction.
  • Putting availability reads on the primary. It slows orders. Use replicas and a short-TTL cache; the order path re-checks.
  • No idempotency key on orders. A retry double-orders. Use the key as the order id.
  • Forgetting packing time. A 60-minute isochrone plus 10 minutes of packing misses the promise.
  • Follow-up: “What if items in one order come from two DCs?” Answer: allowed here, each order line records its dc_id; dispatch may batch pickups.

10. One-page cheat sheet

Topic Key point
Scale 10k DCs, 100k items, 10M orders/day (~115/s), ~2.3k availability/s
Data Inventory 50M rows = 2.5 GB, fits in memory
Nearby DCs Haversine prefilter + precomputed 1-hour isochrones
Availability Replicas + Redis per-DC cache (5 s TTL), p99 < 100 ms
Ordering One ACID tx, FOR UPDATE, quantity >= n, all or nothing
Safety nets CHECK (quantity >= 0), idempotency key as order id
CAP AP for availability reads, CP for orders
Failure Stale isochrones OK, DC offline removes its stock

05. Ticketmaster (Event Ticket Booking) (Medium)

Ticketmaster sells tickets to concerts, sports games, and shows. Users search for events, open an event page with a seat map, pick seats, and pay. The interviewer is really testing how you prevent two people from buying the same seat, how you hold a seat for a few minutes while someone pays, and how you survive the moment a huge on-sale opens and 10 million fans hit the site at once for 50,000 seats.

1. Functional requirements

Core (must have):

  1. Users can view an event: details, venue, performers, and a seat map showing which seats are available.
  2. Users can search for events by keyword, performer, location, date, and type.
  3. Users can book tickets: select seats, hold them while paying, then confirm the purchase.

Below the line (out of scope):

  1. Users can view their past bookings. It is a simple read on the bookings table.
  2. Admins or promoters can create events. Assume events are loaded by another tool.
  3. Dynamic pricing. It changes prices, not the booking mechanics.
  4. Ticket resale and transfer. A separate marketplace with its own rules.

2. Non-functional requirements

  1. No double booking: a seat is sold to at most one person. This needs strong consistency on the booking path.
  2. High availability for view and search: 99.99%. Browsing must keep working even during a huge on-sale.
  3. Low latency for search: p99 under 500 ms.
  4. Read-heavy: about 100 reads (views and searches) for every booking.
  5. Surge handling: support 10M concurrent users trying to book one popular event, with a fair experience.
  6. CAP choice: split by path. Booking is CP: we prefer to reject a request rather than sell a seat twice. Viewing and search are AP: a seat map a second or two stale is fine because the booking step re-checks.

3. Back-of-the-envelope estimates

Assumption Number
Daily active users 10M
Events listed at any time 1M
Average seats per event 10,000 (big stadiums 50k-100k)
Tickets sold per day (normal) 1M
Views + searches per user per day 10
Ticket row size 100 bytes
Hot on-sale 10M users, 50,000 seats, first 10 minutes 
Normal read QPS:     10M x 10 / 86,400       ~= 1,200/s  (peak x5 ~= 6k/s)
Normal booking QPS:  1M / 86,400             ~= 12/s

Hot on-sale:
  Page loads: 10M users refresh in ~1 min    ~= 170k req/s on one event page
  Seat clicks: say 10% try in 1 min          ~= 1M reserve attempts/min
                                             ~= 17k reserve/s, 50k winners

Storage:
  Tickets: 1M events x 10k seats x 100 B     = 1 TB
  Bookings: 1M/day x 365 x 500 B             ~= 180 GB/year
  Events/venues/performers metadata          ~= tens of GB

The normal load is small. The design is shaped by the hot on-sale: 170k reads per second on one page and fierce contention on a few thousand rows.

4. Core entities

  • Event: a single show. Fields: id, venue_id, performer_id, name, date, description.
  • Venue: the place, including its seat map layout (sections, rows, seat coordinates).
  • Performer: the artist or team.
  • Ticket: one seat for one event. Fields: id, event_id, section, row, seat, price, status, booking_id. One row is created per seat when an event is created.
  • Booking: one user’s purchase of one or more tickets. Fields: id, user_id, ticket_ids, total, status (in_progress, confirmed, expired).
  • User: the buyer.
CREATE TABLE tickets (
  id          BIGSERIAL PRIMARY KEY,
  event_id    BIGINT NOT NULL,
  section     TEXT NOT NULL,
  row_label   TEXT NOT NULL,
  seat_number INT  NOT NULL,
  price_cents INT  NOT NULL,
  status      TEXT NOT NULL DEFAULT 'available',  -- available | reserved | sold
  booking_id  BIGINT,
  reserved_until TIMESTAMP,
  UNIQUE (event_id, section, row_label, seat_number)
);
CREATE INDEX idx_tickets_event_status ON tickets (event_id, status);

CREATE TABLE bookings (
  id          BIGSERIAL PRIMARY KEY,
  user_id     BIGINT NOT NULL,
  event_id    BIGINT NOT NULL,
  status      TEXT NOT NULL,          -- in_progress | confirmed | expired
  total_cents INT  NOT NULL,
  payment_ref TEXT UNIQUE,            -- Stripe PaymentIntent id
  created_at  TIMESTAMP NOT NULL DEFAULT now()
);

5. API design

GET /events/{event_id} – event details, venue, performer, and seat map with availability. Public.

// response 200
{"event": {"id": 7, "name": "Taylor Swift - Eras", "date": "2027-06-01T20:00:00Z"},
 "venue": {"id": 3, "name": "MetLife Stadium", "seat_map_url": "https://cdn.../map3.json"},
 "available_ticket_ids": "https://api.../events/7/availability"}

GET /events/{event_id}/availability – current seat statuses (compact). Response 200 {"version": 18231, "available": [10001, 10002, ...]}.

GET /events/search?keyword=swift&city=NYC&start=2027-06-01&end=2027-06-30&type=concert&cursor=.. – search. Response 200 {"events": [...], "next_cursor": "..."}.

POST /bookings/reserve – hold seats for 10 minutes. Requires login. Body {"event_id": 7, "ticket_ids": [10001, 10002]}.

// response 201
{"booking_id": 55012, "status": "in_progress",
 "expires_at": "2027-02-01T10:10:00Z"}

Status codes: 201 held, 409 one or more seats already held or sold, 429 too many attempts, 403 not admitted from the waiting room yet.

POST /bookings/{booking_id}/confirm – pay. Body {"payment_token": "tok_from_stripe_js"}. Response 200 {"status": "confirmed"}, 410 if the hold expired, 402 if payment failed. Card details never touch our servers; Stripe.js turns them into a token in the browser.

GET /events/{event_id}/seats/stream – Server-Sent Events stream of seat changes (deep dive).

One Postgres database holds all core tables. That is fine: the data is tightly linked (bookings need tickets need events), and booking needs ACID transactions. Splitting into a database per service would add distributed transactions for no gain.

How will users view an event?

  1. Client requests GET /events/7.
  2. The gateway forwards to the Event Service.
  3. The Event Service reads the event, venue, and performer rows and returns them.
  4. The client then loads seat availability and draws the map. The static seat layout (shapes, coordinates) comes from the CDN; only the statuses come from our API.
sequenceDiagram
    participant C as Client
    participant G as API gateway
    participant E as Event service
    participant P as Postgres
    participant N as CDN
    C->>G: GET /events/7
    G->>E: forward request
    E->>P: read event venue performer rows
    P-->>E: rows
    E-->>G: event details
    G-->>C: 200 event JSON
    C->>N: fetch static seat layout
    N-->>C: seat map JSON
    C->>G: GET availability
    G->>E: forward request
    E-->>C: available ticket ids

How will users search for events?

  1. Client calls GET /events/search with filters.
  2. The Search Service queries the database by date range, city, and type, with keyword matching.
  3. Results come back sorted by date, 20 per page.

This starts as a SQL query with LIKE, which is slow; the deep dive moves it to Elasticsearch.

How will users book tickets?

  1. User clicks seats and the client calls POST /bookings/reserve.
  2. The Booking Service puts a 10-minute hold on those seats (deep dive) and creates a booking with status = in_progress.
  3. The client shows a countdown timer and the payment form.
  4. The client sends a Stripe token to POST /bookings/{id}/confirm; the service creates a Stripe PaymentIntent.
  5. Stripe calls our webhook when payment succeeds. In one transaction we set the tickets to sold and the booking to confirmed.
  6. If the user walks away, the hold expires after 10 minutes and the seats become available again.

7. Deep dives

How do we reserve a seat while the user pays, without double booking?

The problem: the simple design checks availability only at payment time. A user spends 3 minutes typing card details and then learns someone else bought the seat. We need a hold that (a) only one user can get, (b) disappears on its own if the user leaves, and (c) becomes permanent on payment.

Option How it works Pros Cons
Long-running DB transaction with SELECT ... FOR UPDATE Keep row locked until payment Simple idea Holds DB locks for minutes; connections pile up; terrible at scale
Status column + reserved_until + cleanup job Set status='reserved', expiry time; a cron frees expired rows Durable, all in Postgres Seats stay stuck until cron runs; every read must also check expiry
Distributed lock in Redis with TTL SET ticket:{id} {booking} NX EX 600 Auto-expires exactly on time; very fast; keeps contention off DB Redis failure can drop holds; need DB as final guard

Recommended: Redis lock with a TTL for the hold, with the database as the final source of truth. NX means “set only if the key does not exist”, so only one booking can win a seat. EX 600 means the key deletes itself after 600 seconds, so abandoned holds free up automatically with no cron.

HOLD_SECONDS = 600

def reserve(user_id, event_id, ticket_ids):
    booking_id = new_booking_id()
    won = []
    for t in sorted(ticket_ids):       # sorted order avoids deadlock-ish
        ok = redis.set(f"hold:{t}", booking_id, nx=True, ex=HOLD_SECONDS)
        if not ok:
            for w in won:              # all or nothing: release partial wins
                release_if_owner(w, booking_id)
            raise SeatTaken(t)         # -> 409
        won.append(t)
    db.execute("INSERT INTO bookings (id, user_id, event_id, status, total_cents)"
               " VALUES (%s, %s, %s, 'in_progress', %s)",
               (booking_id, user_id, event_id, price_of(ticket_ids)))
    return booking_id

# Release only if we still own it (Lua keeps check+delete atomic).
RELEASE_LUA = """
if redis.call('GET', KEYS[1]) == ARGV[1] then
  return redis.call('DEL', KEYS[1]) else return 0 end
"""
def release_if_owner(ticket_id, booking_id):
    redis.eval(RELEASE_LUA, 1, f"hold:{ticket_id}", booking_id)

On payment, the webhook does the final write with a guard so the database itself refuses a double sale, even if Redis lost a key:

BEGIN;
UPDATE tickets
SET status = 'sold', booking_id = :booking_id
WHERE id = ANY(:ticket_ids) AND status = 'available';
-- If rows updated != number of tickets: ROLLBACK and refund. Should
-- be rare; it only happens if a Redis hold was lost.
UPDATE bookings SET status = 'confirmed', payment_ref = :pi
WHERE id = :booking_id AND status = 'in_progress';
COMMIT;

The webhook must be idempotent, because Stripe retries webhooks. Checking status = 'in_progress' and the UNIQUE on payment_ref makes a repeated webhook a no-op.

How do we handle a high-demand on-sale? (virtual waiting room)

The problem: 10M fans arrive for 50k seats. If all of them hit the Booking Service at once, Redis and Postgres get hammered, most clicks return “seat taken”, and the site may fall over. It is also unfair: whoever has the fastest connection wins.

Option How Pros Cons
Just autoscale Add servers No new concept Contention is on the same rows; more servers do not help
Rate limit per user/IP Reject over N req/s Protects backend Bots rotate IPs; real users see errors
Virtual waiting room (queue) Users join a queue; admitted in batches at a safe rate Smooth load, fair order, clear UX More moving parts; queue itself must scale

Recommended: a virtual waiting room in front of the booking flow for events flagged as high-demand. Users get a queue position. A controller admits, say, 2,000 users per minute, which is a rate the booking path handles comfortably. Admitted users get a signed, short-lived access token that the Booking Service checks.

# Join: score = arrival time, so earlier users are served first.
def join_queue(event_id, user_id):
    redis.zadd(f"queue:{event_id}", {user_id: time.time()}, nx=True)
    return redis.zrank(f"queue:{event_id}", user_id)   # position

# Admission controller, runs every few seconds per event.
def admit(event_id, batch=200):
    users = redis.zpopmin(f"queue:{event_id}", batch)
    for user_id, _ in users:
        token = sign_jwt({"uid": user_id, "eid": event_id}, ttl=900)
        push_to_client(user_id, {"type": "admitted", "token": token})
Throughput math:
  50,000 seats, average 2 per booking  = 25,000 bookings
  Admit 2,000 users/min, ~70% buy     = 1,400 bookings/min
  Time to sell out                    ~= 18 minutes
  Booking path load                   ~= 2,000 / 60 ~= 35 users/s

Users in the queue hold a WebSocket or SSE connection to see their position, so they do not need to refresh. When the event sells out, everyone still waiting is told immediately instead of waiting for nothing. Bot protection (CAPTCHA at join time, one queue spot per verified account) keeps the queue fair.

How do we make search fast at scale?

The problem: WHERE name LIKE '%swift%' cannot use a B-tree index because of the leading wildcard, so it scans every event. Users also expect typo tolerance and filters on several fields at once.

Option Keyword search Filters + sort Notes
SQL LIKE Full table scan OK Fine at 10k events, not 1M
Postgres full-text (tsvector + GIN index) Indexed OK Good middle ground, one system
Elasticsearch Inverted index, fuzzy, relevance Fast filters, geo, facets Separate system, needs sync

Recommended: Elasticsearch, kept in sync from Postgres using change data capture (CDC, reading the database change log with a tool like Debezium and streaming changes through Kafka). Postgres stays the source of truth.

{
  "query": {
    "bool": {
      "must":   [{"multi_match": {"query": "swift", "fields": ["name^3", "performer", "description"],
                                  "fuzziness": "AUTO"}}],
      "filter": [{"term": {"type": "concert"}},
                 {"term": {"city": "NYC"}},
                 {"range": {"date": {"gte": "2027-06-01", "lte": "2027-06-30"}}}]
    }
  },
  "sort": [{"_score": "desc"}, {"date": "asc"}],
  "size": 20
}

Popular queries repeat a lot (“taylor swift”). Cache full search responses in Redis or at the CDN for 30-60 seconds, keyed by the normalized query string. Elasticsearch also has its own node query cache for repeated filters.

How do we cache event pages for 170k requests per second?

The problem: during an on-sale, millions of users refresh the same event page. Event details almost never change, but seat availability changes every second.

The trick is to split the page into a static part and a dynamic part.

Data Changes how often Cache where TTL
Event, venue, performer info Rarely CDN + Redis Hours, purge on edit
Seat map layout (shapes, coordinates) Never for a venue CDN as a static JSON file Days
Seat availability Every second Redis bitmap, pushed via SSE Live

Recommended: put event details and seat layout on the CDN, so 170k req/s mostly never reach our servers. Keep seat availability in Redis as a compact structure (one bit per seat: 50k seats = about 6 KB) and serve it from an edge-friendly endpoint with a 1-2 second TTL, or push changes over SSE. The Event Service scales horizontally behind a load balancer for the cache misses.

Request mix during a hot on-sale (170k req/s):
  Event details + layout  -> CDN hit rate ~99%  -> ~1.7k req/s to origin
  Availability snapshot   -> 1 s micro-cache    -> ~1 req/s per edge per event
  Seat changes            -> SSE stream, no polling

How do we show a live seat map with Server-Sent Events?

The problem: a seat map loaded 30 seconds ago is wrong during an on-sale. Users click seats that are gone, get 409, click again, and get angry. Polling every second from millions of clients is wasteful.

Option Direction Cost Fit
Polling every 1-2 s Client pulls Many wasted requests OK for small events
Server-Sent Events (SSE) Server pushes over HTTP One long-lived connection, simple Great for one-way updates
WebSockets Two-way More complex infra Overkill; we only push

Server-Sent Events is a standard where the browser opens one HTTP connection and the server keeps writing small text events down it. The browser’s EventSource reconnects on its own if the connection drops.

Recommended: SSE for normal events. When a seat is held, released, or sold, the Booking Service publishes to Redis pub/sub channel seats:{event_id}. SSE servers subscribed to that channel forward the change to every connected client watching that event.

# SSE endpoint (async web framework style)
async def seat_stream(request, event_id):
    async def gen():
        sub = redis.pubsub()
        await sub.subscribe(f"seats:{event_id}")
        snapshot = await availability_snapshot(event_id)
        yield f"event: snapshot\ndata: {json.dumps(snapshot)}\n\n"
        async for msg in sub.listen():
            if msg["type"] == "message":
                # e.g. {"ticket_id": 10001, "status": "reserved", "v": 18232}
                yield f"event: seat\ndata: {msg['data']}\n\n"
    return StreamingResponse(gen(), media_type="text/event-stream")

For the very hottest events, the waiting room changes the picture: only admitted users see the map, so the number of live SSE connections is a few thousand, not millions. Some systems even skip the map and auto-assign “best available” seats to admitted users, which removes the seat-picking race entirely.

Failure handling across the booking path:

Failure Effect Mitigation
Redis primary fails Some holds lost Replica promotion; DB status='available' guard prevents double sale; refund the rare loser
Stripe webhook delayed Hold may expire before confirm Extend hold when payment starts; on late webhook, re-check seats, refund if gone
SSE connection drops Map goes stale EventSource auto-reconnects; server sends a fresh snapshot with a version number
Booking Service crash mid-reserve Partial holds TTL frees them in 10 minutes automatically
Postgres primary fails Confirms fail briefly Multi-AZ failover; webhook retries by Stripe complete the confirm

The waiting room, event, booking and SSE servers run in the service subnet, seat holds in Redis and the Postgres source of truth sit in the data subnet, and Stripe is the only third party.

9. Common mistakes and interviewer follow-ups

  • Checking availability only at payment time. Users lose seats after typing card details. Say: “Hold the seat at selection with a TTL lock.”
  • Holding a DB row lock for the whole checkout. It ties up connections for minutes. Use a Redis TTL hold or a status column with expiry.
  • Trusting Redis alone. A failover can lose a hold. Keep a conditional UPDATE ... WHERE status='available' in the DB as the final guard.
  • A non-idempotent payment webhook. Stripe retries and you double-process. Check booking status and use a unique payment reference.
  • Thinking autoscaling solves the on-sale. Contention is on the same rows. Say: “Virtual waiting room to meter admission.”
  • Serving the whole event page dynamically. Split static (CDN) from dynamic (seat statuses).
  • LIKE '%term%' for search. Full scan. Use Elasticsearch or Postgres full-text with CDC.
  • Follow-up: “Polling or push for the seat map?” Answer: SSE, because updates are one-way; WebSockets only if the client must send too.

10. One-page cheat sheet

Topic Key point
Scale 10M DAU, ~1.2k reads/s normal, 170k req/s on a hot event page
Hot on-sale 10M users, 50k seats, waiting room admits ~2k/min
No double booking Redis SET hold:{t} NX EX 600 + DB WHERE status='available'
Checkout Reserve, then confirm via Stripe webhook (idempotent)
Search Elasticsearch via CDC, fuzzy keyword, filters, 30-60 s result cache
Event page Static on CDN, seat statuses in Redis bitmap (~6 KB for 50k seats)
Live map SSE + Redis pub/sub, snapshot with version on reconnect
CAP CP for booking, AP for view and search
Failure TTL frees crashed holds; DB guard catches lost Redis keys
