06. Instagram (Photo Sharing Feed) (Medium)

Instagram lets people post photos and videos with a caption, follow other people, and scroll a feed of recent posts from everyone they follow. The interviewer is really testing how you build a feed for 500M daily users that loads in under half a second, how you handle celebrities with hundreds of millions of followers, and how you upload and serve huge amounts of media without your servers becoming the bottleneck.

1. Functional requirements

Core (must have):

  1. Users can create a post with one or more photos or videos and a caption.
  2. Users can follow and unfollow other users.
  3. Users can see a feed of recent posts from people they follow, newest first, with infinite scroll.

Below the line (out of scope):

  1. Likes and comments. They are counters and lists attached to a post; they do not change the feed design.
  2. Search for users, hashtags, or places. That needs a search index, a separate topic.
  3. Stories and live video. Ephemeral content and streaming are their own systems.
  4. Ranked (algorithmic) feed. We build a chronological feed; ranking would re-order the same candidates.

2. Non-functional requirements

  1. Low feed latency: p99 under 500 ms to load the first page of the feed.
  2. Fast media: photos (up to 8 MB) and videos (up to 4 GB) should start showing almost instantly, from a nearby CDN.
  3. High availability: 99.99% for feed reads and media serving.
  4. Scale: 500M daily active users, 100M new posts per day.
  5. Consistency: eventual consistency is fine. If a friend’s post shows up in your feed 10-30 seconds late, nobody is hurt. A user should always see their own new post right away (read-your-own-writes).
  6. Durability: uploaded media is never lost.
  7. CAP choice: AP. We prefer to always show a feed, even a slightly stale one, over showing an error.

3. Back-of-the-envelope estimates

Assumption Number
Daily active users 500M
New posts per day 100M
Feed loads per user per day 10
Average follows per user 200
Average media per post (after compression, all sizes) 2 MB
Post metadata 1 KB
Celebrity follower count up to 500M 
Post writes:  100M / 86,400              ~= 1,160 posts/s  (peak x3 ~= 3.5k/s)
Feed reads:   500M x 10 / 86,400         ~= 58,000 feed loads/s (peak ~150k/s)
Read : write  ~= 50 : 1

Media/day:    100M x 2 MB                = 200 TB/day
Media/year:   200 TB x 365               ~= 73 PB/year  (S3 + CDN)
Metadata/yr:  100M x 365 x 1 KB          ~= 36 TB/year

Fan-out on write (naive):
  avg follower count ~200 -> 100M x 200   = 20B feed inserts/day
                                          ~= 230k inserts/s
  one celebrity post with 500M followers  = 500M inserts for ONE post

Feed cache: keep 500 post ids per user x 8 B = 4 KB/user
            500M users x 4 KB             = 2 TB of Redis (sharded)

CDN egress: 58k feed loads/s x 10 images x 200 KB ~= 116 GB/s

The 500M-inserts-for-one-post number is why celebrities need special handling.

4. Core entities

  • User: account. Fields: user_id, username, is_celebrity (follower count above a threshold).
  • Post: one share. Fields: post_id, user_id, caption, media_ids, created_at.
  • Media: one photo or video. Fields: media_id, post_id, s3_key, status, variants (thumbnail, 1080p, HLS for video).
  • Follow: an edge “A follows B”. Fields: follower_id, followee_id, created_at.
  • Feed: a precomputed, per-user list of recent post ids. Lives in a cache.
-- Wide-column / key-value style, shown as SQL for clarity.
CREATE TABLE posts (
  user_id     BIGINT,
  post_id     BIGINT,            -- time-sortable id (Snowflake-style)
  caption     TEXT,
  media_ids   BIGINT[],
  created_at  TIMESTAMP,
  PRIMARY KEY (user_id, post_id) -- "posts by user, newest first" is a range scan
);

CREATE TABLE follows (
  follower_id BIGINT,
  followee_id BIGINT,
  created_at  TIMESTAMP,
  PRIMARY KEY (follower_id, followee_id)   -- "who do I follow?"
);
-- Plus a reverse index: PRIMARY KEY (followee_id, follower_id)
-- for "who follows me?" (needed for fan-out).
// Redis: feed:{user_id} is a sorted set, score = post timestamp
{"feed:42": [[1730620800123, "p_9001"], [1730620700456, "p_8999"]]}

A Snowflake-style id packs a timestamp, a machine id, and a sequence number into 64 bits. Sorting by id is sorting by time, which makes “newest first” free.

5. API design

All endpoints need a logged-in user (JWT). The user id always comes from the token.

POST /posts – create a post. Media is uploaded separately first (see flow).

// request
{"caption": "Sunset in Lisbon", "media_ids": [771, 772]}
// response 201
{"post_id": "p_9001", "created_at": "2026-11-03T18:00:00Z"}

POST /media/uploads – start an upload, get a presigned URL. Body {"content_type": "image/jpeg", "size": 6200000}. Response 201 {"media_id": 771, "upload_url": "https://s3...&X-Amz-Signature=...", "multipart": false}. Large videos get multipart URLs.

POST /users/{user_id}/follow – follow. Response 204. DELETE /users/{user_id}/follow – unfollow. Response 204.

GET /feed?cursor={post_id}&limit=20 – feed page, newest first.

// response 200
{"posts": [{"post_id": "p_9001", "author": {"id": 7, "username": "ana"},
            "caption": "Sunset in Lisbon",
            "media": [{"type": "image", "url": "https://cdn.../771_1080.jpg"}],
            "created_at": "2026-11-03T18:00:00Z"}],
 "next_cursor": "p_8950"}

Status codes: 200, 401 unauthenticated, 400 bad cursor, 429 rate limited.

How will users create a post?

  1. Client calls POST /media/uploads for each photo or video and gets a presigned S3 URL.
  2. Client uploads bytes directly to S3. Our servers never carry the media.
  3. Client calls POST /posts with the caption and media ids.
  4. The Post Service writes the post row with a Snowflake id and returns 201.
  5. An S3 event triggers media processing (resize, transcode) in the background.
sequenceDiagram
    participant C as Client
    participant G as API gateway
    participant P as Post service
    participant S as S3
    participant D as Posts DB
    participant W as Media workers
    C->>G: POST /media/uploads
    G->>P: start upload
    P-->>C: presigned S3 URL and media id
    C->>S: PUT media bytes
    S-->>C: 200 ok
    C->>G: POST /posts with caption and media ids
    G->>P: create post
    P->>D: write post row with Snowflake id
    D-->>P: ok
    P-->>C: 201 post id
    S->>W: S3 event triggers resize and transcode

How will users follow other users?

  1. Client calls POST /users/7/follow.
  2. The Follow Service writes the edge to two tables: (follower_id=42, followee_id=7) and the reverse (followee_id=7, follower_id=42).
  3. Both writes are idempotent: following twice leaves one edge.

How will users see their feed?

In the simplest version (pull on read):

  1. Client calls GET /feed.
  2. Feed Service gets the list of people user 42 follows (about 200).
  3. For each, it reads their newest posts from the Posts DB.
  4. It merges them by time and returns the top 20.

That is 200 queries per feed load, times 58k loads per second. It works for a demo and breaks at scale. The deep dives fix it.

7. Deep dives

How do we build the feed fast? (push vs pull vs hybrid)

The problem: a feed is a merge of recent posts from about 200 accounts. Doing that merge on every read is too slow. Doing it on every write is too expensive for accounts with millions of followers.

Option When work happens Read cost Write cost Celebrity problem
Pull (fan-out on read) At read time ~200 queries + merge 1 insert None, but reads are slow for everyone
Push (fan-out on write) At post time, write post id into every follower’s feed 1 Redis read 1 insert per follower 500M inserts for one post, minutes of lag
Hybrid Push for normal users, pull for celebrities 1 Redis read + a few celebrity reads Bounded by threshold Solved

Recommended: hybrid. Pick a threshold, say 100k followers. For normal authors, a fan-out worker pushes the new post id into each follower’s Redis feed. For celebrities, we do not push. At read time, the Feed Service reads the user’s precomputed feed and also pulls the latest posts from the handful of celebrities they follow, then merges.

CELEB_THRESHOLD = 100_000
FEED_LEN = 500

# Fan-out worker: consumes "post_created" events from Kafka.
def on_post_created(post):
    author = users.get(post.user_id)
    if author.follower_count >= CELEB_THRESHOLD:
        return                                   # pulled at read time
    for batch in follows.followers_of(post.user_id, batch_size=1000):
        pipe = redis.pipeline()
        for follower_id in batch:
            key = f"feed:{follower_id}"
            pipe.zadd(key, {post.post_id: post.ts})
            pipe.zremrangebyrank(key, 0, -FEED_LEN - 1)  # keep newest 500
        pipe.execute()

# Read path
def get_feed(user_id, cursor_ts, limit=20):
    ids = redis.zrevrangebyscore(f"feed:{user_id}", cursor_ts, "-inf",
                                 start=0, num=limit, withscores=True)
    for celeb in follows.celebrities_followed_by(user_id):   # usually < 20
        ids += posts.latest_ids(celeb, before=cursor_ts, limit=limit)
    ids.sort(key=lambda x: x[1], reverse=True)
    return hydrate(ids[:limit])                  # batch-fetch post bodies
Fan-out math after the threshold:
  Normal author, 200 followers:   200 Redis writes, done in ~10 ms
  Author with 99k followers:      99k writes in batches of 1000
                                  = 99 pipelines, ~2-5 s, async
  Celebrity, 500M followers:      0 writes; pulled by readers

The fan-out runs asynchronously through Kafka, so POST /posts returns in milliseconds. To give the author read-your-own-writes, the client inserts the new post at the top of its own feed immediately, and the Feed Service always merges the user’s own latest posts.

A small detail that saves a lot of memory: inactive users (no login in 30 days) are skipped during fan-out. When they come back, we rebuild their feed with a pull once.

How do we upload and serve photos and videos quickly?

The problem: 200 TB of new media per day, files up to 4 GB, and users all over the world who expect images to appear instantly on a phone connection.

Option Upload path Serving Problem
Upload through app servers Client to API to S3 App servers Servers become a bandwidth bottleneck
Presigned URL straight to S3 Client to S3 S3 directly Far from many users; full-size files on mobile
Presigned upload + processing + CDN Client to S3, workers make variants CDN edge, right size per device More pipeline, but standard

Recommended: presigned uploads (multipart for videos above about 100 MB), a processing pipeline, and a CDN. When the upload lands, an S3 event puts a job on a queue. Workers create variants: several image sizes (150 px thumbnail, 640 px, 1080 px) in WebP or AVIF, and for video, HLS renditions. HLS (HTTP Live Streaming) cuts a video into 2-6 second segments at several bitrates, so the player starts quickly at low quality and steps up as bandwidth allows.

 Client --presigned PUT--> S3 raw/ --event--> SQS --> Media workers
                                                     | resize images
                                                     | transcode HLS
                                                     v
                                        S3 processed/ ---> CDN edge
                           Media table: status = ready, variants = {...}
def process_image(media_id, raw_key):
    img = load_from_s3(raw_key)
    variants = {}
    for width in (150, 640, 1080):
        out = resize(img, width).encode("webp", quality=80)
        key = f"processed/{media_id}_{width}.webp"
        s3.put_object(Bucket=B, Key=key, Body=out,
                      CacheControl="public, max-age=31536000, immutable")
        variants[str(width)] = f"https://cdn.example.com/{key}"
    media.update(media_id, status="ready", variants=variants)

Media files never change once written, so they get a one-year cache header. The client picks the variant that fits its screen. A 1080 px WebP is about 200 KB versus a 6 MB original, a 30x saving on mobile data.

How do we paginate the feed?

The problem: users scroll forever. New posts keep arriving at the top while they scroll. Offset pagination (LIMIT 20 OFFSET 40) shows duplicates when new posts push items down, and gets slower the deeper you go.

Option Stable with new posts? Deep page cost Notes
Offset (page=3) No, duplicates and gaps Grows with offset Simple but wrong for feeds
Cursor on timestamp / post id Yes Constant Needs a sortable, unique key
Opaque token encoding cursor + celeb positions Yes Constant Best for hybrid merges

Recommended: cursor pagination using the Snowflake post id (which is time-sortable and unique). The response returns next_cursor = the id of the last post shown. The next call asks for posts strictly older than that.

def page(user_id, cursor=None, limit=20):
    max_score = f"({cursor_ts(cursor)}" if cursor else "+inf"  # "(" = exclusive
    rows = redis.zrevrangebyscore(f"feed:{user_id}", max_score, "-inf",
                                  start=0, num=limit, withscores=True)
    # ...merge celebrity posts older than cursor, as above...
    next_cursor = encode_cursor(rows[-1]) if rows else None
    return rows, next_cursor

When the user reaches the end of the 500 cached ids, the Feed Service falls back to a pull query for older posts. Very few users scroll that far, so the cost is small.

How do we store the follow graph?

The problem: we need two fast questions. “Who does user 42 follow?” (for the celebrity pull and feed rebuild) and “Who follows user 7?” (for fan-out, possibly 99k rows streamed in batches). There are about 500M users x 200 follows = 100B edges.

Option Who-I-follow Who-follows-me Scale
Single SQL table with two indexes Fast Fast 100B rows needs sharding; cross-shard index pain
Graph database Fast Fast Great for multi-hop queries we do not need
Wide-column store, two tables partitioned by each side One partition read One partition read Scales linearly, simple 
Edge storage: 100B edges x ~30 B x 2 tables ~= 6 TB, spread over a cluster

Recommended: a wide-column store like Cassandra or DynamoDB with two tables: following partitioned by follower_id, and followers partitioned by followee_id. Every follow writes both. Each question becomes a single-partition read. Keep follower_count as a separate counter so the fan-out worker can check the celebrity threshold in one lookup.

How do we handle read-heavy traffic with caching, and what if things fail?

The problem: 58k feed loads per second (150k at peak), each needing 20 post bodies plus author info. Hitting the Posts DB for every one is 1M+ row reads per second.

Cache layer What it holds Hit rate TTL
CDN All media variants 95%+ 1 year (immutable)
Feed cache (Redis sorted sets) Post ids per user Very high for active users Rebuilt on miss
Post cache (Redis / Memcached) post_id -> post JSON 90%+ (recent posts are hot) Hours
User cache user_id -> username, avatar 95%+ Hours

Recommended: all four. The feed read becomes one sorted-set read plus one batched MGET for 20 post bodies and authors. Hot keys (a viral celebrity post read millions of times per second) get replicated across several cache nodes or held in a small in-process cache on each Feed Service host for a few seconds.

Feed read latency budget (p99 < 500 ms):
  Gateway + auth                      10 ms
  ZREVRANGE feed:{uid}                 2 ms
  Celebrity pulls (cached, ~10)        10 ms (parallel)
  MGET 20 posts + 20 authors           3 ms
  Serialize + network                 60 ms
  Total                              ~85 ms server+network, images load from CDN
Failure Effect Mitigation
Redis feed shard lost Some users have empty feeds Rebuild on read via pull; Redis replicas
Fan-out workers lag Posts appear late Kafka buffers events; autoscale workers on lag
Media worker fails Post stuck “processing” Queue retries, dead-letter queue, client shows placeholder
Region outage Users in region fail Multi-region read replicas; CDN keeps serving media
Posts DB node down Some writes slow Cassandra replication factor 3, quorum writes

Posting and feed reads go through the gateway to services in the service subnet, fan out workers fill the Redis feed cache from Kafka, and media bytes go straight to S3 and back out through the CDN.

9. Common mistakes and interviewer follow-ups

  • Pure fan-out on write. One celebrity post becomes 500M writes and minutes of lag. Say: “Hybrid: push for normal users, pull for accounts over a threshold.”
  • Pure fan-out on read. 200 queries per feed load at 58k loads/s is ~12M queries/s. Precompute for normal users.
  • Uploading media through app servers. They become a bandwidth bottleneck. Use presigned URLs to S3.
  • Serving the original 6 MB photo to phones. Slow and costly. Make variants and serve via CDN with long cache headers.
  • Offset pagination for the feed. New posts shift pages and cause duplicates. Use a cursor on a time-sortable id.
  • Storing follows only one way. Fan-out needs “who follows me” and the feed needs “who I follow”. Store both directions.
  • Forgetting read-your-own-writes. The author does not see their own post and thinks it failed. Merge the user’s own posts on read.
  • Follow-up: “How would you add ranking?” Answer: keep the same candidate set from the hybrid feed, then score candidates with a model before returning the page.

10. One-page cheat sheet

Topic Key point
Scale 500M DAU, ~1.2k posts/s, ~58k feed loads/s (peak 150k)
Media ~200 TB/day; presigned upload, variants, CDN, 1-year cache
Feed model Hybrid: push for under 100k followers, pull for celebrities
Feed cache Redis sorted set feed:{uid}, newest 500 ids, ~2 TB total
Fan-out Async via Kafka, batched pipelines, skip inactive users
Pagination Cursor on Snowflake post id, exclusive bound
Follow graph Two wide-column tables (following, followers) + counter
Caching CDN, feed cache, post cache, user cache; hot-key replication
Consistency Eventual for feeds, read-your-own-writes for the author
CAP AP: always show a feed

07. Facebook News Feed (Medium)

Facebook News Feed is the scrolling list of posts you see when you open Facebook. It shows recent posts from your friends and from pages and people you follow. You can scroll forever, and new posts keep appearing. The interviewer is really testing three things: how you build a personal feed for billions of people quickly, how you deal with accounts that have millions of followers (the “celebrity problem”), and how you page through a feed that keeps changing under you.

1. Functional requirements

Core (must have):

  1. Users can create a post (text, optionally with a link or a media reference).
  2. Users can follow (or friend) other users. Following is one-way here: A follows B does not mean B follows A.
  3. Users can view a feed of posts from the people they follow, newest or best first.
  4. Users can page through the feed with infinite scroll.

Below the line (out of scope):

  1. Likes, comments, and shares. They are counters and lists attached to a post. They feed the ranking model but do not change the feed pipeline.
  2. Media upload and processing. That is a blob storage and CDN problem, covered in the Instagram and Dropbox chapters.
  3. Privacy settings per post (friends only, custom lists). Real but adds filtering, not new architecture.
  4. Ads in the feed. Ads are inserted by a separate ads system at read time.

2. Non-functional requirements

  1. Low latency: p99 under 500 ms to return the first page of the feed (20 posts).
  2. High availability: 99.99% for feed reads. A slightly stale feed is far better than an error page.
  3. Consistency: eventual. A new post may take up to 1 minute to appear in followers’ feeds. The author must see their own post immediately (read-your-own-writes).
  4. Scale: 2B users, 1B daily active users, up to 100M followers on a single account.
  5. Write durability: an accepted post is never lost.
  6. CAP choice: AP (availability and partition tolerance). During a network split we serve whatever feed we have rather than block. Nobody is harmed by a missing post for a minute.

3. Back-of-the-envelope estimates

Assumption Number
Daily active users (DAU) 1B
Feed loads per user per day 10
Posts per user per day 0.5
Average followers per user 200
Post metadata size 1 KB
Feed cache entry (post ID + score) 16 bytes
Feed cache length per user 500 entries 
Feed reads:
  1B users * 10 loads/day = 10B loads/day
  10B / 86,400 s          ~= 115,000 reads/s average
  peak (x3)               ~= 350,000 reads/s

Post writes:
  1B * 0.5 = 500M posts/day
  500M / 86,400           ~= 5,800 writes/s, peak ~= 17,000/s

Fan-out writes (if we push every post to every follower):
  5,800 posts/s * 200 followers = 1.16M feed inserts/s average

Post storage per year:
  500M * 1 KB = 500 GB/day -> ~180 TB/year (before replication)

Precomputed feed cache:
  1B users * 500 entries * 16 B = 8 TB of RAM (spread over a Redis cluster)

Bandwidth for feed reads:
  350k reads/s * 20 posts * 1 KB = 7 GB/s at peak (metadata only)

The key insight from the math: reads outnumber posts by about 20 to 1, and fan-out turns each post into 200 cache writes. That ratio drives every design choice below.

4. Core entities

  • User: a person or page. Fields: user_id, name, created_at.
  • Follow: a directed edge “follower follows followee”. Fields: follower_id, followee_id, created_at.
  • Post: a piece of content. Fields: post_id, author_id, content, created_at.
  • Feed entry: one item in a user’s precomputed feed. Fields: user_id, post_id, score (time or rank).
  • Cursor: an opaque token that marks where the client is in the feed.
CREATE TABLE posts (
  post_id     BIGINT PRIMARY KEY,      -- Snowflake ID, sortable by time
  author_id   BIGINT NOT NULL,
  content     TEXT,
  created_at  TIMESTAMP NOT NULL
);
CREATE INDEX posts_by_author ON posts (author_id, created_at DESC);

CREATE TABLE follows (
  follower_id BIGINT NOT NULL,
  followee_id BIGINT NOT NULL,
  created_at  TIMESTAMP NOT NULL,
  PRIMARY KEY (follower_id, followee_id)
);
-- Reverse lookup: "who follows X?" is needed for fan-out.
CREATE INDEX follows_by_followee ON follows (followee_id, follower_id);

A Snowflake ID is a 64-bit number made of a timestamp, a machine ID, and a counter. Sorting by it sorts by time, which makes pagination easy.

5. API design

POST /posts – create a post.

// request
{ "content": "Hello world" }
// response 201
{ "post_id": "7182736451", "created_at": "2026-11-03T10:00:00Z" }

Status codes: 201 created, 400 bad input, 401 not logged in. The author comes from the auth token, never from the body.

PUT /users/{user_id}/followers – follow a user. DELETE /users/{user_id}/followers – unfollow.

// response 204, no body

Status codes: 204 ok, 404 user not found, 409 already following.

GET /feed?cursor={cursor}&limit=20 – get a page of the feed.

// response 200
{
  "items": [
    { "post_id": "7182736451", "author_id": "42",
      "content": "Hello world", "created_at": "2026-11-03T10:00:00Z" }
  ],
  "next_cursor": "eyJzIjoxNzMwNjI4MDAwLCJpZCI6NzE4MjczNjQ1MX0"
}

All endpoints require a bearer token. limit is capped at 50 to protect the backend.

How will users create a post?

  1. Client sends POST /posts with the content.
  2. The gateway checks the token and routes to the Post Service.
  3. Post Service creates a Snowflake ID and writes the row to the Posts DB (sharded by post_id).
  4. It publishes a post-created event to Kafka (a durable log that consumers read in order).
  5. It returns 201 to the client right away. Fan-out happens in the background.
sequenceDiagram
    participant C as Client
    participant G as API gateway
    participant P as Post service
    participant D as Posts DB
    participant K as Kafka
    participant W as Fan-out workers
    C->>G: POST /posts with content
    G->>G: check token
    G->>P: route request
    P->>P: create Snowflake ID
    P->>D: write post row
    D-->>P: ok
    P->>K: publish post-created event
    P-->>C: 201 post id
    K->>W: deliver event in background

How will users follow someone?

  1. Client sends PUT /users/42/followers.
  2. Follow Service writes the row (me, 42) into the follows table.
  3. Optional: a background job copies 42’s last few posts into my feed cache so I see them right away.

How will users view their feed?

  1. Client sends GET /feed.
  2. Feed Service reads the user’s sorted list of post IDs from the feed cache.
  3. It merges in recent posts from any celebrities the user follows (see deep dive).
  4. It “hydrates” the IDs: looks up post bodies and author names from the post cache in one batched call.
  5. It passes candidates through the ranking service (optional, see deep dive).
  6. It returns 20 posts plus a next_cursor.

How will users page through the feed?

  1. The client sends back the next_cursor it got last time.
  2. The cursor encodes “the last score and post ID I showed you”. The Feed Service asks Redis for items strictly older than that point.
  3. Repeat until the cache runs out, then fall back to querying the Posts DB directly for older history.

7. Deep dives

Should we fan out on write or fan out on read?

The problem: when a user opens the feed, we need posts from up to hundreds of followed accounts, sorted. We can do that work when the post is written, or when the feed is read.

  • Fan-out on write (push): when Alice posts, copy her post ID into every follower’s feed list.
  • Fan-out on read (pull): when Bob opens the feed, query recent posts of everyone Bob follows and merge them.
Fan-out on write (push) Fan-out on read (pull)
Read cost 1 cache read, very fast N queries + merge, slow for N = 500
Write cost 1 write per follower (200 avg, 100M worst) 1 write
Storage Feed list per user (8 TB RAM) None extra
Freshness Delay while fan-out runs Always fresh
Inactive users Wasted work for users who never log in No waste
Celebrity post 100M writes, minutes of lag Fine

Neither wins alone. Push makes reads fast, which matters because reads are 20x writes. Pull handles celebrities. So we use a hybrid, covered next.

A fan-out worker looks like this:

FEED_LEN = 500

def handle_post_created(event):
    post_id, author_id, ts = event["post_id"], event["author_id"], event["ts"]
    if is_celebrity(author_id):
        return  # celebrities are pulled at read time, not pushed
    for batch in follow_service.followers(author_id, batch_size=1000):
        pipe = redis.pipeline()
        for follower_id in batch:
            if not is_active(follower_id):   # skip users idle > 30 days
                continue
            key = f"feed:{follower_id}"
            pipe.zadd(key, {post_id: ts})
            pipe.zremrangebyrank(key, 0, -FEED_LEN - 1)  # keep newest 500
        pipe.execute()

How do we handle users with millions of followers?

The problem: follower counts are very uneven. Most users have 200 followers. A few have 100M. If a celebrity posts and we push, that is 100M Redis writes. At 1M writes/s per cluster that is 100 seconds of lag, and it starves everyone else’s fan-out.

Option How it works Downside
Push everything, just add workers Scale fan-out horizontally Wastes huge capacity, lag still spikes
Pull everything Merge at read time Slow reads for everyone
Hybrid (recommended) Push for normal users, pull for celebrities Two code paths to maintain

Recommended: hybrid. Mark an account as a “celebrity” when it has more than, say, 100k followers. Their posts are not pushed. Instead each celebrity has a small cache of their own recent posts. At read time, the Feed Service:

  1. Reads the user’s pushed feed from Redis (one call).
  2. Looks up which celebrities the user follows (usually fewer than 50, cached).
  3. Reads each celebrity’s recent posts list (one batched MGET-style call).
  4. Merges everything by score.
def get_feed_candidates(user_id, before_score, limit):
    pushed = redis.zrevrangebyscore(
        f"feed:{user_id}", before_score, "-inf",
        start=0, num=limit, withscores=True)
    celebs = follow_service.celebrities_followed(user_id)   # cached
    pipe = redis.pipeline()
    for c in celebs:
        pipe.zrevrangebyscore(f"posts:{c}", before_score, "-inf",
                              start=0, num=limit, withscores=True)
    pulled = [item for res in pipe.execute() for item in res]
    merged = sorted(pushed + pulled, key=lambda x: x[1], reverse=True)
    return merged[:limit]

Two refinements interviewers like:

  • Skip inactive users during push. If a user has not logged in for 30 days, do not maintain their feed. When they return, build it once with pull. This cuts fan-out work a lot.
  • Use a gradient, not a cliff. Accounts with 10k-100k followers can be pushed only to followers who were active in the last day, and pulled for the rest.

How does the feed ranking service work?

The problem: a pure time-sorted feed shows the newest post, not the most interesting one. Facebook ranks. We need to rank without blowing the 500 ms budget.

Option Latency Quality Notes
Chronological only Lowest Low Simple, good starting point
Rank at write time (store a score) Low Medium Score cannot react to likes after posting
Two-stage rank at read time (recommended) Medium High Candidate fetch, then ML scoring

Recommended: two stages.

  1. Candidate generation: take the top 500 recent candidates from the hybrid fetch above. This is cheap.
  2. Scoring: a Ranking Service scores each candidate with a model using features like author affinity (how often you interact with this person), post age, post type, and early engagement. Return the top 20.
Feed Service
   | 500 candidate IDs
   v
Feature Store (affinity, counts) ---> Ranking Service (model) ---> top 20
   ^                                       |
   | features updated by Kafka streams     | p99 budget ~100 ms

Keep it inside budget: score in batches, cache features, and if the ranker times out, fall back to the chronological order. Rank only the first page with the full model; later pages can use a cheaper model.

A gotcha: if ranking re-orders the feed on every request, page 2 may repeat or skip posts from page 1. The fix is to save the ranked list for this session (in Redis with a 30 minute TTL) and page through that saved list with a cursor.

How do we paginate a feed that keeps changing?

The problem: new posts arrive at the top while the user scrolls. With offset paging (?page=2 means skip 20), a new post shifts everything by one, so the user sees a duplicate.

Option Duplicates/skips Cost of deep pages Notes
Offset (LIMIT 20 OFFSET 40) Yes, when new posts arrive Gets slower the deeper you go Avoid
Cursor on (score, post_id) (recommended) No Constant Stable under inserts
Page token pointing to a saved session list No Constant Needed when ranking re-orders

Recommended: an opaque cursor. It encodes the last item’s score and post ID. The next request asks for items strictly “before” that pair. Including the post ID breaks ties when two posts have the same timestamp.

import base64, json

def encode_cursor(score, post_id):
    raw = json.dumps({"s": score, "id": post_id}).encode()
    return base64.urlsafe_b64encode(raw).decode()

def decode_cursor(cursor):
    if not cursor:
        return float("inf"), None
    d = json.loads(base64.urlsafe_b64decode(cursor))
    return d["s"], d["id"]

The SQL fallback for old history uses the same idea (this is called keyset pagination):

SELECT post_id, author_id, content, created_at
FROM posts
WHERE author_id = ANY(:followees)
  AND (created_at, post_id) < (:last_ts, :last_id)
ORDER BY created_at DESC, post_id DESC
LIMIT 20;

Make the cursor opaque (base64) so clients do not build their own and so you can change its contents later. Sign it with an HMAC if you worry about tampering.

What happens when parts of the system fail?

The problem: fan-out workers crash, Redis nodes die, Kafka lags. The feed must still load.

Failure Effect Mitigation
Fan-out worker crashes mid-batch Some followers miss a post Kafka consumer re-reads from last committed offset; ZADD is idempotent, so replays are safe
Redis feed shard lost Users on that shard have empty feeds Replicas with automatic failover; if both lost, rebuild with pull on next read
Ranking service slow Feed latency breaches 500 ms Timeout at 100 ms, fall back to chronological
Kafka lag spike (big event) Posts appear late Autoscale consumers on lag metric; celebrities already bypass push
Posts DB shard down Hydration fails for some posts Serve from post cache; drop missing items rather than fail the page

Idempotency is the important word. Because the feed is a sorted set keyed by post ID, writing the same post twice is harmless. That lets us use “at least once” delivery from Kafka without worrying.

9. Common mistakes and interviewer follow-ups

  • Picking push only. A 100M-follower post makes fan-out lag for minutes. Say: “push for normal users, pull for celebrities, merge at read time.”
  • Using offset pagination. New posts cause duplicates and deep pages get slow. Say: “cursor on (score, post_id), opaque to the client.”
  • Storing full posts in every feed list. That multiplies storage by 200. Store only post IDs and hydrate from a post cache.
  • Doing fan-out synchronously in the post request. The author waits seconds. Return 201 after the DB write and fan out from Kafka.
  • Maintaining feeds for users who never log in. Huge wasted work. Skip inactive users and rebuild on return.
  • Forgetting the author’s own post. With eventual fan-out the author may not see it. Insert it into the author’s own feed synchronously, or merge it client-side.
  • Follow-up: “What if a user follows 5,000 accounts?” Cap the follow count, or treat heavy followers specially: pushed feed covers them, and pull only for celebrities.
  • Follow-up: “How do you handle a deleted post?” Do not chase it through 200 feeds. Mark it deleted in the Posts DB; hydration drops it at read time.

10. One-page cheat sheet

Topic Key point
Scale 1B DAU, ~350k feed reads/s peak, ~17k posts/s peak
Read/write ratio ~20:1, so optimize reads
Fan-out Hybrid: push for normal, pull for >100k followers
Feed store Redis sorted set feed:{uid}, 500 post IDs, ~8 TB RAM
Posts store Cassandra or sharded MySQL, Snowflake IDs
Async pipeline Kafka post-created -> fan-out workers
Ranking Two stages: 500 candidates -> model -> top 20, fallback to chrono
Pagination Opaque cursor on (score, post_id), keyset SQL for history
Consistency Eventual (< 1 min), read-your-own-writes for author
CAP AP, serve stale feed over error
Failure trick Idempotent ZADD makes Kafka replays safe
Waste saver Skip inactive users during fan-out

Sources

  • Hello Interview: Design Facebook News Feed
  • Facebook Engineering: Serving Facebook Multifeed
  • Facebook Engineering: TAO, the power of the graph
  • System Design Primer (GitHub)

08. Tinder (Dating App Swipe and Match) (Medium)

Tinder shows you a stack of profiles of people near you. You swipe right if you like someone and left if you do not. If two people both swipe right on each other, it is a “match” and both get notified so they can chat. The interviewer is really testing four things: how you make sure a match is never missed when two people swipe at the same moment, how you store billions of swipes cheaply, how you build a stack of nearby profiles quickly, and how you avoid showing someone a profile they have already swiped on.

1. Functional requirements

Core (must have):

  1. Users can create a profile with preferences: age range, gender interest, and maximum distance.
  2. Users can see a stack of nearby profiles that match their preferences.
  3. Users can swipe right (like) or left (pass) on a profile.
  4. Users get a match notification when both people have swiped right on each other.

Below the line (out of scope):

  1. Chat after matching. That is a messaging system, covered in the WhatsApp chapter.
  2. Photo upload and moderation. Blob storage plus CDN, covered elsewhere.
  3. Premium features (super likes, rewind, see who liked you). They reuse the swipe store but add business rules.
  4. ML-based ranking of the stack (desirability scores). We mention it as a hook but do not design the model.

2. Non-functional requirements

  1. Strong consistency for matches: if both users swipe right, a match must be created exactly once, even if they swipe in the same millisecond. Missing a match is the worst bug in the product.
  2. Low swipe latency: p99 under 100 ms. Swiping is a fast physical gesture and must feel instant.
  3. Fast stack loading: p99 under 300 ms to fetch the next batch of profiles.
  4. No repeats: a user should not see a profile they already swiped on (a tiny error rate is OK, under 1 in 1,000).
  5. Scale: 20M daily active users, 100 swipes per user per day.
  6. Availability: 99.9% for swiping. Profile stacks can be slightly stale (a new user nearby may take minutes to appear).
  7. CAP choice: mostly AP for profile discovery, but the match check needs per-pair consistency (CP behaviour on a small key). We get that by co-locating both directions of a pair on one partition and using an atomic operation.

3. Back-of-the-envelope estimates

Assumption Number
Daily active users 20M
Swipes per user per day 100
Right-swipe rate 30%
Match rate of right swipes 5%
Swipe record size 50 bytes
Profile size (metadata, photo URLs) 2 KB
Stack batch size 50 profiles 
Swipe writes:
  20M * 100 = 2B swipes/day
  2B / 86,400 s ~= 23,000 swipes/s average, peak (x3) ~= 70,000/s

Stack fetches:
  100 swipes / 50 per batch = 2 fetches/user/day
  20M * 2 = 40M/day ~= 460/s average, ~1,400/s peak (light)

Matches:
  2B * 0.30 * 0.05 = 30M matches/day ~= 350/s

Swipe storage:
  2B * 50 B = 100 GB/day -> ~36 TB/year (before replication)

Profile storage:
  75M total users * 2 KB = 150 GB (fits in memory on a few nodes)

Bloom filter per user (to avoid repeats):
  say 10,000 swipes stored, 0.1% false positive -> ~14.4 bits/item
  10,000 * 14.4 / 8 ~= 18 KB per user
  20M active users * 18 KB ~= 360 GB of Redis

So swipes are the heavy write path (70k/s peak, 36 TB/year), while stack fetching is read-light but compute-heavy (geo query plus filtering).

4. Core entities

  • User / Profile: who you are. Fields: user_id, name, age, gender, bio, photos, last_location, last_active.
  • Preferences: who you want to see. Fields: user_id, min_age, max_age, interested_in, max_distance_km.
  • Swipe: one decision. Fields: swiper_id, swipee_id, decision (like or pass), created_at.
  • Match: two people who liked each other. Fields: match_id, user_a, user_b, created_at.
  • Stack: a cached, ordered list of candidate profile IDs for one user.
-- Cassandra (CQL). Partition by swiper, so "all my swipes" is one read.
CREATE TABLE swipes (
  swiper_id  bigint,
  swipee_id  bigint,
  decision   text,          -- 'like' or 'pass'
  created_at timestamp,
  PRIMARY KEY ((swiper_id), swipee_id)
);

CREATE TABLE matches (
  user_id    bigint,
  match_id   timeuuid,
  other_user bigint,
  PRIMARY KEY ((user_id), match_id)
) WITH CLUSTERING ORDER BY (match_id DESC);
{
  "user_id": 123,
  "age": 29,
  "gender": "f",
  "prefs": { "min_age": 27, "max_age": 35, "interested_in": "m",
             "max_distance_km": 25 },
  "location": { "lat": 40.7128, "lng": -74.0060, "geohash": "dr5regw" }
}

5. API design

POST /profile – create or update profile and preferences.

// request
{ "age": 29, "gender": "f", "bio": "...",
  "prefs": { "min_age": 27, "max_age": 35, "interested_in": "m",
             "max_distance_km": 25 } }
// response 200
{ "user_id": 123 }

GET /feed?lat=40.71&lng=-74.00 – get the next batch of profiles.

// response 200
{ "profiles": [ { "user_id": 456, "name": "Sam", "age": 31,
                  "distance_km": 3, "photos": ["https://cdn/..."] } ] }

The client sends its current location with each call. The server never trusts a user_id in the query; it comes from the token.

POST /swipe/{target_user_id} – record a swipe.

// request
{ "decision": "like" }
// response 200
{ "matched": true, "match_id": "b1f0..." }

Status codes: 200 ok, 400 invalid decision, 404 target not found, 409 already swiped (idempotent: return the same result again), 429 swipe rate limit hit.

GET /matches?cursor=... – list my matches.

All endpoints need a bearer token. Match notifications go out by push (APNs or FCM), not by polling.

How will users create a profile?

  1. Client sends POST /profile.
  2. Profile Service validates and writes to the Profile DB.
  3. On each app open, the client sends its location. The service updates last_location and its geohash (a short string that names a grid cell on the map; nearby points share a prefix).
sequenceDiagram
    participant U as Client
    participant G as Gateway
    participant P as ProfileService
    participant D as ProfileDB
    U->>G: POST /profile with prefs
    G->>G: Validate token
    G->>P: Forward profile request
    P->>P: Validate fields
    P->>D: Upsert profile and preferences
    D-->>P: ok
    P-->>G: user id
    G-->>U: 200 user id
    U->>G: App open with location
    G->>P: Update location
    P->>D: Set last location and geohash
    D-->>P: ok

How will users see a stack of nearby profiles?

  1. Client calls GET /feed with its location.
  2. Stack Service checks the Stack Cache for a precomputed list for this user. If there are at least 20 left, return the next 50.
  3. If not, it runs a geo query: users within max_distance_km whose age and gender match, who also want someone like me (preferences must match both ways).
  4. It removes profiles I have already swiped on (bloom filter check, see deep dive).
  5. It orders the rest (recently active first, or by a ranking score), saves them to the Stack Cache, and returns the first 50.

How will users swipe?

  1. Client sends POST /swipe/456 with like.
  2. Swipe Service records the swipe and atomically checks whether 456 already liked me (see deep dive).
  3. It adds 456 to my “already swiped” bloom filter.
  4. It returns { matched: true/false } within 100 ms.

How will users get notified of a match?

  1. If the atomic check finds a mutual like, Swipe Service writes two rows to the Matches DB (one per user).
  2. It publishes a match-created event.
  3. Notification Service sends a push to the other user. The swiper already knows from the HTTP response.

7. Deep dives

How do we make sure a match is never missed when both swipe at once?

The problem: Alice and Bob swipe right on each other at the same moment. A naive flow is “write my swipe, then read their swipe”. If both requests write first and then both read before the other write is visible (say, on different replicas), both see “no like yet” and no match is created. Or both see a like and two matches are created.

Option How Problem
Write then read on an eventually consistent DB Two separate operations Race: missed or duplicate matches
Distributed lock per pair Lock pair:alice:bob, then check Extra round trips, lock service is a dependency
Single atomic op on a pair key (recommended) Store both directions under one key, update and check in one Redis Lua script Need pair key routing, Redis durability (backed by Cassandra log)
DB transaction with SERIALIZABLE Postgres row per pair Works, but 70k/s is a lot for one SQL cluster

Recommended: make a pair key from the two IDs sorted, so Alice-Bob and Bob-Alice land on the same key and the same Redis shard. A Lua script runs atomically on that shard (Redis runs one script at a time per shard), so there is no race.

# Key is the same no matter who swipes first.
def pair_key(a, b):
    lo, hi = sorted((a, b))
    return f"swipe:{lo}:{hi}"

# Hash fields: "lo_likes" and "hi_likes". Returns 1 if this swipe created a match.
LUA = """
local key, me_field, other_field = KEYS[1], ARGV[1], ARGV[2]
local decision = ARGV[3]
redis.call('HSET', key, me_field, decision)
redis.call('EXPIRE', key, 7776000)      -- 90 days
if decision == 'like' and redis.call('HGET', key, other_field) == 'like' then
  if redis.call('HSETNX', key, 'matched', 1) == 1 then
    return 1
  end
end
return 0
"""

def swipe(me, target, decision):
    lo, hi = sorted((me, target))
    me_f, other_f = ("lo", "hi") if me == lo else ("hi", "lo")
    matched = redis.eval(LUA, 1, pair_key(me, target),
                         me_f + "_likes", other_f + "_likes", decision)
    kafka.send("swipes", {"swiper": me, "swipee": target, "d": decision})
    if matched:
        create_match(me, target)   # idempotent, keyed by pair
    return bool(matched)

HSETNX on a matched field means only one of two concurrent calls ever returns 1, so we never create a duplicate match. Swipes are also streamed to Kafka and written to Cassandra for durability; if a Redis node is lost, we can rebuild pair state from the log.

How do we store billions of swipes at scale?

The problem: 2B swipes a day, 36 TB a year, and we need two very different reads: “did X like me?” (pair lookup, hot, recent) and “all profiles X has swiped on” (used to filter the stack).

Store Good at Weak at
Postgres Transactions, simple 70k writes/s and 36 TB/year needs heavy sharding
Cassandra (recommended for the log) Huge write throughput, partition by swiper No cross-partition atomicity
Redis (recommended for hot state) Atomic Lua, sub-ms RAM cost, needs TTL
Bloom filter in Redis (recommended for “seen”) 18 KB per user answers “seen?” Small false positive rate, no deletes

Recommended: three layers.

  1. Redis pair hashes for the match check, with a 90-day TTL (most matches happen within days of swiping).
  2. Cassandra swipes table, partitioned by swiper_id, as the durable history. It is written from Kafka, so the swipe request does not wait for it.
  3. A per-user bloom filter of “profiles I have swiped on”, used by the stack builder.

A bloom filter is a compact bit array plus a few hash functions. To add an item, set k bits. To check, see if all k bits are set. It can say “maybe seen” by mistake (false positive) but never “not seen” by mistake. A false positive only means we skip one profile, which is harmless.

import math, mmh3

def bloom_params(n_items, fp_rate):
    m = math.ceil(-n_items * math.log(fp_rate) / (math.log(2) ** 2))  # bits
    k = round(m / n_items * math.log(2))                              # hashes
    return m, k

m, k = bloom_params(10_000, 0.001)   # m ~= 143,776 bits (18 KB), k = 10

def bloom_add(user_id, item):
    for i in range(k):
        redis.setbit(f"seen:{user_id}", mmh3.hash(str(item), i) % m, 1)

def bloom_maybe_seen(user_id, item):
    return all(redis.getbit(f"seen:{user_id}", mmh3.hash(str(item), i) % m)
               for i in range(k))

In production you would use the RedisBloom module (BF.ADD, BF.EXISTS) instead of hand-rolled bits, and pipeline the checks for a whole batch of 500 candidates.

How do we generate a geo-based profile stack quickly?

The problem: find people within 25 km, of the right age and gender, who also want someone like me, out of 75M users, in under 300 ms.

Option How Trade-off
Scan with lat/lng BETWEEN Plain B-tree index Slow, can only index one dimension well
Postgres + PostGIS geo index ST_DWithin on a GiST index Solid; scale reads with replicas
Geohash buckets in Redis or Elasticsearch (recommended) Look up my cell and its 8 neighbours, filter Fast, easy to shard by geohash
Precompute stacks in background (recommended addition) Cron or event-driven job fills Stack Cache Stack may be minutes stale

Recommended: an Elasticsearch (or OpenSearch) index of active profiles with a geo_point field plus age, gender, and preference fields. It supports geo distance filters and multi-field filters in one query, and shards well. Then precompute the stack in the background so GET /feed is usually a cache hit.

{
  "query": { "bool": { "filter": [
    { "geo_distance": { "distance": "25km",
                        "location": { "lat": 40.71, "lon": -74.00 } } },
    { "term":  { "gender": "m" } },
    { "range": { "age": { "gte": 27, "lte": 35 } } },
    { "term":  { "interested_in": "f" } },
    { "range": { "pref_min_age": { "lte": 29 } } },
    { "range": { "pref_max_age": { "gte": 29 } } },
    { "range": { "last_active": { "gte": "now-7d" } } }
  ] } },
  "size": 500
}

The two-way preference check (interested_in and pref_*_age against my own age) is easy to forget and interviewers notice. After the query, filter out seen profiles with the bloom filter, rank, and keep 50 to 200 in the Stack Cache. When the user’s remaining stack drops below 20, kick off a refill in the background so they never wait.

How do we avoid showing repeat profiles?

The problem: if I passed on Sam yesterday, Sam should not show up today. The stack is rebuilt often, and the “seen” set grows forever.

Option Accuracy Cost Notes
Query Cassandra for every candidate Exact 500 reads per stack build Too slow
Exclude list inside the ES query (must_not ids) Exact Query grows with history Breaks down past a few thousand IDs
Bloom filter per user (recommended) 99.9% 18 KB per user, one pipelined call Tiny false positives are fine
Client-side cache of recent IDs Exact for recent Free Good extra layer for the current session

Recommended: bloom filter plus a small client-side list of the last few hundred IDs (covers the gap between swiping and the filter update). Remove stack items from the Stack Cache the moment they are returned, so two devices or two quick refreshes do not get the same profile.

If a filter fills up (say past 10,000 items, the false positive rate starts to rise), rotate: start a new filter, keep the old one for checks, and rebuild from Cassandra in the background.

How do we keep swipes fast and survive failures?

The problem: a swipe must return in 100 ms even at 70k/s peak, and losing a swipe could mean losing a match.

Concern Approach
Latency Only the Redis Lua call is on the hot path (~1 ms). Cassandra write and bloom update go async via Kafka
Client feel Optimistic UI: animate the card away at once, send the request in the background, retry on failure
Duplicate requests (retries) Swipe is idempotent: same pair, same decision, same result. HSETNX matched guards duplicates
Redis shard failure Replica promoted by Redis Cluster; any pair state lost in the gap is rebuilt from the Kafka/Cassandra log, then re-check matches for those pairs
Hot user (very popular profile) Pair keys spread one user’s swipes across many shards, since the key includes the other person
Abuse (bots swiping right on everyone) Rate limit per user (for example 100 likes per 12 hours on free tier) at the gateway 
 swipe request
     |
     v
 Swipe Service --(1 ms Lua)--> Redis pair key  --> response to client
     |
     +--(async)--> Kafka "swipes" --> Cassandra writer
                                  --> Bloom updater
                                  --> Match reconciler (rechecks on failover)

9. Common mistakes and interviewer follow-ups

  • Write-then-read match check on an eventually consistent store. You will miss or duplicate matches under concurrency. Say: “pair key with both directions, checked atomically in one Lua script.”
  • Putting the whole swipe history into the search query as an exclude list. Queries balloon. Say: “bloom filter per user, filter after the geo query.”
  • Only checking my preferences, not theirs. You show people who would never like you back, and the like rate falls. Say: “preferences must match in both directions.”
  • Doing the geo query on every swipe. Wasteful. Precompute stacks and refill in the background below a threshold.
  • Synchronous Cassandra write on the swipe path. Adds latency. Write Redis on the hot path, stream to Cassandra via Kafka.
  • Follow-up: “What if a user travels to a new city?” Location updates on app open; invalidate the Stack Cache when the geohash prefix changes.
  • Follow-up: “How would you rank the stack?” Add a scoring step after filtering: recency of activity, mutual likelihood, a desirability score. Keep the pipeline the same.
  • Follow-up: “Why not one big Postgres?” 70k writes/s and 36 TB/year needs sharding anyway, and you would still need atomic pair handling. Redis plus Cassandra fits the access pattern better.

10. One-page cheat sheet

Topic Key point
Scale 20M DAU, 2B swipes/day, ~70k swipes/s peak, ~36 TB/year
Match correctness Pair key swipe:{lo}:{hi}, atomic Lua, HSETNX matched
Swipe latency Only Redis on hot path, rest async via Kafka, optimistic UI
Durable history Cassandra partitioned by swiper
Stack building Elasticsearch geo_distance + two-way preference filter
Stack serving Precomputed in Redis, refill below 20 left
No repeats Per-user bloom filter, ~18 KB for 10k items at 0.1% FP
Notifications Kafka match-created -> push via APNs / FCM
CAP AP for discovery, atomic per-pair for matches
Failover Rebuild pair state from Kafka/Cassandra log, re-check matches

09. LeetCode (Online Code Judge) (Medium)

LeetCode is a website where people solve coding problems. You read a problem, write code in the browser in a language like Python or Java, and submit it. The site runs your code against hidden test cases and tells you if it passed, how fast it ran, and how much memory it used. It also runs timed contests with a live leaderboard. The interviewer is really testing how you run untrusted code from strangers safely, how you run many test cases quickly, how you build a live leaderboard, and how you survive the traffic spike when 100,000 people start a contest at the same second.

1. Functional requirements

Core (must have):

  1. Users can view a list of problems and open one problem (statement, examples, code stub).
  2. Users can submit code in one of several languages and get a result: accepted, wrong answer, time limit exceeded, runtime error, or compile error.
  3. Users can join a coding contest and see a live leaderboard.

Below the line (out of scope):

  1. Discussion forums and solution posts. Standard CRUD, no new ideas.
  2. “Run” with custom input. It reuses the same execution path as submit with one test case.
  3. Problem authoring tools. Internal, low traffic.
  4. Plagiarism detection. A batch job after the contest.

2. Non-functional requirements

  1. Security: user code must never escape its sandbox, read other users’ code, reach the network, or harm the host. This is the top priority.
  2. Result latency: p95 under 5 seconds from submit to verdict outside contests; under 10 seconds during a contest peak.
  3. Leaderboard freshness: updated within a few seconds of an accepted submission.
  4. Scale: 100k contestants in one contest, each submitting about 20 times over 90 minutes, with a burst at the start and the end.
  5. Availability: 99.9% for browsing problems; submissions may be queued (delayed) under load, but never dropped.
  6. Fairness: the same code on the same tests should get the same verdict and similar timings, whichever worker runs it.
  7. CAP choice: availability for reading problems (AP, cached). For submissions, durability matters more than speed: accept the submission into a durable queue, then process. Leaderboard is eventually consistent.

3. Back-of-the-envelope estimates

Assumption Number
Contestants in a big contest 100,000
Submissions per contestant per contest 20
Contest length 90 minutes
Peak multiplier (first and last 10 min) 5x
Test cases per problem 100
Average CPU time per submission (all tests) 2 s
Submission size (code) 5 KB
Normal-day submissions 2M/day 
Contest submissions:
  100k * 20 = 2M submissions in 90 min = 5,400 s
  average = 2M / 5,400 ~= 370 submissions/s
  peak (x5) ~= 1,850 submissions/s

Worker CPU needed at peak:
  1,850 subs/s * 2 CPU-s = 3,700 CPU cores busy
  with containers using 1 core each, plus 30% headroom ~= 5,000 cores
  at 32 cores per machine ~= 160 machines (scale up only for contests)

Normal day:
  2M / 86,400 ~= 23 subs/s -> ~50 cores. Contest is ~100x normal load.

Storage:
  2M subs/day * 5 KB = 10 GB/day of code -> ~3.6 TB/year
  Problems: 3,000 problems * (statement + tests ~5 MB) = 15 GB

Leaderboard:
  100k entries in one Redis sorted set, ~100 bytes each = 10 MB

The key insight: execution is CPU-bound and contest traffic is about 100 times a normal day. So the design must queue work and autoscale workers, not try to keep 5,000 cores idle all week.

4. Core entities

  • Problem: a coding question. Fields: problem_id, title, statement, difficulty, time_limit_ms, memory_limit_mb, code_stubs per language.
  • TestCase: hidden input and expected output. Fields: problem_id, case_id, input_uri, expected_uri. Stored in blob storage, not the DB.
  • Submission: one attempt. Fields: submission_id, user_id, problem_id, contest_id, language, code, status, runtime_ms, memory_kb, created_at.
  • Contest: a timed event. Fields: contest_id, start_at, end_at, problem_ids.
  • LeaderboardEntry: a user’s contest standing. Fields: contest_id, user_id, score, penalty_minutes.
CREATE TABLE submissions (
  submission_id BIGINT PRIMARY KEY,
  user_id       BIGINT NOT NULL,
  problem_id    INT NOT NULL,
  contest_id    INT,
  language      TEXT NOT NULL,
  code          TEXT NOT NULL,
  status        TEXT NOT NULL DEFAULT 'queued',
  -- queued | running | accepted | wrong_answer | tle | mle | runtime_error
  -- | compile_error
  runtime_ms    INT,
  memory_kb     INT,
  created_at    TIMESTAMP NOT NULL DEFAULT now()
);
CREATE INDEX subs_by_user ON submissions (user_id, created_at DESC);
{
  "problem_id": 1,
  "title": "Two Sum",
  "time_limit_ms": 2000,
  "memory_limit_mb": 256,
  "tests_uri": "s3://judge-tests/1/v7/",
  "stubs": { "python3": "class Solution:\n    def twoSum(self, nums, target):" }
}

5. API design

GET /problems?page=1&difficulty=easy – list problems.

{ "items": [ { "problem_id": 1, "title": "Two Sum", "difficulty": "easy" } ] }

GET /problems/{problem_id} – one problem, with stubs. Public, heavily cached.

POST /problems/{problem_id}/submissions – submit code.

// request
{ "language": "python3", "code": "class Solution: ...", "contest_id": 412 }
// response 202 Accepted
{ "submission_id": "981234", "status": "queued" }

Status codes: 202 queued, 400 unsupported language or code over 64 KB, 401 not logged in, 403 contest not running, 429 too many submissions (for example more than 1 per 5 seconds).

GET /submissions/{submission_id} – poll for the result.

{ "submission_id": "981234", "status": "accepted",
  "runtime_ms": 48, "memory_kb": 16800, "passed": 100, "total": 100 }

Clients poll every 1 second, or use a WebSocket / Server-Sent Events stream for the result.

GET /contests/{contest_id}/leaderboard?offset=0&limit=50 – leaderboard page, plus my own rank.

{ "entries": [ { "rank": 1, "user": "alice", "score": 18, "penalty": 41 } ],
  "me": { "rank": 1532, "score": 11, "penalty": 70 } }

All write endpoints need a bearer token.

How will users view problems?

  1. Client calls GET /problems/1.
  2. The CDN or an in-memory cache answers almost every request, because problem statements rarely change.
  3. On a miss, Problem Service reads Postgres and fills the cache.
sequenceDiagram
    participant U as Client
    participant N as CDN
    participant P as ProblemService
    participant R as Cache
    participant D as Postgres
    U->>N: GET /problems/1
    alt CDN hit
        N-->>U: Cached problem page
    else CDN miss
        N->>P: Forward request
        P->>R: Lookup problem 1
        R-->>P: Miss
        P->>D: SELECT problem 1
        D-->>P: Problem row and stubs
        P->>R: Fill cache
        P-->>N: Problem JSON
        N-->>U: Problem page
    end

How will users submit code and get a result?

  1. Client sends POST /problems/1/submissions.
  2. Submission Service checks rate limits and contest window, writes a row with status queued, and puts a message {submission_id} on the queue.
  3. It returns 202 right away. The browser starts polling GET /submissions/{id}.
  4. A Judge Worker takes the message, loads the code and the problem’s test cases (cached locally), and runs the code in a sandbox against every test.
  5. The worker writes the verdict to the Submissions DB and publishes a submission-judged event.
  6. The next poll returns the verdict.

How will users see the contest leaderboard?

  1. On an accepted contest submission, the Leaderboard Service updates the user’s score in a Redis sorted set.
  2. GET /contests/412/leaderboard reads the top 50 and the caller’s own rank from Redis in two fast calls.

7. Deep dives

How do we run untrusted code safely?

The problem: anyone on the internet can submit code. It might try rm -rf /, open network sockets, fork-bomb (spawn processes until the machine dies), read other submissions, or allocate 100 GB of memory.

Option Isolation strength Start-up time Notes
Run directly on the worker None 0 Never do this
Docker container with hardening (recommended baseline) Good 100-500 ms (less with a warm pool) Shared kernel, so harden it
gVisor or Firecracker microVM (recommended for strongest) Very strong gVisor ~ms; Firecracker ~125 ms Separate kernel or user-space kernel
Full VM per submission Strongest Tens of seconds Too slow and costly

Recommended: a container per submission with layered limits, optionally running on gVisor (a user-space kernel that intercepts system calls) or inside a Firecracker microVM for defence in depth. Each layer stops a different attack:

Layer Stops
No network (--network none) Data theft, calling out to attackers
Read-only root filesystem, small tmpfs for scratch Tampering with the image, filling the disk
Non-root user, all Linux capabilities dropped Privilege escalation
seccomp profile (allow-list of system calls) Dangerous calls like mount, ptrace, reboot
cgroups: CPU, memory, pids limits Infinite loops, memory bombs, fork bombs
Wall-clock timeout, then kill Code that sleeps or blocks forever
One container per submission, destroyed after One user reading another’s leftovers 
docker run --rm \
  --network none \
  --read-only --tmpfs /tmp:rw,size=64m,noexec \
  --user 65534:65534 \
  --cap-drop ALL --security-opt no-new-privileges \
  --security-opt seccomp=/etc/judge/seccomp-python.json \
  --cpus 1 --memory 256m --memory-swap 256m --pids-limit 64 \
  --runtime runsc \
  -v /judge/sub-981234:/sandbox:ro \
  judge-python:3.12 \
  timeout --signal=KILL 3s python3 /sandbox/runner.py

--runtime runsc runs the container under gVisor. Measure CPU time from cgroup stats, not wall clock, so a busy host does not make honest code look slow.

How do we run many test cases quickly and fairly?

The problem: a problem has 100 tests. Starting a fresh container per test costs 100 times the start-up time. But the tests must not share state that lets one test cheat on another, and timing must be fair.

Option Speed Fairness / isolation Notes
New container per test case Slow Best 100 x 300 ms = 30 s overhead
One container per submission, loop over tests inside (recommended) Fast Good, still isolated from other users Stop on first failure
Split tests across many containers in parallel Fastest wall time Good More scheduling cost; use for huge suites

Recommended: one sandbox per submission. Inside it, a small trusted runner program (written by us, mounted read-only) compiles once, then feeds each test input, compares output, and stops at the first failure. Keep a warm pool of pre-started containers per language so start-up is near zero.

# runner.py, runs inside the sandbox. Test files are mounted read-only.
import json, resource, subprocess, time

def run_case(cmd, inp, limit_s):
    start = time.monotonic()
    p = subprocess.run(cmd, input=inp, capture_output=True,
                       timeout=limit_s, text=True)
    return p, time.monotonic() - start

def judge(cmd, cases, limit_s):
    worst = 0.0
    for i, (inp, expected) in enumerate(cases):
        try:
            p, t = run_case(cmd, inp, limit_s)
        except subprocess.TimeoutExpired:
            return {"status": "tle", "failed_case": i}
        if p.returncode != 0:
            return {"status": "runtime_error", "failed_case": i}
        if p.stdout.split() != expected.split():   # ignore whitespace
            return {"status": "wrong_answer", "failed_case": i}
        worst = max(worst, t)
    peak_kb = resource.getrusage(resource.RUSAGE_CHILDREN).ru_maxrss
    return {"status": "accepted", "runtime_ms": int(worst * 1000),
            "memory_kb": peak_kb, "passed": len(cases)}

Other practical points:

  • Cache test cases on each worker’s local disk, keyed by problem_id and a version. They are downloaded once from S3, not per submission.
  • Use one CPU core per sandbox and do not overcommit, or timings get noisy and unfair.
  • For problems with many valid answers (any order, floating point), use a per-problem checker program instead of exact string compare.

How does the contest leaderboard work?

The problem: 100k users, scores change every few seconds near the end, and everybody refreshes the leaderboard. We need top N and “my rank” fast.

Option Top N My rank Notes
SQL ORDER BY score DESC on each request Slow under load COUNT(*) WHERE score > mine, slow Fine for 1k users, not 100k
Precompute every minute in a batch job Fast but stale Fast 1 minute stale feels wrong in a contest
Redis sorted set (recommended) ZREVRANGE, O(log n + k) ZREVRANK, O(log n) 10 MB in RAM per contest

Recommended: one Redis sorted set per contest. A sorted set keeps members ordered by a numeric score. LeetCode ranks by problems solved (higher better), then by penalty time (lower better). Pack both into one number so a single sort works:

BIG = 10**7   # larger than any penalty in seconds

def packed_score(solved, penalty_seconds):
    # More solved wins; for equal solved, lower penalty wins.
    return solved * BIG - penalty_seconds

def on_accepted(contest_id, user_id, solved, penalty_seconds):
    redis.zadd(f"lb:{contest_id}", {user_id: packed_score(solved, penalty_seconds)})

def leaderboard_page(contest_id, offset, limit, me):
    key = f"lb:{contest_id}"
    pipe = redis.pipeline()
    pipe.zrevrange(key, offset, offset + limit - 1, withscores=True)
    pipe.zrevrank(key, me)
    pipe.zscore(key, me)
    top, my_rank, my_score = pipe.execute()
    return top, (None if my_rank is None else my_rank + 1), my_score

Only update the sorted set on the first accepted submission per problem per user (track solved problems in a small Redis hash), so resubmits do not change the score. Cache the top-50 page for 2 seconds; most refreshes then hit that tiny cache instead of Redis. Postgres stays the source of truth; Redis can be rebuilt from accepted submissions if lost.

How do we handle the contest start spike?

The problem: at 10:00:00, 100k people open the problems at once, and by 10:05 a wave of submissions arrives. Normal capacity is about 1% of what we need.

Option Cost Risk
Keep peak capacity always running Very high (5,000 idle cores) Low
Pure reactive autoscaling Low Scaling takes minutes; queue grows during the lag
Scheduled pre-warm plus queue-depth autoscaling plus backpressure (recommended) Medium Low

Recommended, in three parts:

  1. Pre-warm: contests are scheduled, so 30 minutes before start, scale judge workers to the expected peak and pre-pull language images. Pre-load problem statements into the CDN (publish them at start time with a signed URL so they do not leak early).
  2. Queue as a buffer: submissions go into a durable queue (SQS or Kafka). If workers fall behind, users wait a bit longer, but nothing is dropped and the API stays up.
  3. Autoscale on queue depth: add workers when the backlog per worker passes a threshold. Add per-user rate limits (one submission in flight per user) so a few people cannot flood the queue.
# Kubernetes KEDA scaler: scale judge pods on SQS backlog
apiVersion: keda.sh/v1alpha1
kind: ScaledObject
metadata: { name: judge-python }
spec:
  scaleTargetRef: { name: judge-python }
  minReplicaCount: 20
  maxReplicaCount: 3000
  triggers:
    - type: aws-sqs-queue
      metadata:
        queueURL: https://sqs.us-east-1.amazonaws.com/123/judge-python
        queueLength: "5"        # target 5 queued subs per pod

Use one queue per language, so a slow Java compile wave does not delay Python users, and a separate priority queue for contest submissions over practice ones.

How do we make the submission queue reliable?

The problem: a worker can crash mid-judge, a sandbox can hang, or the same message can be delivered twice.

Failure Mitigation
Worker crashes during judging Visibility timeout (SQS) or uncommitted offset (Kafka): message reappears and another worker picks it up
Same submission judged twice Make the result write idempotent: UPDATE ... WHERE submission_id = ? AND status IN ('queued','running')
Poison submission that crashes every worker Max receive count of 3, then move to a dead letter queue and mark “internal error”
Sandbox hangs past timeout Outer watchdog kills the container by cgroup; worker reports TLE
Judge bug gives wrong verdicts Code and test versions are stored with each submission, so we can rejudge later 
-- Idempotent verdict write: a duplicate or late worker does nothing.
UPDATE submissions
SET status = :verdict, runtime_ms = :rt, memory_kb = :mem
WHERE submission_id = :id AND status IN ('queued', 'running');

9. Common mistakes and interviewer follow-ups

  • Running code with only a timeout. Code can still hit the network, fork-bomb, or read files. Say: “container, no network, seccomp, cgroups, non-root, read-only FS, destroyed after.”
  • Judging synchronously inside the HTTP request. A spike ties up web servers and requests time out. Say: “202 plus queue plus poll or SSE.”
  • A new container for every test case. Start-up time dominates. Say: “one sandbox per submission, loop tests inside, warm pool.”
  • Leaderboard computed with SQL per request. Falls over at 100k users. Say: “Redis sorted set, packed score for tie-breaks.”
  • Reactive autoscaling only. Workers arrive after the spike. Say: “contests are scheduled, so pre-warm, then autoscale on queue depth.”
  • Measuring wall-clock time for runtime. Noisy neighbours make honest code look slow. Measure CPU time and pin one core per sandbox.
  • Follow-up: “How do you support a new language?” Build a new judge image with its compiler and a seccomp profile, add a queue and a scaler. Nothing else changes.
  • Follow-up: “How do you stop test cases leaking?” Tests never leave the sandbox host, the sandbox has no network, and failed-case output shown to users is truncated.

10. One-page cheat sheet

Topic Key point
Contest load 2M subs in 90 min, ~1,850 subs/s peak, ~5,000 cores
Normal load ~23 subs/s, so contest is ~100x normal
Submit flow 202 Accepted -> queue -> worker -> DB -> poll or SSE
Sandbox Container + gVisor, no network, seccomp, cgroups, read-only, non-root
Limits 1 CPU, 256 MB, 64 pids, hard kill after time limit
Test running One sandbox per submission, loop tests, stop at first fail
Speed Warm container pool, tests cached on worker disk
Leaderboard Redis ZSET, score = solved * 10^7 - penalty
Spike Pre-warm before start, autoscale on queue depth, per-language queues
Reliability Visibility timeout, idempotent verdict write, DLQ after 3 tries
CAP AP for reading problems, durable queue for submissions

10. WhatsApp (1:1 and Group Chat) (Medium)

WhatsApp is a messaging app. You can send text and media to one person or to a group of up to about 1,000 people. Messages arrive in real time when the other person is online, and are waiting for them when they come back online. You see one tick when a message is sent, two ticks when it is delivered, and blue ticks when it is read. The interviewer is really testing how you keep millions of live connections open, how you route a message to the right server, how you make sure no message is lost when someone is offline, and how you fan out a message to a group.

1. Functional requirements

Core (must have):

  1. Users can send and receive 1:1 messages in real time.
  2. Users can create a group chat and send messages to all members.
  3. Users who were offline receive all missed messages when they reconnect.
  4. Users see delivery and read receipts.
  5. Users can send media (photos, videos, files).

Below the line (out of scope):

  1. Voice and video calls. Real-time media (WebRTC) is a different system.
  2. Status / stories. Ephemeral broadcast content.
  3. Contact discovery from the phone book. A hashing and lookup problem on its own.
  4. Full end-to-end encryption protocol details. We note how it affects the design but do not design the Signal protocol.

2. Non-functional requirements

  1. Low latency: p99 under 500 ms from send to delivery when both users are online.
  2. Guaranteed delivery: a message accepted by the server is never lost, and is delivered at least once. The client removes duplicates, so the user sees it exactly once.
  3. Ordering: messages within one chat appear in the order they were sent.
  4. Scale: 2B users, 500M concurrently connected, 100B messages per day.
  5. Availability: 99.99% for sending. Prefer accepting a message and delivering slightly later over refusing it.
  6. Storage: the server is a relay, not an archive. Messages are deleted from the server after delivery (or after 30 days undelivered). History lives on devices.
  7. CAP choice: AP for delivery (keep accepting messages during partitions), with per-chat ordering provided by a sequence number from a single owner per chat.

3. Back-of-the-envelope estimates

Assumption Number
Daily active users 1B
Concurrent connections at peak 500M
Messages per day 100B
Average message size (text + metadata) 200 bytes
Share of messages to groups 30%
Average group size 20
Connections per chat server 1M (tuned, epoll)
Media messages 5% of messages, 200 KB average 
Message rate:
  100B / 86,400 s ~= 1.16M messages/s average, peak (x2) ~= 2.3M/s

Deliveries (group fan-out):
  70B 1:1 deliveries + 30B group msgs * 20 members = 670B deliveries/day
  ~= 7.8M deliveries/s average

Chat servers:
  500M connections / 1M per server = 500 servers (+50% headroom ~= 750)

Inbox storage (undelivered messages only):
  assume 10% sit undelivered for 1 day on average
  100B * 0.1 * 200 B = 2 TB live in the inbox at any time

Media:
  100B * 5% * 200 KB = 1 PB/day uploaded to blob storage
  (kept 30 days on server -> ~30 PB, served via CDN)

Bandwidth for text:
  7.8M deliveries/s * 200 B ~= 1.6 GB/s

The key insights: connections, not storage, dominate the server count, and media is huge, so it must never pass through chat servers.

4. Core entities

  • User: user_id, phone, public_key, last_seen.
  • Device / Client: one phone or laptop with its own connection. device_id, user_id, push_token.
  • Chat: a 1:1 conversation or group. chat_id, type, created_at.
  • ChatParticipant: membership. chat_id, user_id, role.
  • Message: message_id, chat_id, sender_id, seq, body (encrypted), media_url, created_at.
  • Inbox entry: a message waiting for one device. device_id, message_id.
  • Receipt: message_id, user_id, status (delivered or read), at.
-- Cassandra / DynamoDB style tables.
CREATE TABLE inbox (
  device_id  bigint,
  message_id timeuuid,        -- time ordered
  chat_id    bigint,
  sender_id  bigint,
  payload    blob,            -- encrypted body or media pointer
  PRIMARY KEY ((device_id), message_id)
) WITH default_time_to_live = 2592000;   -- 30 days

CREATE TABLE chat_participants (
  chat_id bigint,
  user_id bigint,
  role    text,
  PRIMARY KEY ((chat_id), user_id)
);
{
  "type": "message",
  "client_msg_id": "c-7f3a",
  "chat_id": 9001,
  "body": "<ciphertext base64>",
  "media": null
}

client_msg_id is made by the sender’s phone. It lets the server and the receiver drop duplicates when the phone retries.

5. API design

Chat uses one long-lived WebSocket per device, because the server must push messages to the client. A WebSocket is a two-way connection that stays open over a single TCP socket. REST is used only for setup and media.

WS /ws – open a connection (auth token in the first frame or header).

Client to server frames:

{ "type": "send", "client_msg_id": "c-7f3a", "chat_id": 9001, "body": "..." }
{ "type": "ack",  "message_ids": ["m-1", "m-2"] }
{ "type": "read", "chat_id": 9001, "up_to_seq": 512 }

Server to client frames:

{ "type": "sent",     "client_msg_id": "c-7f3a", "message_id": "m-9", "seq": 513 }
{ "type": "message",  "message_id": "m-9", "chat_id": 9001, "sender": 42,
  "seq": 513, "body": "..." }
{ "type": "receipt",  "message_id": "m-9", "status": "read", "by": 77 }

POST /chats – create a group.

// request
{ "name": "Family", "members": [42, 77, 88] }
// response 201
{ "chat_id": 9001 }

POST /chats/{chat_id}/members and DELETE /chats/{chat_id}/members/{user_id} – manage group members. Status codes 200, 403 not an admin, 404 not found.

POST /media/upload-url – get a presigned upload URL.

// request
{ "content_type": "image/jpeg", "size": 2400000 }
// response 200
{ "upload_url": "https://media.s3.../abc?X-Amz-Signature=...",
  "media_id": "abc", "expires_in": 600 }

All endpoints require a device auth token.
