How will users send a 1:1 message?

  1. Phone A sends a send frame over its WebSocket to Chat Server 1.
  2. Chat Server 1 assigns a message_id and the next seq for this chat, and writes the message to B’s inbox in Cassandra. This write is what makes it durable.
  3. It sends sent back to A (one tick).
  4. It looks up B’s device in the Chat Registry: “B is on Chat Server 2.”
  5. It publishes the message to Chat Server 2’s channel. Chat Server 2 pushes it down B’s WebSocket.
  6. B’s phone replies with ack. Chat Server 2 deletes the inbox entry and sends a delivered receipt back to A (two ticks).
sequenceDiagram
    participant A as PhoneA
    participant S as ChatServerOne
    participant I as Inbox
    participant R as Registry
    participant T as ChatServerTwo
    participant B as PhoneB
    A->>S: send frame
    S->>I: Write inbox entry for B
    I-->>S: ok
    S-->>A: sent one tick
    S->>R: Lookup B device
    R-->>S: ChatServerTwo
    S->>T: Publish to server channel
    T->>B: message frame
    B-->>T: ack
    T->>I: Delete inbox entry
    T-->>A: delivered receipt two ticks

How will users receive messages sent while they were offline?

  1. While B is offline, step 4 finds no live connection. The message stays in B’s inbox, and a push notification is sent through APNs or FCM.
  2. When B reconnects, the chat server registers B in the registry, then reads B’s inbox in message_id order and streams it down.
  3. B acks in batches; acked entries are deleted.

How will users send a group message?

  1. A sends to chat_id 9001.
  2. The chat server asks the Group Service for the member list (cached).
  3. It writes one inbox entry per member device, then routes to each online member’s chat server (see deep dive).

How will users see delivery and read receipts?

  1. Receipts are just small messages flowing the other way: B’s device sends ack (delivered) and read.
  2. They are routed back to A the same way as a message, and stored in A’s inbox if A is offline.

How will users send media?

  1. A asks for a presigned upload URL and uploads the file directly to blob storage.
  2. A sends a normal message whose payload contains the media_id (and the encryption key, inside the encrypted body).
  3. B downloads the file directly from the CDN.

7. Deep dives

How do we manage millions of WebSocket connections and route to the right server?

The problem: 500M devices are each connected to one of about 750 chat servers. When A on server 1 messages B, server 1 needs to find B’s server fast, and connections drop and move all the time.

Option How Trade-off
Broadcast to all servers Every server checks if it holds B 750x wasted work, does not scale
Consistent hash user to server Load balancer sends B always to one server Rebalancing moves many users, hot servers
Central registry plus pub/sub (recommended) Redis map device -> server, per-server channel One extra lookup, registry must be highly available

Recommended: a Chat Registry. When a device connects, its server writes conn:{device_id} = server_id with a short TTL, and refreshes it with each heartbeat (a small ping every 30 seconds). To deliver, look up the server and publish to that server’s channel. Each chat server subscribes to its own channel only.

HEARTBEAT_TTL = 90  # seconds, 3 missed pings = gone

def on_connect(device_id, ws):
    local_conns[device_id] = ws
    redis.set(f"conn:{device_id}", SERVER_ID, ex=HEARTBEAT_TTL)
    drain_inbox(device_id, ws)

def on_heartbeat(device_id):
    redis.expire(f"conn:{device_id}", HEARTBEAT_TTL)

def on_disconnect(device_id):
    local_conns.pop(device_id, None)
    # Only delete if it still points at us (device may have reconnected elsewhere).
    redis.eval("if redis.call('GET',KEYS[1])==ARGV[1] then "
               "return redis.call('DEL',KEYS[1]) end return 0",
               1, f"conn:{device_id}", SERVER_ID)

def deliver(device_id, msg):
    server = redis.get(f"conn:{device_id}")
    if server is None:
        push_notify(device_id, msg)       # offline; inbox already has it
    else:
        redis.publish(f"server:{server.decode()}", json.dumps(
            {"device_id": device_id, "msg": msg}))

Tuning tips worth saying: use an event loop (epoll / Erlang VM; WhatsApp famously ran on Erlang with very high connections per box), small per-connection buffers, and an L4 (TCP) load balancer so sockets are not terminated twice. When deploying, drain servers slowly so clients reconnect in waves, not all at once.

How do we guarantee delivery when the user is offline?

The problem: the receiver may be offline, the network may drop the frame, or a chat server may crash after accepting a message. The message must still arrive, exactly once from the user’s point of view.

Option Durability Cost Notes
Keep undelivered messages in chat server memory Lost on crash Cheap Not acceptable
Store every message forever in a chat history DB Durable Huge storage Not needed; WhatsApp keeps history on devices
Per-device inbox, delete on ack (recommended) Durable until delivered ~2 TB live Simple, matches “relay” model

Recommended: write to the inbox before acknowledging the sender. Deliver at least once, and let the receiver drop duplicates by message_id.

 A          Chat Srv 1        Inbox (Cassandra)     Chat Srv 2        B
 |--send---->|                     |                    |             |
 |           |---write entry------>|                    |             |
 |<--sent----| (1 tick, durable)   |                    |             |
 |           |---publish------------------------------->|---message-->|
 |           |                     |                    |<----ack-----|
 |           |                     |<---delete entry----|             |
 |<-----------------delivered receipt (2 ticks)---------|             |

Rules that make it correct:

  • The sender keeps the message in its local outbox until it gets sent. On reconnect it resends with the same client_msg_id; the server checks a short-lived dedupe cache and returns the original message_id.
  • The receiver keeps a set of recent message_ids and ignores repeats.
  • Inbox rows have a 30-day TTL, so a phone that never comes back does not keep data forever.
  • Ordering inside a chat uses seq. The receiver shows messages sorted by seq, and can ask for a gap to be resent.

How do we fan out group messages?

The problem: a message to a 1,000-member group means 1,000 inbox writes and up to 1,000 routed deliveries. With 30B group messages a day, fan-out is most of our write load.

Option Write cost Read cost Notes
Fan-out on write to each member’s inbox (recommended for groups up to ~1k) N writes 1 read per device Simple; matches the 1:1 path
Store once per group, members pull 1 write Each device must check every group Complex offline sync and receipts
Hybrid for very large broadcast channels Store once, pull Fine for read-mostly channels Use for “channels” with 100k+ followers

Recommended: fan-out on write, because WhatsApp caps group size (about 1,024), so the worst case is bounded. Do it asynchronously so the sender gets sent after one durable write:

  1. Write the message once to a group_messages log (Kafka topic partitioned by chat_id, which also keeps per-group order).
  2. Return sent to the sender.
  3. Fan-out workers read the log, write one inbox entry per member device, and route to online members, grouping deliveries by destination chat server so one publish carries many devices.
def fanout_group_message(msg):
    members = group_cache.members(msg["chat_id"])   # ~20 avg, <= 1024
    by_server = defaultdict(list)
    batch = cassandra_batch()
    for device_id in devices_of(members):
        if device_id == msg["sender_device"]:
            continue
        batch.insert_inbox(device_id, msg)
        server = registry.get(device_id)
        if server:
            by_server[server].append(device_id)
        else:
            push_queue.put(device_id, msg)
    batch.execute()
    for server, devices in by_server.items():
        pubsub.publish(f"server:{server}", {"devices": devices, "msg": msg})

With end-to-end encryption, the sender actually encrypts the message key for each member (Signal “sender keys” make this cheap for groups), but the server’s fan-out shape is the same.

How do delivery and read receipts work at scale?

The problem: every message creates up to two receipts per recipient. In a 500-member group that is 1,000 receipts for one message. Receipts can overwhelm the system if treated like full messages.

Option Volume Notes
One receipt per message per recipient Highest Simple but noisy
Cumulative “read up to seq N” per chat (recommended) One per chat open Matches how people read
Batch acks every few hundred ms (recommended) Lower Small delay, big saving

Recommended: receipts are cumulative and batched. When B opens the chat, B sends one read up_to_seq 512 frame, which covers all earlier messages. Delivered acks are batched every 200 ms. For large groups, the sender’s phone stores per-member state but the server sends aggregated receipts, and only on demand (“message info” screen) shows the full list. Receipts are best-effort: if one is lost, the next cumulative receipt fixes the state.

How do we send media without overloading chat servers?

The problem: media is about 1 PB a day. If 200 KB files flow through WebSocket servers, those servers become bandwidth bottlenecks and their connection count collapses.

Option Chat server load Notes
Send bytes over the WebSocket Very high Blocks other messages on the same socket
Upload to our API servers, then to storage High Double hop
Presigned URL straight to blob storage, CDN for download (recommended) None Chat message carries only a pointer

A presigned URL is a temporary URL signed by the server that lets the client upload one object directly to S3 for a few minutes, without having storage credentials.

def create_upload_url(user_id, content_type, size):
    if size > 2 * 1024**3:
        raise ValueError("file too large")
    media_id = uuid4().hex
    url = s3.generate_presigned_url(
        "put_object",
        Params={"Bucket": "wa-media", "Key": f"{media_id}",
                "ContentType": content_type},
        ExpiresIn=600)
    return {"upload_url": url, "media_id": media_id}

With end-to-end encryption, the phone encrypts the file with a random key before upload. The server stores only ciphertext, and the key travels inside the encrypted chat message. Set a lifecycle rule on the bucket to delete objects after 30 days.

What about end-to-end encryption and failures?

End-to-end encryption (E2E) means only the sender and receiver devices can read the message. WhatsApp uses the Signal protocol. Effects on our design:

  • The server cannot read, search, or filter content. It routes opaque blobs.
  • Each device has its own keys, so a message to a user with a phone and a laptop is encrypted and delivered once per device. This is why the inbox is per device, not per user.
  • The server stores public keys (a key directory) so senders can start a session with a new contact.
Failure Mitigation
Chat server crashes Clients reconnect to another server via the load balancer; registry entry expires or is overwritten; inbox replays anything not acked
Registry (Redis) node fails Replicas; on miss, treat device as offline: message is still in the inbox and a push is sent
Cassandra replica down Write with quorum across 3 replicas; one node loss is invisible
Push provider slow Push is best-effort; the inbox is the source of truth
Network flapping on phone Exponential backoff with jitter on reconnect to avoid a thundering herd

9. Common mistakes and interviewer follow-ups

  • Sending messages through REST polling. Wastes battery and adds seconds of latency. Say: “one WebSocket per device, push from server, push notification when offline.”
  • Acknowledging the sender before the message is durable. A crash loses it. Say: “write to the inbox first, then send the single tick.”
  • Broadcasting every message to every chat server. Does not scale past a few servers. Say: “registry lookup plus per-server pub/sub channel.”
  • Inbox per user instead of per device. With multiple devices and E2E keys, one device would steal the others’ messages. Say: “inbox per device.”
  • Pushing media through chat servers. Kills their bandwidth. Say: “presigned upload to S3, pointer in the message, CDN download.”
  • Expecting exactly-once from the network. Say: “at-least-once delivery plus dedupe by client_msg_id and message_id.”
  • Follow-up: “How do you keep message order?” Per-chat seq assigned by one owner (the Kafka partition for the chat, or a per-chat counter), and the client sorts by seq.
  • Follow-up: “What about last seen / online status?” Derived from the registry and heartbeats; send presence only to contacts who have the chat open, to avoid a storm of updates.

10. One-page cheat sheet

Topic Key point
Scale 100B msgs/day, ~2.3M msgs/s peak, 500M live connections
Servers ~1M connections per chat server, ~750 servers
Transport WebSocket per device, heartbeat every 30 s
Routing Redis registry conn:{device} with TTL + per-server pub/sub
Durability Write per-device inbox before ack, delete on receiver ack
Delivery semantics At-least-once, dedupe by client_msg_id / message_id
Ordering Per-chat seq number
Groups Fan-out on write via Kafka (cap ~1k members)
Receipts Cumulative “read up to seq”, batched acks
Media Presigned S3 URL, CDN, client-side encrypted, 30-day TTL
E2E Server sees ciphertext only, keys per device
CAP AP: accept and store, deliver when possible

11. Strava (Activity Tracking with GPS) (Medium)

Strava is an app for runners and cyclists. You press start, go for a run or ride, and the phone records your GPS position every second or so. When you finish, the app shows your route on a map, your distance, pace, and elevation, and shares the activity with your friends. You can see friends’ activities in a feed and compare times on popular stretches of road on leaderboards. The interviewer is really testing how you collect location data on a phone that may have no signal, how you store billions of GPS points efficiently, how you compute stats and leaderboards, and how you let friends follow you live.

1. Functional requirements

Core (must have):

  1. Users can start, pause, resume, and stop recording an activity (run or ride).
  2. While recording, users see live stats: elapsed time, distance, current pace.
  3. Users can save an activity and view it later with its route on a map and summary stats.
  4. Users can see a feed of their friends’ recent activities.
  5. Users can share their activity in real time so selected friends can follow along live.

Below the line (out of scope):

  1. Segments with full leaderboards for every stretch of road. We cover a simplified leaderboard, since full segment matching is a geometry project.
  2. Training plans, social clubs, challenges. Product features on top of the same data.
  3. Wearable device sync (Garmin, Apple Watch). Same upload path, different client.
  4. Routing and route suggestions. A maps problem.

2. Non-functional requirements

  1. Offline first: recording must work with no network for hours, with no data loss. The phone is the source of truth during an activity.
  2. Low battery use: sample GPS at about 1 point per second and batch network uploads.
  3. Live tracking latency: friends see a position within 10 seconds when the athlete has signal.
  4. Upload processing: a finished activity’s stats and map are ready within 30 seconds of upload.
  5. Scale: 10M daily active users, 10M activities per day, peak on weekend mornings.
  6. Availability: 99.9% for upload and viewing. An upload that fails must be retried safely (idempotent).
  7. Consistency: eventual for feeds and leaderboards (seconds to a minute is fine). Strong for “my activity was saved”.
  8. CAP choice: AP. Accept uploads and show slightly stale feeds rather than fail.

3. Back-of-the-envelope estimates

Assumption Number
Daily active users 10M
Activities per day 10M
Average activity length 1 hour
GPS sample rate 1 point per second
Raw point size (lat, lng, ele, time, accuracy) ~32 bytes
Compressed point size (delta + varint) ~6 bytes
Feed views per user per day 5
Users live sharing at peak 1% of 2M concurrent = 20k 
GPS points:
  1 hour * 3,600 points = 3,600 points per activity
  10M activities * 3,600 = 36B points/day

Raw storage:
  36B * 32 B ~= 1.15 TB/day -> ~420 TB/year

Compressed storage:
  36B * 6 B ~= 216 GB/day -> ~80 TB/year (about 5x smaller)

Activity uploads:
  10M / 86,400 ~= 115 uploads/s average
  weekend morning peak (x5) ~= 600 uploads/s
  each upload ~ 3,600 * 6 B ~= 22 KB compressed

Feed reads:
  10M * 5 = 50M/day ~= 580 reads/s, peak ~= 3,000/s

Live tracking:
  20k live athletes, 1 batch every 5 s = 4,000 location writes/s
  each viewed by ~3 friends = 12,000 pushes/s

The key insight: GPS points are the bulk of the data, and compressing them gives a 5x saving. Uploads themselves are not high QPS, so the hard parts are offline capture, storage format, and fan-out.

4. Core entities

  • User / Athlete: user_id, name, privacy settings.
  • Friendship / Follow: follower_id, followee_id.
  • Activity: one run or ride. activity_id, user_id, type, start_time, duration_s, distance_m, elevation_gain_m, avg_pace, route_uri, polyline (small simplified route for maps).
  • Route / Track: the full list of GPS points for an activity, stored as a compressed blob.
  • Live session: an in-progress shared activity. session_id, user_id, last_point, viewers.
  • Leaderboard entry: best time per user per segment or per weekly distance.
CREATE TABLE activities (
  activity_id      BIGINT PRIMARY KEY,
  user_id          BIGINT NOT NULL,
  client_id        UUID NOT NULL,          -- made on phone, for idempotency
  type             TEXT NOT NULL,          -- run | ride
  start_time       TIMESTAMPTZ NOT NULL,
  duration_s       INT,
  distance_m       INT,
  elevation_gain_m INT,
  polyline         TEXT,                   -- simplified route, ~1-2 KB
  route_uri        TEXT,                   -- s3://tracks/...
  UNIQUE (user_id, client_id)
);
CREATE INDEX activities_by_user ON activities (user_id, start_time DESC);
{
  "client_id": "5f1c...",
  "type": "run",
  "points": [
    { "t": 1730620800, "lat": 37.77490, "lng": -122.41940, "ele": 16.2 },
    { "t": 1730620801, "lat": 37.77492, "lng": -122.41936, "ele": 16.3 }
  ]
}

5. API design

POST /activities – upload a finished activity (sent as a compressed file).

// request: multipart with metadata + gzip or FIT/GPX file
{ "client_id": "5f1c...", "type": "run", "start_time": "2026-11-01T07:00:00Z" }
// response 202
{ "activity_id": "88812", "status": "processing" }

Status codes: 202 accepted, 200 if the same client_id was already uploaded (returns the existing ID), 400 bad file, 413 too large.

GET /activities/{activity_id} – view an activity: stats, polyline, splits.

{ "activity_id": "88812", "type": "run", "distance_m": 10012,
  "duration_s": 2950, "avg_pace_s_per_km": 295,
  "polyline": "a~l~Fjk~uOwHJy@P", "splits": [298, 294, 293] }

GET /feed?cursor=... – friends’ recent activities, newest first, cursor paginated.

POST /live-sessions – start sharing live. Returns session_id. POST /live-sessions/{session_id}/points – send a batch of recent points.

{ "points": [ { "t": 1730620805, "lat": 37.7750, "lng": -122.4190 } ] }

GET /live-sessions/{session_id}/stream – Server-Sent Events (a one-way stream from server to browser over HTTP) of positions for an allowed viewer.

All endpoints need a bearer token. Live viewers must be on the athlete’s allow list.

How will users record an activity?

  1. User presses start. The app turns on GPS at 1 Hz and writes every point to a local database on the phone (SQLite).
  2. The app computes live stats on the phone from those points: elapsed time, distance, pace. No server is involved, so it works with no signal.
  3. Pause and resume just write marker events into the same local log.
sequenceDiagram
    participant U as User
    participant A as PhoneApp
    participant G as GPS
    participant D as SQLite
    U->>A: Press start
    A->>G: Enable GPS at 1 Hz
    loop every second
        G-->>A: Position fix
        A->>D: Append point in small batch
        A-->>U: Live time distance pace
    end
    U->>A: Press pause
    A->>D: Write pause marker
    U->>A: Press resume
    A->>D: Write resume marker
    U->>A: Press stop
    A->>G: Disable GPS

How will users save and view an activity?

  1. On stop, the app compresses the points and calls POST /activities with a client_id it generated at start.
  2. Activity Service stores the raw file in S3, creates an activities row with status processing, and emits an event.
  3. Processing workers parse the file, clean noisy points, compute distance, elevation gain, splits, and a simplified polyline, then update the row.
  4. When the user opens the activity, GET /activities/{id} returns stats and the polyline from Postgres; the map draws the polyline.

How will users see their friends’ activities?

  1. When processing finishes, an activity-done event goes to Kafka.
  2. A feed fan-out worker adds the activity ID to each follower’s feed list in Redis (most athletes have few followers; pros are pulled at read time).
  3. GET /feed reads the list, hydrates activity summaries, and returns a page with a cursor.

How will users share an activity live?

  1. The athlete starts a live session. Every 5 seconds, when there is signal, the app posts a small batch of points.
  2. Live Service stores the latest point in Redis and publishes to the session’s channel.
  3. Friends watching hold an SSE connection to a Live Service node subscribed to that channel and receive positions as they arrive.

7. Deep dives

How do we record reliably when the phone is offline?

The problem: runners go through tunnels, forests, and mountains. The network can be gone for the whole activity. The app may also be killed by the OS to save memory, or the phone may die.

Option Data safety Battery Notes
Stream every point to the server Lost with no signal Poor, radio always on Not acceptable
Keep points in memory, upload at end Lost if app is killed Good Risky
Write-ahead to local DB, upload on finish with retries (recommended) Survives kill and reboot Good The phone is the source of truth

Recommended: append each point to a local SQLite table in small transactions (every 5-10 points), so a crash loses at most a few seconds. Upload when finished, and keep the local copy until the server confirms. The client_id makes retries safe: uploading twice returns the same activity.

# Pseudocode for the phone-side recorder and upload queue.
def on_gps_fix(fix):
    if fix.accuracy_m > 30:
        return                          # drop very noisy fixes
    buffer.append((fix.t, fix.lat, fix.lng, fix.ele))
    if len(buffer) >= 10:
        db.executemany("INSERT INTO points VALUES (?,?,?,?,?)",
                       [(activity_id, *p) for p in buffer])
        db.commit()
        buffer.clear()

def upload_pending():
    for act in db.query("SELECT * FROM activities WHERE uploaded = 0"):
        try:
            resp = api.post("/activities", client_id=act.client_id,
                            file=compress(load_points(act.id)))
            if resp.status in (200, 202):
                db.execute("UPDATE activities SET uploaded=1 WHERE id=?",
                           (act.id,))
        except NetworkError:
            schedule_retry(backoff_with_jitter())

On the server, idempotency is a unique constraint:

INSERT INTO activities (activity_id, user_id, client_id, type, start_time)
VALUES (:id, :uid, :cid, :type, :start)
ON CONFLICT (user_id, client_id) DO NOTHING
RETURNING activity_id;

If nothing is returned, look up and return the existing ID with 200.

How do we store GPS routes efficiently?

The problem: 36B points a day. Storing each point as a database row would mean 36B rows a day and very slow queries. And most screens only need a rough shape of the route.

Option Size per activity Query pattern Notes
One DB row per point ~3,600 rows, ~200 KB with indexes Slow, huge tables Avoid
Time-series DB (TimescaleDB, InfluxDB) Medium Good for range queries Overkill: we read a route as a whole
Compressed blob in S3 + simplified polyline in DB (recommended) ~22 KB blob + ~1.5 KB polyline Read whole route at once Cheap, simple

Recommended: two forms of each route.

  1. Full track: delta-encode points (store the difference from the previous point, which is tiny), pack as variable-length integers, gzip, and store in S3. About 6 bytes per point.
  2. Display polyline: simplify the route with the Ramer-Douglas-Peucker algorithm (drop points that lie almost on a straight line), then encode with the Google polyline format. A 3,600 point run becomes about 200-400 points, about 1.5 KB, stored directly in the activities row. Map screens and feed cards only ever load this.
def delta_encode(points, scale=1e5):
    # points: list of (t, lat, lng). Returns small ints, easy to compress.
    out, prev = [], (0, 0, 0)
    for t, lat, lng in points:
        cur = (int(t), round(lat * scale), round(lng * scale))
        out.append(tuple(c - p for c, p in zip(cur, prev)))
        prev = cur
    return out   # mostly values like (1, 2, -3) -> 1 byte each as varints

def rdp(points, eps):
    # Ramer-Douglas-Peucker: keep points that bend the line more than eps.
    if len(points) < 3:
        return points
    a, b = points[0], points[-1]
    idx, dmax = 0, 0.0
    for i in range(1, len(points) - 1):
        d = perpendicular_distance(points[i], a, b)
        if d > dmax:
            idx, dmax = i, d
    if dmax <= eps:
        return [a, b]
    return rdp(points[:idx + 1], eps)[:-1] + rdp(points[idx:], eps)

Move tracks older than a year to a cheaper storage class (S3 Infrequent Access or Glacier Instant Retrieval). Users rarely reopen old runs.

How do we compute activity stats and leaderboards?

The problem: raw GPS is noisy. A naive sum of distances between points overstates distance by several percent because the points jitter. Leaderboards must be correct and fast to read.

Stats pipeline in the processing worker:

  1. Filter points with bad accuracy and impossible speeds (for example, a run faster than 12 m/s).
  2. Smooth with a small moving average or Kalman filter (a filter that blends a predicted position with the measured one).
  3. Distance: sum of haversine distances (the great-circle distance on a sphere) between smoothed points, skipping paused spans.
  4. Elevation gain: use a digital elevation model lookup instead of phone GPS altitude, which is noisy.
from math import radians, sin, cos, asin, sqrt

def haversine_m(lat1, lng1, lat2, lng2):
    r = 6_371_000
    p1, p2 = radians(lat1), radians(lat2)
    dp, dl = p2 - p1, radians(lng2 - lng1)
    h = sin(dp / 2) ** 2 + cos(p1) * cos(p2) * sin(dl / 2) ** 2
    return 2 * r * asin(sqrt(h))

Leaderboards:

Option Read speed Freshness Notes
SQL ORDER BY over all efforts Slow at scale Fresh Fine for small segments
Nightly batch Fast Up to a day stale Users expect to see their PR now
Redis sorted set per leaderboard, updated on activity-done (recommended) O(log n) Seconds Rebuildable from Postgres

Recommended: keep two kinds of board in Redis sorted sets. Weekly distance per club or among friends (ZINCRBY lb:week:2026-45:club:7 10012 user_123), and best time per segment (ZADD lb:seg:991 LT 2950 user_123, where LT only updates if the new time is lower). Segment matching itself (does this route pass over segment 991?) runs in the processing worker: index segments by geohash, find candidate segments whose cells the route touches, then check start and end points are passed in order.

How does the friends feed work?

The problem: show friends’ recent activities, newest first, for 3,000 reads/s at peak. Most users have 50-500 followers; some pro athletes have millions.

Option Read cost Write cost Fit
Fan-out on read Query N friends, merge 1 OK for few friends, slow beyond
Fan-out on write One Redis read 1 write per follower Good for typical users
Hybrid (recommended) One read + merge a few pros Bounded Handles pros with millions of followers

Recommended: the same hybrid as a social feed. On activity-done, push the activity ID into each follower’s Redis sorted set feed:{uid} (score = start time), unless the athlete has more than 50k followers. Those pro accounts are pulled at read time and merged. Respect privacy at write time: if an activity is “only me” or “followers only”, fan out only to the allowed set. Use a cursor on (start_time, activity_id) for pages. Feed cards render from the stored polyline and summary, so no S3 reads are needed.

How does real-time sharing work, and what happens on failure?

The problem: 20k athletes stream positions every 5 seconds, each watched by a few friends on different servers. Signal is patchy, so updates arrive late or in bursts.

Option Latency Server cost Notes
Viewers poll every 5 s 0-5 s extra Many empty requests Simple fallback
WebSockets both ways Lowest Stateful connections Overkill: viewers only receive
Athlete posts batches, viewers on SSE fed by Redis pub/sub (recommended) Seconds Light SSE reconnects automatically 
 athlete phone --POST batch (every 5 s)--> Live Service A
                                             | SET live:{sid}:last
                                             | PUBLISH live:{sid}
                                             v
                                       Redis pub/sub
                                             |
                     +-----------------------+---------------+
                     v                                       v
              Live Service B (SSE)                   Live Service C (SSE)
                     |                                       |
                  friend 1                               friend 2

When a viewer connects, the server first sends live:{sid}:last (and the last few minutes of trail from a capped Redis list), then streams new points. When the athlete loses signal, the app buffers and sends the backlog on reconnect; the server forwards points with their original timestamps so the viewer’s map fills in the gap. Live points are short-lived (TTL of a few hours); the full activity still arrives through the normal upload.

Failure handling summary:

Failure Mitigation
Upload fails mid-way Retry with the same client_id; S3 multipart upload resumes
Processing worker crashes Event is redelivered; processing is idempotent (overwrites the same row)
Bad GPS data (spikes, teleporting) Accuracy and speed filters before stats
Redis feed or leaderboard lost Rebuild from Postgres; feed falls back to fan-out on read
Live Service node dies SSE clients reconnect to another node and re-fetch last point

9. Common mistakes and interviewer follow-ups

  • Streaming every GPS point to the server live. Fails with no signal and drains the battery. Say: “phone is the source of truth, local write-ahead log, upload on finish.”
  • Non-idempotent uploads. Retries create duplicate runs. Say: “client-generated client_id with a unique constraint.”
  • One database row per GPS point. Billions of rows a day. Say: “compressed blob in S3 plus a simplified polyline in the activity row.”
  • Summing raw point distances. Jitter inflates distance. Say: “filter by accuracy and speed, smooth, then haversine.”
  • Loading the full track for feed cards. Wasteful. Say: “feed and maps use the 1-2 KB polyline only.”
  • Forgetting privacy zones. Showing where someone’s run starts reveals their home. Say: “trim the first and last few hundred metres near saved private locations before fan-out.”
  • Follow-up: “How do you scale segment matching?” Index segments by geohash, check only segments in cells the route crosses, run it async in workers.
  • Follow-up: “Why SSE over WebSockets for live viewers?” Viewers only receive, SSE works over plain HTTP, reconnects automatically, and is easier to load balance.

10. One-page cheat sheet

Topic Key point
Scale 10M activities/day, 36B GPS points/day, ~600 uploads/s peak
Storage Raw ~420 TB/yr, compressed ~80 TB/yr (delta + varint + gzip)
Offline SQLite write-ahead on phone, upload on finish, retry with backoff
Idempotency client_id + UNIQUE (user_id, client_id)
Route forms Full track blob in S3; RDP-simplified polyline (~1.5 KB) in DB
Stats Filter, smooth, haversine distance, DEM for elevation
Leaderboards Redis ZSET: ZINCRBY for weekly distance, ZADD LT for best time
Feed Hybrid fan-out, pros pulled at read, cursor paging
Live Batches every 5 s, Redis pub/sub, SSE to viewers, last point cached
CAP AP; strong only for “activity saved”

12. Distributed Cache (Redis / Memcached Like) (Medium)

A distributed cache is a fast key-value store that keeps data in memory across many machines. Applications put the results of slow work (database queries, API calls, rendered pages) into it, so the next request can read them in under a millisecond instead of hitting the slow system again. Think Redis or Memcached. The interviewer is really testing how you spread keys across nodes and add or remove nodes without losing most of the cache, how you evict old data when memory is full, how you keep serving when a node dies, and how you deal with one key that gets far more traffic than the rest.

1. Functional requirements

Core (must have):

  1. Clients can set(key, value, ttl) to store a value with an optional time-to-live (TTL, how long the value stays valid).
  2. Clients can get(key) to read a value, or get a miss if it is absent or expired.
  3. Clients can delete(key).
  4. When memory is full, the cache evicts entries using a policy (LRU: least recently used first).

Below the line (out of scope):

  1. Rich data types (lists, sorted sets, streams) like Redis has. They change the value format, not the distribution design.
  2. Persistence to disk (snapshots, append-only file). A cache can be rebuilt from the source of truth; we mention it as an option only.
  3. Transactions and multi-key atomic operations across nodes. Hard in a sharded system and rarely needed for a cache.
  4. Pub/sub messaging.

2. Non-functional requirements

  1. Low latency: p99 under 1 ms for get and set inside a data centre (network round trip included, about 0.2-0.5 ms).
  2. High throughput: 1M+ operations per second overall, about 100k per node.
  3. Scale: 1 TB of hot data, growing; add nodes without downtime.
  4. Availability: 99.99%. A node failure should affect only a small slice of keys, and only briefly.
  5. Consistency: eventual. A read right after a write may return the old value from a replica for a few milliseconds. The cache is not the source of truth.
  6. Elasticity: adding or removing a node moves only about 1/N of the keys.
  7. CAP choice: AP. During a partition, keep serving reads and writes, even if a replica is slightly stale. Correctness belongs to the database behind the cache.

3. Back-of-the-envelope estimates

Assumption Number
Total peak operations 1M ops/s
Read to write ratio 9:1
Hot data size 1 TB
Average key + value size 1 KB
Usable RAM per node (of 64 GB) 50 GB
Per-entry overhead (pointers, hash slot, TTL) ~70 bytes
Throughput per node 100k ops/s
Replication factor 2 (1 primary + 1 replica) 
Entries:
  1 TB / 1 KB = 1 billion entries

Memory with overhead:
  1B * (1,024 + 70) B ~= 1.1 TB

Nodes for memory:
  1.1 TB / 50 GB ~= 22 primaries

Nodes for throughput:
  1M ops/s / 100k ops/s = 10 nodes  -> memory is the limit, so 22

With one replica each:
  22 primaries + 22 replicas = 44 nodes (round to 48 for headroom)

Network per node:
  1M ops/s / 22 nodes ~= 45k ops/s * 1 KB ~= 45 MB/s (~360 Mbps)
  that is fine on a 10 Gbps network card

The key insight: for a cache, memory usually sets the node count, not CPU. And 1 TB fits in a few dozen commodity machines.

4. Core entities

  • Key: a string up to 250 bytes, for example user:123:profile.
  • Value: bytes (up to 1 MB in Memcached, 512 MB in Redis; we cap at 1 MB).
  • Entry: key, value, expires_at, and LRU links (prev, next).
  • Node: one cache server. node_id, address, role (primary or replica), status.
  • Ring / Slot map: which node owns which part of the key space.
  • Client: an application library that knows the slot map, or talks to a proxy.
{
  "cluster": "cache-prod",
  "version": 42,
  "slots": [
    { "range": [0, 5460],     "primary": "10.0.1.11:7000",
      "replicas": ["10.0.2.11:7000"] },
    { "range": [5461, 10922], "primary": "10.0.1.12:7000",
      "replicas": ["10.0.2.12:7000"] },
    { "range": [10923, 16383],"primary": "10.0.1.13:7000",
      "replicas": ["10.0.2.13:7000"] }
  ]
}
from dataclasses import dataclass

@dataclass
class Entry:
    key: str
    value: bytes
    expires_at: float | None   # epoch seconds, None = never
    prev: "Entry | None" = None
    next: "Entry | None" = None

5. API design

A cache uses a compact binary or text protocol over TCP, not REST, because HTTP overhead would dominate a 1 ms budget. Here it is shown as operations.

SET key value [EX seconds] [NX|XX] – store a value. NX = only if absent, XX = only if present.

> SET user:123:profile "{...json...}" EX 300
OK

GET key – read a value.

> GET user:123:profile
"{...json...}"        (or nil on miss)

DEL key – delete. Returns the number of keys removed.

MGET key1 key2 ... – batch read. The client library splits it per node and sends in parallel.

Errors: MOVED <slot> <node> when the client sent a key to the wrong node (its slot map is stale), OOM if the node is out of memory and the policy is “no eviction”, TIMEOUT on the client side.

A client library API might look like:

cache = CacheClient(seeds=["10.0.1.11:7000"], timeout_ms=5)
cache.set("user:123:profile", payload, ttl=300)
value = cache.get("user:123:profile")      # bytes or None
cache.delete("user:123:profile")

Auth: TLS plus a password or ACL per client, and the cluster sits in a private network. Never expose it to the internet.

How will clients set a value?

  1. The app calls cache.set(key, value, ttl).
  2. The client library hashes the key to a slot and looks up the owning primary in its local slot map.
  3. It sends SET over a pooled TCP connection.
  4. The node stores the entry in its hash map, links it at the front of its LRU list, records expires_at, and evicts from the tail if memory is over the limit.
  5. It replies OK, then sends the write to its replica asynchronously.
sequenceDiagram
    participant P as App
    participant L as ClientLib
    participant N as PrimaryNode
    participant R as Replica
    P->>L: set key value ttl
    L->>L: Hash key to slot
    L->>L: Look up primary in slot map
    L->>N: SET over pooled TCP
    N->>N: Store in hash map and LRU head
    N->>N: Evict from LRU tail if over limit
    N-->>L: OK
    L-->>P: OK
    N->>R: Replicate write async

How will clients get a value?

  1. The client hashes the key to the same slot and node.
  2. The node looks the key up in its hash map. If found and not expired, it moves the entry to the front of the LRU list and returns the value.
  3. If missing or expired, it returns nil. The app then reads the database and calls set (this pattern is called cache-aside).

How will clients delete a value?

  1. Same routing. The node removes the entry from the hash map and the LRU list, and replicates the delete.

How does eviction happen?

  1. Each node has a memory limit (for example 50 GB).
  2. On any write that pushes memory over the limit, the node removes entries from the LRU tail until it is back under the limit.

7. Deep dives

How do we spread keys across nodes and rebalance when nodes change?

The problem: with 22 nodes, the simple rule node = hash(key) % 22 works until we add a 23rd node. Then almost every key maps to a different node, the cache is effectively empty, and the database gets flooded (a “cache stampede”).

Option Keys moved when N -> N+1 Notes
hash(key) % N ~ N/(N+1), about 96% at N = 22 Do not use
Consistent hashing with virtual nodes (recommended, Memcached style) ~ 1/(N+1), about 4% Ring of points, walk clockwise
Fixed hash slots, e.g. 16,384, mapped to nodes (recommended, Redis Cluster style) Only the slots you choose to move Explicit, easy to reason about

Consistent hashing places each node at many points on a ring of hash values (these are “virtual nodes”, say 150 per physical node, which evens out the load). A key goes to the first node point clockwise from its own hash. Adding a node takes over small arcs from its neighbours only.

import bisect, hashlib

def h(s: str) -> int:
    return int.from_bytes(hashlib.md5(s.encode()).digest()[:8], "big")

class HashRing:
    def __init__(self, nodes, vnodes=150):
        self.vnodes = vnodes
        self.ring = []          # sorted list of (hash, node)
        for n in nodes:
            self.add(n)

    def add(self, node):
        for i in range(self.vnodes):
            bisect.insort(self.ring, (h(f"{node}#{i}"), node))

    def remove(self, node):
        self.ring = [(k, n) for k, n in self.ring if n != node]

    def node_for(self, key):
        i = bisect.bisect(self.ring, (h(key), ""))
        return self.ring[i % len(self.ring)][1]

Hash slots work the same way but with a fixed number of buckets: slot = crc16(key) % 16384, and a table maps slots to nodes. To add a node, move a chosen set of slots to it. During the move, the old node answers ASK (try the new node for this key) for keys already migrated, and once the slot is fully moved, clients get MOVED and refresh their map.

Rebalancing safely:

  1. Add the new node empty.
  2. Move slots (or let the ring take over arcs) a few at a time, throttled, so the database does not see a wave of misses.
  3. Optionally warm the new node by copying entries for moving slots from the old owner instead of starting cold.

How do we implement LRU eviction efficiently?

The problem: when memory is full we must find the least recently used entry instantly, and every get must mark an entry as recently used. Both must be O(1), because a node handles 100k ops/s.

Option Get Evict Memory Notes
Scan all entries for oldest timestamp O(1) O(n) Low Too slow
Min-heap on last access time O(log n) O(log n) Medium Every get reorders the heap
Hash map + doubly linked list (recommended, exact LRU) O(1) O(1) 2 pointers per entry Classic answer
Sampled LRU (Redis approach) O(1) O(k) samples Lowest Approximate, saves pointer memory

Recommended: hash map plus doubly linked list. The hash map finds an entry by key in O(1). The list keeps entries in recency order: most recent at the head, least recent at the tail. On access, unlink the node and move it to the head (O(1) because each node knows its neighbours). To evict, remove the tail. Sentinel head and tail nodes remove edge cases.

import threading, time

class Node:
    __slots__ = ("key", "value", "expires_at", "size", "prev", "next")
    def __init__(self, key=None, value=b"", expires_at=None):
        self.key, self.value, self.expires_at = key, value, expires_at
        self.size = len(value) + (len(key) if key else 0)
        self.prev = self.next = None

class LRUCache:
    def __init__(self, max_bytes):
        self.max_bytes, self.used = max_bytes, 0
        self.map = {}
        self.head, self.tail = Node(), Node()   # sentinels
        self.head.next, self.tail.prev = self.tail, self.head
        self.lock = threading.Lock()

    def _unlink(self, n):
        n.prev.next, n.next.prev = n.next, n.prev

    def _push_front(self, n):
        n.prev, n.next = self.head, self.head.next
        self.head.next.prev = n
        self.head.next = n

    def _remove(self, n):
        self._unlink(n)
        del self.map[n.key]
        self.used -= n.size

    def get(self, key):
        with self.lock:
            n = self.map.get(key)
            if n is None:
                return None
            if n.expires_at is not None and n.expires_at <= time.time():
                self._remove(n)            # lazy expiry
                return None
            self._unlink(n)
            self._push_front(n)            # mark as most recently used
            return n.value

    def set(self, key, value, ttl=None):
        with self.lock:
            if key in self.map:
                self._remove(self.map[key])
            exp = time.time() + ttl if ttl else None
            n = Node(key, value, exp)
            self.map[key] = n
            self._push_front(n)
            self.used += n.size
            while self.used > self.max_bytes and self.tail.prev is not self.head:
                self._remove(self.tail.prev)   # evict least recently used

    def delete(self, key):
        with self.lock:
            n = self.map.get(key)
            if n:
                self._remove(n)

Production notes worth mentioning: Redis uses approximate LRU (sample 5 keys, evict the oldest) to save the two pointers per key, and also offers LFU (least frequently used), which resists one-off scans pushing out popular keys. Real servers avoid one global lock by sharding the map into many segments, or by running one single-threaded event loop per core (Redis, and Memcached’s per-thread design).

How do we replicate and fail over when a node dies?

The problem: if a node with 50 GB of hot data dies, all its keys miss at once and that traffic hits the database. We want a standby ready to take over within seconds.

Option Write latency Data loss on failover Notes
No replication Lowest Whole node’s data Acceptable only for tiny caches
Async primary-replica (recommended) Lowest Last few ms of writes Fine: the cache is not the source of truth
Sync replication / quorum writes Higher (extra round trip) None Too costly for a cache

Recommended: each primary streams writes asynchronously to one replica in a different availability zone. A membership service (or the nodes themselves via gossip, as in Redis Cluster) health-checks every node.

 1. Node B misses heartbeats for 3 s  -> marked "suspect" by peers
 2. Majority of primaries agree       -> marked "failed"
 3. Replica B' is promoted            -> slot map version 43 published
 4. Clients get MOVED or refresh map  -> traffic goes to B'
 5. New empty replica is attached     -> full sync from B'

Pitfalls to name:

  • Split brain: the old primary is only cut off, not dead, and keeps taking writes. Require a majority vote to promote and have a primary stop accepting writes when it cannot reach a majority.
  • Read from replicas only if stale reads are OK. Default to reading from primaries for simpler consistency; use replicas to scale reads for hot keys.
  • Keep TTLs in absolute time on replicas, so expiry is the same after failover.

How do we handle hot keys?

The problem: one key (a celebrity profile, a flash-sale item, a config blob) can get 200k reads/s. That is more than one node can serve, and the node holding it overloads while others are idle. Consistent hashing does not help, because one key always maps to one node.

Option How Trade-off
Local in-process cache on app servers (recommended first step) Keep hot keys in app memory for 1-5 s Slightly stale, uses app RAM
Read from replicas Spread reads across primary + replicas Only 2-3x more capacity
Key splitting / replication across nodes (recommended for extreme cases) Store key#0..key#9 on different nodes, read a random copy Writes must update all copies
Request coalescing (single flight) One miss fetches, others wait Fixes stampedes, not steady hot reads

Recommended: detect hot keys (sample request counts per key on the server, or count in the client), then:

  1. Serve them from a small local cache in each app server with a short TTL (a few seconds). This alone often removes over 90% of the load.
  2. For extreme keys, write N copies with suffixes so they land on different nodes, and read a random copy.
import random

HOT_COPIES = 10

def get_hot(cache, key):
    v = local_cache.get(key)               # in-process, TTL 2 s
    if v is not None:
        return v
    v = cache.get(f"{key}#{random.randrange(HOT_COPIES)}")
    if v is not None:
        local_cache.set(key, v, ttl=2)
    return v

def set_hot(cache, key, value, ttl):
    for i in range(HOT_COPIES):            # same value on 10 nodes
        cache.set(f"{key}#{i}", value, ttl=ttl)

Also protect against stampedes on popular keys that expire: when a hot key misses, let one request rebuild it (a short SET lock:key NX EX 5) while others briefly serve the stale value or wait.

How do TTL and expiry work without wasting CPU?

The problem: a billion keys each have their own TTL. Checking every key every second is impossible, but expired keys must not be served and should not use memory for long.

Option CPU Memory reclaimed Notes
Timer per key Huge Exact Millions of timers, not practical
Lazy expiry only (check on read) None Never for keys nobody reads Leaks memory
Lazy + periodic sampling (recommended, Redis approach) Small, bounded Most expired keys within seconds Simple and effective

Recommended: both.

  1. Lazy: on every get, if expires_at has passed, delete and return a miss (shown in the LRU code above).
  2. Active sampling: about 10 times a second, sample 20 keys from the set of keys that have a TTL, delete the expired ones, and if more than 25% were expired, repeat at once. This keeps expired keys under roughly 25% of memory without scanning everything.
def active_expire_cycle(store, sample=20, max_ms=25):
    start = time.monotonic()
    while True:
        keys = store.random_keys_with_ttl(sample)
        expired = [k for k in keys if store.is_expired(k)]
        for k in expired:
            store.delete(k)
        if len(expired) <= sample // 4:
            break                          # few expired, stop for now
        if (time.monotonic() - start) * 1000 > max_ms:
            break                          # cap CPU per cycle

Add a small random jitter to TTLs (for example 300 s plus or minus 10%) so keys written at the same time do not all expire together and stampede the database.

Should clients route directly or go through a proxy?

The problem: something must turn a key into a node address. That logic can live in every client or in a proxy tier.

Option Latency Client complexity Operations
Smart client with slot map (recommended for latency) 1 hop Needs a library per language, handles MOVED No extra tier
Proxy tier (Twemproxy, Envoy, mcrouter) 2 hops (+0.1-0.3 ms) Dumb clients, any language Proxies must scale and be HA
Sidecar proxy on each app host ~1 hop (localhost) Dumb clients One proxy per host to deploy

Recommended: smart clients when you control the languages (lowest latency, as in Redis Cluster clients). Use a proxy or sidecar (Facebook’s mcrouter is the famous example) when many languages or teams share the cache, or when you need central features like connection pooling, routing rules, and shadow traffic. Either way, the client must cache the slot map, refresh it on MOVED, and use short timeouts (a few ms) with a circuit breaker, so a sick cache degrades to “go to the database” rather than hanging app threads.

9. Common mistakes and interviewer follow-ups

  • Using hash(key) % N. Adding one node remaps almost every key and floods the database. Say: “consistent hashing with virtual nodes, or fixed hash slots.”
  • LRU with a timestamp scan or a heap. Too slow at 100k ops/s. Say: “hash map plus doubly linked list, O(1) get and evict.”
  • Synchronous replication for a cache. Doubles write latency for data you can rebuild. Say: “async replication, the database is the source of truth.”
  • Ignoring hot keys. One node melts while others idle. Say: “local short-TTL cache on app servers, then split the key into copies.”
  • Same TTL for everything written at once. Mass expiry causes a stampede. Say: “add TTL jitter and single-flight rebuilds.”
  • No client timeouts. A slow cache node hangs every app thread. Say: “few-ms timeouts, circuit breaker, fall back to the database.”
  • Follow-up: “How do you keep the cache consistent with the database?” Cache-aside: update the DB, then delete the cache key (not set it), so the next read reloads fresh data; keep TTLs as a safety net.
  • Follow-up: “LRU or LFU?” LRU is simple and good for recency-heavy workloads; LFU protects popular keys from being pushed out by one-time scans.

10. One-page cheat sheet

Topic Key point
Sizing 1B entries * ~1.1 KB = 1.1 TB, 50 GB per node -> 22 primaries + 22 replicas
Throughput ~100k ops/s per node, p99 < 1 ms
Partitioning Consistent hashing (150 vnodes) or 16,384 hash slots
Rebalance Move ~1/N of keys, throttled, MOVED / ASK redirects
Eviction Hash map + doubly linked list, O(1); Redis samples approx LRU / LFU
Expiry Lazy on read + active sampling (20 keys, repeat if > 25% expired)
Replication Async primary -> replica in another AZ
Failover Majority vote, promote replica, bump slot map version
Hot keys Local 2 s cache, split into key#0..#9, single-flight on miss
Routing Smart client (1 hop) or proxy/sidecar (mcrouter, Envoy)
CAP AP; database is the source of truth

13. Rate Limiter (Medium)

A rate limiter decides, for every incoming API request, “is this client allowed to make one more call right now?” If yes, the request goes through. If no, the server answers with HTTP 429 Too Many Requests. It protects services from abuse, runaway scripts, and traffic bursts, and keeps usage fair between customers. The interviewer is really testing three things: do you know the classic algorithms and their trade-offs, can you make the counting correct when many servers share one counter (race conditions), and do you know what to do when the limiter itself breaks.

1. Functional requirements

Core (must have):

  1. Identify the client by user ID, API key, or IP address.
  2. Apply configurable rules, for example “100 requests per minute per user” or “10 searches per second per IP”.
  3. Reject requests over the limit with HTTP 429 and return helpful headers: limit, remaining, and when the window resets.
  4. Support different rules per endpoint and per customer tier (free vs paid).

Below the line (out of scope):

  1. Analytics dashboards on who got limited. Useful, but it is a separate reporting pipeline.
  2. Long-term storage of counters. Counters only matter for seconds or minutes.
  3. Billing and quotas per month. That is a metering system with different accuracy needs.

2. Non-functional requirements

  1. Low overhead: the limit check adds less than 10 ms at p99, ideally 1-2 ms.
  2. Scale: 1 million requests per second across 100 million daily active users.
  3. High availability: 99.99%. If the limiter is down, the API must not go down with it.
  4. Accuracy: a client may overshoot its limit by a small amount (say under 1%) during races or failover. We do not need perfect global accuracy.
  5. CAP choice: we pick availability over strong consistency (AP). A few extra requests slipping through is much cheaper than blocking all traffic because one counter node is unreachable.
  6. Rule changes take effect within about 1 minute.

3. Back-of-the-envelope estimates

Assumption Number
Peak requests per second 1,000,000
Daily active users 100,000,000
Active clients in any one minute 10,000,000
Bytes per counter in Redis (key + value + overhead) ~100 B
Rules per client checked per request 1-3 
Redis operations:
  1M req/s x 1 check each        = 1M Redis ops/s
  one Redis node handles ~100k simple ops/s
  1M / 100k                      = 10 shards minimum
  add 2x headroom                = ~20 shards (plus replicas)

Memory for token bucket state (2 fields per key):
  10M active clients x 100 B     = 1 GB
  x 3 rules                      = 3 GB total  -> fits in memory easily

Network:
  each check ~200 B round trip
  1M/s x 200 B                   = 200 MB/s across the cluster

The lesson: memory is small, but operations per second force us to shard.

4. Core entities

  • Rule: the policy. Fields: rule_id, match (endpoint, tier), key_type (user, ip, api_key), algorithm, limit, window_seconds or refill_rate.
  • Client: the thing being limited. Identified by a key such as user:42 or ip:1.2.3.4.
  • Counter / Bucket state: the live numbers for one client and one rule, for example tokens left and last refill time.
  • Request: the incoming call, with headers and path, used to pick the rule and the client key.
  • Decision: allow or deny, plus remaining and reset time.
# rules.yaml - stored in a config service, cached in every gateway
- rule_id: search_per_ip
  match: { path: "/v1/search", method: GET }
  key: ip
  algorithm: token_bucket
  capacity: 20          # max burst
  refill_per_sec: 10    # steady rate
- rule_id: free_tier_user
  match: { tier: free }
  key: user_id
  algorithm: sliding_window_counter
  limit: 1000
  window_seconds: 3600
{
  "key": "rl:search_per_ip:ip:203.0.113.7",
  "tokens": 13.5,
  "last_refill_ms": 1762205400123
}

5. API design

A rate limiter is mostly internal, so its “API” is a check call plus the response headers clients see.

POST /internal/ratelimit/check – ask whether one request is allowed.

// request
{ "rule_ids": ["search_per_ip"], "client_key": "ip:203.0.113.7", "cost": 1 }
// response 200
{ "allowed": true, "limit": 20, "remaining": 12, "reset_ms": 800 }

Auth: mTLS between gateway and limiter; never exposed to the internet.

Client-facing behavior on a denied request:

HTTP/1.1 429 Too Many Requests
X-RateLimit-Limit: 20
X-RateLimit-Remaining: 0
X-RateLimit-Reset: 1762205401
Retry-After: 1

PUT /admin/rules/{rule_id} – create or update a rule. Body is one rule (as in the YAML above). Returns 200, or 400 on invalid config. Admin auth only.

GET /admin/rules – list rules, used by gateways to refresh their local cache. Returns 200 with a version number so gateways can skip unchanged data.

How will the system identify the client?

  1. The request reaches the gateway.
  2. The gateway validates the JWT or API key. If valid, the key is user:<id> or key:<api_key>.
  3. If the request is anonymous, it uses the client IP from the load balancer (the X-Forwarded-For header set by our own LB, never one the client sent).
  4. The gateway now has a client key and the request path.
sequenceDiagram
    participant C as Client
    participant L as LoadBalancer
    participant G as Gateway
    participant A as AuthCheck
    participant R as Redis
    C->>L: API request with JWT or API key
    L->>G: Forward request with LB seen IP
    G->>A: Validate JWT or API key
    alt credentials valid
        A-->>G: user id
        G->>G: Build key user id
    else anonymous
        A-->>G: no identity
        G->>G: Build key from LB client IP
    end
    G->>R: Run Lua check for client key
    R-->>G: allowed and remaining
    G-->>C: Response with rate limit headers

How will the system apply configurable rules?

  1. The gateway keeps all rules in memory, refreshed from the Rule Config Service every 30 seconds.
  2. It matches the request (path, method, tier) to 1-3 rules.
  3. For each rule it builds a Redis key like rl:<rule_id>:<client_key>.
  4. It runs one atomic Lua script on Redis per rule (details in the deep dives). The script returns allowed and remaining.

How will the system reject requests with helpful headers?

  1. If any rule says “deny”, the gateway returns 429 with the headers shown above. The backend never sees the request.
  2. If all rules allow, the gateway forwards the request and still adds X-RateLimit-Remaining to the response so good clients can slow down on their own.

7. Deep dives

Which rate limiting algorithm should we use?

There are five classic algorithms. You should be able to explain each in one sentence and write it.

Algorithm Idea Memory per key Bursts Accuracy
Fixed window counter Count per clock minute 1 int 2x burst at window edge Low
Sliding window log Store every timestamp O(limit) None Exact
Sliding window counter Weighted mix of current and previous window 2 ints Small Very good (approx)
Token bucket Tokens refill at rate r, cap c 2 numbers Allows bursts up to c Good
Leaky bucket Queue drained at fixed rate queue Smooths all bursts Good, adds delay

Fixed window counter. Simple, but a client can send 100 at 12:00:59 and 100 more at 12:01:00, so 200 in two seconds.

import time
counters = {}  # (key, window) -> count

def fixed_window(key, limit, window_s):
    window = int(time.time() // window_s)
    k = (key, window)
    counters[k] = counters.get(k, 0) + 1
    return counters[k] <= limit

Sliding window log. Keep a list of timestamps. Exact, but 1,000 requests per hour means storing 1,000 timestamps per user.

from collections import deque
logs = {}

def sliding_log(key, limit, window_s):
    now = time.time()
    q = logs.setdefault(key, deque())
    while q and q[0] <= now - window_s:
        q.popleft()             # drop old timestamps
    if len(q) < limit:
        q.append(now)
        return True
    return False

Sliding window counter. Keep counts for the current and previous fixed windows. Estimate the last full window as prev * (overlap fraction) + curr. Cloudflare reported this approach was within about 0.003% of exact in their traffic.

def sliding_counter(key, limit, window_s):
    now = time.time()
    curr_w = int(now // window_s)
    elapsed = (now % window_s) / window_s      # 0.0 .. 1.0
    prev = counters.get((key, curr_w - 1), 0)
    curr = counters.get((key, curr_w), 0)
    estimate = prev * (1 - elapsed) + curr
    if estimate < limit:
        counters[(key, curr_w)] = curr + 1
        return True
    return False

Token bucket. Each client has a bucket holding up to capacity tokens. Tokens refill at rate per second. Each request takes one token. Allows short bursts but enforces the average rate. Used by AWS API Gateway and Stripe.

buckets = {}  # key -> (tokens, last_ts)

def token_bucket(key, capacity, rate):
    now = time.time()
    tokens, last = buckets.get(key, (capacity, now))
    tokens = min(capacity, tokens + (now - last) * rate)  # refill
    if tokens >= 1:
        buckets[key] = (tokens - 1, now)
        return True
    buckets[key] = (tokens, now)
    return False

Leaky bucket. Requests enter a queue; a worker drains it at a fixed rate. Output is perfectly smooth, which is great for protecting a fragile downstream (like a payment provider), but requests wait.

import queue, threading
q = queue.Queue(maxsize=100)    # bucket size

def leaky_submit(req):
    try:
        q.put_nowait(req)       # full bucket = reject
        return True
    except queue.Full:
        return False

def drain(rate_per_s, handle):
    while True:
        handle(q.get())
        time.sleep(1 / rate_per_s)

Recommendation: token bucket as the default for user-facing APIs (it is cheap, two numbers per key, and burst-friendly). Use sliding window counter when the product says “1,000 per hour” and customers will complain about edge bursts. Use leaky bucket only in front of a downstream that cannot take bursts.

How do we make the counter atomic across many gateways?

The problem: 50 gateway servers check the same Redis key. A naive “GET tokens, compute, SET tokens” has a race. Two gateways both read tokens=1, both allow, both write 0. The client got 2 requests for 1 token.

Option How Problem
GET then SET from gateway Two round trips Race condition, double spend
WATCH / MULTI / EXEC Optimistic transaction Retries under contention, slow
INCR + EXPIRE (fixed window) Single atomic op Only works for fixed window
Lua script on Redis Whole read-modify-write runs atomically Script must stay tiny and fast

Redis runs one Lua script at a time on a shard, so the script is atomic. Recommended token bucket script:

-- KEYS[1] = bucket key
-- ARGV: capacity, refill_per_ms, now_ms, cost
local cap   = tonumber(ARGV[1])
local rate  = tonumber(ARGV[2])
local now   = tonumber(ARGV[3])
local cost  = tonumber(ARGV[4])

local b = redis.call('HMGET', KEYS[1], 'tokens', 'ts')
local tokens = tonumber(b[1]) or cap
local ts     = tonumber(b[2]) or now

tokens = math.min(cap, tokens + (now - ts) * rate)
local allowed = 0
if tokens >= cost then
  tokens = tokens - cost
  allowed = 1
end
redis.call('HSET', KEYS[1], 'tokens', tokens, 'ts', now)
-- expire idle buckets: time to refill fully, plus margin
redis.call('PEXPIRE', KEYS[1], math.ceil(cap / rate) + 1000)
return { allowed, math.floor(tokens) }
# gateway side (redis-py); script is loaded once, called by SHA
lua = r.register_script(TOKEN_BUCKET_LUA)

def allow(key, cap, rate_per_s):
    now_ms = int(time.time() * 1000)
    allowed, remaining = lua(keys=[key],
                             args=[cap, rate_per_s / 1000, now_ms, 1])
    return allowed == 1, remaining

A detail interviewers like: clock skew. If 50 gateways send their own now_ms, a gateway with a fast clock can over-refill. Fix it by calling redis.call('TIME') inside the script so Redis is the single clock.

How does the system scale to 1M requests per second?

  1. Shard Redis by key. Redis Cluster hashes each key to one of 16,384 slots spread over ~20 primaries. All state for one client and rule lives on one shard, so the Lua script never crosses shards.
  2. Keep connections warm. Each gateway uses a connection pool and pipelines when a request matches several rules.
  3. Hot keys. One abusive IP at 100k req/s hits one shard. Add a local, in-process pre-check on each gateway: if the gateway already denied this key in the last second, deny locally without calling Redis. This caps the damage from a single attacker.
  4. Optional local batching. For very high-volume keys, each gateway can take a “lease” of 10 tokens at once from Redis and spend them locally. This cuts Redis traffic 10x at the cost of small overshoot.
 Gateway A ---\                 +---------+ slot 0-5460
 Gateway B ----+-- hash(key) -->| Redis 1 |
 Gateway C ---/       |         +---------+
                      +-------->| Redis 2 | slot 5461-10922
                      |         +---------+
                      +-------->| Redis 3 | slot 10923-16383
                                +---------+

What happens when Redis is slow or down: fail open or fail closed?

Choice Behavior when limiter is unreachable Good for Risk
Fail open Allow the request Normal APIs, revenue paths Abuse slips through during outage
Fail closed Reject with 429 or 503 Login, password reset, SMS sending, costly APIs Your own outage takes the API down
Fail to local Use an in-memory limiter per gateway at limit / N Most systems Approximate limits

Recommended: fail open by default with a strict timeout (for example 5 ms), but fall back to a local in-memory token bucket set to limit / number_of_gateways. For security-sensitive rules (login attempts), fail closed. Make this a per-rule flag.

def check(rule, key):
    try:
        return redis_allow(rule, key, timeout_ms=5)
    except (TimeoutError, ConnectionError):
        metrics.incr("ratelimit.redis_error")
        if rule.fail_mode == "closed":
            return False, 0
        return local_bucket(rule, key, share=1 / NUM_GATEWAYS)

Also add a circuit breaker: after many Redis errors in a row, stop calling Redis for 10 seconds so you do not add timeout latency to every request. Redis replicas with automatic failover (Sentinel or Cluster) shorten outages; losing a few seconds of counters on failover is fine because counters are short-lived.

Where should the rate limiter live, and how are rules configured?

Placement Pros Cons
Client side Saves network Cannot be trusted, easy to bypass
API gateway / edge One place, blocks bad traffic early, language neutral Gateway must know user identity and rules
Middleware in each service Fine-grained, knows business context Duplicated logic across services and languages
Sidecar (Envoy + rate limit service) Language neutral, per-service Extra hop, more ops work

Recommended: put the global limits in the API gateway (Envoy, Kong, or AWS API Gateway style), and allow a service to add its own in-process limit for business rules like “5 password resets per hour”.

Rules: store them in a config service or database with a version number. Gateways poll every 30 seconds (or get a push via a watch on etcd/ZooKeeper) and swap the in-memory rule table atomically. Never read rules from a database on the hot path.

9. Common mistakes and interviewer follow-ups

  • Mistake: GET then SET from the gateway. It causes double spending under concurrency. Say instead: “the read-modify-write runs as one Lua script so it is atomic per key.”
  • Mistake: choosing fixed window without mentioning the edge burst. It hurts because the interviewer will ask about it. Say: “fixed window allows 2x at boundaries; sliding window counter fixes that with two integers.”
  • Mistake: storing counters in a SQL database. Disk writes at 1M/s are far too slow. Say: “in-memory store, data is short-lived, losing it on failover is acceptable.”
  • Mistake: no plan for limiter failure. Say: “fail open with a 5 ms timeout and a local fallback, fail closed only for security rules.”
  • Mistake: trusting the client’s X-Forwarded-For. Attackers rotate it to dodge IP limits. Say: “use the IP our own load balancer saw.”
  • Mistake: using gateway clocks inside the algorithm. Clock skew breaks refills. Say: “use Redis TIME inside the script.”
  • Follow-up: “How would you rate limit by cost, not count?” Answer: pass cost to the script, for example an expensive search costs 5 tokens.
  • Follow-up: “How do you limit across regions?” Answer: limit per region with limit / regions as the share, and accept small global overshoot; strong global counters would add 100 ms of cross-region latency.

10. One-page cheat sheet

Topic Key point
Goal Allow or deny each request, 429 on deny
Scale 1M req/s, 100M DAU, ~20 Redis shards
Latency budget < 10 ms p99, aim for 1-2 ms
Default algorithm Token bucket (capacity + refill rate)
No edge bursts Sliding window counter (prev * overlap + curr)
Smooth output Leaky bucket (queue, fixed drain)
Atomicity One Redis Lua script per check, Redis TIME as clock
Sharding Redis Cluster by key, all client state on one shard
Hot keys Local deny cache, token leases
Failure Fail open + local fallback; fail closed for login/SMS
Placement API gateway for global, service middleware for business
Rules Config service, cached in gateway, refresh 30 s
Headers X-RateLimit-Limit, -Remaining, -Reset, Retry-After
CAP AP: small overshoot is OK, outages are not

14. Online Auction (Medium)

An online auction site like eBay lets sellers list an item with a starting price and an end time. Buyers place bids, and each new bid must be higher than the current highest bid. When the clock runs out, the highest bidder wins. The interviewer is really testing one hard correctness problem (two people bid at the same moment, who wins, and do we ever accept a lower bid by mistake), one real-time problem (showing the new highest bid to thousands of watchers within a second), and how you end auctions exactly on time.

1. Functional requirements

Core (must have):

  1. Sellers can create an auction for an item with a starting price and an end time.
  2. Buyers can place a bid. A bid is accepted only if it is higher than the current highest bid (and at least the starting price).
  3. Anyone can view an auction, including the current highest bid, and see it update in real time.
  4. When an auction ends, the system picks the winner and notifies the winner and seller.

Below the line (out of scope):

  1. Search, categories, and sorting. They are a separate search system (Elasticsearch) fed from the auction DB.
  2. Payments and shipping. They start after the auction closes and belong to a checkout service.
  3. Proxy bidding (eBay’s “bid up to $X for me”). Nice extension, mention it if time allows.
  4. Fraud and shill bidding detection. An offline ML pipeline.

2. Non-functional requirements

  1. Strong consistency for bids: we must never accept a bid that is not higher than the true current highest bid, and never lose an accepted bid. This is the CP part.
  2. Availability for viewing: browsing auctions should stay up (99.99%) even if the bidding path is degraded. Reads can be slightly stale (a second or two).
  3. Low latency: place-bid p99 < 300 ms; new highest bid visible to watchers within 1 second.
  4. Scale: 10 million concurrent auctions, about 100 bids per second on average, peaks of thousands of bids per second on one hot auction in its final minute.
  5. Fairness: bids are judged in the order the server received them; ties go to the earlier bid.
  6. Durability: every accepted bid is stored durably (audit trail, disputes).

CAP choice: per-auction bid acceptance is CP (correctness beats availability, we would rather reject a bid than accept a wrong one). Everything else is AP.

3. Back-of-the-envelope estimates

Assumption Number
Active auctions 10,000,000
New auctions per day 1,000,000
Average bids per auction 100
Bid size stored 200 B
Auction row size (with metadata) 2 KB
Views per bid 100
Hot auction final-minute peak 1,000 bids/s 
Writes:
  1M auctions/day x 100 bids  = 100M bids/day
  100M / 86,400 s             = ~1,150 bids/s average
  peak (5x)                   = ~6,000 bids/s globally

Reads:
  100 views per bid           = ~115k reads/s average, ~600k peak

Storage per year:
  bids:     100M/day x 200 B x 365   = ~7.3 TB
  auctions: 1M/day x 2 KB x 365      = ~730 GB
  images live in S3, not counted here

Real-time fanout:
  hot auction: 50k watchers x 1 update/s = 50k messages/s for one item

4. Core entities

  • Auction: the listing. Fields: auction_id, seller_id, item_id, starting_price, end_time, status (active, ended), current_max_bid, current_winner_id, version.
  • Item: what is sold. Fields: item_id, title, description, image_urls.
  • Bid: one offer. Fields: bid_id, auction_id, bidder_id, amount, created_at, status (accepted, rejected).
  • User: buyer or seller. Fields: user_id, name, rating.
  • Notification: message to winner, seller, outbid users.
CREATE TABLE auctions (
  auction_id       BIGINT PRIMARY KEY,
  seller_id        BIGINT NOT NULL,
  item_id          BIGINT NOT NULL,
  starting_price   NUMERIC(12,2) NOT NULL,
  end_time         TIMESTAMPTZ NOT NULL,
  status           TEXT NOT NULL DEFAULT 'active',
  current_max_bid  NUMERIC(12,2),
  current_winner   BIGINT,
  version          BIGINT NOT NULL DEFAULT 0
);
CREATE INDEX ON auctions (status, end_time);

CREATE TABLE bids (
  bid_id      BIGINT PRIMARY KEY,
  auction_id  BIGINT NOT NULL REFERENCES auctions,
  bidder_id   BIGINT NOT NULL,
  amount      NUMERIC(12,2) NOT NULL,
  status      TEXT NOT NULL,          -- accepted / rejected
  created_at  TIMESTAMPTZ NOT NULL DEFAULT now()
);
CREATE INDEX ON bids (auction_id, amount DESC);

Use NUMERIC (or integer cents), never floats, for money.

5. API design

POST /v1/auctions – create an auction.

// request
{ "item": { "title": "Vintage camera", "description": "...",
            "image_ids": ["img_1"] },
  "starting_price": 50.00, "end_time": "2026-11-10T18:00:00Z" }
// 201
{ "auction_id": "a_123", "status": "active" }

Status: 201 created, 400 bad input (end time in the past). Auth: seller JWT.

POST /v1/auctions/{auction_id}/bids – place a bid.

// request (Idempotency-Key header to make retries safe)
{ "amount": 120.00 }
// 201 accepted
{ "bid_id": "b_987", "status": "accepted", "current_max_bid": 120.00 }
// 409 rejected
{ "status": "rejected", "reason": "bid_too_low", "current_max_bid": 125.00 }

Status: 201, 409 too low, 410 auction ended, 429 too many bids. Auth: buyer JWT; bidder_id comes from the token, never the body.

GET /v1/auctions/{auction_id} – view the auction (item, current max bid, end time). 200 or 404. Public.

GET /v1/auctions/{auction_id}/stream – Server-Sent Events stream of bid updates.

event: bid
data: {"auction_id":"a_123","current_max_bid":130.00,"bid_count":42}
