How will sellers create an auction?

  1. Client uploads images to S3 with a pre-signed URL and gets image IDs.
  2. Client calls POST /v1/auctions. Auction Service validates and inserts the item and auction rows in one transaction.
  3. The service registers the end time with the End Scheduler (see deep dives).
  4. Returns 201 with the auction ID.
sequenceDiagram
    participant S as Seller
    participant I as ImageStore
    participant G as Gateway
    participant A as AuctionService
    participant D as Postgres
    participant E as EndScheduler
    S->>G: Request pre-signed upload URL
    G-->>S: Pre-signed URL
    S->>I: Upload images
    I-->>S: Image IDs
    S->>G: POST /v1/auctions
    G->>A: Create auction
    A->>D: INSERT item and auction in one transaction
    D-->>A: Committed
    A->>E: Register end time
    A-->>G: auction id
    G-->>S: 201 auction id

How will buyers place a bid?

  1. Client calls POST /bids with an idempotency key.
  2. Bid Service checks the auction is active and now < end_time.
  3. Bid Service runs a conditional update so it only succeeds if the new amount is higher than the current max (details in deep dives).
  4. On success, it inserts the bid row, commits, and publishes a bid event.
  5. Returns 201. On failure returns 409 with the current max so the UI can refresh.

How will users view an auction and see live updates?

  1. Client calls GET /auctions/{id}. Auction Service reads from cache (Redis) or Postgres.
  2. Client opens GET /auctions/{id}/stream. The Realtime Service subscribes to channel auction:{id} in Redis pub/sub.
  3. Every accepted bid is published to that channel and pushed down all open SSE connections.

How will the system end an auction?

  1. At end_time, the End Scheduler marks the auction ended with a conditional update.
  2. It reads the winning bid, then emits an auction_ended event.
  3. Notification Service emails the winner and seller; Checkout starts.

7. Deep dives

How do we guarantee the highest bid is correct under concurrency?

The problem: current max is $100. Alice bids $110 and Bob bids $105 at the same instant. Both read “max = 100”, both think they are higher, both write. If Bob’s write lands last, the auction shows $105 and Alice’s higher bid is lost.

Option How it works Pros Cons
Read then write, no lock Read max, compare in app, write Simple Wrong under races
Pessimistic lock (SELECT ... FOR UPDATE) Lock the auction row while bidding Correct, easy to reason Lock waits on hot auctions
Optimistic locking (version column) Update only if version unchanged, retry on conflict No lock held, fast when low contention Many retries at peak
Conditional atomic update UPDATE ... WHERE current_max_bid < :amount One statement, no retry needed Only works for a single-row rule
SERIALIZABLE isolation DB detects conflicts Correct for complex logic Aborts and retries, more expensive

Recommended: a conditional atomic update. The rule “new bid beats current max” is checked and applied inside one statement, so the database’s row lock serializes it. A losing bid simply updates zero rows. No retry loop.

BEGIN;
UPDATE auctions
   SET current_max_bid = :amount,
       current_winner  = :bidder_id,
       version         = version + 1
 WHERE auction_id = :auction_id
   AND status = 'active'
   AND end_time > now()
   AND :amount > COALESCE(current_max_bid, starting_price - 0.01)
RETURNING version;
-- 1 row  -> accepted: insert bid as accepted
-- 0 rows -> rejected: insert bid as rejected (audit)
INSERT INTO bids (bid_id, auction_id, bidder_id, amount, status)
VALUES (:bid_id, :auction_id, :bidder_id, :amount, :status);
COMMIT;

If you prefer optimistic locking (for example, more complex rules like minimum increments that depend on other tables), the pattern is:

def place_bid(auction_id, bidder, amount, retries=3):
    for _ in range(retries):
        a = db.one("SELECT current_max_bid, version FROM auctions "
                   "WHERE auction_id=%s", auction_id)
        if amount <= a.current_max_bid:
            return "rejected"
        n = db.execute("UPDATE auctions SET current_max_bid=%s, "
                       "current_winner=%s, version=version+1 "
                       "WHERE auction_id=%s AND version=%s",
                       amount, bidder, auction_id, a.version)
        if n == 1:
            return "accepted"
    return "retry_later"

Why not SERIALIZABLE everywhere? It works, but at peak a hot auction would see many aborted transactions. The conditional update gives the same correctness for this single-row rule at lower cost.

How do we keep bid ordering fair and survive spikes on hot auctions?

The problem: in the last 30 seconds a popular auction can get 1,000 bids per second (“sniping”). Every bid hits the same Postgres row, so they queue on the row lock. If the DB is slow, requests time out and users do not know if their bid counted.

Option How Pros Cons
Direct DB writes Each request updates the row Simple, immediate answer Row lock contention, timeouts at peak
Kafka partitioned by auction_id Bids are queued; one consumer per partition processes in order Durable, strict per-auction order, absorbs spikes Async, client waits for result
Redis per-auction Lua Atomic compare-and-set in memory, then persist Very fast Must handle Redis loss carefully

Recommended for large scale: write each bid to Kafka with key auction_id. Kafka guarantees order inside a partition, and all bids for one auction land in the same partition. A single consumer per partition processes bids one by one, so there is no lock contention at all, and the arrival order is the fairness order. The bid is durable the moment Kafka acks it, so a DB hiccup does not lose it.

 Bid API --(key=auction_id)--> Kafka topic "bids" (64 partitions)
                                 | p0 | p1 | ... | p63 |
                                   |
                       Bid Processor (one per partition)
                         - compare with in-memory max
                         - conditional UPDATE in Postgres
                         - publish result
                                   |
                     +-------------+--------------+
                     v                            v
            Redis pub/sub (viewers)     result to bidder (SSE)
# Bid processor loop, one consumer per partition
for msg in consumer:                     # ordered per auction
    bid = json.loads(msg.value)
    accepted = conditional_update(bid)   # SQL from previous deep dive
    publish(f"auction:{bid['auction_id']}", bid, accepted)
    consumer.commit()                    # after DB commit

The client gets a fast 202 Accepted with a bid ID, and the final accepted/rejected result arrives on its SSE stream, usually within 100 ms. Processing is at-least-once, so the bid ID is the primary key and a replayed message is ignored.

For a medium-scale interview answer, it is fine to start with direct conditional updates and say “if one auction gets hot, I put Kafka in front, partitioned by auction ID”.

How do viewers see new bids in real time?

Option How Pros Cons
Polling every 2 s GET /auction/{id} repeatedly Simple, cacheable Wasteful, up to 2 s stale
Long polling Request hangs until change Fewer requests Reconnect after each update
Server-Sent Events One HTTP stream, server pushes One-way is all we need, works through proxies, auto-reconnect One direction only
WebSocket Full duplex socket Two-way More complex, sticky connections

Recommended: SSE. Viewers only need to receive updates; bids go through normal POST. Each Realtime server holds many SSE connections and subscribes to Redis pub/sub channels only for auctions its clients watch.

# Realtime server (async)
async def stream(request, auction_id):
    sub = redis.pubsub()
    await sub.subscribe(f"auction:{auction_id}")
    async def events():
        async for m in sub.listen():
            if m["type"] == "message":
                yield f"event: bid\ndata: {m['data']}\n\n"
    return EventSourceResponse(events())

Scaling note: 50,000 watchers on one hot auction spread over 50 Realtime servers means the Bid Processor publishes once, Redis delivers to 50 subscribers, each server writes to 1,000 sockets. Coalesce updates (send at most 5 per second per auction) so a bidding war does not flood phones.

How do we end auctions exactly on time?

The problem: 1 million auctions end per day, and the end must be precise. A bid at 17:59:59.900 must count; a bid at 18:00:00.100 must not.

Option How Pros Cons
Cron scanning the DB every minute WHERE end_time < now() Simple Up to 60 s late, heavy query
Delayed message queue (SQS delay, Kafka timer) Message delivered at end time Precise, scalable Delay limits (SQS max 15 min)
Redis sorted set by end time Poller pops due auctions every 100 ms Precise, cheap Needs a durable backup

Recommended: two layers. The truth is in the DB: every bid checks end_time > now() in its own SQL, so no late bid is ever accepted even if the closer is slow. The closer only does housekeeping (mark ended, notify), so a delay of a second there is harmless. A worker scans a Redis sorted set (score = end time) for auctions due in the next second; a slow DB sweep every few minutes catches anything missed.

while True:
    now = time.time()
    due = r.zrangebyscore("auction_end", 0, now, start=0, num=500)
    for aid in due:
        if r.zrem("auction_end", aid):           # claim it
            close_auction(aid)                    # idempotent SQL
    time.sleep(0.1)
-- close_auction is idempotent
UPDATE auctions SET status = 'ended'
 WHERE auction_id = :id AND status = 'active' AND end_time <= now();

Many auction sites also add “soft close”: a bid in the last 2 minutes extends the end time by 2 minutes, which kills sniping. If you support it, the bid update also bumps end_time and re-scores the sorted set.

How do we handle read load with caching?

Reads are 100x writes. Cache the auction page (item, image URLs, current max) in Redis with key auction:{id}. The Bid Processor updates the cached current_max_bid right after a successful DB commit (write-through), so the cache is never far behind. Static parts (title, images) go to the CDN. Cache staleness of a second is fine for viewing because the authoritative check happens at bid time in the DB.

9. Common mistakes and interviewer follow-ups

  • Mistake: reading the max bid, comparing in code, then writing. Two bidders race and the lower bid can win. Say: “the comparison happens inside the UPDATE’s WHERE clause, so the DB serializes it.”
  • Mistake: storing money as floats. Rounding errors create disputes. Say: “integer cents or NUMERIC.”
  • Mistake: relying only on the closer job to stop bids. If it is late, late bids get accepted. Say: “each bid checks end_time > now() itself; the closer is just cleanup.”
  • Mistake: polling every second for live updates. 50k watchers x 1 req/s is 50k QPS for one item. Say: “SSE plus pub/sub, publish once, fan out per server.”
  • Mistake: no idempotency on bid retries. A network retry could create duplicate bid rows. Say: “Idempotency-Key header, bid_id as primary key.”
  • Mistake: one global Kafka partition. It kills throughput. Say: “partition by auction_id; order only matters within one auction.”
  • Follow-up: “How would you add proxy (automatic) bidding?” Store each user’s max secretly; on a new bid, the processor computes the result of all proxies and writes only the final price, still one ordered step per auction.
  • Follow-up: “What about clock differences between servers?” Use the DB’s now() (or the Kafka broker timestamp) as the single clock, never the client’s.

10. One-page cheat sheet

Topic Key point
Scale 10M active auctions, ~1.2k bids/s avg, 1k/s on one hot item
Reads vs writes ~100:1, cache auction page in Redis + CDN
Correctness UPDATE ... WHERE :amount > current_max_bid (one atomic statement)
Alternative Optimistic locking with version column, retry on 0 rows
Hot auctions Kafka keyed by auction_id, one consumer per partition, ordered
Fairness Server arrival order (Kafka offset), DB clock
Real time SSE + Redis pub/sub, coalesce to ~5 updates/s
Ending Bid SQL checks end_time; Redis ZSET closer + DB sweep
Anti-sniping Soft close: extend end by 2 min on late bids
Idempotency Idempotency-Key, bid_id primary key
Money Integer cents / NUMERIC
CAP CP for bid acceptance, AP for viewing

15. YouTube (Medium)

YouTube lets anyone upload a video and lets anyone else watch it, on any device, on any network speed. The two user actions sound simple, “upload” and “watch”, but the files are huge (up to tens of gigabytes), uploads fail halfway, raw video does not play on every phone, and hundreds of millions of people watch every day. The interviewer is really testing whether you can design a large file upload pipeline, a transcoding (format conversion) pipeline, adaptive bitrate streaming so playback never stalls, and a CDN strategy to serve it all cheaply.

1. Functional requirements

Core (must have):

  1. Users can upload a video (up to tens of GB) with a title and description.
  2. Users can watch (stream) a video smoothly on web and mobile, even on slow networks.
  3. Uploads can be resumed after a network failure without starting over.
  4. Users see a view count on each video.

Below the line (out of scope):

  1. Search, recommendations, comments, subscriptions. Each is its own system.
  2. Live streaming. Different latency problem (seconds, not minutes, to publish).
  3. Content moderation and copyright matching. Important, but an async ML side pipeline.
  4. Monetization and ads.

2. Non-functional requirements

  1. Availability over consistency (AP): watching must be up 99.99%. It is fine if a new video takes a few minutes to appear or a view count lags.
  2. Large files: support uploads up to 50 GB.
  3. Low latency playback: video starts in under 2 seconds (p95), and rebuffering stays under 1% of watch time.
  4. Works on bad networks: quality adapts automatically from 144p to 4K.
  5. Scale: 1 million uploads per day, 100 million videos watched per day (closer to billions in real YouTube).
  6. Durability: an uploaded video is never lost (11 nines in object storage).
  7. Processing time: a 10 minute video is watchable within about 10 minutes of upload finishing.

3. Back-of-the-envelope estimates

Assumption Number
Uploads per day 1,000,000
Average raw video size 500 MB
Output renditions (144p … 4K) total size vs raw ~1.5x raw
Videos watched per day 100,000,000
Average watch time 5 minutes
Average streaming bitrate 3 Mbps
Metadata per video 2 KB 
Upload bandwidth:
  1M x 500 MB / 86,400 s     = ~5.8 GB/s = ~46 Gbps ingress

Storage per day:
  raw:         1M x 500 MB    = 500 TB
  renditions:  500 TB x 1.5   = 750 TB
  total                       = ~1.25 PB/day -> ~450 PB/year

Streaming egress:
  100M views x 300 s x 3 Mbps = 9e10 Mbit/day
  / 86,400 s                  = ~1 Tbps average (peak ~3 Tbps)
  -> only a CDN can serve this

Metadata:
  write QPS: 1M / 86,400       = ~12/s
  read QPS:  100M / 86,400     = ~1,200/s (x5 peak = 6k/s)
  storage:   1M x 2 KB x 365   = ~730 GB/year

The takeaways: metadata is small and easy; video bytes are enormous and must never pass through our app servers.

4. Core entities

  • User: uploader or viewer. Fields: user_id, name.
  • Video: the logical video. Fields: video_id, uploader_id, title, description, status (uploading, processing, ready, failed), duration.
  • Upload: one in-progress upload. Fields: upload_id, video_id, total_size, chunk_size, chunks_done.
  • Rendition: one encoded version. Fields: video_id, resolution, bitrate, codec, manifest_url.
  • Segment: a 2-6 second piece of one rendition stored in object storage.
  • ViewCount: aggregated views per video.
CREATE TABLE videos (
  video_id     TEXT PRIMARY KEY,
  uploader_id  BIGINT NOT NULL,
  title        TEXT NOT NULL,
  description  TEXT,
  status       TEXT NOT NULL,          -- uploading/processing/ready
  duration_s   INT,
  master_manifest_url TEXT,
  created_at   TIMESTAMPTZ DEFAULT now()
);

CREATE TABLE uploads (
  upload_id    TEXT PRIMARY KEY,       -- S3 multipart upload id
  video_id     TEXT REFERENCES videos,
  total_bytes  BIGINT,
  chunk_bytes  INT,                    -- e.g. 16 MB
  parts_done   INT[]                   -- list of completed part numbers
);

5. API design

POST /v1/videos – start an upload, returns pre-signed chunk URLs.

// request
{ "title": "My trip", "description": "...", "file_size": 2147483648,
  "content_type": "video/mp4" }
// 201
{ "video_id": "v_abc", "upload_id": "u_123", "chunk_size": 16777216,
  "part_urls": [{ "part": 1, "url": "https://s3.../part1?sig=..." }] }

Auth: uploader JWT. Status: 201, 400 too large or bad type, 401.

GET /v1/uploads/{upload_id} – which parts are done (for resume).

{ "upload_id": "u_123", "parts_done": [1, 2, 3, 5], "missing": [4, 6] }

POST /v1/uploads/{upload_id}/complete – tell the server all parts are uploaded.

// request
{ "parts": [{ "part": 1, "etag": "\"a1b2\"" }] }
// 202
{ "video_id": "v_abc", "status": "processing" }

GET /v1/videos/{video_id} – metadata plus the playback manifest URL.

{ "video_id": "v_abc", "title": "My trip", "status": "ready",
  "manifest_url": "https://cdn.example.com/v_abc/master.m3u8",
  "views": 10234 }

Public for public videos; 404 if missing, 409 if still processing.

POST /v1/videos/{video_id}/views – record a view (fire and forget). Returns 202.

How will users upload a video?

  1. Client calls POST /v1/videos. Video Service writes a videos row with status uploading, starts an S3 multipart upload, and returns pre-signed URLs for each 16 MB part.
  2. Client PUTs parts directly to object storage, several in parallel. Our servers never touch the bytes.
  3. Client calls /complete with each part’s ETag (checksum). Video Service completes the multipart upload.
  4. Storage emits an “object created” event. Video Service sets status processing and starts the transcoding pipeline.
sequenceDiagram
    participant C as Client
    participant V as VideoService
    participant D as MetadataDB
    participant S as ObjectStore
    participant T as TranscodePipeline
    C->>V: POST /v1/videos
    V->>D: INSERT video status uploading
    V->>S: Start multipart upload
    S-->>V: upload id
    V-->>C: 201 video id and pre-signed part URLs
    loop each 16 MB part in parallel
        C->>S: PUT part
        S-->>C: ETag
    end
    C->>V: POST complete with ETags
    V->>S: Complete multipart upload
    S->>V: Object created event
    V->>D: UPDATE status processing
    V->>T: Start transcoding

How will users watch a video?

  1. Client calls GET /v1/videos/{id} and gets the master manifest URL on the CDN.
  2. The player downloads the manifest, which lists the available qualities.
  3. The player picks a quality based on measured bandwidth and downloads 4 second segments from the CDN.
  4. It keeps measuring and switches quality between segments as the network changes.

How will uploads resume after a failure?

  1. The client stores upload_id locally.
  2. After reconnecting, it calls GET /v1/uploads/{upload_id}, learns which parts are missing, and uploads only those.

How will view counts work?

  1. The player sends POST /views after a few seconds of playback.
  2. Events go to Kafka and are counted in batches (deep dive below).

7. Deep dives

How do we handle uploads of tens of GB reliably?

Option How Pros Cons
Single POST through app servers Client streams file to our API Simple App servers become a bandwidth bottleneck; one failure restarts the whole file
Single pre-signed PUT to S3 Client uploads straight to storage Offloads servers 5 GB S3 single PUT limit; no resume
Chunked multipart upload with pre-signed URLs Split into 16 MB parts, upload in parallel, track parts Resumable, parallel, no app bandwidth Client logic is more complex

Recommended: multipart upload. A 10 GB file at 16 MB parts is 640 parts. Losing the network costs at most one part. Uploading 4 parts in parallel uses the full uplink. Each part has an MD5 checksum so corruption is caught.

# client side, simplified
CHUNK = 16 * 1024 * 1024

def upload(path, upload_id, part_urls, done):
    with open(path, "rb") as f:
        for p in part_urls:
            if p["part"] in done:
                continue                      # resume: skip finished
            f.seek((p["part"] - 1) * CHUNK)
            data = f.read(CHUNK)
            resp = http.put(p["url"], data=data, timeout=60)
            resp.raise_for_status()
            save_etag(upload_id, p["part"], resp.headers["ETag"])

A small trick: let the client fingerprint the file (hash of size + first and last MB) so a user re-uploading the same file after a crash finds the old upload_id automatically.

How does the transcoding pipeline work?

The problem: a raw upload might be a 4K MOV from an iPhone. Phones on 3G need 240p H.264, smart TVs want 4K VP9 or AV1. Encoding a one hour 4K video on one machine can take hours. We need it in minutes.

The idea: split the video into short pieces, encode pieces in parallel, then stitch. This forms a DAG (directed acyclic graph) of jobs, where some steps depend on others.

                     +--> encode seg1 @ 1080p --+
 raw.mp4 --> split --+--> encode seg1 @ 720p ---+
   |        (GOP-    +--> encode seg2 @ 1080p --+--> package --> manifests
   |         aligned)+--> ...  (N x M jobs)  ---+    (HLS/DASH)   + publish
   |                                            |
   +--> extract audio --> encode AAC/Opus ------+
   +--> thumbnails
   +--> moderation / copyright scan (async)
Option Pros Cons
One worker encodes whole file Simple Very slow for long videos
Split into segments, parallel workers, DAG orchestrator Minutes even for long videos, retries per piece Need an orchestrator and segment alignment
Managed service (AWS Elemental MediaConvert) No ops Cost, less control

Recommended: a DAG orchestrator (like Temporal, Airflow, or AWS Step Functions) fans out segment x resolution jobs to a pool of worker machines via a queue. Segments are cut on keyframe (GOP) boundaries so they can be encoded independently. Each job is idempotent: its output path is deterministic, so a retry just overwrites.

# orchestrator sketch
def transcode(video_id, raw_key):
    segs = split_on_keyframes(raw_key, seconds=10)    # e.g. 360 for 1 h
    jobs = [enqueue("encode", video_id, s, r)
            for s in segs for r in ["240p","480p","720p","1080p"]]
    wait_all(jobs, retries=3)
    audio = enqueue("encode_audio", video_id, raw_key)
    wait_all([audio])
    package_hls_dash(video_id)                         # write manifests
    db.update_status(video_id, "ready")

Math: 1 hour video, 360 segments x 4 resolutions = 1,440 jobs. If each takes 30 seconds and we give it 200 workers, it finishes in about 1,440 / 200 x 30 s = 3.6 minutes.

How does adaptive bitrate streaming keep playback smooth?

Adaptive bitrate (ABR) streaming means each quality is cut into small segments (2-6 s), and a text manifest lists them. The player picks the best quality the network can sustain right now, and can switch at every segment boundary. The two standard formats are HLS (Apple, .m3u8) and MPEG-DASH (.mpd). Both work over plain HTTP, so any CDN can cache them.

Option Pros Cons
Progressive download of one MP4 Simple Stalls on slow networks, wastes data if user leaves
HLS Plays natively on iOS/Safari, widely supported Historically slightly higher latency
DASH Codec-agnostic open standard, good on Android/web Not native on Safari
CMAF segments + both manifests One set of segment files, two small manifests Slightly more packaging work

Recommended: encode once into CMAF (fragmented MP4) segments and write both an HLS and a DASH manifest pointing to them.

# master.m3u8 (HLS master playlist)
#EXTM3U
#EXT-X-STREAM-INF:BANDWIDTH=400000,RESOLUTION=426x240
240p/index.m3u8
#EXT-X-STREAM-INF:BANDWIDTH=1500000,RESOLUTION=854x480
480p/index.m3u8
#EXT-X-STREAM-INF:BANDWIDTH=3000000,RESOLUTION=1280x720
720p/index.m3u8
#EXT-X-STREAM-INF:BANDWIDTH=6000000,RESOLUTION=1920x1080
1080p/index.m3u8

# 720p/index.m3u8 (media playlist)
#EXTM3U
#EXT-X-TARGETDURATION:4
#EXTINF:4.0,
seg_00001.m4s
#EXTINF:4.0,
seg_00002.m4s
# simplified player ABR rule (throughput based)
def pick_rendition(renditions, measured_bps, buffer_s):
    safety = 0.8 if buffer_s > 10 else 0.5     # be careful when buffer low
    ok = [r for r in renditions if r.bandwidth <= measured_bps * safety]
    return max(ok, key=lambda r: r.bandwidth) if ok else renditions[0]

How do we serve 1+ Tbps of video cheaply with a CDN?

The problem: 1 Tbps average egress cannot come from one data center, and a viewer in Mumbai should not fetch bytes from Virginia.

Option Pros Cons
Serve from origin object store Simple Expensive egress, high latency far away
Third-party CDN (CloudFront, Akamai) Global, quick to adopt Cost at YouTube scale
Own edge caches inside ISPs (Google Global Cache, Netflix Open Connect) Cheapest per GB at huge scale, closest to user Big investment

Recommended: a CDN in front of the segment bucket, with a tiered cache (edge -> regional shield -> origin). Video views follow a long-tail pattern: a small set of popular videos makes most traffic, so edge hit ratios of 90%+ are common. For new viral videos, pre-warm the edge by pushing the first segments of the top renditions. Segment URLs are immutable (content never changes), so set Cache-Control: max-age=31536000, immutable. Long-tail old videos can be stored in cheaper storage classes and only a few renditions kept hot.

 viewer -> Edge PoP (hit 90%) -> Regional shield (hit 8%) -> Origin S3 (2%)

How do we count views at scale without hurting the database?

Viral videos get thousands of views per second. UPDATE videos SET views = views + 1 would lock one row thousands of times per second.

Option Pros Cons
Increment DB row per view Exact, simple Hot row, slow
Redis INCR per video Fast Memory only, lose on crash unless persisted
Kafka events + stream aggregation, batch write Scales, durable, allows dedup and fraud filtering Counts lag by seconds to minutes

Recommended: send view events to Kafka, aggregate per video in a stream processor (Flink) every 10 seconds, and add the totals to the DB and a Redis cache. Real YouTube also validates views (bots, refresh spam), which this pipeline makes possible.

# stream job: tumbling 10 s window
counts = defaultdict(int)
for ev in kafka.consume("views", window_s=10):
    if is_valid(ev):            # dedup by (user, video, 30 s)
        counts[ev.video_id] += 1
for vid, n in counts.items():
    db.execute("UPDATE videos SET views = views + %s WHERE video_id=%s",
               n, vid)
    redis.incrby(f"views:{vid}", n)

What happens when transcoding workers fail?

Each job is a message on a queue with a visibility timeout. If a worker crashes, the message reappears and another worker picks it up. Jobs write to deterministic paths, so a duplicate run is harmless. After 3 failures a job goes to a dead letter queue, and the video is marked failed with an alert. The raw file stays in storage, so we can always re-run the whole DAG.

9. Common mistakes and interviewer follow-ups

  • Mistake: sending video bytes through API servers. 46 Gbps of uploads would need a huge fleet. Say: “pre-signed URLs, client uploads straight to object storage.”
  • Mistake: one huge upload request. A failure at 95% restarts from zero. Say: “multipart chunks, track finished parts, resume.”
  • Mistake: storing one MP4 and streaming it. It stalls on slow networks. Say: “ABR with HLS/DASH, 4 s segments, several renditions.”
  • Mistake: encoding the whole video on one machine. A 1 hour 4K video takes hours. Say: “split on keyframes, fan out to many workers, DAG with retries.”
  • Mistake: counting views with a DB update per view. Hot row locks. Say: “Kafka plus windowed aggregation, batch writes.”
  • Mistake: forgetting the CDN math. 1 Tbps from origin is impossible and expensive. Say: “edge + shield caches, immutable segment URLs, 90%+ hit ratio.”
  • Follow-up: “How do you save storage?” Answer: keep fewer renditions for rarely watched videos, move old raw files to cold storage, and re-encode popular videos with AV1 for 30% smaller files.
  • Follow-up: “How do you make a video playable faster?” Answer: publish the low resolutions first, then add higher ones to the manifest as they finish.

10. One-page cheat sheet

Topic Key point
Scale 1M uploads/day, 100M views/day
Upload ingress ~46 Gbps; storage ~1.25 PB/day
Egress ~1 Tbps avg, CDN required
Metadata Tiny: ~12 writes/s, ~6k reads/s peak
Upload Multipart, 16 MB parts, pre-signed URLs, resumable
Transcode Split on keyframes, DAG, parallel workers, idempotent jobs
Formats CMAF segments, HLS (.m3u8) + DASH (.mpd), 2-6 s segments
ABR Player picks rendition by bandwidth and buffer
CDN Edge -> shield -> origin, immutable URLs, pre-warm viral
Views Kafka + Flink 10 s windows, batch DB updates
Failures Queue retries, DLQ, raw kept for re-run
CAP AP; new video can take minutes to appear

16. Job Scheduler (Medium)

A distributed job scheduler is “cron for a whole company”. Users say “run this task now”, “run it at 3 pm Friday”, or “run it every day at 10 am”, and the system makes sure it runs on time on some worker machine, records whether it worked, and retries if it failed. Think Airflow, AWS EventBridge Scheduler, or Kubernetes CronJobs at large scale. The interviewer is really testing scheduling precision (running jobs within a couple of seconds of their time when there are billions of future jobs), at-least-once execution without accidental double runs, and how workers fail and recover.

1. Functional requirements

Two terms first. A task is the reusable piece of work, like “send an email”. A job is one scheduled instance of a task with parameters and a time, like “send an email to john@example.com at 10:00 Friday”. Each actual run of a job is an execution.

Core (must have):

  1. Users can schedule a job to run immediately, at a future time, or on a recurring schedule (a cron expression such as 0 10 * * *).
  2. Users can see the status of each job and its executions (pending, running, succeeded, failed) with logs.
  3. Failed executions are retried with backoff, then moved to a dead letter queue.
  4. Users can cancel a job.

Below the line (out of scope):

  1. DAGs of dependent jobs (job B after job A). That is a workflow engine, a layer on top.
  2. Resource-aware placement (GPUs, memory). Assume homogeneous workers.
  3. Multi-tenant billing and quotas.

2. Non-functional requirements

  1. Precision: a job starts within 2 seconds of its scheduled time (p99).
  2. Throughput: 10,000 job executions per second at peak.
  3. Reliability: at-least-once execution. A scheduled job is never silently skipped. Duplicate runs are rare and handled with idempotency.
  4. Durability: once the API returns 201, the job survives any single machine or zone failure.
  5. Availability: 99.9% for scheduling API; execution keeps going even if the API is down.
  6. Status reads may be eventually consistent (a few seconds old).
  7. CAP: the job store prefers consistency for claiming work (two workers must not both believe they own a job for long), while status views are AP.

3. Back-of-the-envelope estimates

Assumption Number
Peak executions per second 10,000
Average executions per second 2,000
Job definition size 1 KB
Execution record size 500 B
Average job runtime 30 s
Retention of execution history 1 year 
Executions per day:
  2,000/s x 86,400              = ~173M per day

Storage for executions:
  173M x 500 B                  = ~86 GB/day
  x 365                         = ~31 TB/year  -> partition by time

Concurrent running jobs (Little's law: L = rate x time):
  10,000/s x 30 s               = 300,000 running at peak
  if one worker runs 50 jobs at once -> 6,000 workers at peak

Scheduler reads:
  every 1 s, fetch jobs due in next window
  10,000 due per second -> one indexed range query per second per shard

4. Core entities

  • Task: the code to run. Fields: task_id, name, handler (container image or function), default timeout.
  • Job: a schedule for a task. Fields: job_id, user_id, task_id, params, schedule (one-off time or cron), next_run_at, status (active, paused, cancelled).
  • Execution: one run. Fields: execution_id, job_id, scheduled_at, status, attempt, worker_id, started_at, finished_at, error.
  • Worker: a machine that runs executions. Fields: worker_id, heartbeat_at, capacity.
  • Lease: a time-limited claim of an execution by a worker.
CREATE TABLE jobs (
  job_id       UUID PRIMARY KEY,
  user_id      BIGINT NOT NULL,
  task_id      TEXT NOT NULL,
  params       JSONB,
  cron_expr    TEXT,                  -- null for one-off jobs
  next_run_at  TIMESTAMPTZ NOT NULL,
  status       TEXT NOT NULL DEFAULT 'active'
);

CREATE TABLE executions (
  execution_id  UUID PRIMARY KEY,
  job_id        UUID NOT NULL,
  scheduled_at  TIMESTAMPTZ NOT NULL,
  status        TEXT NOT NULL,        -- pending/running/succeeded/failed
  attempt       INT NOT NULL DEFAULT 0,
  worker_id     TEXT,
  lease_until   TIMESTAMPTZ,
  error         TEXT,
  UNIQUE (job_id, scheduled_at)       -- one execution per tick
);
CREATE INDEX ON executions (status, scheduled_at);

The UNIQUE (job_id, scheduled_at) constraint is quietly important: it stops two schedulers from creating the same execution twice.

5. API design

POST /v1/jobs – create a job.

// request
{ "task_id": "send_email",
  "params": { "to": "john@example.com", "template": "weekly" },
  "schedule": { "type": "cron", "expr": "0 10 * * *",
                "tz": "America/New_York" },
  "max_retries": 3, "timeout_s": 300 }
// 201
{ "job_id": "j_42", "next_run_at": "2026-11-04T15:00:00Z" }

schedule.type can be immediate, at (with run_at), or cron. Status: 201, 400 bad cron, 401. Auth: user JWT; header Idempotency-Key makes retries of this call safe.

GET /v1/jobs/{job_id} – job definition and next run. 200 / 404.

GET /v1/jobs/{job_id}/executions?status=failed&cursor=... – execution history, newest first.

{ "executions": [
    { "execution_id": "e_9", "scheduled_at": "2026-11-03T15:00:00Z",
      "status": "failed", "attempt": 3, "error": "SMTP timeout" } ],
  "next_cursor": "e_8" }

DELETE /v1/jobs/{job_id} – cancel future runs. Returns 204.

How will users schedule a job?

  1. Client calls POST /v1/jobs.
  2. Job API validates the cron expression and computes next_run_at in UTC.
  3. It inserts the job row. If next_run_at is within the next few minutes, it also creates the execution right away (see two-tier design below).
  4. Returns 201 with the job ID.
sequenceDiagram
    participant U as User
    participant A as JobAPI
    participant D as JobDB
    participant R as RedisDueSet
    U->>A: POST /v1/jobs with Idempotency-Key
    A->>A: Validate cron and compute next run in UTC
    A->>D: INSERT job row
    D-->>A: ok
    alt next run within a few minutes
        A->>D: INSERT pending execution
        A->>R: ZADD execution with run time score
    end
    A-->>U: 201 job id and next run time

How will jobs actually run?

  1. The Scheduler finds executions whose time has arrived.
  2. It puts each one on a queue.
  3. A free worker pulls a message, marks the execution running with a lease, and runs the task.
  4. On success it marks succeeded. On failure it schedules a retry or marks failed.
  5. For recurring jobs, after creating an execution, the Scheduler computes the next cron time and updates jobs.next_run_at.

How will users monitor jobs?

  1. Workers write status and a pointer to logs (stored in S3) on the execution row.
  2. GET /executions reads from the DB, or a read replica, by job_id.

7. Deep dives

How do we start jobs within 2 seconds of their scheduled time?

The problem: there might be billions of future jobs. Polling the database every second with WHERE next_run_at <= now() across all of them is heavy, and polling less often makes jobs late.

Option How Pros Cons
Poll DB every second Range query on index Simple Heavy DB load at scale, lock contention between pollers
Poll DB every minute Cheaper Simple Up to 60 s late
Two-tier: DB + in-memory/Redis sorted set Every few min load jobs due soon into a fast timer store; fire from there Precise and cheap Two components to keep in sync
Delayed queue (SQS delay up to 15 min) Message invisible until due Managed, precise 15 min max delay, so still needs a DB tier

Recommended: two tiers.

  • Tier 1 (durable): the database holds every job and execution. Every 5 minutes, a watcher queries “executions due in the next 5 minutes” and loads them into tier 2.
  • Tier 2 (precise): a Redis sorted set where the score is the run time (epoch ms). A loop checks every 100-500 ms for items whose score is now or earlier and pushes them to the work queue.
 Job DB  --(every 5 min: due in next 5 min)-->  Redis ZSET "due"
                                                 score = run_at ms
                                                     |
                               every 200 ms: ZRANGEBYSCORE 0 now
                                                     v
                                               Work queue -> workers

Popping must be atomic so two scheduler instances never both take the same item. A small Lua script does “get due items and remove them” in one step:

-- KEYS[1] = due zset, KEYS[2] = ready list
-- ARGV[1] = now_ms, ARGV[2] = batch size
local items = redis.call('ZRANGEBYSCORE', KEYS[1], 0, ARGV[1],
                         'LIMIT', 0, ARGV[2])
for _, id in ipairs(items) do
  redis.call('ZREM', KEYS[1], id)
  redis.call('LPUSH', KEYS[2], id)
end
return #items

A job created for “in 30 seconds” skips the 5 minute wait: the API inserts it into the DB and also directly into the Redis set. If Redis is lost, the next watcher pass reloads everything still pending from the DB, so nothing is skipped, just delayed by up to one pass.

An alternative Hello Interview mentions is replacing Redis with SQS delayed messages (delay up to 15 minutes), which removes the need to run Redis yourself.

How do we guarantee at-least-once execution?

At-least-once means every job runs one or more times; never zero. The danger points are: the scheduler crashes after reading a job but before enqueuing it, or a worker crashes halfway through.

Failure Protection
Scheduler crashes before enqueue Execution row stays pending in DB; next watcher pass re-adds it
Queue loses message Use a durable queue (SQS, Kafka); DB sweep for old pending rows
Worker crashes mid-run Lease expires, message becomes visible again, another worker retries
Worker hangs forever Timeout per task; lease not renewed, so it is reclaimed
Task throws an error Retry with exponential backoff, then dead letter

Leases are the core idea. A worker does not own an execution forever; it owns it until lease_until, and it renews the lease with a heartbeat every few seconds while running.

-- claim: only succeeds if no one else holds a live lease
UPDATE executions
   SET status = 'running', worker_id = :me,
       lease_until = now() + interval '30 seconds',
       attempt = attempt + 1
 WHERE execution_id = :id
   AND (status = 'pending'
        OR (status = 'running' AND lease_until < now()))
RETURNING attempt;
def run(execution_id):
    if not claim(execution_id):           # 0 rows -> someone else has it
        return
    stop = start_heartbeat(execution_id, every_s=10)  # extend lease
    try:
        execute_task(execution_id, timeout_s=300)
        mark(execution_id, "succeeded")
    except Exception as e:
        handle_failure(execution_id, e)
    finally:
        stop()

With SQS, the visibility timeout plays the same role: a message received but not deleted becomes visible again after the timeout. Workers extend it with ChangeMessageVisibility while working.

How do we prevent duplicate execution, and what if it happens anyway?

At-least-once means duplicates are possible (a worker finishes the work but crashes before marking success, so the lease expires and someone runs it again). We reduce them and make them harmless.

Layer Technique
Creating executions UNIQUE (job_id, scheduled_at) so two schedulers cannot create the same tick
Claiming Conditional UPDATE / lease, so only one live owner
Stale owner Fencing token: the attempt number. Side effects carry it, and old attempts are rejected
Side effects Idempotency key = execution_id passed to downstream APIs 
# task code: make side effects idempotent
def send_email(execution_id, to, template):
    # the email provider dedups on this key for 24 h
    provider.send(to=to, template=template,
                  idempotency_key=str(execution_id))

The honest answer to “can you guarantee exactly once?” is: not across a network with crashes. You get at-least-once delivery plus idempotent handlers, which is “effectively once”.

How do retries and the dead letter queue work?

Option Pros Cons
Immediate retry Fast recovery from blips Hammers a broken dependency
Fixed delay Simple Many jobs retry at the same moment
Exponential backoff with jitter Spreads load, gives systems time to recover Slower recovery

Recommended: exponential backoff with jitter (random spread). Retry is just scheduling a new attempt time back into the same sorted set.

import random

def handle_failure(execution_id, err, max_retries=3, base_s=10):
    ex = load(execution_id)
    if ex.attempt >= max_retries:
        mark(execution_id, "failed", error=str(err))
        dlq.send(execution_id)                 # humans / alerts look here
        return
    delay = base_s * (2 ** (ex.attempt - 1))    # 10, 20, 40 s
    delay = random.uniform(0, delay)            # full jitter
    reschedule(execution_id, run_at=now() + delay, status="pending")

The dead letter queue holds executions that failed all attempts. Operators get an alert, can inspect the error, fix the bug, and re-drive (re-enqueue) them.

How does the system scale to 10k executions per second?

  1. Partition the job store. Shard the DB (or use DynamoDB) by job_id. Each watcher instance owns a set of shards, so range queries stay small. A DynamoDB-style design uses a partition key of time bucket (for example the minute) plus a random suffix, so “due this minute” is a few targeted queries.
  2. Multiple scheduler instances. Each owns a subset of shards, assigned by a coordinator (ZooKeeper, etcd, or a simple lease table). If one dies, its shards move to another within seconds.
  3. Queue in the middle. The queue decouples “it is time” from “a worker is free”. Spikes (every job at midnight) just make the queue deeper for a minute.
  4. Autoscale workers on queue depth. 300,000 concurrent runs at peak, about 6,000 workers at 50 slots each. Scale up when queue age passes a few seconds.
  5. Spread hot times. Many users pick 0 0 * * *. Allow users to opt into jitter (“run between 00:00 and 00:05”) to flatten the midnight spike.
 Watchers (one per shard group)
   W1: shards 0-31   W2: shards 32-63   W3: shards 64-95
       \                 |                  /
        +--> Redis ZSET (sharded) --> SQS --> autoscaled workers

9. Common mistakes and interviewer follow-ups

  • Mistake: polling the whole DB every second. At billions of rows it melts the DB. Say: “two tiers: DB for durability, sorted set for the next few minutes.”
  • Mistake: claiming “exactly once”. It cannot be guaranteed with crashes. Say: “at-least-once plus idempotent tasks keyed by execution_id.”
  • Mistake: a worker deletes the queue message before running the job. A crash then loses the job. Say: “delete or ack only after success; use leases and visibility timeouts.”
  • Mistake: no lease expiry. A crashed worker’s job is stuck “running” forever. Say: “lease_until plus heartbeats; expired leases are reclaimable.”
  • Mistake: storing cron times in local time. Daylight saving makes jobs skip or double. Say: “store the cron with a time zone, compute next_run_at in UTC.”
  • Mistake: retrying instantly forever. It floods a broken dependency. Say: “exponential backoff with jitter, max retries, DLQ.”
  • Follow-up: “What if the whole Redis tier is lost?” Answer: executions are still pending in the DB; the next watcher pass reloads them, so the worst case is a few minutes late, never skipped.
  • Follow-up: “How do you support job dependencies?” Answer: a workflow layer marks a child job runnable only when parents succeed, then hands it to this same scheduler.

10. One-page cheat sheet

Topic Key point
Terms Task = code, Job = schedule + params, Execution = one run
Scale 10k exec/s peak, ~173M/day, ~31 TB/year history
Concurrency 10k/s x 30 s = 300k running, ~6k workers
Precision Two-tier: DB (5 min scan) + Redis ZSET (200 ms pop)
Atomic pop Lua: ZRANGEBYSCORE + ZREM in one step
No dup ticks UNIQUE (job_id, scheduled_at)
Ownership Leases + heartbeats; conditional UPDATE to claim
Guarantee At-least-once + idempotent handlers
Retries Exponential backoff + jitter, max 3, then DLQ
Scaling Shard store by job_id, watchers own shards, queue, autoscale
Time zones Cron with tz, next_run_at in UTC
CAP Consistent claims, eventually consistent status

17. Facebook Live Comments (Medium)

While someone streams a live video on Facebook, viewers type comments and everyone watching sees those comments scroll by almost instantly. A new viewer who joins late can also scroll back to see earlier comments. The interviewer is really testing real-time push at large scale: how you deliver a comment to possibly millions of viewers of one video in under 200 ms, which transport you choose (polling, Server-Sent Events, WebSockets), how you route messages only to the servers that need them, and how you store and page through comments.

1. Functional requirements

Core (must have):

  1. Viewers can post a comment on a live video.
  2. Viewers see new comments in near real time while watching.
  3. Viewers can load comments posted before they joined (scroll back).

Below the line (out of scope):

  1. Replies and reactions on comments. Same pipeline, more event types.
  2. Spam and hate speech moderation. An async classifier that can hide comments after the fact.
  3. Comments on recorded (non-live) videos. A normal paginated read, much easier.
  4. The live video stream itself. Owned by a separate video team.

2. Non-functional requirements

  1. Low latency: a comment reaches other viewers within 200 ms p95 (humans perceive under 200 ms as instant).
  2. Scale: millions of concurrent live videos, up to thousands of comments per second on one video, and millions of viewers on the most popular video.
  3. Availability over consistency (AP): 99.99% for watching comments. It is fine if two viewers see a slightly different order or a comment arrives a second late.
  4. Durability: a posted comment is stored and visible later (no loss after 201).
  5. Read history fast: loading the last 50 comments takes under 100 ms.
  6. Graceful degradation: on a giant video, it is acceptable to show a sample of comments rather than every single one.

3. Back-of-the-envelope estimates

Assumption Number
Concurrent live videos 1,000,000
Concurrent viewers total 100,000,000
Average comments per video per second 1
Hot video: viewers 5,000,000
Hot video: comments per second 2,000
Comment size 200 B
Connections per realtime server 100,000 
Write QPS:
  1M videos x 1 comment/s          = 1M comments/s total (peak)

Fanout (deliveries):
  average video: 100 viewers x 1/s  = 100 deliveries/s per video
  total: 100M viewers x ~1 msg/s    = ~100M deliveries/s
  hot video: 5M viewers x 2,000/s   = 10 BILLION deliveries/s  (!!)
    -> impossible to send all; we must sample/batch (deep dive)

Connections:
  100M viewers / 100k per server    = 1,000 realtime servers

Storage:
  1M/s x 200 B                      = 200 MB/s
  x 86,400                          = ~17 TB/day

The hot video line is the whole interview: you cannot push every comment to every viewer.

4. Core entities

  • User: a viewer or broadcaster. Fields: user_id, name, avatar_url.
  • LiveVideo: the stream being commented on. Fields: video_id, broadcaster_id, status (live, ended). Owned by another team.
  • Comment: one message. Fields: comment_id, video_id, author_id, text, created_at.
  • Connection: one viewer’s open real-time stream. Fields: connection_id, user_id, video_id, server_id.
-- Cassandra / DynamoDB style: partition by video, cluster by time
CREATE TABLE comments (
  video_id    BIGINT,
  comment_id  TIMEUUID,          -- time-ordered unique id
  author_id   BIGINT,
  text        TEXT,
  PRIMARY KEY ((video_id), comment_id)
) WITH CLUSTERING ORDER BY (comment_id DESC);
{
  "comment_id": "01JC8Z7Q5R9X2M3N4P5Q6R7S8T",
  "video_id": 123,
  "author": { "id": 42, "name": "Alice", "avatar": "https://cdn/.../42.jpg" },
  "text": "This is amazing",
  "created_at": "2026-11-03T21:40:00.123Z"
}

5. API design

POST /v1/videos/{video_id}/comments – post a comment.

// request
{ "text": "This is amazing" }
// 201
{ "comment_id": "01JC8Z7Q...", "created_at": "2026-11-03T21:40:00.123Z" }

Auth: session token or JWT; the author ID comes from the token, never the body. Status: 201, 400 empty or too long (over 500 chars), 404 video not live, 429 rate limited.

GET /v1/videos/{video_id}/comments?before={comment_id}&limit=50 – older comments (scroll back), newest first.

{ "comments": [ { "comment_id": "01JC8Z...", "text": "..." } ],
  "next_cursor": "01JC8Y..." }

GET /v1/videos/{video_id}/comments/stream – Server-Sent Events stream of new comments.

id: 01JC8Z7Q5R9X2M3N4P5Q6R7S8T
event: comment
data: {"comment_id":"01JC8Z7Q...","author":{"name":"Alice"},"text":"Hi"}

The id: line lets the browser send Last-Event-ID on reconnect, so the server can fill the gap.

How will viewers post a comment?

  1. Client calls POST /comments. Gateway authenticates and rate limits (for example 1 comment per 2 seconds per user).
  2. Comment Service generates a time-ordered ID, writes the comment to Cassandra under partition video_id.
  3. It publishes the comment to the pub/sub channel video:{video_id}.
  4. Returns 201. The client shows its own comment immediately (optimistic UI).
sequenceDiagram
    participant V as Viewer
    participant G as Gateway
    participant C as CommentService
    participant D as Cassandra
    participant P as PubSub
    participant R as RealtimeServer
    V->>G: POST comment
    G->>G: Authenticate and rate limit
    G->>C: Forward comment
    C->>C: Generate time ordered ID
    C->>D: Write to partition video id
    D-->>C: ok
    C->>P: Publish to video channel
    C-->>G: 201 comment id
    G-->>V: 201 and show comment optimistically
    P->>R: Deliver comment to subscribed servers

How will viewers see new comments in real time?

  1. When a viewer opens the video, the client opens an SSE connection to a Realtime server.
  2. That server records “connection C watches video V” in memory and subscribes to channel video:V if it is not already subscribed.
  3. When a comment is published on video:V, the server receives it once and writes it to every local connection watching V.

How will viewers see comments from before they joined?

  1. On open, the client calls GET /comments?limit=50 to fill the screen with the latest 50.
  2. Scrolling up calls the same endpoint with before=<oldest id on screen>.
  3. Cassandra reads one partition in clustering order, which is a fast sequential read.

7. Deep dives

Which real-time transport should we use?

Option How Latency Cost Fit
Short polling Client GETs every 2-3 s 0-3 s Huge request volume, mostly empty Poor
Long polling Request waits until data or timeout Low Re-open after each message, header overhead OK fallback
Server-Sent Events One HTTP response stays open, server writes events Low One connection, plain HTTP, auto reconnect with Last-Event-ID Great for one-way
WebSocket Full duplex TCP channel Low Needs upgrade, sticky routing, custom reconnect Great for two-way chat

Recommended: SSE. Comments flow mostly from server to client: thousands of reads per write. Posting is rare, so a normal POST is fine. SSE runs over regular HTTP/2, passes through proxies and CDNs easily, and the browser handles reconnect. WebSocket is a fine answer too if you explain the choice; it shines when the client sends often (multiplayer games, collaborative editing).

# Realtime server: one coroutine per connection (FastAPI style)
@app.get("/v1/videos/{vid}/comments/stream")
async def stream(vid: int, request: Request):
    q = asyncio.Queue(maxsize=200)
    local_subs[vid].add(q)
    await ensure_subscribed(vid)              # pub/sub channel once
    async def gen():
        try:
            while not await request.is_disconnected():
                c = await q.get()
                yield f"id: {c['comment_id']}\nevent: comment\n" \
                      f"data: {json.dumps(c)}\n\n"
        finally:
            local_subs[vid].discard(q)
    return StreamingResponse(gen(), media_type="text/event-stream")

How do we route a comment only to the servers that need it?

The problem: 1,000 realtime servers. Viewers of video V are scattered across them. If every comment is broadcast to all 1,000 servers, each server processes 1M comments per second, almost all for videos it has no viewers for.

Option How Pros Cons
Broadcast to all servers Every server gets every comment Simple 1,000x wasted work
Pub/sub channel per video Server subscribes to video:V only when it has a viewer of V Each server only gets relevant comments Many channels; subscription churn
Partitioned pub/sub (N topics, hash(video) % N) Server subscribes to topic partitions it needs Bounded number of channels Some extra messages per partition
Colocate viewers by video on the same servers Load balancer routes by video_id Each video touches few servers, fewer subscriptions Hot video still needs many servers

Recommended: pub/sub channel per video (Redis pub/sub or a partitioned Kafka/NATS layer), combined with routing viewers of the same video to a small set of servers. With colocation, a video with 300 viewers lives on 1 server instead of 300, so that comment is delivered to 1 server, not 300.

 Without colocation:                With colocation (route by video_id):
 video V viewers on 300 servers     video V viewers on 1-3 servers

 pubsub --> S1 S2 S3 ... S300       pubsub --> S17
          (each sends to 1 viewer)            (sends to 300 viewers)

How to colocate: the client first asks a lightweight “which server?” endpoint, and a consistent hash ring maps video_id to a server group. Or the L7 load balancer hashes on the video_id in the path. For a video too big for one server, the ring assigns it a larger group (see next deep dive). Facebook’s own engineering talk on live comments describes a similar idea: a dispatcher layer knows which edge servers have viewers for each video and forwards only there.

How do we handle a hot video with millions of viewers?

The problem from the estimates: 5M viewers x 2,000 comments/s is 10 billion deliveries per second, and nobody can read 2,000 comments per second anyway. Phones would drown.

Option What it does Pros Cons
Deliver everything Push all 2,000/s to everyone Complete Impossible bandwidth, useless UX
Batch Server flushes every 200-500 ms as one message 10-50x fewer network writes Up to 500 ms extra delay
Sample / rank Send each viewer at most ~10-20 comments/s, prefer friends and high-quality Fits human reading speed Viewers see different subsets
Fanout tree Pub/sub -> regional relays -> edge servers Spreads the fanout over layers More hops (~10-20 ms each)

Recommended: combine all three. A fanout tree spreads delivery to the ~50 servers hosting the video’s viewers (5M / 100k). Each server batches messages every 250 ms. Each server also caps output at about 15 comments per second per connection, always keeping comments from the viewer’s friends and the broadcaster, and sampling the rest.

# per video, per realtime server: batch + sample every 250 ms
async def flush_loop(vid):
    while True:
        await asyncio.sleep(0.25)
        batch = buffers[vid].drain()           # all comments last 250 ms
        for q in local_subs[vid]:
            pick = [c for c in batch if c.author in q.friends][:4]
            rest = [c for c in batch if c not in pick]
            pick += random.sample(rest, min(len(rest), 4 - len(pick)))
            q.put_nowait({"type": "batch", "comments": pick})

Sampling is safe because all comments are stored; anyone can still scroll back through the full list. Also protect the write side: per-user rate limits and slow mode (one comment per 10 s per user) during huge events.

How do we store comments and paginate them?

Writes are append-only, and reads are “latest N for one video, then older”. That matches a wide-column store partitioned by video_id and clustered by time.

Option Pros Cons
Postgres with index (video_id, created_at) Familiar, transactions 1M writes/s needs heavy sharding
Cassandra / DynamoDB (partition = video_id) High write throughput, fast range reads Hot partitions for giant videos
Redis list of last 1,000 + cold store Very fast recent reads Second system to maintain

Recommended: Cassandra (or DynamoDB) as the source of truth, plus a Redis list of the latest 200 comments per live video for instant first page. For a giant video, split its partition by time bucket, for example (video_id, minute), so one partition does not get every write.

Cursor pagination, not offset. With OFFSET 1000, new comments arriving at the top shift everything and the user sees duplicates. A cursor (“give me comments older than this ID”) is stable and uses the index directly.

-- first page
SELECT * FROM comments WHERE video_id = ? LIMIT 50;
-- next page: strictly older than the last id we showed
SELECT * FROM comments WHERE video_id = ? AND comment_id < ? LIMIT 50;

How do we order comments, and what if a viewer disconnects?

Ordering: we promise “roughly the order they were posted”. Each comment gets a time-ordered ID at the Comment Service (TIMEUUID, ULID, or Snowflake: timestamp bits + machine bits + sequence). Clients insert by ID, so small network reordering is fixed on screen. Strict global order would require a single sequencer per video, adding latency for little user benefit.

Disconnects: phones lose signal constantly. On reconnect, the browser sends Last-Event-ID. The server reads comments newer than that ID from the Redis recent list (or Cassandra) and sends them before resuming live. If the gap is huge, it sends only the latest 50 and a “jump to live” marker.

async def resume(vid, last_id, q):
    missed = await recent_after(vid, last_id, limit=50)   # Redis/Cassandra
    for c in missed:
        q.put_nowait(c)

If a realtime server dies, its 100k clients reconnect (with random backoff to avoid a thundering herd) to other servers, which subscribe to the needed channels. Nothing is lost because comments live in the database, not in the server.

9. Common mistakes and interviewer follow-ups

  • Mistake: polling every second. 100M viewers means 100M requests per second, mostly empty. Say: “SSE, one long-lived connection per viewer.”
  • Mistake: broadcasting every comment to every realtime server. Each server drowns in irrelevant traffic. Say: “channel per video, subscribe only when you have a viewer.”
  • Mistake: trying to deliver all comments of a hot video to all viewers. 10 billion messages per second. Say: “batch every 250 ms, cap and sample per viewer, keep everything in storage.”
  • Mistake: offset pagination. New comments shift pages and cause duplicates. Say: “cursor on comment_id.”
  • Mistake: keeping comments only in server memory. A crash loses them. Say: “write to Cassandra first, then publish.”
  • Mistake: putting WebSocket in without explaining why. It is not wrong, but say why; SSE is simpler for one-way.
  • Follow-up: “How do you scale the realtime tier?” Answer: it is stateless except for connections; add servers, and reconnecting clients spread out with jittered backoff.
  • Follow-up: “Global users?” Answer: realtime servers in each region, pub/sub replicated between regions; cross-region adds ~100 ms but stays within budget.

10. One-page cheat sheet

Topic Key point
Latency target < 200 ms post-to-screen
Scale 1M live videos, 100M viewers, 1M comments/s
Connections ~100k per server, ~1,000 realtime servers
Transport SSE for receive, POST for send, Last-Event-ID on reconnect
Routing Pub/sub channel per video, subscribe on first viewer
Colocation Route viewers of one video to the same server group
Hot video Fanout tree + 250 ms batching + per-viewer sampling
Storage Cassandra, partition video_id, cluster by time-ordered id
Recent Redis list of last 200 per live video
Pagination Cursor (comment_id < ?), never offset
Ordering Approximate, time-ordered IDs, client sorts
CAP AP; eventual consistency is fine

18. News Aggregator (Medium)

A news aggregator like Google News collects articles from thousands of publishers around the world, groups articles that describe the same story, and shows each user a fresh, ranked feed they can scroll forever. Clicking a headline sends the reader to the publisher’s site. The interviewer is really testing four things: ingesting content from many sources on a schedule (crawling and RSS), detecting near-duplicate articles and clustering them into stories, ranking and personalizing the feed, and serving a feed with low latency while keeping it fresh, especially during breaking news spikes.

1. Functional requirements

Core (must have):

  1. The system ingests articles from thousands of publishers (RSS feeds, sitemaps, and web pages).
  2. Users see an aggregated feed of recent news, with duplicate articles about the same event grouped into one story.
  3. Users can scroll the feed “infinitely” (paginated).
  4. Clicking an article redirects the user to the publisher’s site.
  5. Users can view topic feeds (World, Sports, Tech) and a personalized “For you” feed.

Below the line (out of scope):

  1. Full-text search over articles. A separate Elasticsearch system.
  2. Hosting article bodies. We only keep title, snippet, image, and link (copyright and publisher traffic).
  3. Comments, sharing, paywall handling.
  4. Advanced misinformation detection. Important, but an ML pipeline of its own.

2. Non-functional requirements

  1. Freshness: a new article appears in feeds within 30 minutes of publication (target 5 minutes for major publishers).
  2. Low latency: feed requests p99 under 200 ms.
  3. Scale: 100 million daily active users, read-heavy (about 1,000 reads per article write).
  4. Spikes: breaking news can cause 10x traffic in minutes; the system must stay up.
  5. Availability over consistency (AP): 99.99% for feed reads. Two users can see slightly different feeds; a story may take a minute to merge.
  6. Politeness: never overload a publisher’s site; obey robots.txt and rate limits per domain.

3. Back-of-the-envelope estimates

Assumption Number
Publishers (sources) 50,000
New articles per day 2,000,000
Article metadata size 2 KB
DAU 100,000,000
Feed requests per user per day 10
Items per feed page 20
Feed response size 20 KB 
Ingestion:
  2M articles / 86,400 s          = ~23 new articles/s (peak ~100/s)
  polling: 50k sources every 5 min = 50,000 / 300 = ~170 fetches/s

Feed reads:
  100M x 10 / 86,400 s            = ~11,600 req/s average
  breaking news 10x               = ~120k req/s peak

Storage:
  2M x 2 KB                       = 4 GB/day
  x 365                           = ~1.5 TB/year (metadata only)
  thumbnails: 2M x 50 KB          = 100 GB/day in object storage

Bandwidth:
  11,600 x 20 KB                  = ~230 MB/s of feed JSON (CDN helps)

Reads dwarf writes, and writes are tiny. The hard parts are freshness, dedup, and caching, not raw storage.

4. Core entities

  • Source (Publisher): where news comes from. Fields: source_id, domain, feed_urls, crawl_interval, authority_score.
  • Article: one item from one publisher. Fields: article_id, source_id, url, title, snippet, image_url, published_at, simhash, category, cluster_id.
  • Story (Cluster): a group of articles about the same event. Fields: cluster_id, lead_article_id, article_ids, first_seen, last_updated, score.
  • User: a reader. Fields: user_id, followed_topics, interest vector.
  • Feed: an ordered list of story IDs for a user or topic.
CREATE TABLE articles (
  article_id    BIGINT PRIMARY KEY,
  source_id     INT NOT NULL,
  url           TEXT UNIQUE NOT NULL,      -- canonical URL
  title         TEXT NOT NULL,
  snippet       TEXT,
  image_url     TEXT,
  category      TEXT,
  published_at  TIMESTAMPTZ NOT NULL,
  simhash       BIGINT,                    -- 64-bit fingerprint
  cluster_id    BIGINT
);
CREATE INDEX ON articles (category, published_at DESC);

CREATE TABLE stories (
  cluster_id      BIGINT PRIMARY KEY,
  lead_article_id BIGINT,
  article_count   INT,
  first_seen      TIMESTAMPTZ,
  last_updated    TIMESTAMPTZ,
  score           REAL
);

5. API design

GET /v1/feed?topic=top&cursor=...&limit=20 – a page of stories for a topic, or for the user when topic=for_you.

{
  "stories": [
    { "cluster_id": 991,
      "lead": { "article_id": 5, "title": "Storm hits coast",
                "source": "Example Times", "image": "https://cdn/i/5.jpg",
                "published_at": "2026-11-03T20:55:00Z" },
      "more_coverage": 37 }
  ],
  "next_cursor": "eyJzY29yZSI6MC44MSwiaWQiOjk5MX0="
}

Auth: optional. Logged-out users get topic feeds; for_you needs a JWT. Status: 200, 400 bad cursor.

GET /v1/stories/{cluster_id} – all articles in one story (“full coverage”). 200 / 404.

GET /v1/articles/{article_id}/click – log the click and redirect.

HTTP/1.1 302 Found
Location: https://publisher.example.com/2026/11/03/storm-hits-coast

POST /v1/admin/sources – add a publisher (domain, feed URLs). Admin only. 201.

How will the system ingest articles from thousands of publishers?

  1. A scheduler reads the Source DB and enqueues “fetch this feed” tasks based on each source’s interval (popular sources every 1-5 min, small ones every 30-60 min).
  2. Crawler workers fetch RSS/Atom feeds (and sitemaps) using conditional GET (If-Modified-Since, ETag) so unchanged feeds cost almost nothing.
  3. For each new item, the crawler fetches the page to get the canonical URL, the main image, and the first paragraph.
  4. Raw articles go onto Kafka topic raw_articles.
sequenceDiagram
    participant S as Scheduler
    participant D as SourceDB
    participant C as Crawler
    participant P as Publisher
    participant K as Kafka
    S->>D: Read sources due by interval
    D-->>S: Feed URLs
    S->>C: Enqueue fetch feed task
    C->>P: Conditional GET feed with ETag
    alt feed unchanged
        P-->>C: 304 Not Modified
    else new items
        P-->>C: 200 RSS items
        C->>P: Fetch article page
        P-->>C: Canonical URL, image, first paragraph
        C->>K: Produce to raw articles topic
    end

How will users see an aggregated, de-duplicated feed?

  1. A processing consumer normalizes the article (canonical URL, clean title), computes a fingerprint, and checks for duplicates.
  2. It assigns the article to an existing story cluster or creates a new one.
  3. It classifies the category (Sports, Tech) and updates the story score.
  4. It updates per-topic ranked lists in Redis: feed:topic:tech is a sorted set of cluster IDs scored by rank.
  5. GET /feed reads the top 20 from the sorted set and hydrates story details from cache.

How will users scroll infinitely?

  1. The response includes an opaque cursor encoding the last item’s (score, id).
  2. The next request asks for items after that cursor (deep dive on stable pagination).

How will clicks redirect to publishers?

  1. The story card links to /articles/{id}/click.
  2. The service logs a click event to Kafka (used for ranking) and returns 302 to the publisher URL.

7. Deep dives

How do we crawl and ingest at scale while staying fresh and polite?

The problem: 50,000 sources, some publish every minute, some once a week. Fetching all of them every minute is 830 requests per second of mostly “nothing new”, and may get us blocked. Fetching all every hour misses the 30 minute freshness goal.

Option How Pros Cons
Fixed interval polling Every source every N minutes Simple Too slow for big sources or too wasteful for small
Adaptive polling Interval based on each source’s recent publish rate Fresh where it matters, cheap elsewhere Needs tuning
Push (WebSub / PubSubHubbub, publisher APIs) Publisher notifies us on new content Near real time, no waste Only some publishers support it
Full web crawl Follow links across sites Finds sources without feeds Expensive, slow, complex

Recommended: adaptive polling of RSS/sitemaps as the backbone, push (WebSub) where publishers support it, and a light page fetch per new item. Each domain gets a per-domain rate limit (for example at most 1 request per second) and a robots.txt cache.

def next_interval(source):
    # aim to fetch about twice per expected new article,
    # clamped between 1 and 60 minutes
    per_hour = max(source.articles_last_24h / 24, 0.1)
    minutes = 60 / (2 * per_hour)
    return min(max(minutes, 1), 60)

def fetch_feed(source):
    r = http.get(source.feed_url, headers={
        "If-None-Match": source.etag or "",
        "If-Modified-Since": source.last_modified or ""}, timeout=10)
    if r.status_code == 304:
        return []                          # nothing new, very cheap
    source.etag = r.headers.get("ETag")
    return [i for i in parse_rss(r.text) if not seen(i.link)]

seen(url) is a check against a Bloom filter (a compact, probabilistic “have I seen this?” set) plus a lookup on the unique canonical URL in the DB. Canonical URL means stripping tracking parameters (utm_*), using the page’s <link rel="canonical">, and lowercasing the host.

With 50k sources and adaptive intervals averaging 5 minutes, we need about 170 fetches per second, which a few dozen crawler workers handle easily.

How do we detect duplicates and cluster articles into stories?

The problem: one event is covered by hundreds of outlets. Wire stories (AP, Reuters) are syndicated almost word for word. Other outlets rewrite them. Users want one card per story with “37 more sources”, not 37 identical headlines.

Two separate steps:

  1. Near-duplicate detection: is this text basically the same as one we have? (syndicated copies)
  2. Story clustering: is this a different article about the same event?
Technique What it detects How it works Cost
Exact hash (SHA of text) Identical copies Hash of normalized text Very cheap, misses small edits
SimHash Near duplicates 64-bit fingerprint; similar texts differ in few bits (Hamming distance) Cheap, great for syndication
MinHash + LSH Near duplicates by shingle overlap (Jaccard similarity) Many hash minimums, banded into buckets Moderate, tunable
Embeddings + nearest neighbors Same event, different wording Sentence embedding of title + lead, cosine similarity Higher cost, best for clustering

Recommended: SimHash on title + first paragraph for near duplicates (cheap, catches syndicated wire copy), then embedding similarity plus entity overlap (people, places) within a time window of 48 hours to attach the article to a story cluster.

SimHash in a few lines. Each word “votes” on each of 64 bits; the result flips only a few bits when the text changes slightly.

import hashlib

def simhash(text, bits=64):
    v = [0] * bits
    for word in text.lower().split():
        h = int(hashlib.md5(word.encode()).hexdigest(), 16)
        for i in range(bits):
            v[i] += 1 if (h >> i) & 1 else -1
    return sum(1 << i for i in range(bits) if v[i] > 0)

def hamming(a, b):
    return bin(a ^ b).count("1")

# near-duplicate if fingerprints differ in <= 3 of 64 bits
is_dup = hamming(simhash(t1), simhash(t2)) <= 3

To find candidates fast without comparing against every article, split the 64 bits into 4 blocks of 16 and index each block. Two fingerprints within 3 bits must match exactly on at least one block (pigeonhole principle), so we look up only those buckets. MinHash with LSH (locality sensitive hashing) uses the same banding trick for Jaccard similarity.

Clustering sketch:

def assign_cluster(article):
    vec = embed(article.title + " " + article.snippet)
    cands = ann_index.search(vec, k=20, max_age_hours=48)  # vector DB
    best = max(cands, key=lambda c: c.similarity, default=None)
    if best and best.similarity > 0.82 and shares_entities(article, best):
        return best.cluster_id
    return new_cluster(article)

Clustering is eventually consistent: two articles may briefly sit in separate clusters and be merged a few minutes later by a periodic re-clustering job.

How do we rank and personalize the feed?

A story score combines a few understandable signals.

Signal Why Example weight
Freshness (time decay) News gets old fast half-life of 6 hours
Coverage (cluster size, growth rate) Many outlets covering it means it matters log(sources)
Source authority Trusted, original reporting 0.5 to 1.5
Engagement (CTR) Users find it interesting clicks / impressions, smoothed
Personal affinity User’s topics and past clicks cosine(user, story) 
import math, time

def story_score(s, now=None):
    now = now or time.time()
    age_h = (now - s.first_seen) / 3600
    decay = 0.5 ** (age_h / 6)                    # half-life 6 h
    coverage = math.log1p(s.source_count)
    ctr = (s.clicks + 1) / (s.impressions + 20)   # smoothed
    return decay * (1.0 * coverage + 0.6 * s.authority + 2.0 * ctr)

def personal_score(story, user):
    return story_score(story) * (1 + 0.5 * cosine(user.vec, story.vec))
Personalization approach Pros Cons
Precompute a feed per user Fastest reads 100M feeds to update on every new story, heavy writes, wasted for inactive users
Compute on request from candidate lists Fresh, no per-user storage More CPU per request
Hybrid: shared topic lists + light per-user re-rank Fast and fresh Slightly less personal

Recommended: hybrid. Keep global and per-topic ranked lists in Redis (a few hundred lists, not 100 million). On a for_you request, merge the user’s top 3-5 topics’ lists (about 500 candidates), re-rank with personal_score, and cache the result for that user for 5 minutes.

How do we keep feeds fresh but still serve them from cache in under 200 ms?

Option Freshness Latency Cost
Compute from DB on every request Perfect Slow (heavy queries) High
CDN cache whole feed for 10 min Up to 10 min stale Very fast Low
Redis sorted sets updated on ingest + short CDN TTL ~1 min stale Fast Low

Recommended: precomputed ranked lists in Redis that the processing pipeline updates as articles arrive, so the data is fresh by construction. The logged-out topic feeds (the same for everyone) are cached at the CDN for 60 seconds, which absorbs breaking-news spikes: 120k requests per second turn into a few hundred origin requests. Scores decay with time, so a job re-scores the top 2,000 stories per topic every minute.

# on ingest: update the topic list
r.zadd(f"feed:topic:{story.category}", {story.cluster_id: story_score(story)})
r.zremrangebyrank(f"feed:topic:{story.category}", 0, -2001)  # keep top 2000
 120k req/s --> CDN (TTL 60 s, hit ~99%) --> ~1k req/s --> Feed Svc --> Redis

How do we paginate an infinite feed when rankings keep changing?

The problem: with ?page=2, if new stories are inserted at the top between requests, page 2 repeats items from page 1, or skips some.

Option Pros Cons
Offset (page=2) Simple Duplicates and gaps when list changes
Cursor on (score, id) Stable relative to last seen item Scores change over time, items can still move
Snapshot the ranked list per session Perfectly consistent scrolling Memory per session

Recommended: on the first request, snapshot the top 500 story IDs for that user into Redis with a 30 minute TTL and return a cursor that is (snapshot_id, position). Further pages read from the snapshot. Pull-to-refresh creates a new snapshot. This is what keeps “infinite scroll” free of duplicates.

def get_feed(user, cursor=None, limit=20):
    if cursor is None:
        ids = rank_for(user)[:500]
        snap = f"snap:{uuid4()}"
        r.rpush(snap, *ids); r.expire(snap, 1800)
        pos = 0
    else:
        snap, pos = decode(cursor)
    page = r.lrange(snap, pos, pos + limit - 1)
    return hydrate(page), encode(snap, pos + limit)

What happens when a publisher or the pipeline fails?

Crawler failures are isolated per source: a site that times out gets exponential backoff and a lower priority, not a retry storm. Kafka between crawling and processing means a processing outage only delays articles; when consumers return they catch up from the last committed offset. Processing is idempotent because the canonical URL is unique, so replays do not create duplicate articles. If Redis is lost, feeds are rebuilt from the Article DB by a backfill job in minutes, and the CDN keeps serving the last cached topic feeds meanwhile.

9. Common mistakes and interviewer follow-ups

  • Mistake: polling every source at the same fixed interval. Either stale or wasteful, and you may get banned. Say: “adaptive intervals from publish rate, conditional GET, push where available, per-domain limits.”
  • Mistake: dedup by exact URL only. Syndicated wire stories have different URLs and near-identical text. Say: “canonical URL plus SimHash or MinHash for near duplicates, embeddings for same-event clustering.”
  • Mistake: precomputing a feed for all 100M users. Huge write amplification for users who never open the app. Say: “shared topic lists in Redis, light per-user re-rank on request.”
  • Mistake: offset pagination. Duplicates when new stories arrive. Say: “snapshot plus cursor.”
  • Mistake: storing and serving full article text. Legal risk and takes traffic from publishers. Say: “title, snippet, thumbnail, and a redirect.”
  • Mistake: ignoring breaking-news spikes. Say: “CDN with 60 s TTL on shared feeds turns 120k req/s into ~1k at origin.”
  • Follow-up: “How do you get articles into feeds within 5 minutes?” Answer: shorter intervals for high-volume sources, WebSub push, and streaming processing (seconds per article) rather than batch jobs.
  • Follow-up: “How would you avoid filter bubbles?” Answer: blend a share of top general stories into every personalized feed and diversify sources within a story.

10. One-page cheat sheet

Topic Key point
Scale 50k sources, 2M articles/day, 100M DAU, ~12k feed req/s
Ratio Reads ~1000x writes; metadata only ~1.5 TB/year
Freshness < 30 min (target 5), adaptive polling + WebSub push
Polite crawling robots.txt, per-domain rate limit, conditional GET
Dedup Canonical URL + Bloom filter; SimHash (<= 3 bits of 64)
Clustering Embeddings + entities, 48 h window, periodic re-merge
Ranking Time decay (6 h half-life) x coverage, authority, CTR
Personalization Topic ZSETs in Redis + per-user re-rank, 5 min cache
Latency Precomputed lists in Redis, < 200 ms
Spikes CDN 60 s TTL on shared feeds
Pagination Snapshot of top 500 + cursor
CAP AP; clusters and feeds eventually consistent
