19. Price Tracking Service like CamelCamelCamel (Medium)

A price tracker watches the prices of Amazon products over time. Users can see a chart of a product’s price history, and they can say “email me when this drops below $50.” Services like CamelCamelCamel also ship a browser extension that shows the chart right on the Amazon page. The interviewer is really testing three things: how you collect data from a website you do not own without hammering it (crawling politely at a scale of hundreds of millions of products), how you store a huge amount of time-series data cheaply, and how you match a price change against millions of user alerts quickly without sending duplicate emails.

1. Functional requirements

Core (must have):

  1. Users can view the price history of an Amazon product (website or browser extension).
  2. Users can subscribe to a price drop alert with a target price (“tell me when it is below $X”).
  3. Users get a notification (email or push) when the price drops below their target.
  4. Users can list and delete their alerts.

Below the line (out of scope):

  1. Product search and discovery. It is a separate search problem (an inverted index) and not the core of this question.
  2. Price comparison across many retailers. Same design, more crawlers; it adds breadth, not depth.
  3. Reviews and ratings. Unrelated data.
  4. Sub-minute “real time” prices. Amazon prices do not change that fast for most items, and chasing it would multiply crawl cost.

2. Non-functional requirements

  1. Scale: track about 500 million products and 10 million alerts from a few million users.
  2. Latency: price history chart loads with p99 < 500 ms. The extension is on the Amazon page, so slow means useless.
  3. Freshness: a price drop should trigger a notification within 1 hour for popular products and within 24 hours for long-tail products.
  4. Politeness: stay under a fixed request budget per second toward Amazon (for example 1,000 requests per second total) and respect rate limits and robots rules. Getting blocked kills the product.
  5. Availability over consistency (AP in CAP terms). If a chart is a few minutes stale, nobody is hurt. Reads should be 99.9% available.
  6. Correctness for alerts: each user gets at most one notification per price-drop event (no spam), and should not miss a drop that lasted longer than one crawl interval.
  7. Durability: price history is the product’s core asset. It must never be lost (replicated storage, 11 nines style object storage for cold data).

CAP choice: we choose availability. Price data is eventually consistent. The only place we want stronger guarantees is the “already notified” record, so we do not double-send, and that is handled with idempotent writes, not with a globally consistent database.

3. Back-of-the-envelope estimates

Assumption Number
Products tracked 500 M
Hot products (tracked by alerts or viewed often) 10 M
Crawl interval, hot every 1 hour
Crawl interval, long tail every 1 to 7 days
Active alerts 10 M
Extension users (daily) 1 M
Chart views per day 20 M
Size of one price point ~16 bytes (time 8, price 4, extras 4)
Price changes actually stored only when price changes, ~1 per product per day avg 
Crawl rate
  hot:  10M / 3600 s              ~= 2,800 req/s
  tail: 490M / (3 days * 86400 s) ~= 1,900 req/s
  total                           ~= 4,700 req/s  (above our 1,000 budget!)
  -> we cannot crawl everything directly; we need other data sources
     (extension crowd-sourcing, Amazon Product API, smart scheduling)

Read QPS (charts)
  20M / 86400 ~= 230 req/s average, peak x5 ~= 1,200 req/s

Alert writes
  say 200k new alerts/day -> ~2 writes/s (tiny)

Storage per year (change-only encoding)
  500M products * 365 changes * 16 B ~= 2.9 TB/year raw
  with compression (delta + varint)  ~= 1 TB/year
  10 years ~= 10 TB -> fits easily in a time-series DB + S3

Notification volume
  maybe 1% of alerts fire per day -> 100k notifications/day (~1/s)

The key insight from the math: crawling is the bottleneck, not storage or reads.

4. Core entities

  • Product: an Amazon item. Fields: asin (Amazon’s product id), title, url, current_price, last_crawled_at, crawl_priority.
  • PricePoint: one observed price. Fields: asin, observed_at, price_cents, source (crawler, extension, API).
  • Alert (subscription): a user’s rule. Fields: alert_id, user_id, asin, target_price_cents, status (active, triggered, paused).
  • User: account. Fields: user_id, email, push tokens, preferences.
  • Notification: a record of something we sent. Fields: notification_id, alert_id, price_event_id, sent_at, channel.
  • CrawlTask: a scheduled fetch. Fields: asin, next_run_at, priority.
CREATE TABLE products (
  asin             VARCHAR(16) PRIMARY KEY,
  title            TEXT,
  current_price    INT,           -- cents
  last_crawled_at  TIMESTAMP,
  next_crawl_at    TIMESTAMP,
  priority         SMALLINT       -- 0 = hottest
);

CREATE TABLE alerts (
  alert_id     BIGINT PRIMARY KEY,
  user_id      BIGINT NOT NULL,
  asin         VARCHAR(16) NOT NULL,
  target_cents INT NOT NULL,
  status       VARCHAR(12) DEFAULT 'active',
  last_fired_price INT
);
-- the most important index: find alerts for a product, cheapest first
CREATE INDEX alerts_by_product ON alerts (asin, target_cents)
  WHERE status = 'active';

-- price history in a time-series table (TimescaleDB style)
CREATE TABLE price_points (
  asin        VARCHAR(16),
  observed_at TIMESTAMPTZ,
  price_cents INT,
  PRIMARY KEY (asin, observed_at)
);

5. API design

GET /products/{asin}/history?range=1y – price history for the chart.

// response 200
{
  "asin": "B08N5WRWNW",
  "currency": "USD",
  "points": [[1730592000, 4999], [1730678400, 4599]],
  "low": 3999, "high": 5999
}

Status: 200, 404 if unknown asin (we may enqueue it for crawling and return 202). No auth needed; it is public and cacheable.

POST /alerts – create a price drop alert. Auth: user token.

// request
{ "asin": "B08N5WRWNW", "target_price_cents": 3999, "channel": "email" }
// response 201
{ "alert_id": 98765, "status": "active" }

Status: 201, 400 bad price, 401 not logged in, 409 duplicate alert for same asin.

GET /alerts – list my alerts. Auth required. Response: list of alert objects. 200.

DELETE /alerts/{alert_id} – remove an alert. Auth required, owner only. 204, 404.

POST /extension/observations – the extension reports the price the user is seeing. Auth: extension install token, rate limited.

{ "asin": "B08N5WRWNW", "price_cents": 4599, "seen_at": 1730678400 }

Response 202 Accepted (queued, verified later).

How will users view price history?

  1. The extension sees the user is on an Amazon page and reads the asin from the URL.
  2. It calls GET /products/{asin}/history.
  3. The Product Service checks Redis (key hist:{asin}:1y). On a hit it returns in a few ms.
  4. On a miss it queries the time-series database: SELECT observed_at, price_cents FROM price_points WHERE asin = ? AND observed_at > now() - interval '1 year'. It downsamples to about 365 points (one per day) since a chart cannot show more anyway, caches the result for 15 minutes, and returns it.
sequenceDiagram
    participant E as Extension
    participant G as Gateway
    participant P as ProductService
    participant R as Redis
    participant T as TimeSeriesDB
    E->>G: GET product history for asin
    G->>P: Forward request
    P->>R: GET hist key for asin
    alt cache hit
        R-->>P: Cached chart points
    else cache miss
        R-->>P: Not found
        P->>T: Range query last year
        T-->>P: Price points
        P->>P: Downsample to daily points
        P->>R: SET chart with 15 min TTL
    end
    P-->>G: Chart JSON
    G-->>E: 200 price history

How will users subscribe to an alert?

  1. User clicks “alert me below $39.99” in the extension.
  2. POST /alerts hits the Alert Service, which inserts a row in the alerts table.
  3. The Alert Service also bumps the product’s crawl priority, because someone now cares about it. A product with alerts goes into the hourly tier.
  4. If the product is new to us, the service enqueues an immediate crawl.

How do price changes get detected and turned into notifications?

  1. The Scheduler picks products whose next_crawl_at has passed and pushes them to the crawl queue.
  2. A crawler fetches the page (or the Product Advertising API), parses the price, and compares it with current_price.
  3. If the price did not change, it just updates last_crawled_at. If it changed, it writes a PriceChanged event to Kafka.
  4. The History Writer consumes the event and appends a row to the time-series DB.
  5. The Alert Matcher consumes the same event, finds all active alerts for that asin with target_cents >= new_price, and pushes one notification job per alert.
  6. The Notification workers send the email or push and record that it was sent.

7. Deep dives

How do we crawl 500 million products without getting blocked?

The math said a naive crawl needs ~4,700 requests per second, but we only want to send about 1,000 per second to Amazon. We have to be smarter about which products we fetch and when.

Option How it works Pros Cons
Fixed round-robin crawl Visit every product every N days Simple Wastes budget on dead products; popular items too stale
Priority scheduling Crawl interval depends on demand and volatility Spends budget where users care Needs a scoring function and a scheduler
Crowd-sourced from extension + verify Extension users report prices they see Free, very fresh for popular items Data can be wrong or malicious, must verify

Recommended: priority scheduling plus extension crowd-sourcing. The score combines how many alerts a product has, how often it is viewed, and how often its price has changed in the past. A product with 5,000 alerts that changes price daily gets crawled hourly. A dusty item with no alerts gets crawled weekly.

def next_interval_seconds(p):
    # demand: alerts + recent views; volatility: changes per week
    demand = p.alert_count * 10 + p.views_7d
    volatility = p.changes_last_30d / 30.0
    if demand > 1000 or volatility > 1:
        return 3600            # hourly
    if demand > 10:
        return 6 * 3600        # every 6 hours
    return 7 * 86400           # weekly

def schedule(p, now):
    p.next_crawl_at = now + next_interval_seconds(p)

Politeness rules for the crawler fleet:

  • A global token bucket (stored in Redis) caps total requests per second. Every crawler takes a token before a fetch. If no token, it waits.
  • Spread requests out over time (add jitter) so we never burst.
  • Back off exponentially on HTTP 429 or 503, and pause the whole fleet if the error rate passes a threshold.
  • Prefer the official Product Advertising API where allowed; it is cheaper and does not risk blocking.

Extension reports go to a verification step: if three independent users report the same new price within an hour, or one report disagrees with our last crawl, we schedule a priority re-crawl to confirm. That way the extension acts as a free “change detector,” and crawlers only confirm.

How should we store price history efficiently?

Prices are classic time-series data: (key, time, value), append-only, read by time range.

Option Pros Cons
One row per crawl in Postgres Simple, SQL 500M x 24 rows/day is billions of rows of duplicates
Store only changes in a time-series DB (TimescaleDB, InfluxDB) Compression, fast range scans, built-in downsampling Another system to run
Wide-column (Cassandra), row per asin per month Huge write scale, easy sharding Less query flexibility

Recommended: store only changes (a price point is written when the price differs from the last one) in a time-series store, partitioned by asin, with old data rolled into daily summaries. Change-only storage cuts volume by 10 to 50 times because most crawls see the same price.

-- TimescaleDB hypertable partitioned by time and hashed by asin
SELECT create_hypertable('price_points', 'observed_at',
       partitioning_column => 'asin', number_partitions => 64);

-- continuous aggregate for fast yearly charts
CREATE MATERIALIZED VIEW price_daily
WITH (timescaledb.continuous) AS
SELECT asin, time_bucket('1 day', observed_at) AS day,
       min(price_cents) AS low, max(price_cents) AS high,
       last(price_cents, observed_at) AS close
FROM price_points GROUP BY asin, day;

Data older than 2 years can be exported as compressed Parquet files to S3, with the daily summary staying in the hot DB. With ~1 TB per year after compression, storage is cheap. Charts read from price_daily and are cached in Redis, so a chart is a single fast lookup.

When a price changes, how do we find matching alerts fast?

A naive approach scans all 10 million alerts on every price change. With thousands of changes per second, that is impossible.

Option How Cost per price change
Full scan of alerts Compare every alert O(all alerts), far too slow
Index by asin WHERE asin = ? then filter by price O(alerts on that product)
Index by (asin, target) sorted Range scan target >= new_price O(matches), only touches alerts that fire

Recommended: a composite index on (asin, target_cents). When the price drops to P, we only read alerts whose target is at least P. Because the index is sorted, the database jumps straight to them.

SELECT alert_id, user_id
FROM alerts
WHERE asin = :asin
  AND status = 'active'
  AND target_cents >= :new_price
  AND (last_fired_price IS NULL OR last_fired_price > :new_price);

Hot products (a popular TV with 200,000 alerts on Black Friday) can produce a big result. The matcher pages through results in batches of 1,000 and pushes them to the notification queue, so one giant product does not block other events. Partition Kafka by asin so all events for one product are processed in order by one matcher.

Edge case: only fire when the price crosses the threshold downward. If the price goes $50 -> $38 -> $37, the user with target $40 should get one email, not two. That leads to the next deep dive.

How do we avoid sending duplicate notifications?

Duplicates happen for three reasons: Kafka redelivers a message after a crash (at-least-once delivery), the price bounces around the threshold, and two crawlers observe the same change.

Option Pros Cons
Hope it does not happen Zero work Users get spammed and unsubscribe
Idempotency key per (alert, price_event) Retries become safe Need a dedup store
Alert state machine (active -> triggered, re-arm on recovery) Stops threshold flapping Need re-arm rule

Recommended: both. Each price change gets an event_id. The notifier writes (alert_id, event_id) with a unique constraint before sending. The alert itself moves to triggered and only re-arms if the price goes back above the target by some margin (say 5%) or after a cooldown of 7 days.

def handle_match(alert, event):
    key = f"notif:{alert.id}:{event.id}"
    # SET NX = only set if not exists; 7 day TTL
    if not redis.set(key, 1, nx=True, ex=7 * 86400):
        return  # already handled this exact event
    db.execute("""UPDATE alerts SET status='triggered',
                  last_fired_price=%s WHERE alert_id=%s
                  AND status='active'""", (event.price, alert.id))
    if db.rowcount == 1:          # we won the race
        notify_queue.put({"alert": alert.id, "price": event.price,
                          "idempotency_key": key})

The conditional UPDATE ... AND status='active' acts as a compare-and-set. Even if two matchers race, only one sees rowcount == 1.

How does the system scale to millions of tracked products and users?

  • Crawlers are stateless workers pulling from a queue (SQS or Kafka). Add more workers up to the politeness budget; use many IP egress points only within the provider’s terms.
  • The scheduler should not scan a 500M-row table. Keep a Redis sorted set per shard with score = next_crawl_at, and pop due items with ZRANGEBYSCORE key 0 now LIMIT 0 1000.
  • Alerts DB: 10M rows is small for Postgres. Shard by asin only when needed. Read replicas serve “list my alerts.”
  • Chart reads: CDN plus Redis caching. The top 1% of products get most views, so the hit rate is high.
  • Notification fan-out: a separate notification service with its own queue and rate limits per email provider.
Redis ZSET "crawl:due:shard7"
  score = next_crawl_at (unix), member = asin
Scheduler loop:
  due = ZRANGEBYSCORE crawl:due:shard7 0 NOW LIMIT 0 1000
  push due to crawl queue
  ZADD crawl:due:shard7 (NOW + interval) asin   # reschedule

Failure handling: if a crawler dies mid-task, the queue’s visibility timeout returns the task. If the matcher dies, Kafka consumer offsets let it resume from the last committed event; the idempotency key makes replays safe. If Amazon blocks us, the circuit breaker pauses crawling and we rely on extension reports until we recover.

Crawlers are the only part of the VPC that talks to Amazon, and every price change flows through one Kafka topic in the data subnet to both the history store and the alert matcher.

9. Common mistakes and interviewer follow-ups

  • Mistake: crawling every product every hour. Why it hurts: it is 140,000 requests per second and you will be blocked. Say instead: tier crawl frequency by demand and volatility, and use extension data as a change detector.
  • Mistake: storing every crawl result. Why it hurts: billions of duplicate rows. Say instead: store only changes and keep daily rollups.
  • Mistake: scanning all alerts per price change. Why it hurts: O(N) per event. Say instead: index alerts by (asin, target) and range scan.
  • Mistake: ignoring duplicates. Why it hurts: at-least-once delivery plus price flapping spams users. Say instead: idempotency key per (alert, event) and a triggered/re-arm state machine.
  • Mistake: trusting extension data blindly. Why it hurts: anyone can fake a $1 price. Say instead: verify with a crawl or multiple independent reports.
  • Follow-up: “What if Amazon blocks your crawlers?” Answer: circuit breaker, back off, fall back to the official API and extension reports, alert the on-call.
  • Follow-up: “How do you support other retailers?” Answer: a parser plugin per retailer and a per-domain token bucket; the rest of the pipeline is the same.
  • Follow-up: “How do you guarantee the 1 hour freshness?” Answer: any product with an alert is in the hourly tier; monitor crawl lag as a metric.

10. One-page cheat sheet

Topic Key point
Scale 500M products, 10M alerts, ~1k req/s crawl budget
Bottleneck Crawling, not storage
Crawl Priority tiers (hourly/6h/weekly), token bucket, backoff, extension as detector
Storage Change-only time series, ~1 TB/year, daily rollups, S3 archive
Chart reads Redis + CDN, p99 < 500 ms, downsample to ~365 points
Alert match Index (asin, target_cents), range scan target >= price
Dedup Redis SET NX on (alert, event) + triggered state, re-arm rule
Events Kafka partitioned by asin
CAP AP; eventual consistency for prices
Failure Queue visibility timeout, Kafka offsets, idempotent replays, circuit breaker

20. Notification System (Medium)

A notification system is an internal platform. Other teams (chat, orders, marketing) hand it a message and a recipient, and it delivers that message over push (iOS/Android), SMS, or email. The product teams never talk to Apple, Twilio, or SendGrid directly. The interviewer is testing whether you can build a reliable pipeline on top of unreliable third-party providers: fan-out through queues, at-least-once delivery without spamming users twice, per-user preferences and rate limits, retries with a dead letter queue, priority lanes so a password reset is never stuck behind a marketing blast, and failover when a provider goes down.

1. Functional requirements

Core (must have):

  1. Internal services can send a notification to one user on one or more channels (push, SMS, email).
  2. Internal services can send a bulk notification to a large audience (for example 50 million users for a campaign).
  3. Users can set preferences: opt out of a channel or a category (for example “no marketing SMS”), and set quiet hours.
  4. The system tracks delivery status of each notification (queued, sent, delivered, failed) and callers can query it.
  5. Notifications support templates with variables (for example “Hi {name}, your order {id} shipped”).

Below the line (out of scope):

  • In-app notification inbox UI (it is a separate read-heavy feature, we can mention it as an extra consumer).
  • Building our own SMS or push gateway. We use providers like APNs, FCM, Twilio, SES.
  • Rich analytics dashboards on open rates. We emit events; analytics is another team.
  • Content authoring tools for marketers.

2. Non-functional requirements

  1. Scale: 1 billion notifications per day on average, peaks of 10x for campaigns.
  2. Latency: critical (transactional) notifications such as OTP codes and chat messages reach the provider within p99 < 2 seconds of the API call. Promotional notifications can take minutes.
  3. Reliability: at-least-once delivery. A notification accepted by the API is never silently lost (durability 99.999%).
  4. No duplicates visible to the user: the same logical notification is delivered at most once per channel, even with retries. We achieve “effectively once” with idempotency keys.
  5. Availability: 99.99% for the send API. If a downstream provider fails, we fail over or queue, we do not reject the caller.
  6. Isolation: a 50M-user marketing blast must not delay an OTP. Priority lanes.
  7. Respect user preferences and per-user rate limits (for example at most 3 marketing pushes per day).
  8. CAP choice: we pick availability (AP) for the send path. Accept the message, store it, deliver eventually. Preferences can be eventually consistent (a few seconds stale is fine). Deduplication needs a strongly consistent check per key (a conditional write).

3. Back-of-the-envelope estimates

Assumption Number
Notifications per day 1 billion
Split: push / email / SMS 70% / 25% / 5%
Peak factor 10x
Avg payload stored per notification 1 KB
Status events per notification 3 (queued, sent, delivered)
Retention of notification log 30 days hot, 1 year cold
Users 500 million 
Average send QPS = 1e9 / 86,400       ~ 11,600 /s
Peak send QPS    = 11,600 * 10        ~ 116,000 /s

Per channel at peak:
  push  = 0.70 * 116k ~ 81,000 /s
  email = 0.25 * 116k ~ 29,000 /s
  SMS   = 0.05 * 116k ~  5,800 /s   (SMS costs money, often ~$0.0075 each)

Storage (notification log):
  1e9 * 1 KB = 1 TB per day
  30 days hot = 30 TB ; 1 year cold = 365 TB (compressed ~100 TB)

Status writes: 3 * 11,600 ~ 35,000 writes/s average, 350k/s peak

Bandwidth to providers at peak: 116k * 1 KB ~ 116 MB/s ~ 1 Gbps
SMS bill: 50M SMS/day * $0.0075 ~ $375k/day  -> rate limits matter!

The SMS line is a good thing to say out loud. It shows why dedup and rate limiting are money problems, not just user-experience problems.

4. Core entities

  • Notification: one logical message to one user. Fields: notification_id, idempotency_key, user_id, category, priority, channels, template_id, variables, created_at.
  • Delivery: one attempt to deliver a notification on one channel. Fields: delivery_id, notification_id, channel, provider, status, attempts, last_error.
  • Template: a reusable message body per channel and locale. Fields: template_id, channel, locale, subject, body.
  • UserPreference: what a user allows. Fields: user_id, category, channel, enabled, quiet_hours.
  • DeviceToken / Contact: where to send. Fields: user_id, push tokens (per device), phone, email, verified flag.
  • Campaign: a bulk send. Fields: campaign_id, audience query or segment id, template_id, schedule, status.
CREATE TABLE notification (
  notification_id   UUID PRIMARY KEY,
  idempotency_key   TEXT NOT NULL,
  caller_service    TEXT NOT NULL,
  user_id           BIGINT NOT NULL,
  category          TEXT NOT NULL,      -- 'otp', 'chat', 'marketing'
  priority          SMALLINT NOT NULL,  -- 0 = critical, 1 = normal, 2 = bulk
  template_id       TEXT NOT NULL,
  variables         JSONB,
  created_at        TIMESTAMPTZ NOT NULL,
  UNIQUE (caller_service, idempotency_key)
);

CREATE TABLE delivery (
  delivery_id     UUID PRIMARY KEY,
  notification_id UUID NOT NULL,
  channel         TEXT NOT NULL,        -- 'push', 'sms', 'email'
  provider        TEXT,                 -- 'apns', 'fcm', 'twilio', 'ses'
  status          TEXT NOT NULL,        -- queued/sent/delivered/failed/skipped
  attempts        INT DEFAULT 0,
  last_error      TEXT,
  updated_at      TIMESTAMPTZ
);
{
  "user_id": 42,
  "preferences": {
    "marketing": {"push": true, "email": true, "sms": false},
    "security":  {"push": true, "email": true, "sms": true}
  },
  "quiet_hours": {"start": "22:00", "end": "07:00", "tz": "America/New_York"},
  "devices": [{"token": "fcm:abc...", "platform": "android", "last_seen": "2026-10-01"}]
}

5. API design

All endpoints are internal and authenticated with service-to-service auth (mTLS or signed tokens). Each caller service has a quota.

POST /v1/notifications – send to one user.

{
  "idempotency_key": "order-123-shipped",
  "user_id": 42,
  "category": "order_update",
  "priority": "normal",
  "channels": ["push", "email"],
  "template_id": "order_shipped_v2",
  "variables": {"name": "Ana", "order_id": "123"},
  "expires_at": "2026-11-06T00:00:00Z"
}

Response 202 Accepted:

{"notification_id": "9f1c...", "status": "queued"}

Status codes: 202 accepted, 200 with the same body if the idempotency key was already seen (duplicate request), 400 bad template or variables, 429 caller over quota.

POST /v1/campaigns – bulk send to a segment.

{
  "idempotency_key": "black-friday-2026",
  "segment_id": "active_us_users",
  "category": "marketing",
  "template_id": "bf_promo",
  "channels": ["push"],
  "send_at": "2026-11-27T14:00:00Z",
  "expires_at": "2026-11-28T00:00:00Z"
}

Response 202 Accepted with {"campaign_id": "c-77", "status": "scheduled"}.

GET /v1/notifications/{id} – delivery status per channel.

{"notification_id": "9f1c...",
 "deliveries": [
   {"channel": "push", "status": "delivered", "attempts": 1},
   {"channel": "email", "status": "sent", "attempts": 2}]}

PUT /v1/users/{user_id}/preferences – user (via the app backend) updates opt-outs and quiet hours. Auth: the user’s session token, checked by the app gateway. Returns 200.

POST /v1/users/{user_id}/devices – register or refresh a push token. Returns 201.

POST /v1/providers/{provider}/callbacks – webhook for provider delivery receipts (Twilio, SES). Verified with the provider’s signature. Returns 200.

How will a service send a notification to one user?

  1. The caller sends POST /v1/notifications with an idempotency key.
  2. The API validates the request and checks the caller’s quota.
  3. It inserts a row in the notification table. The unique constraint on (caller_service, idempotency_key) catches duplicate calls. If the insert conflicts, return the existing id with 200.
  4. It publishes the notification id and payload to the Kafka topic for its priority. It returns 202. The caller is now done.
  5. A router consumes the event. It loads the user’s preferences and contacts (from a cache in front of the DB). It drops channels the user opted out of and writes skipped deliveries for them.
  6. It renders the template per channel and locale, then enqueues one message per channel onto the channel queues.
  7. Channel workers call the provider (FCM, SES, Twilio), record sent, and handle errors.
  8. Providers later send delivery receipts via webhook. We update the delivery row to delivered or failed.
sequenceDiagram
    participant C as Caller
    participant A as API
    participant D as NotificationDB
    participant K as Kafka
    participant R as Router
    participant W as Worker
    participant P as Provider
    C->>A: POST notification with idempotency key
    A->>D: INSERT with unique key
    D-->>A: ok or conflict
    A->>K: Publish to priority topic
    A-->>C: 202 queued
    K->>R: Consume event
    R->>R: Load prefs, drop opt outs, render template
    R->>W: Enqueue per channel message
    W->>P: Send via FCM, SES or Twilio
    P-->>W: Accepted
    W->>D: Record sent
    P-->>A: Delivery receipt webhook
    A->>D: Update delivered or failed

How will a service send a bulk campaign?

  1. Marketing calls POST /v1/campaigns. We store the campaign and schedule it.
  2. At send_at, a campaign fan-out job reads the segment (a list of user ids, often from a data warehouse export or a segment service) in pages of 10,000.
  3. For each page it creates notification records with deterministic idempotency keys like campaign_id:user_id and publishes them to the bulk topic.
  4. From there the flow is the same as the single-user flow, on the bulk lane.

How will users manage preferences?

  1. The app backend calls PUT /v1/users/{id}/preferences.
  2. We write to the preference DB (a key-value store keyed by user_id) and invalidate the cache entry.
  3. The router reads preferences on every notification, so the change takes effect within seconds.

How will callers see delivery status?

  1. Workers and webhooks write status events to a status topic.
  2. A consumer updates the delivery table (Cassandra or DynamoDB, keyed by notification_id).
  3. GET /v1/notifications/{id} reads that table.

7. Deep dives

How do we fan out to millions of users without melting anything?

The problem: one campaign call can mean 50 million notifications. If the API tried to do this inline, the request would time out and a crash halfway would leave us not knowing who got the message.

Option How it works Pros Cons
Loop in the API API iterates users and calls providers Simple Times out, no recovery, no backpressure
One queue message per user, produced by a fan-out job Job pages through segment, publishes per-user events Resumable, parallel, backpressure Fan-out job must checkpoint
Send one “campaign” event, let workers expand Each worker expands a shard of the segment Very parallel Harder to reason about progress

Recommended: a fan-out job that pages through the segment and checkpoints the last page it published. Kafka absorbs the burst. Workers drain at the rate providers allow.

def fan_out(campaign):
    cursor = load_checkpoint(campaign.id)        # resume after crash
    while True:
        page, cursor = segment.read(campaign.segment_id, cursor, size=10_000)
        if not page:
            break
        events = [{
            "idempotency_key": f"{campaign.id}:{uid}",
            "user_id": uid,
            "template_id": campaign.template_id,
            "priority": "bulk",
            "expires_at": campaign.expires_at,
        } for uid in page]
        kafka.send_batch("notif.bulk", events, key=lambda e: e["user_id"])
        save_checkpoint(campaign.id, cursor)     # after publish succeeds
    mark_done(campaign.id)

If the job crashes between publish and checkpoint, it republishes one page. That is fine because the idempotency key campaign:user makes the duplicate harmless (next deep dive). 50M users at 10k per page is 5,000 pages, so with 20 parallel partitions the publish phase finishes in a few minutes.

How do we get at-least-once delivery without sending duplicates?

The problem: queues give at-least-once delivery. A worker can call Twilio, succeed, then crash before committing the Kafka offset. Another worker picks up the same message and sends the SMS again. The user gets two OTPs and we pay twice.

Exactly-once across a network to a third party is not possible in general. What we can do is make our side idempotent: before sending, claim the delivery; after sending, record it. Many providers also accept an idempotency key.

Option Pros Cons
No dedup, accept duplicates Simplest Users annoyed, extra SMS cost
Dedup table with conditional write (claim before send) Strong per-key guarantee One extra write per send
Redis SETNX with TTL Very fast Lost on Redis failure, needs persistence

Recommended: a dedup record keyed by notification_id:channel, written with a conditional put (DynamoDB attribute_not_exists or Redis SET NX backed by the DB). States go claimed -> sent. A claim older than a timeout (for example 60 s) without sent can be retried.

def deliver(msg):
    key = f"{msg.notification_id}:{msg.channel}"
    claimed = dedup.put_if_absent(key, state="claimed", ttl_s=7*86400,
                                  claim_ts=now())
    if not claimed:
        rec = dedup.get(key)
        if rec.state == "sent":
            return ack(msg)                     # duplicate, drop it
        if now() - rec.claim_ts < 60:
            return retry_later(msg)             # someone else is sending
        dedup.cas(key, expect=rec, new={"state": "claimed", "claim_ts": now()})
    resp = provider.send(msg, idempotency_key=key)  # pass key if supported
    dedup.update(key, state="sent", provider_id=resp.id)
    ack(msg)

There is still a tiny window: crash after provider.send returns but before state=sent. After 60 s someone retries and may send twice. We shrink that window by passing the key to providers that support it (many email APIs and some SMS APIs do). Say this honestly in the interview: “effectively once, with a small, bounded duplicate risk”.

Idempotency also exists at the API edge: the unique constraint on (caller_service, idempotency_key) stops a caller’s retry from creating a second notification.

How do we apply user preferences and per-user rate limits?

The problem: users must never get a channel they opted out of, and must not be spammed (for example 10 marketing pushes in an hour). The check runs on every one of the 116k/s messages, so it must be cheap.

Option Pros Cons
Read preference DB every time Always fresh 116k DB reads/s
Cache preferences in Redis with TTL + invalidate on write Fast, fresh within seconds Cache miss storms during campaigns
Embed preferences in the campaign segment No lookups Stale if user opts out after segment built

Recommended: Redis cache in front of the preference store with invalidation on write. For rate limiting use a per-user, per-category counter in Redis with a fixed or sliding window.

def allowed(user_id, category, channel):
    prefs = pref_cache.get(user_id) or load_and_cache(user_id)
    if not prefs.enabled(category, channel):
        return "skipped_optout"
    if category != "security" and prefs.in_quiet_hours(now()):
        return "defer"                          # re-enqueue for quiet_end
    limit = LIMITS.get((category, channel))     # e.g. marketing push: 3/day
    if limit:
        k = f"rl:{user_id}:{category}:{channel}:{today()}"
        n = redis.incr(k)
        if n == 1:
            redis.expire(k, 86400)
        if n > limit:
            return "skipped_ratelimit"
    return "ok"

Security and OTP categories bypass quiet hours and marketing limits but have their own abuse limit (for example 5 OTP SMS per phone per hour) to stop SMS pumping fraud.

How do we handle retries, provider errors, and dead letters?

The problem: providers fail in different ways. A 503 from FCM is transient. An “invalid device token” is permanent. Retrying permanent failures wastes money; not retrying transient ones loses messages.

Error type Example Action
Transient 429, 503, timeout Retry with exponential backoff and jitter
Permanent, user data Invalid token, unsubscribed email, bad number Do not retry. Mark failed. Clean up token.
Permanent, our bug Template render error Send to dead letter queue (DLQ), alert
Expired Promo past expires_at Drop, mark expired 
channel queue --> worker --fail(transient)--> retry topic (delay 2^n s)
                     |                              |
                     | fail after 6 attempts        v
                     +-------------------------> DLQ --> alert + replay tool

Retry topics with delays (for example 5 s, 30 s, 2 min, 10 min, 1 h) keep the main queue moving. Never block a partition sleeping on one message. A DLQ holds messages that failed all attempts so an engineer can inspect and replay them after a fix. Always check expires_at before each retry: a “sale ends tonight” push sent tomorrow is worse than no push.

How do we keep critical notifications fast during a huge campaign?

The problem: if OTPs and a 50M marketing blast share one queue, the OTP waits behind millions of messages.

Option Pros Cons
Single queue with priority field Simple Head-of-line blocking, Kafka has no priority
Separate topics and worker pools per priority Strong isolation More infra to run
Separate topics plus provider quota reservation Isolation all the way to the provider Need quota accounting

Recommended: three lanes (critical, normal, bulk), each with its own Kafka topic, its own consumer group, and its own worker pool. We also reserve provider throughput. If Twilio gives us 1,000 SMS/s, critical gets a guaranteed 300/s, and bulk uses only what is left.

lanes:
  critical: {topic: notif.critical, workers: 200, provider_share: 0.3, max_lag_s: 2}
  normal:   {topic: notif.normal,   workers: 400, provider_share: 0.5}
  bulk:     {topic: notif.bulk,     workers: 400, provider_share: 0.2,
             borrow_unused: true}

Alert on consumer lag for the critical lane above 2 seconds.

What happens when a provider goes down?

The problem: SendGrid has an outage, or Twilio is slow in one region. We promised 99.99% availability.

Recommended: keep at least two providers per channel (email: SES + SendGrid, SMS: Twilio + Vonage; push only has APNs for iOS and FCM for Android, so for push we can only retry and queue). Wrap each provider in a circuit breaker. When the error rate passes a threshold, the breaker opens and traffic shifts to the backup.

class ProviderRouter:
    def __init__(self, providers):
        self.providers = providers               # ordered by preference/cost

    def send(self, msg):
        for p in self.providers:
            if p.breaker.is_open():
                continue
            try:
                r = p.client.send(msg, timeout=2.0)
                p.breaker.record_success()
                return r
            except TransientError:
                p.breaker.record_failure()       # opens at >50% errors / 30 s
        raise AllProvidersDown()                  # -> retry topic

Because the dedup key is ours, switching providers mid-retry does not cause our own double send, although the first provider might still deliver late. That is an acceptable rare duplicate.

9. Common mistakes and interviewer follow-ups

  • Mistake: calling providers synchronously from the API. It couples caller latency to Twilio’s latency. Say instead: accept, persist, enqueue, return 202.
  • Mistake: claiming “exactly once”. The interviewer will push on the crash-after-send window. Say: at-least-once from the queue plus idempotent claims gives effectively once, with a small bounded duplicate risk.
  • Mistake: one queue for everything. A campaign blocks OTPs. Say: separate lanes, separate worker pools, reserved provider quota.
  • Mistake: retrying every error. Invalid tokens and unsubscribed emails are permanent. Say: classify errors, retry only transient ones, prune dead tokens.
  • Mistake: ignoring expiry. Late promos hurt. Say: carry expires_at and check before every attempt.
  • Mistake: reading preferences from the DB on every message. Say: cache with invalidation on write.
  • Follow-up: “How do you build an in-app inbox?” Add a consumer that writes each notification to a per-user feed table (Cassandra, partition by user_id, sorted by time).
  • Follow-up: “How do you stop SMS pumping fraud on OTP?” Per-phone and per-IP rate limits, country allowlists, and cost alarms.

Storage ~1 TB/day of logs, 30 days hot
API POST /notifications returns 202, idempotency key required
Pipeline API -> Kafka lanes -> router -> channel queues -> workers -> providers
Dedup Unique key at API; conditional claim notif_id:channel before send
Delivery At-least-once from queue, effectively once to user
Preferences Redis cache, invalidate on write; quiet hours defer; security bypasses
Rate limit Redis INCR per user/category/channel/day
Retries Backoff topics 5s to 1h, classify errors, DLQ + replay
Priority critical/normal/bulk topics, separate pools, reserved provider share
Failover Two providers per channel, circuit breakers
CAP AP for send path; strong only for dedup key writes

21. YouTube Top K (Hard)

We want to show the K most viewed YouTube videos (for example the top 100) over a few time windows: the last hour, the last day, the last month, and all time. Views arrive as a firehose of events from players all over the world. The product looks tiny, one list on a page, but the interviewer is testing data-intensive design: how to count billions of events per day, how to keep counts per time window without recounting everything, when approximate counting (count-min sketch) is good enough versus when you need exact numbers, how to deal with one viral video that gets a huge share of traffic, how to serve the list in milliseconds, and how to recover counts after a node dies.

1. Functional requirements

Core (must have):

  1. Clients can query the top K videos (K up to 1,000) by view count.
  2. Supported windows: last 1 hour, last 1 day, last 30 days, and all time.
  3. The system ingests every view event emitted by video players.
  4. Results are fresh: a view should be reflected in the ranking within about 1 minute.

Below the line (out of scope):

  • Arbitrary time ranges like “March 3 to March 9”. We support fixed windows only. Arbitrary ranges are a data warehouse query.
  • Per-country or per-category top K. We can mention it as an extension (it multiplies the number of keys).
  • Deciding what counts as a “valid” view (bot filtering, minimum watch time). Assume an upstream service emits only valid views.
  • Personalized ranking. That is a recommendation system.

2. Non-functional requirements

  1. Ingest: sustain ~700k view events per second on average and ~3.5M per second at peak.
  2. Query latency: p99 < 50 ms for a top K read.
  3. Freshness: results lag real views by at most 60 seconds.
  4. Accuracy: exact counts are preferred for the published list (top K is shown publicly and creators care). Small approximation in the candidate selection step is acceptable if the final ranking is correct within a tiny error for the top 1,000.
  5. Availability: 99.99% for reads. A stale result is better than an error.
  6. Durability: counts must survive node failures. We must not double count or lose large chunks of views.
  7. CAP choice: AP. Reads may be up to a minute stale, and different readers may briefly see different lists. Counting must be eventually exact.

3. Back-of-the-envelope estimates

Assumption Number
Views per day 60 billion (roughly 700k/s)
Peak factor 5x
Total videos 4 billion (about 3.6 billion with at least one view)
Videos with a view in a given hour ~200 million
View event size ~100 bytes (video_id, user, ts, region)
K up to 1,000
Top K read QPS ~10,000/s (cached heavily) 
Ingest QPS:
  avg  = 60e9 / 86,400          ~ 700,000 events/s
  peak = 700k * 5               ~ 3.5 million events/s

Raw event volume:
  60e9 * 100 B = 6 TB/day   -> keep in Kafka 3 days ~ 18 TB (x3 replicas)

Counter state, exact, all time:
  4e9 videos * (8 B id + 8 B count) = 64 GB   -> fits in a sharded KV store

Counter state per minute bucket (videos active in that minute):
  ~20M videos * 16 B = 320 MB per minute bucket
  1 hour of minute buckets = 60 * 320 MB ~ 19 GB (too much to keep raw)
  -> keep minute buckets only for the last hour, hour buckets for 30 days

Hour buckets for 30 days:
  200M active videos/hour * 16 B = 3.2 GB/hour * 720 hours ~ 2.3 TB
  -> store on disk (time series / KV), not RAM

Count-min sketch per minute (width 2^20, depth 5, 4-byte cells):
  2^20 * 5 * 4 B = 20 MB  (vs 320 MB exact)

Read side: 4 windows * 1,000 entries * 16 B = 64 KB total. Trivially cached.

The key numbers to say out loud: 700k writes per second and a tiny 64 KB result. The whole problem is reducing a huge write stream to a tiny, frequently read answer.

4. Core entities

  • ViewEvent: one view. Fields: video_id, event_id, timestamp, region.
  • Counter: the number of views for a video in one bucket. Fields: video_id, bucket_start, granularity (minute, hour, day), count.
  • Window: a named time range (1h, 1d, 30d, all). It is made of buckets.
  • TopKList: the published ranking for one window. Fields: window, computed_at, entries (video_id, count).
  • Checkpoint: the Kafka offset per partition that a counter has fully applied. Used for recovery.
-- Exact per-bucket counts, stored in a wide-column store
CREATE TABLE view_counts (
  video_id     BIGINT,
  granularity  TEXT,         -- 'min', 'hour', 'day'
  bucket_start TIMESTAMP,
  views        BIGINT,
  PRIMARY KEY ((granularity, bucket_start), video_id)
);

CREATE TABLE all_time_counts (
  video_id BIGINT PRIMARY KEY,
  views    BIGINT
);
{
  "window": "1h",
  "computed_at": "2026-11-05T19:07:00Z",
  "entries": [
    {"video_id": "dQw4w9WgXcQ", "views": 1840221},
    {"video_id": "9bZkp7q19f0", "views": 1203117}
  ]
}

5. API design

GET /v1/top-videos?window=1h&k=100 – get the top K for a window.

Response 200:

{
  "window": "1h",
  "as_of": "2026-11-05T19:07:00Z",
  "videos": [{"video_id": "dQw4w9WgXcQ", "views": 1840221, "rank": 1}]
}

Status codes: 200 OK, 400 for unknown window or k > 1000. Public read, no auth, but rate limited per IP at the edge.

POST /v1/views (internal) – the player backend emits a view event. In practice this is a direct Kafka produce from the view-tracking service, not an HTTP call per view.

{"event_id": "e-8f2a...", "video_id": "dQw4w9WgXcQ", "ts": 1793905620123}

Response 202. Auth: service-to-service only.

How will the system ingest views?

  1. The player reports a view to the view-tracking service, which validates it.
  2. The service produces the event to Kafka, keyed by video_id. Keying by video means all views of one video land on the same partition, so one worker owns that video’s count.
  3. Kafka keeps events for 3 days. That replay buffer is our safety net for recovery.
sequenceDiagram
    participant P as Player
    participant V as ViewTracking
    participant K as Kafka
    participant W as CounterWorker
    participant S as CountStore
    P->>V: Report view event
    V->>V: Validate view
    V->>K: Produce keyed by video id
    K-->>V: Ack, retained 3 days
    V-->>P: 202 accepted
    K->>W: Deliver events for partition
    W->>W: Increment minute map
    W->>S: Flush minute bucket on close
    S-->>W: ok
    W->>K: Commit offset

How will the system keep counts?

  1. Each counter worker consumes a set of partitions.
  2. It keeps an in-memory map video_id -> count for the current minute.
  3. When the minute closes (by event time, with a small allowed lateness), it flushes the minute bucket to the count store and adds the minute counts to its hour and all-time counters.
  4. It commits the Kafka offset only after the flush succeeds.

How will users get the top K?

  1. Every worker computes its local top N (N a bit bigger than K, for example 2,000) for each window from its own videos.
  2. The aggregator merges the local lists from all workers into a global top K per window.
  3. It writes the result to Redis as a small JSON blob per window and pushes it to the CDN.
  4. GET /v1/top-videos reads from the CDN or Redis. It never touches the count store.

The merge is correct because of partitioning by video: a video’s full count lives on exactly one worker, so the global top K must be inside the union of the local top K lists. Say this explicitly, it is the main insight.

7. Deep dives

Should we count exactly, or use a count-min sketch and a heap?

The problem: at 3.5M events per second, keeping a hash map of every active video per window is a lot of memory. A count-min sketch is a fixed-size probabilistic counter that answers “about how many times did I see X?” using far less memory, but it can overcount.

How a count-min sketch works: it is a small 2D array with d rows and w columns. Each row has its own hash function. To add an item, hash it with every row’s function and increment one cell per row. To estimate a count, take the minimum of those d cells. Collisions only ever add, so the minimum is the closest to the truth and never undercounts.

import mmh3, heapq

class CountMinSketch:
    def __init__(self, width=2**20, depth=5):
        self.w, self.d = width, depth
        self.t = [[0] * width for _ in range(depth)]

    def add(self, key, n=1):
        for i in range(self.d):
            self.t[i][mmh3.hash(key, i) % self.w] += n

    def estimate(self, key):
        return min(self.t[i][mmh3.hash(key, i) % self.w] for i in range(self.d))

class SketchTopK:
    """Sketch for counts + min-heap of size K for the current leaders."""
    def __init__(self, k):
        self.k, self.cms, self.heap, self.inheap = k, CountMinSketch(), [], {}

    def add(self, vid):
        self.cms.add(vid)
        c = self.cms.estimate(vid)
        if vid in self.inheap:
            self.inheap[vid] = c                  # lazy update, heap fixed later
        elif len(self.heap) < self.k or c > self.heap[0][0]:
            heapq.heappush(self.heap, (c, vid)); self.inheap[vid] = c
            if len(self.heap) > self.k:
                _, out = heapq.heappop(self.heap); self.inheap.pop(out, None)

Error bound: with width w, the overcount is at most about (e / w) * total_events with probability 1 - e^-d. With w = 2^20 and 40M events in a minute, the max overcount is about 2.7 * 40M / 1M ~ 104 views. For the top 1,000 videos (each with tens of thousands of views per minute) that is noise.

Approach Memory per minute Accuracy Merge across nodes Notes
Exact hash map ~320 MB Exact Add maps Simple, memory heavy
Count-min sketch + heap ~20 MB Overcounts slightly Add sketches cell by cell Cannot list keys, needs heap
Exact streaming + periodic batch Map + batch job Exact eventually Batch recompute Lambda architecture

Recommended: exact counting per worker, because partitioning by video keeps each worker’s map manageable (320 MB per minute spread across ~200 workers is ~1.6 MB each). Use the sketch if the interviewer removes partition-by-video (for example events arrive randomly to any node) or asks for a much larger key space like search queries. A strong hybrid: sketch to pick candidates fast, then fetch exact counts for those candidates from the count store before publishing.

How do we maintain sliding windows without recounting?

The problem: “last hour” moves every minute. Recounting 60 minutes of raw events each minute is wasteful.

The trick: buckets. Keep counts in fixed-size buckets and keep a running window total. When a new bucket enters the window, add it. When the oldest bucket leaves, subtract it.

 minute buckets for one video (last hour window):

  t-60 t-59 ...  t-2  t-1   t
  [ 5 ][ 7 ] ... [ 9 ][12 ][ 4 ]
     ^ leaves window          ^ enters window
  window_total = window_total + b[t] - b[t-60]
Window Bucket size Buckets kept Update rule each minute
1 hour 1 minute 60 +newest minute, -minute from 60 ago
1 day 1 hour 24 (+ current partial hour) +minute into current hour; on hour roll, -hour from 24 ago
30 days 1 day (or hour) 30 same idea at day granularity
All time none 1 only add 
def on_minute_close(minute_counts, t):
    for vid, c in minute_counts.items():
        h1[vid] += c; d1[vid] += c; d30[vid] += c; all_time[vid] += c
    expired = store.read_bucket("min", t - 60)       # leaves the 1h window
    for vid, c in expired.items():
        h1[vid] -= c
        if h1[vid] == 0: del h1[vid]
    if is_hour_boundary(t):
        for vid, c in store.read_bucket("hour", t - 24*60).items():
            d1[vid] -= c
    if is_day_boundary(t):
        for vid, c in store.read_bucket("day", t - 30*1440).items():
            d30[vid] -= c

The 1-day window is “hopping” at hour granularity: it is accurate to within the current hour. Mention this trade-off. If the interviewer wants minute accuracy on the daily window, keep 1,440 minute buckets, which costs more storage.

Late events: use event time, not arrival time. Allow a lateness of, say, 2 minutes. A minute bucket closes 2 minutes after its end. Events later than that go to the current bucket (slight misattribution) or are dropped and counted only in a nightly exact batch.

How do we get exact results and still be fast?

The problem: interviewers often ask, “Is approximate OK?” Creators and press quote these numbers, so the published top 100 should be exact.

Option Freshness Exactness Cost
Streaming exact counters (above) ~1 min Exact if no data loss Medium
Sketch only Seconds Approximate Low
Lambda: fast approximate stream + nightly batch Stream fresh, batch exact Exact after batch Two code paths
Kappa: one exact stream with replay ~1 min Exact One code path

Recommended: Kappa style. One streaming job with exact counts, exactly-once state via checkpoints (Flink checkpoints with Kafka offsets), and replay from Kafka for repair. Add a daily batch job over the raw events in the data lake as an audit that compares totals and alerts on drift above 0.1%.

What about a hot video that gets a huge share of all views?

The problem: a viral video can get 200k views per second. Partitioning by video_id sends all of them to one Kafka partition and one worker. That worker falls behind and the whole window is delayed.

Option Pros Cons
Do nothing Simple One hot partition lags
Pre-aggregate at the producer (batch per second) Shrinks events 100x+ Producers hold small state
Salt hot keys: video_id#0..N Spreads load Must merge salted counts before ranking
Two-stage aggregation: random partition, then by key Fully balanced Extra stage, more latency

Recommended: pre-aggregate at the edge plus salting for known hot keys. The view-tracking service buffers for 1 second and emits {video_id, count} instead of one event per view. A viral video then produces one message per second per tracking host instead of 200k.

# in each view-tracking host
buffer = Counter()
def on_view(video_id):
    buffer[video_id] += 1

def flush_every_second():
    for vid, n in buffer.items():
        key = vid
        if hot_keys.contains(vid):                 # detected by a sampler
            key = f"{vid}#{random.randrange(16)}"  # spread over 16 partitions
        kafka.send("views", key=key, value={"vid": vid, "n": n, "ts": now()})
    buffer.clear()

When we salt, the “one video lives on one worker” rule breaks. Fix it with a second, tiny merge stage keyed by the real video_id that sums the salted partial counts. The second stage sees only a few messages per second per hot video, so it is cheap.

How do we serve top K in under 50 ms?

The problem: 10k reads per second, and computing a top K from billions of counters on read is impossible.

Recommended: precompute. The answer is 64 KB total for four windows. Recompute every 30 to 60 seconds and serve it from memory.

 workers --local top 2000 per window--> aggregator
 aggregator: k-way merge (heap) -> global top 1000 per window
          -> Redis SET topk:1h <json> ; topk:1d ; topk:30d ; topk:all
          -> CDN purge or short TTL (30 s)
 API: read Redis -> slice first k -> return
def merge_local_lists(lists, k=1000):
    # each list is already sorted desc by count; videos are disjoint
    return heapq.nlargest(k, itertools.chain.from_iterable(lists),
                          key=lambda e: e["views"])

Why N = 2,000 local and not 1,000? It costs little and protects against salted keys whose partial counts are split. With exact partitioning by video, local K is enough.

Serving numbers: a Redis GET of 16 KB takes well under 1 ms. The CDN absorbs nearly all public traffic with a 30-second TTL, which also matches our freshness goal.

How do we recover if a counter node dies?

The problem: a worker holds in-memory counts for a minute or more. If it crashes, those counts are gone. If we simply restart from the last committed offset we may also double count events that were already flushed.

Option Pros Cons
Restart from latest offset Fast Loses events in flight
Replay from last committed offset, idempotent bucket writes No loss, no double count Must make writes idempotent
Flink checkpoints (state + offsets snapshotted together) Exactly-once state Checkpoint overhead

Recommended: snapshot state and offsets together, and make bucket writes idempotent by writing absolute values (SET count = X for a bucket) instead of increments.

 every 30 s:
   checkpoint = {partition offsets, in-memory counters}  -> S3 / HDFS
 on crash:
   new worker loads latest checkpoint
   seeks Kafka to checkpointed offsets
   replays events since then (at most 30 s of data)
 bucket flush:
   UPSERT view_counts (bucket, video_id) = absolute_count   -- idempotent

Because the bucket write sets an absolute value, replaying the same minute twice writes the same number twice. No double count. The all-time counter is rebuilt from the checkpoint plus replay, never by “increment again”.

The aggregator is stateless. If it dies, a standby takes over and rebuilds the top K from workers in one cycle. Redis keeps the last published list, so readers see a slightly stale list instead of an error.

The write firehose and the read path meet only at Redis: views flow from tracking hosts through Kafka and Flink into the count store, while readers only ever touch the CDN, the Top K API and one small Redis blob.

9. Common mistakes and interviewer follow-ups

  • Mistake: querying a database with ORDER BY views DESC LIMIT K on every read. At 4B rows and 700k updates/s this cannot keep up. Say: precompute and cache, the answer is tiny.
  • Mistake: random partitioning, then trying to merge local top K. A video’s count is split across nodes, so local top K lists can miss the global winner. Say: partition by video_id, or add a merge stage.
  • Mistake: using a sketch and claiming exact results. Say clearly that the sketch overcounts and give the error bound, then offer the exact path.
  • Mistake: recomputing windows from raw events. Say: buckets plus add-new, subtract-expired.
  • Mistake: increments on replay. Replaying +1 double counts. Say: snapshot state with offsets, write absolute bucket values.
  • Mistake: ignoring hot keys. Say: pre-aggregate at the edge and salt known hot keys.
  • Follow-up: “Top K per country?” Add country to the key, counts grow by the number of countries but most videos are active in few countries. The top K blobs grow to about 200 x 64 KB, still tiny.
  • Follow-up: “Arbitrary time range?” Sum hour buckets from the count store in a batch query, or use an OLAP store like Druid or Pinot.

10. One-page cheat sheet

Topic Key point
Scale 60B views/day, ~700k/s avg, ~3.5M/s peak
Output 4 windows x 1,000 entries ~ 64 KB, cache it
Partitioning Kafka keyed by video_id so one worker owns a video
Counting Exact per worker; count-min sketch (20 MB vs 320 MB) when keys are huge or unpartitioned
CMS error about e/w * N overcount, never undercount
Windows Minute buckets for 1h, hour buckets for 1d, day for 30d; add new, subtract expired
Merge Local top N per worker, k-way heap merge for global top K
Hot keys 1 s pre-aggregation at edge, salt vid#0..15, second merge stage
Serving Recompute every 30-60 s, Redis + CDN, p99 < 50 ms
Recovery Flink checkpoints (state + offsets), replay Kafka, idempotent absolute upserts
Correctness Kappa stream + nightly batch audit
CAP AP, up to 60 s stale

22. Uber (Hard)

Uber connects riders who need a trip with nearby drivers. A rider enters a destination, sees a fare estimate, and requests a ride. The system finds a close, available driver, offers them the trip, and once they accept, both sides track the trip until drop-off. The interviewer is testing real-time geospatial design: how to absorb millions of driver location updates per minute, how to find the nearest drivers fast, how to make sure one driver is never sent two rides at once (and a rider never gets two drivers), and how the system behaves when a matching server dies mid-request.

1. Functional requirements

Core (must have):

  1. Riders can enter a pickup and destination and get a fare estimate (with ETA).
  2. Riders can request a ride based on that estimate.
  3. The system matches the rider with a nearby available driver. The driver can accept or decline. On decline or timeout, the next driver is tried.
  4. Drivers send their location continuously while online.
  5. Riders and drivers can follow the trip through its states (requested, matched, arriving, in progress, completed, cancelled), including the driver’s live position.

Below the line (out of scope):

  • Payments, tipping, and payouts (a separate payments system).
  • Ratings and reviews.
  • Ride types beyond a single standard type (pooling changes matching a lot).
  • Scheduled rides in the future.
  • Fraud detection and driver onboarding.

2. Non-functional requirements

  1. Matching latency: a rider is matched (or told no drivers are available) within p99 < 1 minute. Finding candidate drivers takes < 100 ms.
  2. Location ingestion: handle ~2.5M location updates per second at peak, with a driver’s position at most ~5 seconds stale.
  3. Strong consistency for dispatch: a driver is offered at most one ride at a time, and a ride is assigned to at most one driver.
  4. Availability: 99.99% for requesting rides. Location tracking can briefly degrade (stale positions) without blocking new rides.
  5. Durability: once a trip is accepted, its state is never lost.
  6. Regional scale: millions of concurrent drivers worldwide; traffic is local, so we can shard by city or region.
  7. CAP choice: CP for the ride and driver assignment (correctness over availability for that small piece), AP for location data (fast and approximately fresh is fine).

3. Back-of-the-envelope estimates

Assumption Number
Drivers online at peak (worldwide) 10 million
Location update interval every 4 seconds
Rides per day 30 million
Peak factor for ride requests 3x
Location update size ~100 bytes
Fare estimates per ride ~3 (people check before booking)
Trip record size ~2 KB 
Location writes:
  10M drivers / 4 s              = 2.5M updates/s at peak
  bandwidth = 2.5M * 100 B       = 250 MB/s ingest

Ride requests:
  avg = 30M / 86,400             ~ 350 rides/s
  peak = 350 * 3                 ~ 1,000 rides/s
Fare estimates:
  peak ~ 3,000 /s

Driver location index (only latest position):
  10M * ~100 B                   = 1 GB  -> fits in memory (Redis)

Trip storage:
  30M * 2 KB                     = 60 GB/day ~ 22 TB/year

Location history (if we keep it for trips, 1 point / 4 s):
  2.5M * 100 B * 86,400          ~ 21 TB/day raw -> sample, compress, cold store

Main takeaway: the write firehose is location updates (2.5M/s). Ride requests are tiny by comparison (1k/s), but each one needs strong correctness.

4. Core entities

  • Rider: user who requests trips. Fields: rider_id, name, payment_method_id.
  • Driver: user who drives. Fields: driver_id, vehicle, status (offline, available, offered, on_trip).
  • Location: latest position of a driver. Fields: driver_id, lat, lng, heading, ts.
  • Fare: a price quote. Fields: fare_id, rider_id, pickup, dropoff, price, eta, surge_multiplier, expires_at.
  • Ride: one trip. Fields: ride_id, rider_id, driver_id, fare_id, status, timestamps.
  • Offer: one attempt to give a ride to a driver. Fields: ride_id, driver_id, sent_at, expires_at, response.
CREATE TABLE ride (
  ride_id      UUID PRIMARY KEY,
  rider_id     BIGINT NOT NULL,
  driver_id    BIGINT,
  fare_id      UUID NOT NULL UNIQUE,     -- one ride per fare (idempotency)
  status       TEXT NOT NULL,            -- requested, matched, ...
  pickup       GEOGRAPHY(POINT),
  dropoff      GEOGRAPHY(POINT),
  price_cents  INT NOT NULL,
  version      INT NOT NULL DEFAULT 0,   -- optimistic concurrency
  created_at   TIMESTAMPTZ,
  updated_at   TIMESTAMPTZ
);

CREATE TABLE fare (
  fare_id     UUID PRIMARY KEY,
  rider_id    BIGINT,
  price_cents INT,
  surge       NUMERIC(3,2),
  eta_seconds INT,
  expires_at  TIMESTAMPTZ
);
{"driver_id": 7781, "lat": 37.7749, "lng": -122.4194,
 "heading": 270, "speed_mps": 8.1, "ts": 1793905620}

5. API design

All rider and driver calls require a JWT session token from the auth service. The user id comes from the token, never from the request body.

POST /v1/fares – get a fare estimate.

{"pickup": {"lat": 37.77, "lng": -122.41}, "dropoff": {"lat": 37.80, "lng": -122.27}}

Response 201: {"fare_id": "f-1", "price_cents": 2350, "surge": 1.2, "eta_seconds": 240, "expires_at": "..."}

POST /v1/rides – request a ride from a fare. The fare_id doubles as the idempotency key.

{"fare_id": "f-1"}

Response 202: {"ride_id": "r-9", "status": "requested"}. Status 409 if the fare expired, 200 with the existing ride if the same fare was already booked.

POST /v1/drivers/location – driver app sends location (batched, every ~4 s).

{"lat": 37.7749, "lng": -122.4194, "heading": 270, "ts": 1793905620}

Response 204. (At scale, this is better over a persistent connection, see deep dives.)

PATCH /v1/drivers/status – go online or offline. Body {"status": "available"}. Response 200.

POST /v1/rides/{ride_id}/accept and /decline – driver responds to an offer. Response 200, or 409 if the offer expired or the ride was taken.

PATCH /v1/rides/{ride_id} – driver advances state: {"status": "arrived"}, "in_progress", "completed". Rider can send "cancelled". Response 200 or 409 for an invalid transition.

GET /v1/rides/{ride_id} and a WebSocket /v1/rides/{ride_id}/stream – rider sees status and live driver position.

How will riders get a fare estimate?

  1. The rider app calls POST /v1/fares with pickup and dropoff.
  2. The fare service calls a routing/ETA service (map graph, see deep dives) for distance and duration.
  3. It reads the current surge multiplier for the pickup area.
  4. It computes price = (base + per_km * km + per_min * min) * surge, stores the fare with a short expiry (for example 5 minutes), and returns it.
sequenceDiagram
    participant R as RiderApp
    participant G as Gateway
    participant F as FareService
    participant E as ETAService
    participant S as SurgeStore
    participant D as FareDB
    R->>G: POST fares with pickup and dropoff
    G->>F: Forward with rider id from JWT
    F->>E: Route distance and duration
    E-->>F: km and minutes
    F->>S: Get surge for pickup cell
    S-->>F: Multiplier 1.2
    F->>F: Compute price
    F->>D: Store fare with 5 min expiry
    D-->>F: ok
    F-->>G: Fare id, price, ETA
    G-->>R: 201 fare estimate

How will riders request a ride?

  1. The app calls POST /v1/rides with the fare_id.
  2. The ride service inserts a ride row with status requested. The unique constraint on fare_id makes the request idempotent: a double tap creates one ride.
  3. It hands the ride to the matching service (via a queue so the request survives a crash, see deep dives) and returns 202.

How will drivers report location?

  1. The driver app sends a location every 4 seconds over a persistent connection.
  2. The location service writes it to the Redis geo index with GEOADD and stores a heartbeat timestamp.
  3. Drivers whose heartbeat is older than ~30 s are treated as offline.

How will the system match a rider with a driver?

  1. The matching service queries Redis for available drivers within a radius of the pickup, sorted by distance.
  2. It re-ranks the top few by real ETA (road distance, not straight line).
  3. For the best candidate it tries to take a short lock on that driver. If it gets the lock, it sends an offer push and waits up to 10 s.
  4. On accept, it updates the ride (status matched, driver_id) in the DB with a conditional write. On decline or timeout, it releases the lock and tries the next driver.

How will riders and drivers track the trip?

  1. The driver app advances the state: arrived, in progress, completed.
  2. The ride service validates each transition and writes it.
  3. The rider’s WebSocket subscribes to the ride channel. Driver location updates for that driver are forwarded to the rider every few seconds.

7. Deep dives

How do we handle 2.5 million location updates per second?

The problem: a relational database cannot take 2.5M updates per second on one table, and we only care about the latest position for matching.

Option Write throughput Proximity query Notes
Postgres + PostGIS Tens of thousands/s per node Good (R-tree) Index churn kills it at this rate
Redis GEO (geohash in a sorted set) ~100k+/s per shard GEOSEARCH radius In-memory, shard by region
Custom in-memory grid (H3 cells) Very high Look up neighbor cells What Uber built (H3)

What is a geohash? It turns a (lat, lng) into a string by repeatedly splitting the world in half. Nearby points share a prefix. 9q8yy is a cell of about 5 km x 5 km in San Francisco. Redis GEO stores each driver in a sorted set with a 52-bit geohash as the score, so a radius query becomes a few range scans.

Recommended: Redis GEO sharded by city (or by geohash prefix for huge cities), with the location service as the only writer. Batch updates on the client and use a persistent connection to cut per-request overhead.

# location service: one update
def on_location(driver_id, lat, lng, ts):
    shard = shard_for(lat, lng)                 # e.g. city or geohash[:4]
    if shard != last_shard.get(driver_id):      # driver crossed a boundary
        redis_for(last_shard[driver_id]).zrem("drivers:geo", driver_id)
        last_shard[driver_id] = shard
    r = redis_for(shard)
    pipe = r.pipeline()
    pipe.geoadd("drivers:geo", (lng, lat, driver_id))
    pipe.set(f"drv:hb:{driver_id}", ts, ex=30)  # heartbeat with TTL
    pipe.execute()
 2.5M/s total; each Redis shard ~100k writes/s comfortably
 -> 25-40 primary shards worldwide (+ replicas), split by city load

Further reduction: adaptive update rates. A parked driver can report every 15 s; a moving driver every 4 s; a driver on a trip every 2 s for smooth tracking. Only “available” drivers need to be in the matching index at all; drivers on a trip go to a separate tracking path.

How do we find the nearest driver for a rider?

The problem: straight-line distance is a poor proxy. A driver 300 m away across a river may be 10 minutes out.

Recommended two-step: cheap filter, then accurate rank.

def find_candidates(pickup, k=10):
    r = redis_for(shard_for(pickup.lat, pickup.lng))
    for radius_km in (1, 2, 5):                  # expand ring if empty
        ids = r.geosearch("drivers:geo", longitude=pickup.lng,
                          latitude=pickup.lat, radius=radius_km, unit="km",
                          sort="ASC", count=50)
        ids = [d for d in ids if is_available(d) and heartbeat_fresh(d)]
        if ids:
            break
    etas = eta_service.batch_eta(origins=ids, dest=pickup)   # road network
    return sorted(zip(ids, etas), key=lambda x: x[1])[:k]

The ETA service uses a road graph with live traffic. Uber’s production system precomputes routes over a partitioned graph (contraction hierarchies style) so a one-to-many ETA call takes a few milliseconds. In the interview, it is enough to say “a routing service with a road graph and historical plus live speeds per road segment, cached by cell pair”.

How do we make sure a driver is never sent two rides at once?

The problem: two matching servers handle two riders near the same driver at the same moment. Both see the driver as available and both send an offer. The driver accepts both, or accepts one and the other rider waits.

Option Pros Cons
Check status in DB, then send offer Simple Race between check and update
DB row lock / conditional update on driver status Strong DB on the hot path, lock held for 10 s offer
Distributed lock in Redis with TTL (SET NX PX) Fast, auto-expires Must handle lock expiry and fencing
Single owner per region (one matcher per city shard) No cross-node race Hot spot, failover needed

Recommended: a Redis lock per driver with a TTL equal to the offer timeout plus a margin, and a final conditional write on the ride row as the source of truth.

OFFER_TTL_MS = 12_000

def offer(ride_id, driver_id):
    token = str(uuid4())
    got = redis.set(f"lock:driver:{driver_id}", f"{ride_id}:{token}",
                    nx=True, px=OFFER_TTL_MS)
    if not got:
        return False                              # someone else is offering
    push.send(driver_id, {"type": "offer", "ride_id": ride_id,
                          "expires_in_s": 10})
    return token
-- on driver accept: only succeeds if ride is still unassigned
UPDATE ride
SET driver_id = :driver_id, status = 'matched', version = version + 1
WHERE ride_id = :ride_id AND status = 'requested' AND driver_id IS NULL;
-- 0 rows updated -> ride taken or cancelled, tell driver 409

Why TTL? If the matcher crashes after locking, the driver is not stuck forever. After 12 s the lock disappears and the driver is available again. Why the SQL guard too? Locks with TTL can expire early (GC pause, clock issues). The conditional update is the fencing check that guarantees one driver per ride. The driver’s accept call must also verify that it still holds the lock value it was offered (compare the ride id in the lock).

Release on decline uses a compare-and-delete so we never delete someone else’s lock:

-- Lua script, atomic in Redis
if redis.call("GET", KEYS[1]) == ARGV[1] then
  return redis.call("DEL", KEYS[1])
end
return 0

What if the matching service crashes in the middle of a request?

The problem: the rider is waiting. The matcher that owned their ride crashed after offering to driver 1. Nobody is trying driver 2. The rider sees a spinner forever.

Option Pros Cons
Matching in the request thread Simple Crash loses the request
Durable queue of ride requests, consumer acks after match Survives crashes, retries Possible duplicate processing
Workflow engine (Temporal / Step Functions) with timers Built-in retries and timeouts Extra infra

Recommended: put each ride on a durable queue (Kafka or SQS) and use a visibility timeout. The matcher processes one ride at a time and only acks after the ride is matched or no_drivers. If it dies, the message becomes visible again and another matcher takes it. Matching is idempotent because the ride row and driver locks hold the real state.

def match_loop():
    for msg in queue.receive(visibility_timeout_s=30):
        ride = db.get_ride(msg.ride_id)
        if ride.status != "requested":
            queue.ack(msg); continue              # already done by someone
        tried = set(ride.tried_drivers or [])
        for driver_id, eta in find_candidates(ride.pickup):
            if driver_id in tried:
                continue
            db.append_tried(ride.ride_id, driver_id)   # persist progress
            if offer(ride.ride_id, driver_id) and wait_accept(ride, driver_id, 10):
                break
            queue.extend_visibility(msg, 30)      # heartbeat while working
        else:
            db.set_status(ride.ride_id, "no_drivers")
        queue.ack(msg)

The tried_drivers list stops a new matcher from re-offering to drivers who already declined. The rider app polls or listens on the ride channel, so it simply sees the status change.

How do we model the trip so states never get out of sync?

The problem: driver taps “complete” while the rider taps “cancel”. Network retries resend old transitions.

Recommended: an explicit state machine with allowed transitions, enforced with optimistic concurrency (a version column).

 requested --match--> matched --arrive--> arriving --start--> in_progress
     |                   |                    |                    |
     +--cancel/no_drv-+  +------cancel--------+               complete
                      v                       v                    v
                  cancelled               cancelled            completed
ALLOWED = {
    "requested":   {"matched", "cancelled", "no_drivers"},
    "matched":     {"arriving", "cancelled"},
    "arriving":    {"in_progress", "cancelled"},
    "in_progress": {"completed"},
}

def transition(ride_id, new_status, expected_version):
    ride = db.get(ride_id)
    if new_status not in ALLOWED.get(ride.status, set()):
        raise Conflict(f"{ride.status} -> {new_status} not allowed")
    n = db.execute("""UPDATE ride SET status=%s, version=version+1
                      WHERE ride_id=%s AND version=%s""",
                   (new_status, ride_id, expected_version))
    if n == 0:
        raise Conflict("stale version, reload")
    events.publish("ride.status", {"ride_id": ride_id, "status": new_status})

Each transition publishes an event that drives notifications, billing, and the driver’s status (back to available on completion or cancel).

How does surge pricing work, and how do we handle a demand spike?

The problem: a concert ends and 20,000 people open the app in one neighborhood. Demand is far higher than supply.

Surge: every 30-60 seconds, a stream job counts open requests and available drivers per cell (geohash or H3 cell) and sets a multiplier. Higher prices reduce demand and pull drivers in.

def surge_for_cell(demand, supply):
    ratio = demand / max(supply, 1)
    if ratio < 1.2:
        return 1.0
    return min(round(1.0 + 0.5 * (ratio - 1.2), 1), 3.0)   # capped at 3x

The multiplier is stored in Redis per cell and locked into the fare quote (fare.surge), so a rider pays what they saw. For the request spike itself: matching is sharded by city, the ride queue buffers bursts, and fare estimates are cacheable per cell pair for a few seconds.

9. Common mistakes and interviewer follow-ups

  • Mistake: storing every location update in Postgres. 2.5M writes/s with index churn will not hold. Say: in-memory geo index for latest position, stream history to cold storage.
  • Mistake: matching by straight-line distance only. Say: geo filter for candidates, then rank by road ETA.
  • Mistake: “check driver is free, then assign” without atomicity. Say: Redis lock with TTL plus a conditional update as the fencing check.
  • Mistake: no plan for a crashed matcher. Say: durable queue, visibility timeout, persisted list of tried drivers.
  • Mistake: one global Redis. Say: shard by city or geohash prefix; rides are local.
  • Mistake: free-form status updates. Say: explicit state machine with optimistic concurrency.
  • Follow-up: “Driver crosses a shard boundary?” The location service moves the driver to the new shard and removes it from the old one. Matching near a border queries both shards.
  • Follow-up: “How do you scale across regions?” Each region is independent (cells of cities). Global data like user profiles is replicated; rides stay in the region where they start.

10. One-page cheat sheet

Topic Key point
Scale 10M drivers, 2.5M location writes/s, ~1k ride requests/s peak
Location index Redis GEO (geohash sorted set), sharded by city, ~1 GB total
Freshness Updates every 2-15 s adaptive, heartbeat TTL 30 s
Matching GEOSEARCH radius ring 1/2/5 km, rank by road ETA
No double dispatch SET lock:driver NX PX 12000 + UPDATE ride ... WHERE driver_id IS NULL
Idempotency fare_id unique per ride
Failure Ride queue with visibility timeout, tried_drivers persisted
Trip State machine + version column, events on each transition
Surge Per-cell demand/supply every 30-60 s, locked into fare quote
CAP CP for assignment, AP for locations
