23. Robinhood (Hard)

Robinhood is a stock brokerage app. Users watch live prices, place market and limit orders, cancel them, and see their order status. Robinhood is not the stock exchange. It forwards orders to an exchange (or a market maker) and receives fills back. The interviewer is testing two very different systems in one design: a huge, loss-tolerant price stream to millions of phones, and a small but money-critical order path that must never lose, duplicate, or mis-state an order. Strong answers say this split out loud and give each side different guarantees.

1. Functional requirements

Core (must have):

  1. Users can see live prices for stocks (a watchlist and a symbol detail page).
  2. Users can place orders: market orders (buy now at the best price) and limit orders (buy only at or below a price, sell only at or above).
  3. Users can cancel an open order.
  4. Users can see their orders and their status (pending, open, partially filled, filled, cancelled, rejected).

Below the line (out of scope):

  • Building the exchange or matching engine. Exchanges do this.
  • Options, crypto, margin, short selling.
  • Portfolio charts and tax documents (read models built from fills).
  • Funding the account (bank transfers). Assume a buying-power service exists.
  • Charting history (OHLC candles) beyond a mention.

2. Non-functional requirements

  1. Price latency: a price change reaches a watching client within p99 < 500 ms of arriving from the market data feed.
  2. Price fan-out scale: 10M concurrently connected clients during market open, each watching about 20 symbols.
  3. Order correctness: no lost orders, no duplicate orders. Order status must be strongly consistent with what the exchange says.
  4. Order latency: order submit to exchange in p99 < 200 ms inside our system.
  5. Availability: 99.99% for order placement during market hours (9:30 to 16:00 ET). Price streaming can degrade (coalesce, slower updates) but should stay up.
  6. Burst handling: 10x to 20x traffic spike in the first minutes after market open and on meme-stock days.
  7. Auditability: every order event is kept immutable for at least 7 years (broker-dealer rules such as SEC 17a-4 and FINRA CAT reporting).
  8. CAP choice: orders are CP (prefer to reject or delay than to be wrong). Prices are AP (stale by a second is better than an error).

3. Back-of-the-envelope estimates

Assumption Number
Daily active users 20 million
Peak concurrent connected clients 10 million
Symbols watched per client 20
US-listed symbols ~10,000
Market data updates (all symbols) ~100k/s, peaks 1M/s
Orders per day 10 million
Peak order rate (open, 30x average over trading hours) ~13,000/s
Price message size ~60 bytes
Order event size ~500 bytes 
Orders:
  trading day = 6.5 h = 23,400 s
  avg = 10M / 23,400            ~ 430 orders/s
  peak (30x at open)            ~ 13,000 orders/s
  order events (submit, ack, fills, cancel) ~ 4 per order -> 52k events/s peak

Price fan-out (naive: every tick to every watcher):
  subscriptions = 10M clients * 20 symbols = 200M subscriptions
  if each watched symbol ticks 5x/s -> 1 billion messages/s  (too much)
  coalesce to 1 update/s per symbol per client:
    10M * 20 * 1/s = 200M msgs/s * 60 B = 12 GB/s outbound
  only ~5 symbols visible on screen at a time:
    10M * 5 * 1/s = 50M msgs/s * 60 B = 3 GB/s (24 Gbps) across the edge fleet

Connections:
  10M WebSockets / 50k per server ~ 200 edge servers (+ headroom ~300)

Order storage:
  10M * 4 events * 500 B = 20 GB/day ~ 5 TB/year; 7 years ~ 35 TB (WORM storage)

The two lines to remember: price fan-out is tens of millions of messages per second and must be coalesced; orders are only ~13k per second but must be perfect.

4. Core entities

  • User / Account: holder of cash and positions. Fields: account_id, buying_power, status.
  • Symbol: a tradable stock. Fields: ticker, exchange, tick size, trading status (halted or not).
  • Quote: latest price for a symbol. Fields: ticker, bid, ask, last, ts, seq.
  • Order: a user’s instruction. Fields: order_id, client_order_id, account_id, ticker, side, type, qty, limit_price, status, filled_qty, avg_price, exchange_order_id.
  • Execution (fill): a trade confirmation from the exchange. Fields: exec_id, order_id, qty, price, ts.
  • OrderEvent: immutable log row for each state change (for audit).
CREATE TABLE orders (
  order_id          UUID PRIMARY KEY,
  account_id        BIGINT NOT NULL,
  client_order_id   TEXT NOT NULL,          -- idempotency from the app
  ticker            TEXT NOT NULL,
  side              TEXT NOT NULL,          -- buy / sell
  type              TEXT NOT NULL,          -- market / limit
  qty               NUMERIC(18,6) NOT NULL,
  limit_price       NUMERIC(18,4),
  status            TEXT NOT NULL,
  filled_qty        NUMERIC(18,6) DEFAULT 0,
  exchange_order_id TEXT,
  version           INT NOT NULL DEFAULT 0,
  created_at        TIMESTAMPTZ NOT NULL,
  UNIQUE (account_id, client_order_id)
);

CREATE TABLE order_events (                 -- append-only audit log
  event_id   BIGSERIAL PRIMARY KEY,
  order_id   UUID NOT NULL,
  type       TEXT NOT NULL,                 -- created, sent, acked, fill, ...
  payload    JSONB NOT NULL,
  ts         TIMESTAMPTZ NOT NULL
);
{"ticker": "AAPL", "bid": 227.41, "ask": 227.43, "last": 227.42,
 "ts": 1793905620123, "seq": 88123401}

5. API design

All endpoints require the user’s OAuth access token. Account id comes from the token.

GET /v1/quotes?symbols=AAPL,TSLA – snapshot of latest prices. Response 200 with a list of quotes.

WS /v1/stream – live price stream. Client sends:

{"action": "subscribe", "symbols": ["AAPL", "TSLA"]}

Server pushes {"type": "quote", "ticker": "AAPL", "last": 227.42, "seq": 88123401}. (SSE GET /v1/stream?symbols=... is an alternative for read-only streams.)

POST /v1/orders – place an order.

{"client_order_id": "c9a1-...", "ticker": "AAPL", "side": "buy",
 "type": "limit", "qty": 10, "limit_price": 225.00, "time_in_force": "gfd"}

Response 202: {"order_id": "o-55", "status": "pending"}. 200 with the same order if client_order_id was already used. 400 invalid, 403 insufficient buying power, 409 symbol halted, 429 rate limited.

DELETE /v1/orders/{order_id} – request cancel. Response 202 {"status": "cancel_pending"}. Cancel is a request to the exchange; it is final only when the exchange confirms.

GET /v1/orders?status=open and GET /v1/orders/{order_id} – order status and fills. Order updates are also pushed on the same WebSocket as {"type": "order", ...}.

How will users see live prices?

  1. Market data ingest connects to exchange feeds (or a consolidated feed such as the SIP), normalizes messages, and publishes each quote to the price bus on a topic per symbol (or per symbol shard).
  2. Ingest also updates the latest quote per symbol in Redis for snapshots.
  3. A client opens a WebSocket to a stream edge server and subscribes to its symbols.
  4. The edge server subscribes to those symbols on the bus (once per server, not per client) and forwards updates, coalesced to at most a few per second per symbol.
  5. On subscribe, the edge first sends the Redis snapshot so the screen is filled instantly.
sequenceDiagram
    participant F as ExchangeFeed
    participant I as Ingest
    participant B as PriceBus
    participant R as Redis
    participant E as EdgeServer
    participant C as Client
    C->>E: WebSocket subscribe AAPL and TSLA
    E->>B: Subscribe symbol channels once
    E->>R: GET latest quotes
    R-->>E: Snapshot
    E-->>C: Snapshot quotes
    F->>I: Raw ticks
    I->>R: Update latest quote
    I->>B: Publish normalized quote
    B->>E: Quote for AAPL
    E->>E: Keep latest, coalesce 250 ms
    E-->>C: Coalesced quote update

How will users place an order?

  1. The app generates a client_order_id (UUID) and calls POST /v1/orders.
  2. The order service checks idempotency (unique account_id, client_order_id), validates the symbol and quantity, and reserves buying power.
  3. In one DB transaction it inserts the order with status pending and appends an created event to the order events table (and an outbox row for publishing).
  4. It returns 202. The exchange gateway picks the order up from the outbox, sends a FIX NewOrderSingle with our order_id as the FIX ClOrdID, and marks the order sent.
  5. The exchange replies with an ack (order is open) and later fills. The gateway writes each into the DB and pushes updates to the user.

How will users cancel an order?

  1. DELETE /v1/orders/{id} sets cancel_pending if the order is open.
  2. The gateway sends a FIX OrderCancelRequest.
  3. The exchange replies with cancelled (or “too late to cancel” if it already filled). The order moves to its final state accordingly.

How will users see order status?

  1. Every state change is written to the order DB and the event log.
  2. A publisher pushes order updates to the user’s WebSocket channel.
  3. GET /v1/orders reads from the order DB (or a read replica for history).

7. Deep dives

How do we stream live prices to 10 million clients?

The problem: 200M symbol subscriptions and millions of ticks. Sending every tick to every client is impossible and useless (a human cannot read 20 updates per second).

Transport options:

Option Pros Cons
Client polling every 1 s Simple, cacheable 10M req/s, wasted calls, latency up to 1 s
Server-Sent Events (SSE) One-way, HTTP friendly, auto-reconnect Server-to-client only (fine for prices)
WebSocket Two-way: subscribe and unsubscribe on one connection Stateful connections, needs sticky routing

Recommended: WebSocket (SSE is a fine answer too). Three ideas make fan-out tractable:

  1. Shard by symbol upstream. The bus has a topic or channel per symbol. An edge server subscribes to a symbol once and fans it out locally to all its clients who want it.
  2. Coalesce. The edge keeps only the latest quote per symbol and flushes every 250 ms to 1 s. Ten ticks become one message.
  3. Subscribe only to what is on screen. The app unsubscribes when a symbol scrolls off.
class EdgeServer:
    def __init__(self):
        self.subs = defaultdict(set)      # ticker -> set of connections
        self.latest = {}                  # ticker -> newest quote
        self.dirty = set()

    def on_client_subscribe(self, conn, tickers):
        for t in tickers:
            if not self.subs[t]:
                bus.subscribe(f"quotes.{t}", self.on_quote)   # once per server
            self.subs[t].add(conn)
            conn.send(redis.get(f"quote:{t}"))                # snapshot first

    def on_quote(self, q):
        self.latest[q.ticker] = q          # overwrite, older ticks dropped
        self.dirty.add(q.ticker)

    async def flush_loop(self):
        while True:
            await asyncio.sleep(0.25)
            for t in self.dirty:
                msg = encode(self.latest[t])
                for conn in self.subs[t]:
                    conn.send_nowait(msg)  # drop if client buffer is full
            self.dirty.clear()
 Market feed -> ingest -> pub/sub (channel per symbol, sharded)
                                |
          +---------------------+---------------------+
          v                     v                     v
     edge-1 (50k conns)    edge-2 (50k conns)  ...  edge-300
     subscribes AAPL,TSLA  subscribes AAPL,NVDA
          |                     |
       clients               clients

Hot symbols (TSLA on a news day) are subscribed by nearly every edge server. That is 300 subscribers per symbol at the bus, which Redis pub/sub or NATS handles easily. Clients connect through a load balancer; any edge can serve any client, so no client stickiness is needed beyond the connection itself. Slow clients get their messages dropped rather than buffered, since only the latest price matters. Sequence numbers let the client ignore out-of-order updates.

How do we place orders with the exchange reliably?

The problem: the order service writes to its DB and also must send to the exchange. These are two systems. If we send first and crash before writing, we have a live order we do not know about. If we write first and crash before sending, the user’s order never goes out.

Option Pros Cons
Send to exchange, then write DB Fast Crash leaves unknown live order (worst case)
Write DB, then send in the same request Simple Crash after write leaves order stuck in pending
Write DB + outbox in one transaction, separate sender Never lose an order Sender must be idempotent

Recommended: transactional outbox. The DB row is the source of truth. The exchange gateway reads pending outbox rows and sends them. Because we use our order_id as the FIX ClOrdID, and exchanges reject duplicate ClOrdIDs per session/day, a resend after a crash is detected instead of creating a second order.

def place_order(account_id, req):
    with db.transaction():
        existing = db.find_order(account_id, req.client_order_id)
        if existing:
            return existing                       # idempotent replay
        buying_power.reserve(account_id, estimate_cost(req))   # same txn/lock
        order = db.insert_order(account_id, req, status="pending")
        db.insert_event(order.id, "created", req)
        db.insert_outbox(topic="orders.new", key=order.id, payload=order)
    return order

def gateway_sender():
    for row in db.poll_outbox("orders.new", limit=500):
        fix.send_new_order_single(cl_ord_id=row.key, **row.payload)
        db.mark_order_sent(row.key)               # status pending -> sent
        db.delete_outbox(row.id)

Ambiguous case: we sent, then lost the connection before the ack. We do not know if the exchange has the order. Do not resend blindly. Send a FIX OrderStatusRequest with the ClOrdID, or wait for the exchange’s resend on session recovery (FIX sessions have sequence numbers and replay missed messages on reconnect). Until resolved, the order shows pending to the user, and cancel is still allowed.

How do we keep order state consistent and idempotent?

The problem: fills can arrive out of order, duplicated (FIX replay), or race with a user’s cancel. A partially filled order can get a cancel and another fill at the same time.

Recommended: an explicit state machine, idempotency per exchange execution id, and optimistic concurrency on the order row.

 pending -> sent -> open -> partially_filled -> filled
    |         |       |            |
    |         |       +--> cancel_pending --> cancelled
    |         |                    |              (or filled if too late)
    +-> rejected  <---------------+ rejected by exchange
def on_execution_report(er):                       # from FIX gateway
    with db.transaction():
        if db.exists("executions", exec_id=er.exec_id):
            return                                 # duplicate fill, ignore
        o = db.lock_order(er.cl_ord_id)            # SELECT ... FOR UPDATE
        if er.type == "fill":
            db.insert_execution(er)
            o.filled_qty += er.last_qty
            o.status = "filled" if o.filled_qty == o.qty else "partially_filled"
            positions.apply(o.account_id, o.ticker, o.side, er.last_qty, er.last_px)
        elif er.type == "cancelled":
            o.status = "cancelled"
            buying_power.release_unfilled(o)
        elif er.type == "rejected":
            o.status = "rejected"; buying_power.release_unfilled(o)
        db.update_order(o)
        db.insert_event(o.id, er.type, er.raw)
        db.insert_outbox("orders.updates", o.account_id, o)  # push to user

The exchange is the source of truth for fills. Once a day we reconcile our orders and executions against the exchange’s (and the clearing firm’s) end-of-day files and alert on any mismatch.

Database choice: orders need transactions and strong consistency, so a relational database (Postgres, Aurora) sharded by account_id. At ~13k orders/s and ~52k events/s peak, 8 to 16 shards with headroom are enough.

How do we support limit orders triggered by price?

The problem: “Sell AAPL if it reaches $240.” There are two ways to do this, and the interviewer wants to hear the trade-off.

Option How Pros Cons
Send the limit order to the exchange right away Exchange holds it in its book Exchange does matching, fair priority, simplest Supported only for real limit orders, not every order type
Hold it in our own trigger engine We watch prices, send a market/limit order when triggered Supports stop orders, conditional orders, extended features We must watch every tick, latency and fairness on us

Recommended: true limit orders go straight to the exchange (it is the exchange’s job). For stop and stop-limit orders (which trigger on a price but are not on the book), run a trigger engine sharded by symbol.

# one trigger worker owns a set of symbols
# per symbol: two sorted structures of resting triggers
buy_stops  = SortedList(key=lambda o: o.stop_price)   # trigger when price >= stop
sell_stops = SortedList(key=lambda o: o.stop_price)   # trigger when price <= stop

def on_trade(ticker, price):
    while buy_stops[ticker] and buy_stops[ticker][0].stop_price <= price:
        fire(buy_stops[ticker].pop(0))
    while sell_stops[ticker] and sell_stops[ticker][-1].stop_price >= price:
        fire(sell_stops[ticker].pop())

def fire(o):
    order_service.submit_child(o.id, type="market" if o.kind == "stop" else "limit")

Each check is O(log n) per tick. The trigger worker consumes the full-rate price stream (not the coalesced one). Its state lives in the order DB; on restart it reloads resting triggers for its symbols.

How do we survive the market-open spike?

The problem: at 9:30 ET, orders that were queued overnight plus a rush of new ones hit at once. Meme-stock days add 10x more. Connections also spike as users open the app.

Recommended mix:

Technique What it does
Pre-scale before 9:30 Scheduled autoscaling of edge, API, and order services; warm caches
Queue overnight orders Orders placed when closed are stored and released to the exchange at a paced rate at open
Rate limits per user and per symbol Stop a single client or bot from flooding
Admission control If the order path is saturated, return 503 with retry-after fast rather than time out
Degrade prices, never orders Raise the coalescing interval from 250 ms to 1-2 s under load
Connection jitter Clients reconnect with random backoff to avoid a thundering herd 
# token bucket in front of the exchange gateway per FIX session
class Pacer:
    def __init__(self, rate_per_s, burst):
        self.rate, self.tokens, self.burst, self.t = rate_per_s, burst, burst, time()

    def acquire(self):
        now = time()
        self.tokens = min(self.burst, self.tokens + (now - self.t) * self.rate)
        self.t = now
        if self.tokens >= 1:
            self.tokens -= 1
            return True
        return False                              # caller waits or queues

Exchanges limit messages per session, so we spread load across many FIX sessions and pace each.

How do we keep an audit trail regulators accept?

The problem: broker-dealers must keep order records for years in a form that cannot be altered, and report order lifecycle events to regulators (for example the FINRA Consolidated Audit Trail).

Recommended: the order_events table is append-only (no UPDATE or DELETE grants). A change data capture (CDC) stream copies every event to Kafka and then to write-once storage, such as S3 Object Lock in compliance mode with a 7-year retention. A daily job builds the regulatory report from the same events.

 Order DB (order_events, append-only)
        | CDC (Debezium)
        v
 Kafka "order-events" --> S3 (Object Lock, WORM, 7 yr) --> daily CAT report
                      \-> reconciliation job vs exchange/clearing files

Each event carries timestamps from our system and the exchange, plus the user and device ids, so we can reconstruct exactly who did what and when.

The lossy price path and the exact order path share only the VPC: quotes flow from exchange feeds through ingest and per-symbol pub sub to the stream edges, while orders go through the API gateway and Postgres outbox to the FIX gateway.

9. Common mistakes and interviewer follow-ups

  • Mistake: designing a matching engine. Robinhood is a broker. Say: we route orders to exchanges; we do not match them.
  • Mistake: one system for prices and orders with the same guarantees. Say: prices are AP and coalesced; orders are CP and transactional.
  • Mistake: sending every tick to every client. Say: per-symbol channels, one subscription per edge server, coalescing, only visible symbols.
  • Mistake: no idempotency on order submit. A retry on a flaky phone network buys 20 shares instead of 10. Say: client_order_id unique per account, and order_id as FIX ClOrdID.
  • Mistake: “send then save” to the exchange. Say: transactional outbox and FIX session recovery for ambiguous sends.
  • Mistake: treating cancel as instant. Say: cancel_pending until the exchange confirms; a fill can still win.
  • Follow-up: “Where does buying power live?” In the same transaction as the order on the account’s shard, so reserve and insert succeed or fail together.
  • Follow-up: “What about after-hours?” Same design, different trading sessions and order flags; overnight orders wait in our queue until the session opens.

10. One-page cheat sheet

Topic Key point
Two systems Prices: AP, lossy, coalesced. Orders: CP, exact, audited
Price scale 10M clients, 200M subs, coalesce to <= 4/s, ~300 edge servers
Fan-out Channel per symbol, edge subscribes once, local fan-out, snapshot on subscribe
Order scale ~430/s avg, ~13k/s at open
Idempotency client_order_id unique per account; order_id = FIX ClOrdID; exec_id dedup
Exchange integration Transactional outbox, FIX sessions with sequence replay
State pending, sent, open, partial, filled, cancel_pending, cancelled, rejected
Limit orders Real limits go to exchange; stops in trigger engine sharded by symbol
Open spike Pre-scale, pace FIX sessions, rate limits, degrade prices not orders
Audit Append-only events, CDC to S3 Object Lock 7 years, daily reconciliation

24. Google Docs (Hard)

Google Docs lets several people edit the same document at the same time from different browsers. Each person sees the others’ typing within a fraction of a second, sees their cursors, and nobody’s edit is lost even when two people type in the same sentence. The interviewer is testing whether you understand the core problem of concurrent edits: why “last write wins” destroys work, how Operational Transformation (OT) or CRDTs fix it, how to route every editor of a document to the same collaboration server, how to store a stream of tiny operations plus periodic snapshots, and how offline edits merge back in.

1. Functional requirements

Core (must have):

  1. Users can create a document and open an existing one.
  2. Multiple users can edit the same document at the same time, and all of them converge to the same content.
  3. Users see other editors’ changes in near real time.
  4. Users see who else is in the document and where their cursors are (presence).
  5. Users can keep editing while briefly offline; their edits merge when they reconnect.

Below the line (out of scope):

  • Permissions and sharing UI (assume an access service answers “can user U edit doc D?”).
  • Comments, suggestions mode, and version history browsing (we mention history as a by-product of storing operations).
  • Rich formatting details (bold, tables, images). We model plain text; formatting is attributes on ranges and uses the same machinery.
  • Full-text search across documents.

2. Non-functional requirements

  1. Latency: a keystroke shows locally instantly (optimistic) and reaches other editors within p99 < 200 ms in the same region.
  2. Consistency: eventual consistency with strong convergence. After all edits are delivered, every replica has the identical text. No edit is silently lost.
  3. Concurrency: up to 100 simultaneous editors per document (Google caps active editors around this size); unlimited viewers via a degraded path.
  4. Scale: 1 billion documents, 10 million documents open concurrently.
  5. Durability: an acknowledged edit is never lost (11 nines object storage for snapshots, replicated log for ops).
  6. Availability: 99.99% for opening and editing. A collaboration server crash should cost at most a reconnect of a few seconds.
  7. CAP choice: AP per document across regions, with a single ordering server per document to make OT simple. Inside a document we favor availability and convergence over a global lock.

3. Back-of-the-envelope estimates

Assumption Number
Total documents 1 billion
Average document size 50 KB
Concurrently open documents 10 million
Average active editors per open doc 2
Typing rate of an active editor ~3 operations/s (batched every ~100 ms)
Operation size ~100 bytes with metadata
Snapshot every 1,000 operations or 5 minutes 
Concurrent editors = 10M docs * 2 = 20M WebSocket connections
  -> at 50k connections per server ~ 400 collaboration servers

Operation rate = 20M editors * 3 ops/s = 60M ops/s (peak, if all typing)
  realistic: ~20% typing at once -> ~12M ops/s
  each op is broadcast to the other editors (avg 1) -> ~12M msgs/s out

Op log storage:
  12M ops/s * 100 B = 1.2 GB/s ~ 100 TB/day raw
  ops are compacted into snapshots and old ops archived -> keep 30 days hot

Document storage:
  1B docs * 50 KB = 50 TB of current snapshots (object store)

Per-document load: 100 editors * 3 ops/s = 300 ops/s on one doc
  -> easily handled by one server holding the doc in memory

Two takeaways: total load is large but spread over millions of documents, and a single document is small enough to live in one server’s memory. That is why we shard by document.

4. Core entities

  • Document: metadata. Fields: doc_id, title, owner_id, created_at, latest_snapshot_version.
  • Operation: one edit. Fields: doc_id, version (server sequence number), client_id, base_version, type (insert or delete), position, text or length.
  • Snapshot: full document content at a version. Fields: doc_id, version, content (blob pointer).
  • Session / Presence: an editor connected to a doc. Fields: doc_id, user_id, client_id, cursor position, selection, color, last_seen.
  • Client: one browser tab. Fields: client_id, pending (unacknowledged) ops.
CREATE TABLE documents (
  doc_id            UUID PRIMARY KEY,
  owner_id          BIGINT NOT NULL,
  title             TEXT,
  snapshot_version  BIGINT NOT NULL DEFAULT 0,
  snapshot_uri      TEXT,                      -- s3://docs/<doc>/<ver>
  updated_at        TIMESTAMPTZ
);

-- wide-column store (Cassandra / Bigtable), one partition per doc
CREATE TABLE doc_ops (
  doc_id      UUID,
  version     BIGINT,                         -- assigned by server, 1,2,3...
  client_id   TEXT,
  client_seq  BIGINT,                         -- idempotency per client
  op          BLOB,                           -- encoded operation
  ts          TIMESTAMP,
  PRIMARY KEY ((doc_id), version)
);
{"type": "op", "doc_id": "d-1", "client_id": "c-7", "client_seq": 42,
 "base_version": 1051, "ops": [{"retain": 12}, {"insert": "hello"}]}

5. API design

REST for document lifecycle, WebSocket for collaboration. All calls carry the user’s session token; the server checks edit permission with the access service on connect.

POST /v1/docs – create a document. Body {"title": "Plan"}. Response 201 {"doc_id": "d-1"}.

GET /v1/docs/{doc_id} – load the latest snapshot plus ops since it.

{"doc_id": "d-1", "version": 1051, "content": "Hello world...", "title": "Plan"}

Status 200, 403 no access, 404 missing.

WS /v1/docs/{doc_id}/collab – the collaboration channel. Messages:

Client to server:

{"type": "op", "client_seq": 42, "base_version": 1051,
 "ops": [{"retain": 5}, {"insert": "X"}]}
{"type": "cursor", "pos": 17, "sel_end": 17}
{"type": "sync", "since_version": 1040}

Server to client:

{"type": "ack", "client_seq": 42, "version": 1052}
{"type": "op", "version": 1053, "client_id": "c-9", "ops": [{"retain": 3}, {"delete": 2}]}
{"type": "presence", "users": [{"user_id": 8, "name": "Bo", "pos": 30}]}

GET /v1/docs/{doc_id}/ops?from=1000&to=1051 – fetch missing operations (used for catch-up and history).

How will users open a document?

  1. The client calls GET /v1/docs/{id}. The document service reads the latest snapshot from the object store and the ops after it from the op log, applies them, and returns the content at version V.
  2. The client opens the WebSocket. The router sends it to the collaboration server that owns this document.
  3. The client sends sync since_version=V. The server sends any ops newer than V.
sequenceDiagram
    participant C as Client
    participant D as DocService
    participant O as ObjectStore
    participant L as OpLog
    participant R as Router
    participant S as CollabServer
    C->>D: GET doc by id
    D->>O: Read latest snapshot
    O-->>D: Snapshot at v5000
    D->>L: Read ops after snapshot
    L-->>D: Ops v5001 to V
    D-->>C: Content at version V
    C->>R: Open WebSocket for doc
    R->>S: Route to owner by hash
    C->>S: sync since version V
    S-->>C: Newer ops if any

How will users edit together?

  1. The user types. The client applies the edit locally right away (so typing feels instant) and sends it with base_version = the last server version it has seen.
  2. The collaboration server holds the document in memory. If other ops were applied after base_version, it transforms the incoming op against them (OT, see deep dives).
  3. It assigns the next version number, appends the op to the op log, and only then acks to the sender.
  4. It broadcasts the transformed op to all other connected editors of that document.
  5. Each receiving client transforms the incoming op against its own unacknowledged local ops and applies it.

How will users see each other’s cursors?

  1. Clients send cursor updates (throttled to ~10/s) over the same WebSocket.
  2. The server keeps presence in memory for the document and broadcasts it. Presence is not stored durably.
  3. When an op is applied, every cursor position is shifted by the same transform rules, so cursors stay on the right character.

How will offline edits work?

  1. While offline, the client keeps queuing local ops with their base version.
  2. On reconnect it sends sync to fetch missed server ops, rebases its queued ops on top, and sends them.
  3. Details in the deep dives.

7. Deep dives

How do we merge concurrent edits correctly: OT or CRDT?

The problem: Alice and Bob both start from the text "abc" (version 1).

  • Alice inserts "X" at position 1 -> she sees "aXbc".
  • Bob deletes the character at position 2 ("c") -> he sees "ab".

If the server applies them naively in order, Alice’s insert then Bob’s raw “delete at 2” removes "b" instead of "c". Result "aXc". Wrong, Bob wanted to delete "c". Last-write-wins on the whole document would instead throw away one person’s work.

Operational Transformation (OT): when an op was made without seeing another concurrent op, adjust (transform) its position as if it had. Bob’s delete at 2 is transformed against Alice’s insert at 1: the insert happened before position 2, so shift Bob’s delete to 3.

 start "abc"                        (version 1)
 Alice: insert("X", 1)   -> v2      server applies first: "aXbc"
 Bob:   delete(2), base v1          arrives second, base is stale
 transform(delete(2), against insert(1)) = delete(3)
 apply delete(3) to "aXbc"          -> "aXb"
 Alice receives delete(3) -> "aXb"; Bob receives insert(1) -> "aXb"
 Both converge to "aXb". Correct.
def transform(op, other):
    """Return op adjusted so it applies after `other` (both made on same base)."""
    if other.kind == "insert":
        if op.pos > other.pos or (op.pos == other.pos and op.client > other.client):
            return op.shift(len(other.text))
        return op
    if other.kind == "delete":
        if op.pos >= other.pos + other.length:
            return op.shift(-other.length)
        if op.kind == "insert" and op.pos > other.pos:
            return op.at(other.pos)                # insert inside deleted range
        if op.kind == "delete":
            return op.trim_overlap(other)          # avoid deleting twice
        return op

The tie-break on equal positions (by client id) is important: both sides must pick the same order, or they diverge.

CRDT (Conflict-free Replicated Data Type): give every character a unique, ordered id instead of an integer position. Inserts say “put X after character id (A,1)”. Deletes mark a character id as removed (a tombstone). Because ids never change, ops commute: any order of application gives the same result, no central server needed.

 "abc" as CRDT:  a(1,s)  b(2,s)  c(3,s)
 Alice: insert X with id (1,alice) after a(1,s)
 Bob:   delete id c(3,s)
 Apply in any order -> a  X  b  [c tombstone]  -> "aXb"
Aspect OT (central server) CRDT (Yjs, Automerge)
Needs a central ordering server Yes, simplest with one No, peer to peer possible
Metadata overhead Small (positions) Larger (ids and tombstones per char)
Offline / long divergence Harder, must rebase many ops Natural, merge anytime
Implementation difficulty Transform functions are tricky to get right Data structure is tricky, but libraries exist
Used by Google Docs Figma (CRDT-like), many newer editors

Recommended: OT with a single authoritative collaboration server per document, which is what Google Docs does. It keeps memory small and the server gives a total order. Mention that a CRDT is a strong alternative when offline-first or peer-to-peer matters. Either answer is fine if you explain the trade-off.

How do we route all editors of a document to the same server?

The problem: OT with a central order requires one server to own each document. If Alice is on server 1 and Bob on server 2, they cannot agree on an order without another layer.

Option Pros Cons
Any server + pub/sub between servers Stateless servers No single order, need distributed OT or locks
Consistent hashing on doc_id Simple, no lookup Rebalancing moves docs when servers join/leave
Directory service (doc -> server) in ZooKeeper/etcd Explicit control, easy failover Extra lookup on connect

Recommended: consistent hashing of doc_id to a collaboration server, with the ring membership stored in ZooKeeper or etcd so all routers agree. When a server joins, only the documents that hash to it move.

class Router:
    def __init__(self, ring):
        self.ring = ring                      # sorted list of (hash, server)

    def server_for(self, doc_id):
        h = mmh3.hash(doc_id)
        i = bisect.bisect(self.ring, (h,)) % len(self.ring)
        return self.ring[i][1]

# on WebSocket connect at the edge/load balancer
def on_connect(ws, doc_id):
    target = router.server_for(doc_id)
    proxy(ws, target)                         # sticky for the connection life

A single document at 100 editors and 300 ops/s is light, so one owner per doc never becomes a hot spot. A rare “celebrity doc” with 10,000 viewers: let only up to 100 people be editors; viewers get a read-only stream fed by a pub/sub fan-out from the owner server.

How do we store operations and snapshots?

The problem: we need every op durably (so no acked edit is lost), fast load times (replaying a million ops on open is slow), and version history.

Option Pros Cons
Store only the full document on each edit Simple reads 50 KB write per keystroke, no history
Store only the op log Full history, tiny writes Loading = replay all ops
Op log + periodic snapshots Small writes, fast loads, history Two stores, compaction job

Recommended: append every op to an op log partitioned by doc_id (Cassandra or Bigtable, or Kafka plus a DB), then take a snapshot every 1,000 ops or 5 minutes.

def apply_client_op(doc, msg):
    # idempotency: a reconnecting client may resend the same op
    if doc.seen(msg.client_id, msg.client_seq):
        return send_ack(msg, doc.version_of(msg.client_id, msg.client_seq))
    op = msg.op
    for past in doc.ops_since(msg.base_version):     # in-memory recent ops
        op = transform(op, past)
    new_version = doc.version + 1
    oplog.append(doc.id, new_version, msg.client_id, msg.client_seq, op)  # durable
    doc.apply(op, new_version)
    send_ack(msg, new_version)
    broadcast(doc, op, new_version, exclude=msg.client_id)
    if new_version - doc.snapshot_version >= 1000:
        snapshot_queue.put((doc.id, new_version))
 load doc:
   snapshot @ v5000 (object store, 50 KB)  +  ops v5001..v5420 (op log)
   -> apply 420 ops in memory -> content @ v5420   (a few ms)

Write the op to the log before acking. If we ack first and crash, the client believes the edit is saved but it is gone. Old ops beyond 30 days can be archived to cold storage; history views use snapshots plus archived ops.

How do we handle offline edits and reconnection?

The problem: Bob’s laptop goes offline on a train for 20 minutes. He types 300 ops. Meanwhile Alice makes 500 ops. When Bob reconnects, both sets must merge.

Recommended: the client keeps two buffers: inflight (sent, not acked) and pending (not sent yet). On reconnect:

def on_reconnect(client):
    missed = server.sync(since_version=client.last_server_version)  # Alice's 500
    for server_op in missed:
        # transform server op over my local unacked ops, and my ops over it
        for i, mine in enumerate(client.inflight + client.pending):
            server_op, mine_t = transform(server_op, mine), transform(mine, server_op)
            replace_local(client, i, mine_t)
        client.apply_remote(server_op)
        client.last_server_version = server_op.version
    client.resend(client.inflight + client.pending,
                  base_version=client.last_server_version)

Because each op carries (client_id, client_seq), if the server already received some of Bob’s ops before the drop, resending them is safe: the server acks the duplicate with its existing version and does not apply it twice.

For very long offline periods (days), rebasing thousands of ops is slow and the result can surprise users. That is the case where CRDTs shine, and where some products show a “your version vs theirs” warning instead.

How do we show cursors and presence efficiently?

The problem: cursors change on every keystroke and mouse click. Storing them durably would be wasteful.

Recommended: presence is in-memory on the owner server only. Clients throttle cursor messages to about 10 per second. The server batches presence broadcasts every 50-100 ms. When a client disconnects (or misses heartbeats for 30 s), it is removed. Cursor positions are transformed by every applied op, the same way as pending text ops, so a cursor after "abc" stays after "abc" when someone inserts earlier.

Data Where Durable? Update rate
Text ops Op log Yes Every edit
Snapshots Object store Yes Every 1,000 ops
Cursors and presence Owner server memory No Throttled ~10/s

What happens when a collaboration server crashes?

The problem: the owner server for 25,000 documents dies. Its in-memory state is gone.

Recommended: nothing in memory is the only copy. Every acked op is already in the op log. ZooKeeper/etcd notices the lost heartbeat (session expiry in a few seconds) and removes the server from the ring. Clients see their WebSocket close and reconnect with backoff; the router now sends them to the new owner. The new owner loads snapshot plus op log for each document on first connect, and clients sync and resend their unacked ops.

 t=0    server 7 dies
 t=3s   etcd lease expires, ring updated, routers reload ring
 t=3-5s clients reconnect (jittered), new owner loads doc:
        snapshot + ops since snapshot -> in-memory state
        clients resend inflight ops (dedup by client_id, client_seq)
 result: no acked edit lost; un-acked edits are resent by clients

Split brain guard: before accepting writes, the new owner takes a lease (fencing token) for the document in etcd. The op log write includes the token, and the log rejects writes with an older token. This stops a zombie old server from appending ops after it lost ownership.

How do we scale to many concurrent editors and documents?

The problem: 20M connections and 12M ops/s overall, plus the occasional document with very many people.

Recommendations:

  • Horizontal: ~400+ collaboration servers, documents spread by consistent hashing. Add servers to grow; only a fraction of docs move.
  • Batching: clients send ops every ~100 ms instead of every keystroke, which cuts message count 3-5x. The server also batches broadcasts.
  • Edit cap: limit active editors per doc (for example 100). Extra people join as viewers who receive a delayed broadcast from a pub/sub topic.
  • Idle docs: unload a document from memory after 10 minutes with no connections; it reloads from snapshot on demand.
  • Regions: the owner server lives in one region. Users far away get slightly higher latency (100-200 ms) but local echo hides it.

9. Common mistakes and interviewer follow-ups

  • Mistake: last write wins on the whole document. Concurrent typing loses work. Say: OT or CRDT so every edit survives and replicas converge.
  • Mistake: locking the document or a paragraph while someone types. It feels broken and blocks collaboration. Say: optimistic local apply plus transformation.
  • Mistake: stateless servers behind round-robin for OT. Editors of the same doc land on different servers. Say: one owner per doc via consistent hashing.
  • Mistake: acking before the op is durable. Say: append to the op log, then ack.
  • Mistake: saving the full document on every keystroke. Say: op log plus periodic snapshots.
  • Mistake: forgetting to transform cursors. Say: cursors are positions and get the same transform as text ops.
  • Follow-up: “Version history?” Snapshots every N ops plus the op log give any past version by loading the nearest snapshot and replaying.
  • Follow-up: “Why not CRDT?” Valid choice, especially offline-first; costs more metadata per character and needs garbage collection of tombstones.

10. One-page cheat sheet

Topic Key point
Scale 1B docs, 10M open, 20M connections, ~400 collab servers
Per doc <= 100 editors, ~300 ops/s, fits in one server’s memory
Merge OT with a single owner server per doc; CRDT as offline-first alternative
OT core transform(op, concurrent) shifts positions; deterministic tie-break
Routing Consistent hash(doc_id), ring in etcd/ZK
Write path transform, assign version, append op log, ack, broadcast
Storage Op log (Cassandra) + snapshot every 1,000 ops (S3)
Idempotency (client_id, client_seq) on every op
Offline inflight + pending buffers, sync since version, rebase, resend
Presence In memory only, throttled 10/s, transformed with ops
Failure Lease/fencing per doc, clients reconnect and resend, no acked edit lost
CAP Convergent eventual consistency, availability first

25. Web Crawler (Hard)

A web crawler starts from a few seed URLs, downloads each page, pulls out the links on it, and repeats for every new link, until it has fetched a large part of the web. The output (raw HTML and extracted text) feeds a search index or a machine learning dataset. The goal here is 10 billion pages in a few days. The interviewer is testing large-scale batch-style systems: a URL frontier that decides what to fetch next, politeness so we never hammer one website, deduplication of both URLs and page content, DNS as a hidden bottleneck, crawler traps, and how to resume after crashes without starting over.

1. Functional requirements

Core (must have):

  1. Start from a list of seed URLs and crawl outward by following links.
  2. Fetch the HTML of each page and store it.
  3. Extract links from each page and add new ones to the set of URLs to crawl.
  4. Extract the text content and store it for downstream use (indexing, LLM training).
  5. Respect robots.txt and per-domain politeness.

Below the line (out of scope):

  • Building the search index or ranking (a separate consumer of our output).
  • Fetching images, video, or PDFs (we store HTML only, maybe note the extension).
  • Continuous re-crawling and freshness scheduling (we mention it briefly).
  • Logged-in pages and forms.

2. Non-functional requirements

  1. Scale: crawl 10 billion pages within 5 days.
  2. Politeness: at most 1 request per second per domain by default, and honor Crawl-delay and Disallow rules in robots.txt.
  3. Fault tolerance: a crashed fetcher or parser loses no progress beyond a few seconds of work; the crawl resumes, it never restarts from zero.
  4. No duplicate work: each URL is fetched at most once per crawl; pages with identical content are stored once.
  5. Robustness: survive bad HTML, slow servers (timeouts), huge pages (size caps), and crawler traps (infinite URL spaces).
  6. Efficiency: keep fetchers busy; DNS and slow sites must not stall the pipeline.
  7. CAP choice: availability and partition tolerance. It is fine if two workers briefly race on the same URL (dedup will catch it), but the crawl must keep moving.

3. Back-of-the-envelope estimates

Assumption Number
Pages to crawl 10 billion
Time budget 5 days
Average page size (HTML) ~100 KB compressed on the wire, ~500 KB uncompressed
Extracted text per page ~20 KB
Links per page ~50 (most already seen)
Unique domains ~100 million (a few million with most pages)
Network per fetcher machine ~1 Gbps usable 
Fetch rate:
  10e9 pages / (5 * 86,400 s) = 10e9 / 432,000 ~ 23,000 pages/s

Bandwidth:
  23,000 * 100 KB (on the wire) = 2.3 GB/s ~ 18.4 Gbps
  at ~1 Gbps useful per machine (with overhead) -> ~20-30 fetcher machines
  network is not the hard limit; latency (wait time per request) is

Concurrency needed:
  avg page fetch ~ 1 s (DNS + connect + TLS + download)
  concurrent requests = 23,000 * 1 s = 23,000 in flight
  with async I/O at ~1,000-2,000 concurrent per machine -> ~15-25 machines
  plan for ~50 fetchers for headroom and slow sites

Storage:
  raw HTML (stored compressed ~100 KB) = 10e9 * 100 KB = 1 PB
  text = 10e9 * 20 KB = 200 TB
  URL metadata (URL ~100 B + state ~50 B) = 10e9 * 150 B = 1.5 TB

Links discovered:
  23,000 pages/s * 50 links = 1.15M links/s to dedup
  bloom filter for 10B URLs at 1% false positive:
    bits = -n ln(p) / (ln 2)^2 = 10e9 * 4.6 / 0.48 ~ 96e9 bits ~ 12 GB

The numbers to repeat: ~23k pages per second, ~1 PB of HTML, ~1M link checks per second, and a 12 GB Bloom filter.

4. Core entities

  • URL record: one URL we know about. Fields: url_hash, url, domain, depth, priority, status (queued, fetched, failed, skipped), last_fetched, content_hash.
  • Domain: per-site politeness state. Fields: domain, robots rules, crawl_delay, next_allowed_fetch_time, ip, error_count.
  • Page: fetched content. Fields: url_hash, http_status, fetched_at, s3_key for HTML, s3_key for text, content_hash.
  • Frontier entry: a URL waiting to be fetched. Fields: url, domain, priority, enqueue_time.
  • Content fingerprint: hash (and optionally SimHash) of page text, used for duplicate detection.
-- URL metadata in a wide-column or key-value store (DynamoDB/Cassandra)
CREATE TABLE urls (
  url_hash      BINARY(16) PRIMARY KEY,     -- hash of normalized URL
  url           TEXT,
  domain        TEXT,
  depth         INT,
  status        TEXT,                        -- queued/fetched/failed/skipped
  attempts      INT,
  content_hash  BINARY(16),
  html_key      TEXT,                        -- s3://crawl/html/...
  fetched_at    TIMESTAMP
);

CREATE TABLE domains (
  domain             TEXT PRIMARY KEY,
  robots_txt         TEXT,
  robots_fetched_at  TIMESTAMP,
  crawl_delay_ms     INT DEFAULT 1000,
  next_fetch_at      TIMESTAMP,
  consecutive_errors INT DEFAULT 0
);
{"url": "https://example.com/a/b?id=7", "domain": "example.com",
 "depth": 3, "priority": 0.62, "discovered_from": "https://example.com/"}

5. API design

A crawler is mostly an internal pipeline, but a small control API helps operators and shows the interviewer the system boundaries. All endpoints are internal, behind service auth.

POST /v1/crawls – start a crawl.

{"name": "web-2026-11", "seeds": ["https://en.wikipedia.org/", "https://www.bbc.com/"],
 "max_pages": 10000000000, "max_depth": 20, "default_crawl_delay_ms": 1000}

Response 201 {"crawl_id": "cr-1", "status": "running"}.

GET /v1/crawls/{crawl_id} – progress.

{"crawl_id": "cr-1", "fetched": 2140000000, "queued": 5300000000,
 "failed": 41000000, "pages_per_sec": 23400}

POST /v1/crawls/{crawl_id}/pause and /resume – operator control. Response 202.

POST /v1/domains/{domain}/block – stop crawling a site (owner complaint, trap). Response 200.

Internal message formats (queues):

{"type": "fetch_task", "url": "https://example.com/x", "url_hash": "9a1f...", "attempt": 1}
{"type": "parse_task", "url_hash": "9a1f...", "html_key": "s3://crawl/html/9a/9a1f.gz"}

How will the crawler fetch pages?

  1. The frontier hands a fetcher the next URL whose domain is allowed to be fetched now (politeness, see deep dives).
  2. The fetcher resolves DNS through a local cache, opens a connection (reusing keep-alive connections per host), and downloads with a 10-second timeout and a 5 MB size cap.
  3. It writes the raw HTML (gzip) to the object store, records status in the URL metadata store, and puts a parse task on a queue.
sequenceDiagram
    participant F as Frontier
    participant W as Fetcher
    participant D as DNS cache
    participant S as Website
    participant O as Object store
    participant M as Metadata store
    participant Q as Parse queue
    W->>F: Request next ready URL
    F-->>W: URL whose domain is allowed now
    W->>D: Resolve host
    D-->>W: IP address
    W->>S: HTTP GET with timeout and size cap
    S-->>W: HTML response
    W->>O: Put gzipped HTML
    W->>M: Update status fetched
    W->>Q: Send parse task

How will the crawler extract links and text?

  1. A parser worker takes the parse task and reads the HTML from the object store.
  2. It extracts the visible text and stores it.
  3. It computes a content hash. If the hash was seen before, it marks the page as a duplicate and does not follow its links again.
  4. It extracts links, resolves relative links to absolute URLs, and sends them to the URL filter.

How will new URLs get into the frontier?

  1. The filter normalizes each URL (lowercase host, drop fragments, sort query params, strip tracking params like utm_*).
  2. It checks the Bloom filter. If maybe-seen, it confirms in the metadata store; if new, it inserts the URL record and adds it to the frontier with a priority.
  3. It checks robots.txt rules for the domain (cached) and drops disallowed URLs.

How will the crawl respect politeness?

  1. Each domain has its own queue in the frontier and a next_fetch_at time.
  2. A fetcher only takes a URL from a domain whose next_fetch_at has passed, then sets next_fetch_at = now + crawl_delay.

7. Deep dives

How do we design the URL frontier and prioritize what to crawl?

The problem: billions of URLs wait to be fetched. We want important pages first (a news homepage before page 900 of a forum), and we must not let a single domain dominate.

Option Pros Cons
One FIFO queue (BFS) Simple No priority, one huge site floods the queue, impolite
Single priority queue Important pages first Still no per-domain politeness
Two-level: priority front queues + per-domain back queues (Mercator style) Priority and politeness together More moving parts

Recommended: the Mercator design. Front queues hold URLs by priority bucket. Back queues hold one domain each. A min-heap orders back queues by the time they are next allowed to fetch.

 incoming URLs
      |
      v
 [prioritizer] -> F1 (high)  F2  F3  ...  Fn (low)      front queues
                     \        |    |       /
                      v       v    v      v
                 [back-queue router: domain -> queue]
                  B(example.com) B(bbc.com) B(wiki) ...  back queues
                         \           |          /
                          v          v         v
                 [heap of (next_fetch_at, back_queue)]
                                |
                                v
                            fetchers

Priority signals: inverse depth, domain importance (for example a PageRank-like score from a previous crawl), freshness needs (news sites), and number of inbound links seen so far.

def priority(url_rec, domain_score):
    depth_term   = 1.0 / (1 + url_rec.depth)
    inlink_term  = min(1.0, math.log1p(url_rec.inlinks) / 10)
    return 0.5 * domain_score + 0.3 * depth_term + 0.2 * inlink_term

At 10B URLs the frontier does not fit in RAM. Store the queues on disk with an in-memory buffer at the head and tail of each queue (Mercator did exactly this), or use a durable queue system. Partition the frontier across machines by hash(domain), so all URLs of one domain live on one frontier node. That makes politeness a local decision on that node.

How do we stay polite to each website?

The problem: 23k fetches per second spread badly could send 1,000 requests per second to one small site and knock it over. Site owners will block us, and it is the wrong thing to do.

Recommended: per-domain rate limiting from the back-queue heap, robots.txt honored and cached, and adaptive backoff.

def next_task(frontier_node):
    while True:
        next_at, domain = heapq.heappop(frontier_node.heap)
        if next_at > now():
            sleep(next_at - now())
        url = frontier_node.back_queue[domain].pop()
        rules = robots_cache.get(domain) or fetch_robots(domain)   # cached 24 h
        delay = max(rules.crawl_delay_ms or 0, DEFAULT_DELAY_MS)
        if frontier_node.back_queue[domain]:
            heapq.heappush(frontier_node.heap, (now() + delay / 1000, domain))
        if rules.allowed(USER_AGENT, url):
            return url

def on_response(domain, status, latency_s):
    d = domains[domain]
    if status in (429, 503) or latency_s > 5:
        d.crawl_delay_ms = min(d.crawl_delay_ms * 2, 60_000)    # back off
    elif status == 200:
        d.crawl_delay_ms = max(DEFAULT_DELAY_MS, int(d.crawl_delay_ms * 0.9))

robots.txt is fetched once per domain and cached for about a day. If robots.txt returns 5xx, be conservative and treat the site as disallowed for a while. Identify the crawler with a clear User-Agent and contact URL. Also limit per IP address, not just per domain, because many small domains share one shared-hosting server.

Math check: at 1 request per second per domain, 23k pages per second needs at least 23k domains active at any moment. With millions of domains in the frontier that is easy, but it means the frontier must interleave domains, never drain one at a time.

How do we avoid fetching the same URL or storing the same content twice?

The problem: about 1.15M discovered links per second, most already seen. And many different URLs return the same page (mirrors, ?sessionid=, http vs https, printer versions).

URL dedup options:

Option Memory for 10B URLs Exact? Notes
Hash set in memory ~160 GB (16 B hash each) Yes Needs sharding across machines
DB lookup per URL Small RAM Yes 1.15M reads/s on the DB
Bloom filter + DB confirm on “maybe” ~12 GB at 1% FP No false negatives Fast path in RAM

A Bloom filter is a bit array plus k hash functions. To add a URL, set k bits. To check, see if all k bits are set. If any bit is 0, the URL is definitely new. If all are 1, it is probably seen (1% false positive at our sizing). It never says “new” for a URL we already added.

Recommended: normalize first, then a Bloom filter sharded by URL hash. For a crawler, a 1% false positive means we skip 1% of truly new URLs, which is often acceptable. If not, confirm “maybe seen” answers against the metadata store with a conditional insert.

def normalize(url):
    p = urlsplit(url)
    host = p.hostname.lower().rstrip(".")
    query = "&".join(sorted(q for q in p.query.split("&")
                            if q and not q.startswith(("utm_", "sessionid="))))
    path = re.sub(r"/+", "/", p.path or "/")
    return f"{p.scheme.lower()}://{host}{path}" + (f"?{query}" if query else "")

def maybe_enqueue(url, depth):
    n = normalize(url)
    h = hash128(n)
    if bloom.might_contain(h):
        return                                  # seen (or 1% false positive)
    bloom.add(h)
    if metadata.put_if_absent(h, url=n, status="queued", depth=depth):
        frontier.add(n, depth)

Content dedup: compute a hash (for example SHA-256 or a 128-bit hash) of the extracted text. If it is already in the content-hash table, store a pointer instead of a second copy and do not re-extract links. For near-duplicates (same article with a different ad banner), use SimHash: similar documents produce fingerprints that differ in only a few bits.

def handle_page(url_hash, text):
    ch = sha256(text.encode()).digest()[:16]
    if not content_index.put_if_absent(ch, url_hash):
        metadata.mark_duplicate(url_hash, of=content_index.get(ch))
        return False                            # skip link extraction
    return True

Why is DNS a bottleneck, and how do we fix it?

The problem: every new domain needs a DNS lookup. Public resolvers often take 10 to 200 ms, can rate-limit us, and standard library resolvers are often blocking (one thread waits per lookup). At 23k fetches per second, slow DNS caps throughput.

Option Pros Cons
OS resolver per request No work Blocking, slow, rate-limited
Local caching resolver on each fetcher (for example Unbound) Cache hits in microseconds Cache per machine
Shared DNS cache service + async resolver High hit rate across fleet Another service to run

Recommended: run an async, caching resolver on every fetcher machine, pre-resolve domains when they enter the back queue (so the IP is ready when the fetch is due), and respect TTLs (cache at least a few minutes, at most the record’s TTL or a cap of ~1 day).

 back queue for domain X becomes non-empty
        |
        v
 prefetch DNS(X) async ---> local cache (TTL)  ---> fetch at next_fetch_at
                                 ^
            hit rate high because many URLs per domain

Because the frontier groups URLs by domain, one lookup serves hundreds or thousands of fetches.

How do we handle failures and resume the crawl?

The problem: over 5 days with 50 fetchers and many parsers, machines will crash, and networks will fail. We cannot restart a 10B-page crawl.

Recommended: make every stage a consumer of a durable queue, store state in a durable store, and make each step idempotent.

Stage Durable state Recovery
Frontier Disk-backed queues + URL metadata status Rebuild in-memory heads from disk; re-queue URLs left in fetching too long
Fetch Task in queue with visibility timeout (SQS) or Kafka offset Unacked task reappears; fetching twice is harmless
Parse Parse task in queue; HTML already in S3 Re-parse from S3, link inserts are idempotent (put_if_absent)
Bloom filter Periodic snapshot to S3 Reload snapshot; misses since snapshot caught by metadata conditional insert 
def fetch_worker():
    for task in fetch_queue.receive(visibility_timeout_s=60):
        try:
            resp = http.get(task.url, timeout=10, max_bytes=5_000_000)
            key = f"html/{task.url_hash[:2]}/{task.url_hash}.gz"
            s3.put(key, gzip(resp.body))                 # same key -> idempotent
            metadata.update(task.url_hash, status="fetched", html_key=key)
            parse_queue.send({"url_hash": task.url_hash, "html_key": key})
            fetch_queue.ack(task)
        except TransientError:
            if task.attempt < 3:
                fetch_queue.retry(task, delay_s=30 * 2 ** task.attempt)
            else:
                metadata.update(task.url_hash, status="failed")
                fetch_queue.ack(task)

Retries use exponential backoff, and a domain that keeps failing gets its crawl delay raised or is paused, so we do not spend fetcher time on dead hosts.

How do we handle crawler traps and dynamic pages?

The problem: some sites generate infinite URLs. A calendar with “next month” links forever, /a/b/a/b/a/b/... paths from relative-link bugs, or session ids in every URL. A trap can eat millions of fetches.

Defenses:

Trap Defense
Infinite depth (/a/b/a/b/...) Max URL length (~2,000 chars), max path depth, detect repeated path segments
Calendars, infinite pagination Max pages per domain per crawl, max depth from seed
Session ids in URLs Normalization strips known session params
Many URLs, same content Content hash dedup stops link expansion
Spider traps that slow-drip bytes Read timeout and total download timeout
Huge pages Size cap (5 MB) 
def looks_like_trap(url, depth, domain_stats):
    path = urlsplit(url).path
    segs = [s for s in path.split("/") if s]
    if len(url) > 2000 or len(segs) > 15 or depth > 20:
        return True
    if any(segs.count(s) > 3 for s in set(segs)):      # /a/b/a/b/a/b
        return True
    if domain_stats.pages > domain_stats.budget:       # per-domain budget
        return True
    return False

Dynamic (JavaScript-rendered) pages: plain HTTP fetch returns an empty shell for some single-page apps. Rendering with a headless browser (Chromium) costs 10-100x more CPU per page. Recommended: fetch plain HTML for everything, detect pages with little text and heavy scripts, and send only those (and only for high-priority domains) to a separate, smaller rendering pool.

How do we scale the fetchers?

The problem: we need ~23k pages per second with many slow servers, so most time is waiting.

Recommendations:

  • Async I/O (asyncio, Netty, Go goroutines): one machine holds thousands of connections open while waiting. Threads per request do not scale this far.
  • Partition by domain: route a domain’s tasks to the fetcher co-located with its frontier partition so politeness, DNS cache, and keep-alive connections are all local.
  • Connection reuse: HTTP keep-alive per host saves TCP and TLS handshakes (often 100+ ms each).
  • Separate fast and slow lanes: domains that respond slowly go to a pool with longer timeouts so they do not block fast ones.
  • Geographic placement: run fetchers in several regions and send a domain’s fetches from the region nearest to its servers.
  • Autoscale on frontier backlog of “ready now” URLs, not on CPU.
 per fetcher: ~1,500 concurrent requests, ~1 s avg -> ~1,500 pages/s
 needed: 23,000 pages/s -> 16 fetchers minimum, run ~50 for slow sites,
         retries, and failures

9. Common mistakes and interviewer follow-ups

  • Mistake: one global FIFO queue. It ignores priority and floods single domains. Say: Mercator-style front (priority) and back (per-domain) queues.
  • Mistake: forgetting robots.txt and per-domain rate limits. Say: cached robots rules, crawl delay per domain and per IP, adaptive backoff on 429/503.
  • Mistake: dedup with a plain DB lookup per link. 1M+ lookups per second. Say: normalize, Bloom filter first, conditional insert to confirm.
  • Mistake: only URL dedup. Different URLs serve the same page. Say: content hash, plus SimHash for near duplicates.
  • Mistake: ignoring DNS. Say: async caching resolver, prefetch per domain, respect TTL.
  • Mistake: no story for crashes. Say: durable queues with visibility timeouts, HTML in S3 before parse, idempotent steps, Bloom snapshots.
  • Mistake: rendering every page in a headless browser. 10-100x cost. Say: plain fetch first, render only flagged pages.
  • Follow-up: “How do you recrawl for freshness?” Track change rate per URL; schedule next crawl sooner for pages that change often (news) and later for static ones. Use If-Modified-Since and ETag to save bandwidth.

10. One-page cheat sheet

Topic Key point
Scale 10B pages / 5 days ~ 23k pages/s, ~18 Gbps, ~1 PB HTML
Concurrency ~23k requests in flight; async fetchers, ~50 machines
Frontier Front priority queues + per-domain back queues + next_fetch_at heap
Partitioning hash(domain) -> frontier node + fetcher, politeness stays local
Politeness 1 req/s/domain default, robots.txt cached 24 h, backoff on 429/503
URL dedup Normalize, Bloom filter (~12 GB at 1% FP), put_if_absent
Content dedup SHA of text; SimHash for near duplicates
DNS Local async caching resolver, prefetch per domain
Fault tolerance Durable queues, visibility timeout, S3 before parse, idempotent writes
Traps URL length/depth caps, repeated segments, per-domain budget, timeouts
Dynamic pages Plain fetch first, headless render only when needed
CAP AP: keep crawling, dedup cleans up races

26. Ad Click Aggregator (Hard)

An ad click aggregator records every time a user clicks an ad, sends the user on to the advertiser’s website, and counts those clicks so advertisers can see how each ad is doing, per minute, per hour, and per day. The counts also decide how much money the advertiser is billed, so they must be correct. The interviewer is really testing whether you can design a high-volume event pipeline: how you ingest a flood of tiny events without losing any, how you count them in near real time with stream processing, how you avoid counting the same click twice, and how you make the final numbers trustworthy enough to bill against.

1. Functional requirements

Core (must have):

  1. When a user clicks an ad, the system records the click and redirects the user to the advertiser’s landing page.
  2. Advertisers can query click counts for their ads over a time range, at minute, hour, and day granularity (a “rollup” is a total over a bigger time bucket).
  3. Advertisers can filter or group counts by a few dimensions, such as ad, campaign, country, and device.

Below the line (out of scope, and why):

  • Ad serving and targeting (choosing which ad to show). That is a separate, very large system.
  • Fraud detection with machine learning. We will do simple dedup and mention where a fraud model would plug in.
  • Impressions and conversions. Same pipeline shape as clicks, so the design generalizes; we keep scope to clicks.
  • The billing system itself. We produce the trusted daily numbers it consumes.

2. Non-functional requirements

  1. Scale: peak 10,000 clicks per second, average about 2,000 per second (about 170 million clicks per day), 10 million active ads. We size for the peak.
  2. Redirect latency: p99 under 100 ms from click to the 302 response. The user must never wait on the counting pipeline.
  3. Freshness: aggregated counts visible to advertisers within 1 minute of the click (near real time).
  4. Query latency: p99 under 1 second for a dashboard query over any range up to 1 year.
  5. Correctness: no click lost after it is acknowledged (durability), and each unique click counted exactly once in the final billing numbers. Real-time numbers may be slightly off for a few minutes; the daily reconciled numbers must be exact.
  6. Availability: 99.99% for click capture and redirect. Losing clicks loses money.
  7. CAP choice: favor availability (AP) on the ingest path. Accept a click even during a partial outage and reconcile later. For billing we get correctness by recomputing from the raw log, not by blocking writes.

3. Back-of-the-envelope estimates

Assumption Number
Peak clicks per second 10,000
Average clicks per second 2,000
Clicks per day (average) ~170 million
Raw click event size ~200 bytes
Active ads 10 million
Dimensions per aggregate row ad, campaign, country, device
Dashboard query QPS ~1,000 at peak 
Write path
  Peak ingest            = 10,000 events/s
  Raw bytes/s at peak    = 10,000 * 200 B = 2 MB/s  (tiny for Kafka)
  Raw per day            = 170M * 200 B   = 34 GB/day
  Raw per year           = 34 GB * 365    = ~12 TB/year (S3, cheap)

Aggregates (minute buckets)
  Worst case rows/min    = ads clicked that minute, not all 10M.
  Say 1M distinct ads/min * 1 row each = 1M rows/min
  Row size ~ 50 B        = 50 MB/min = 72 GB/day of minute rows
  Keep minute rows 7 days, hour rows 1 year, day rows forever:
    minute: 72 GB * 7       = ~500 GB
    hour:   (1M rows/hr*50B)*24*365 = ~440 GB/year
    day:    much smaller, ~20 GB/year

Read path
  1,000 dashboard QPS, each scanning at most a few thousand
  pre-aggregated rows -> easy for an OLAP store.

The lesson from the math: ingest bandwidth is small, but the event count is high and every event matters. The design is about correctness and freshness, not raw bytes.

4. Core entities

  • Click event: one raw click. Fields: click_id, impression_id, ad_id, user_id (or anonymous id), timestamp, country, device, ip.
  • Ad: the thing being clicked. Fields: ad_id, campaign_id, advertiser_id, redirect_url.
  • Impression: one showing of an ad to a user. Fields: impression_id, ad_id, user_id, shown_at, signature. It lets us tie a click to a real view.
  • Aggregate (rollup row): a count for one ad over one time bucket. Fields: ad_id, bucket_start, granularity, country, device, clicks.
  • Advertiser: owner of ads. Fields: advertiser_id, name.
{
  "click_id": "c_9f2a1e",
  "impression_id": "imp_77b3",
  "ad_id": "ad_123",
  "user_id": "u_555",
  "event_time": "2026-11-05T19:01:12.345Z",
  "country": "US",
  "device": "ios"
}
-- OLAP table for aggregates (ClickHouse style)
CREATE TABLE ad_clicks_minute (
  ad_id        String,
  campaign_id  String,
  bucket_start DateTime,      -- start of the minute
  country      LowCardinality(String),
  device       LowCardinality(String),
  clicks       UInt64
) ENGINE = SummingMergeTree
PARTITION BY toDate(bucket_start)
ORDER BY (ad_id, bucket_start, country, device);

5. API design

GET /click?impression_id=imp_77b3&ad_id=ad_123&sig=... – record a click and redirect.

// response: no body, just a redirect
// 302 Found
// Location: https://advertiser.example.com/landing?utm=...

Status codes: 302 on success, 400 if the signature is invalid (we still redirect to a safe fallback page so users are not stranded), 404 if the ad does not exist. Auth: none for the user, but the impression id is signed by the ad server so it cannot be forged.

GET /ads/{ad_id}/metrics?from=...&to=...&granularity=minute|hour|day&group_by=country – read aggregated counts.

// response 200
{
  "ad_id": "ad_123",
  "granularity": "hour",
  "series": [
    {"bucket": "2026-11-05T18:00:00Z", "country": "US", "clicks": 1520},
    {"bucket": "2026-11-05T19:00:00Z", "country": "US", "clicks": 1733}
  ],
  "is_final": false
}

Status codes: 200, 400 (bad range), 403 (advertiser does not own the ad). Auth: advertiser OAuth token; the service checks the ad belongs to the caller.

GET /campaigns/{campaign_id}/metrics?... – same shape, grouped at campaign level.

The is_final flag tells the client whether the numbers come from the reconciled batch (final) or the real-time stream (provisional).
