How will users click an ad and get redirected?

  1. The ad server renders the ad with a link to our Click Service that carries a signed impression id and the ad id.
  2. The user clicks. The browser calls GET /click?....
  3. The Click Service verifies the signature (a quick HMAC check, no database).
  4. It looks up the redirect URL for the ad from an in-memory cache (10 million ads * ~200 bytes = 2 GB, fits in a Redis cluster or local cache).
  5. It builds the click event and produces it to Kafka with acks=all, so the event is durably stored on several brokers.
  6. Once Kafka acknowledges, it returns 302 Found with the landing page URL.
sequenceDiagram
    participant U as User
    participant C as Click Service
    participant R as Redirect cache
    participant K as Kafka
    participant A as Advertiser site
    U->>C: GET click with signed impression id
    C->>C: Verify HMAC signature
    C->>R: Look up redirect URL for ad
    R-->>C: Landing page URL
    C->>K: Produce click event with acks all
    K-->>C: Ack from replicas
    C-->>U: 302 Found to landing page
    U->>A: GET landing page

Why produce before redirecting? If we redirect first and the service crashes, we lose a billable click. The Kafka produce takes a few milliseconds, well under the 100 ms budget.

Why a server-side redirect rather than letting the browser go straight to the advertiser and send a beacon? Beacons get blocked by ad blockers and dropped when the page unloads. The server redirect guarantees we see every click.

How will advertisers query click metrics?

  1. Kafka holds every click, partitioned by ad_id.
  2. A Flink job (Flink is a stream processing engine that runs continuous computations over event streams) reads the topic, groups events by ad and by one-minute window, and counts them.
  3. When a minute window closes, Flink writes the count rows to the OLAP store (OLAP means Online Analytical Processing: a database built for fast aggregate queries over many rows, like ClickHouse, Druid, or Pinot).
  4. The dashboard calls the Query Service, which runs a SUM(clicks) ... GROUP BY against the right rollup table and returns the series.
SELECT toStartOfHour(bucket_start) AS bucket, country, sum(clicks) AS clicks
FROM ad_clicks_minute
WHERE ad_id = 'ad_123'
  AND bucket_start >= '2026-11-05 00:00:00'
  AND bucket_start <  '2026-11-06 00:00:00'
GROUP BY bucket, country
ORDER BY bucket;

How will advertisers get minute, hour, and day rollups?

We do not keep only minute rows and sum them at query time for a year range; that would scan 525,600 minutes per ad. Instead we keep three tables. Flink writes minute rows; the OLAP store builds hour and day rows using materialized views (a view that is stored and kept updated as new rows arrive). A query for a year at day granularity reads 365 rows.

7. Deep dives

Should we use stream processing or batch processing to count clicks?

The problem: advertisers want counts within a minute, but batch jobs that run hourly or daily are slow. Stream processing is fast but historically harder to make exact.

Option Freshness Correctness Cost / complexity
Batch only (Spark over S3 every hour) 1 hour+ Exact, easy to rerun Low
Stream only (Flink over Kafka) Seconds Good with checkpoints, but bugs and late data can drift Medium
Stream + batch reconciliation (Lambda style) Seconds for provisional, daily for final Exact final numbers Higher, two code paths

Recommended: stream processing for the real-time view, plus a daily batch reconciliation job that recomputes the truth from the raw S3 log. This is the classic Lambda architecture (two paths: a fast “speed layer” and a slow, exact “batch layer”). Many teams simplify it toward Kappa (one streaming path, replay Kafka to fix mistakes), but for billing, a separate batch recount is the safer answer to give.

A minimal Flink job, written in Flink SQL:

-- Tumbling one-minute windows on event time
INSERT INTO ad_clicks_minute_sink
SELECT
  ad_id,
  campaign_id,
  TUMBLE_START(event_time, INTERVAL '1' MINUTE) AS bucket_start,
  country,
  device,
  COUNT(*) AS clicks
FROM clicks_dedup        -- stream after dedup, see next deep dive
GROUP BY
  ad_id, campaign_id, country, device,
  TUMBLE(event_time, INTERVAL '1' MINUTE);

A “tumbling window” is a fixed, non-overlapping time bucket: 19:00-19:01, 19:01-19:02, and so on.

How do we make sure each click is counted exactly once?

The problem has two parts. First, duplicate events: a user double-clicks, a browser retries, or a bot hammers the link, so the same logical click arrives several times. Second, duplicate processing: a Flink worker crashes and replays events from Kafka, which could count them again.

For duplicate processing, Flink gives “exactly-once state” through checkpoints. A checkpoint is a consistent snapshot of every operator’s state plus the Kafka offsets it has read. After a crash, Flink restores the snapshot and rereads Kafka from the saved offsets, so state is never double-updated. To make the output exactly-once too, the sink must either be transactional (Flink two-phase commit with Kafka) or idempotent (writing the same row twice gives the same result).

For duplicate events, we need a dedup key:

Dedup approach How Pros Cons
Client-generated click id Browser sends a random UUID Simple Easy to forge, bots send fresh UUIDs
Signed impression id Ad server signs impression; one click per impression counts Hard to forge, ties click to a real view Needs signing and key rotation
Heuristic (user + ad + 10 s window) Drop repeat clicks in a short window Catches double clicks Fuzzy, may drop real repeats

Recommended: the signed impression id. The ad server signs impression_id|ad_id|timestamp with HMAC. The Click Service rejects bad signatures. Downstream, we keep a dedup set keyed by impression id: only the first click for an impression is billable.

Where to keep the dedup set? At 10k/s with a 24-hour window, that is up to ~860 million ids. Two good places:

  1. Flink keyed state with a TTL (time to live), keyed by impression id. It lives on local RocksDB disks and is checkpointed, so it is exactly-once with the rest of the job.
  2. A Redis SET NX with expiry in the Click Service. Fast, but Redis is not checkpointed together with Flink, so it can drift on failures.
# Flink-style dedup operator (pseudo-Python)
class DedupByImpression(KeyedProcessFunction):
    def open(self, ctx):
        desc = ValueStateDescriptor("seen", Types.BOOLEAN())
        desc.enable_time_to_live(StateTtlConfig.new_builder(Time.hours(24)).build())
        self.seen = ctx.get_state(desc)

    def process_element(self, click, ctx):
        # key = click.impression_id
        if self.seen.value():
            ctx.output(DUPLICATES_TAG, click)   # side output for audits
            return
        self.seen.update(True)
        yield click

On the write side, make the OLAP write idempotent by using a deterministic row key (ad_id, bucket_start, country, device, flink_window_id) and a table engine that replaces rows with the same key (for example ReplacingMergeTree), so a retried write overwrites instead of adding.

How do we handle a hot ad that gets far more clicks than others?

The problem: Kafka and Flink partition by ad_id so all clicks for one ad land on one partition and one Flink task. A Super Bowl ad might get 5,000 clicks per second, half our peak, all on one worker. That worker falls behind while others sit idle.

Option How it works Pros Cons
Bigger machines Vertical scale Simple Has a ceiling, wastes money
Key salting Partition by ad_id:N with N in 0..K-1, then sum the K partial counts Spreads load evenly Extra merge step
Local pre-aggregation Each Click Service host counts per ad for 1 s and emits one summary event Cuts event volume a lot Loses per-event dedup unless done carefully

Recommended: key salting for ads known to be hot. The Click Service keeps a small list of hot ad ids (pushed from a config service or detected by a heavy-hitter counter). For those, it appends a random suffix 0-9 to the partition key. Flink counts per salted key, then a second, small aggregation step sums the 10 partials per ad and minute.

HOT_ADS = load_hot_ads()          # refreshed every 30 s
SALT_BUCKETS = 10

def partition_key(click):
    if click.ad_id in HOT_ADS:
        return f"{click.ad_id}:{random.randrange(SALT_BUCKETS)}"
    return click.ad_id

Note that dedup must still be keyed by impression id, not by salted ad key, so run the dedup operator before the salted aggregation (dedup is keyed by impression id, which is already spread evenly).

How do we reconcile real-time counts with the truth?

The problem: even with checkpoints, things go wrong. A bug in the Flink job, a misconfigured watermark, or a lost partition can make streaming counts drift. Billing cannot depend on that.

Recommended: a daily batch reconciliation job.

  1. Kafka Connect (or Flink) continuously writes every raw click to S3 as Parquet files, partitioned by hour.
  2. Once a day, after the late-data cutoff (say 2 hours past midnight UTC), a Spark job reads the whole day, applies the same dedup logic, and computes exact per-ad, per-minute counts.
  3. It compares the batch counts with the streaming counts. If they differ beyond a tiny threshold, it raises an alert and overwrites the OLAP rows for that day with the batch numbers, marking them is_final = true.
  4. The billing system reads only final rows.
-- Spark SQL: the recount
WITH dedup AS (
  SELECT *, ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY impression_id ORDER BY event_time) AS rn
  FROM raw_clicks
  WHERE dt = '2026-11-05' AND sig_valid = true
)
SELECT ad_id, date_trunc('minute', event_time) AS bucket_start,
       country, device, COUNT(*) AS clicks
FROM dedup
WHERE rn = 1
GROUP BY 1, 2, 3, 4;
          real time path                      batch path
 Kafka --> Flink --> OLAP (is_final=false)
   |                                         daily Spark
   +--> S3 Parquet ----------------------->  recount ----> diff ---> alert
                                                |
                                                v
                                    OLAP overwrite (is_final=true)
                                                |
                                                v
                                             Billing

How do we handle events that arrive late?

The problem: a click happens at 19:00:58 on a phone in a tunnel and arrives at 19:03:10. If our one-minute window for 19:00 already closed and wrote its count, the click is missed or lands in the wrong bucket.

Two kinds of time matter. Event time is when the click actually happened (from the event). Processing time is when Flink sees it. Advertisers care about event time.

A watermark is Flink’s running estimate of “I have probably seen all events up to time T.” A window closes when the watermark passes its end.

Option Behavior Trade-off
Processing-time windows Bucket by arrival time Simple, but wrong buckets for late events
Event-time windows, short watermark delay (5 s) Fast results More events arrive after the window closes
Event-time windows, watermark delay + allowed lateness Emit early, then update the window when late events come Slightly more state, correct buckets

Recommended: event time, a bounded-out-of-orderness watermark of about 10 seconds, plus allowed lateness of a few minutes. When a late event arrives within allowed lateness, Flink re-fires the window with an updated count, and our idempotent upsert overwrites the row. Events later than that go to a side output, are logged, and are picked up by the daily batch recount (which sees everything).

WatermarkStrategy
  .<Click>forBoundedOutOfOrderness(Duration.ofSeconds(10))
  .withTimestampAssigner((c, ts) -> c.eventTimeMillis());

clicks
  .keyBy(Click::adId)
  .window(TumblingEventTimeWindows.of(Time.minutes(1)))
  .allowedLateness(Time.minutes(5))
  .sideOutputLateData(lateTag)
  .aggregate(new CountAgg());

Also guard against clients with bad clocks: if the event time is more than a few minutes in the future or more than a day in the past, replace it with the server receive time.

How do we serve aggregated counts quickly, and what if parts fail?

Serving: the OLAP store holds pre-aggregated minute, hour, and day tables. Queries pick the coarsest table that covers the requested granularity. A popular dashboard can also be cached in Redis for 30 seconds keyed by the query parameters, which absorbs refresh storms.

Store Strength Weakness
Postgres with rollup tables Familiar Struggles with billions of rows and wide group-bys
Cassandra with precomputed keys Fast point reads No ad-hoc group-by
ClickHouse / Druid / Pinot Fast group-by on billions of rows, columnar Another system to run

Recommended: an OLAP store such as ClickHouse or Pinot.

Failure handling, component by component:

  • Click Service host dies: stateless, load balancer routes around it. Clients retry; dedup by impression id absorbs retries.
  • Kafka unreachable from a Click Service host: buffer events to a local disk queue and redirect anyway (availability first), then drain the buffer when Kafka returns. This trades a tiny risk of loss on host disk failure for never blocking users.
  • Kafka broker dies: replication factor 3 with min.insync.replicas=2 keeps writes going.
  • Flink job crashes: restart from the last checkpoint (every 30-60 s); Kafka keeps 7 days of data so nothing is lost.
  • OLAP store down: Flink sink retries with backoff; Kafka backs up; dashboards show stale data with a banner. Billing is unaffected because it uses the batch path.

9. Common mistakes and interviewer follow-ups

  • Writing every click straight into a relational database and running COUNT(*). It melts at 10k writes per second and makes queries scan billions of rows. Say: log to Kafka, pre-aggregate with a stream job, query rollups in an OLAP store.
  • Redirecting before the event is durable. A crash loses billable clicks. Say: produce to Kafka with acks=all, then redirect; or buffer to local disk if Kafka is down.
  • Claiming “Flink is exactly-once, so we are done.” Exactly-once state does not remove duplicate clicks from users or bots, and the sink must be idempotent too. Say: dedup on a signed impression id and use idempotent upserts.
  • Bucketing by processing time. Late mobile events land in the wrong minute. Say: event-time windows with watermarks and allowed lateness, with the batch job as the final safety net.
  • Ignoring hot ads. One partition becomes the bottleneck. Say: detect heavy hitters and salt their keys, then merge partial counts.
  • No reconciliation. Billing on a stream with no audit is risky. Say: daily Spark recount from S3, compare, alert, and overwrite to produce final numbers.
  • Follow-up: “How would you add fraud filtering?” Answer: a Flink operator or async ML scorer that tags suspicious clicks; tagged clicks are still stored but excluded from billable counts, and the batch job can apply an updated model.
  • Follow-up: “Why not Kappa only?” Answer: Kappa (replay Kafka to fix mistakes) works and is simpler, but needs long Kafka retention and the same code for both paths; for money, a separate recount from cold storage gives an independent check.

10. One-page cheat sheet

Topic Key point
Scale 10k clicks/s peak, 2 MB/s, ~34 GB raw/day, ~12 TB/year
Latency Redirect p99 < 100 ms; counts visible < 1 min; query p99 < 1 s
Click path Verify HMAC, produce to Kafka (acks=all), then 302
Log Kafka partitioned by ad_id, RF=3, 7-day retention
Counting Flink event-time tumbling 1-minute windows
Dedup Signed impression id; Flink keyed state with 24 h TTL
Exactly-once Flink checkpoints + idempotent upsert keys in the sink
Late data 10 s watermark, 5 min allowed lateness, side output, batch fix
Hot ads Salt key into N buckets, merge partials
Rollups Minute (7 days), hour (1 year), day (forever) via materialized views
Store ClickHouse / Pinot / Druid for group-by queries
Truth Raw clicks in S3 Parquet; daily Spark recount marks rows final
Billing Reads only is_final = true rows
CAP Availability on ingest, correctness via recompute

27. Facebook Post Search (Hard)

Facebook Post Search lets a user type one or more keywords and get back posts that contain them, sorted either by most recent or by most liked. The twist in the interview version is that you are not allowed to just say “use Elasticsearch.” You must explain how a search index is built and kept fresh while billions of posts are being created and liked every day. The interviewer is really testing whether you understand inverted indexes, how to shard them, how to handle a very high write rate (new posts and, even more, new likes), how to rank cheaply, and how to keep storage cost under control.

1. Functional requirements

Core (must have):

  1. Users can create posts and like posts (these are the writes that the search system must absorb).
  2. Users can search posts by one or more keywords.
  3. Users can sort search results by recency (newest first) or by like count (most liked first).
  4. Results are paginated (the user can load more).

Below the line (out of scope, and why):

  • Privacy filtering (friends-only posts). Real Facebook does it, but it is its own deep problem; we assume all posts are public.
  • Fuzzy matching, typos, stemming, and synonyms. They change the tokenizer, not the architecture.
  • Personalized ranking with machine learning. We do two simple sort orders.
  • Searching images or videos. Text only.

2. Non-functional requirements

  1. Query latency: p99 under 500 ms for a search.
  2. Freshness: a new post is searchable within 1 minute of being created. Like counts used for sorting can be up to a few minutes stale.
  3. Scale: 1 billion users, ~1 billion new posts per day, ~10 billion likes per day, ~10,000 search QPS average.
  4. Availability: 99.99% for search. If an index shard is down, return partial results rather than an error.
  5. Durability: the post store is the source of truth; the index can be rebuilt from it.
  6. CAP choice: availability over consistency for search. Eventual consistency is fine: a just-liked post can rank slightly wrong for a minute. The post and like stores themselves are durable.
  7. Recall: search must find every post (not a sample) that matches, at least for the recency sort. Old posts must still be reachable, even if slower.

3. Back-of-the-envelope estimates

Assumption Number
Daily active users 1 billion
New posts per day 1 billion
Likes per day 10 billion
Searches per day 1 billion (avg 1 per user)
Average post length 100 words, ~60 unique terms after stop words
Post retention 10 years
Posting list entry 8 bytes (post id) 
Writes
  Posts/s   = 1e9 / 86,400       = ~12,000/s  (peak ~3x = 36k/s)
  Likes/s   = 1e10 / 86,400      = ~115,000/s (peak ~350k/s)

Reads
  Search/s  = 1e9 / 86,400       = ~12,000/s  (peak ~36k/s)

Raw post storage
  1e9 posts/day * 1 KB           = 1 TB/day
  per year                       = 365 TB
  10 years                       = ~3.6 PB  (blob/KV store)

Index postings
  1e9 posts/day * 60 terms       = 6e10 postings/day
  * 8 B                          = 480 GB/day
  per year                       = ~175 TB, 10 years ~1.75 PB
  (two sort orders roughly doubles it; compression cuts 3-5x)

Two things jump out. First, likes outnumber posts 10 to 1, so updating like counts in the index on every like is the scariest write path. Second, the index for 10 years is petabytes, so keeping all of it in memory is not affordable. Both drive deep dives.

4. Core entities

  • Post: the content. Fields: post_id, author_id, text, created_at.
  • Like: one user liking one post. Fields: user_id, post_id, created_at.
  • User: author or searcher. Fields: user_id, name.
  • Keyword (term): a normalized word extracted from post text. It is the key of the index.
  • Posting list: for one term, the list of post ids that contain it, kept in a chosen sort order.
  • Like counter: aggregated like count per post, used for sorting.
-- Source-of-truth tables (could be a sharded KV store like Cassandra)
CREATE TABLE posts (
  post_id    BIGINT PRIMARY KEY,  -- Snowflake id, time ordered
  author_id  BIGINT,
  text       TEXT,
  created_at TIMESTAMP
);

CREATE TABLE likes (
  post_id    BIGINT,
  user_id    BIGINT,
  created_at TIMESTAMP,
  PRIMARY KEY (post_id, user_id)
);
// Index entries, conceptually
{
  "term:pizza:recent": [9012, 9007, 8800, 8122],
  "term:pizza:likes":  [{"post": 8122, "score": 5401}, {"post": 9007, "score": 312}]
}

5. API design

POST /posts – create a post.

// request
{"text": "Best pizza in Chicago is deep dish"}
// response 201
{"post_id": "9012", "created_at": "2026-11-05T19:00:00Z"}

POST /posts/{post_id}/likes – like a post. Response 204 No Content; 409 if already liked (idempotent from the client’s view).

GET /search?q=pizza+chicago&sort=recent|likes&cursor=...&limit=25 – search.

// response 200
{
  "results": [
    {"post_id": "9012", "author_id": "77", "snippet": "Best pizza in Chicago...",
     "created_at": "2026-11-05T19:00:00Z", "likes": 41}
  ],
  "next_cursor": "eyJzaGFyZCI6Li4ufQ=="
}

Status codes: 200, 400 (empty query), 429 (rate limited). Auth: user session token on every endpoint; search is rate limited per user. The cursor is an opaque token that encodes where each shard left off, so the next page continues correctly.

How will users create and like posts?

  1. The client calls POST /posts. The Post Service writes the post to the Posts DB (source of truth) and publishes a PostCreated event to Kafka.
  2. The client calls POST /posts/{id}/likes. The Like Service inserts into the Likes DB (the primary key prevents double likes) and publishes a PostLiked event.
  3. Both services return as soon as the DB write and Kafka publish succeed. Search indexing happens asynchronously, which is why freshness is “within 1 minute,” not instant.
sequenceDiagram
    participant U as Client
    participant P as Post Service
    participant D as Posts DB
    participant K as Kafka
    participant I as Indexer
    participant X as Index
    U->>P: POST posts with text
    P->>D: Insert post
    D-->>P: ok
    P->>K: Publish PostCreated
    K-->>P: ack
    P-->>U: 201 post id
    K->>I: Deliver PostCreated
    I->>I: Tokenize text into terms
    I->>X: Append post id to each posting list

How will users search by keyword?

The core structure is an inverted index. A normal (“forward”) index maps a post to its words. An inverted index flips that: it maps each word to the list of posts that contain it.

  1. The Indexer consumes PostCreated, tokenizes the text (lowercase, split on spaces and punctuation, drop stop words like “the”), and for each term appends the post id to that term’s posting list.
  2. The client calls GET /search?q=pizza chicago&sort=recent.
  3. The Search Service tokenizes the query the same way, giving terms pizza and chicago.
  4. It fetches both posting lists and intersects them (AND semantics: a post must contain both words).
  5. It takes the top 25 by the chosen sort, hydrates them (fetches text and author from the Posts DB or a cache), and returns them.
def tokenize(text: str) -> list[str]:
    words = re.findall(r"[a-z0-9#@']+", text.lower())
    return sorted({w for w in words if w not in STOP_WORDS})

def search_recent(terms, limit=25):
    # each list is sorted by post_id DESC; Snowflake ids are time ordered
    lists = [index.get(f"{t}:recent") for t in terms]
    lists.sort(key=len)                      # start with the rarest term
    result = set(lists[0])
    for lst in lists[1:]:
        result &= set(lst)
    return sorted(result, reverse=True)[:limit]

How will users sort by recency or by likes?

We keep two posting lists per term. The recency list is ordered by post id (Snowflake ids embed the creation time, so higher id means newer). The likes list is ordered by like count. In Redis, a sorted set (ZSET) is a natural fit: each member has a numeric score and Redis keeps members ordered by score.

ZADD term:pizza:recent  9012  9012      (score = post_id ~ time)
ZADD term:pizza:likes     41  9012      (score = like count)
ZREVRANGE term:pizza:likes 0 24         (top 25 by likes)

7. Deep dives

How do we build and shard an inverted index this large?

The problem: a year of postings is ~175 TB before compression. No single machine holds it. We must split the index across many machines (shards), and the way we split decides how expensive each query is.

Sharding option How Query cost Write cost Main risk
By term (term-partitioned) All postings for “pizza” live on one shard Touch only shards for the query terms (1-3) A post with 60 terms writes to up to 60 shards Hot terms (“the”, trending hashtags) overload one shard; intersections need cross-shard data movement
By document (doc-partitioned) Each shard owns a subset of posts and a full mini index for them Fan out to every shard, each returns its top K, merge A post writes to exactly one shard Fan-out to all shards for every query; tail latency grows with shard count
Hybrid (doc-partitioned + time tiers) Doc partition within a time range; recent tiers first Fan out within the hot tier only for most queries One shard More moving parts

Recommended: shard by document, grouped into time-based tiers. Doc partitioning keeps writes to one shard, makes intersections local (each shard has both “pizza” and “chicago” lists for its posts), and spreads hot terms evenly. The fan-out cost is real, so we bound it with tiers (next deep dives) and by scatter-gather with a timeout: each shard returns its local top K; the aggregator merges them; slow shards are dropped from the response and the answer is marked partial.

async def scatter_gather(terms, sort, k=25, timeout_ms=200):
    tasks = [shard.search(terms, sort, k) for shard in hot_tier_shards()]
    done = await gather_with_timeout(tasks, timeout_ms)   # drop slow shards
    merged = heapq.nlargest(k, chain(*done), key=lambda r: r.score)
    return merged, len(done) < len(tasks)                 # results, is_partial

Inside each shard, postings are stored compressed. Because post ids in a recency list are sorted, we store the differences between neighbors (delta encoding), which are small numbers, then pack them with variable-byte encoding. That routinely gives 3-5x compression.

How do we rank by recency and by likes without slow queries?

The problem: for “pizza,” there may be 500 million matching posts. Sorting them all at query time is impossible within 500 ms.

Option How Pros Cons
Sort at query time Fetch all matches, sort Simple Way too slow for common terms
One index, sort by recency, re-rank top N by likes Read newest 10k matches, sort those by likes One index Misses old viral posts entirely
Two indexes per term (recency and likes) Each posting list is pre-sorted Top K is just “read the head” Double storage, and likes keep reordering the likes list

Recommended: two pre-sorted indexes. The recency index is append-only (new posts always go on top), so it is cheap. The likes index is the hard one because scores change. To keep it affordable, store only the top N (say 1,000) posts per term per shard in the likes index; a user scrolling past the 1,000th most-liked “pizza” post is rare. For multi-term queries sorted by likes, intersect the recency lists to find candidates and then sort by a like-count lookup, but cap the candidate set (for example, check the top 1,000 of the rarest term’s likes list first, which usually yields enough matches).

pizza:likes (capped ZSET, top 1000)
  8122 -> 5401
  7740 -> 4980
  ...
  1033 -> 120   <- lowest score kept; new entries below this are dropped
ZADD term:pizza:likes 130 9012 ; ZREMRANGEBYRANK term:pizza:likes 0 -1001

How do we absorb 115,000 likes per second into the index?

The problem: each like changes a post’s score. If a post has 60 terms, one like could mean 60 index updates. At 115k likes per second that is ~7 million index writes per second. Unworkable.

Option How Pros Cons
Update index on every like 60 ZADDs per like Always fresh 7M writes/s
Batch likes per post Count likes in a short window, update once Cuts writes hugely A few seconds to minutes stale
Update only at milestones Re-index a post’s score when its count crosses 1, 2, 4, 8, 16… (powers of 2) Updates per post grow as log of likes Score in index is approximate
Two-stage: approximate index + exact lookup Index uses milestone score; at query time fetch exact counts for the top candidates and re-sort Correct final order, cheap writes Extra lookup at query time

Recommended: combine batching, milestones, and two-stage ranking.

  1. A Like Counter service (Kafka consumer) aggregates like events per post in 30-second windows and writes the exact count to a Like Count store (Redis or Cassandra).
  2. It only pushes a score update to the search index when the count crosses a power of 2. A post with 1 million likes has been re-indexed only about 20 times.
  3. At query time, the Search Service reads, say, the top 2K candidates by approximate score, fetches their exact like counts in one batched call, re-sorts, and returns the top K.
def on_like_batch(post_id: int, new_count: int, old_count: int):
    like_store.set(post_id, new_count)                 # exact, always
    if new_count.bit_length() > old_count.bit_length():
        # crossed a power of two: refresh index score
        for term in post_terms(post_id):
            index.zadd(f"{term}:likes", {post_id: new_count})
like events --> Kafka --> Like Counter (30 s windows)
                               |            |
                       exact   v            v  only at 2^n
                     +-------------+   +-----------------+
                     | Like Count  |   | Index likes ZSET|
                     | store       |   | (approx score)  |
                     +-------------+   +-----------------+
                               ^            |
                               +-- re-rank top 2K at query time

New posts follow a similar path: the Indexer batches writes per shard (for example, 500 ms micro-batches) so each shard gets a few large writes instead of thousands of small ones. That still meets the 1-minute freshness target.

How do we keep popular searches fast?

The problem: search traffic is skewed. Trending topics and common words make up a big share of queries, and every one of them fans out to many shards.

Option How Pros Cons
No cache Always query the index Always fresh Wasteful for repeated queries
Result cache in Redis Key = normalized query + sort + page, TTL 30-60 s Big hit rate on trending queries Results up to a minute stale
CDN edge cache Cache public search responses at the edge Lowest latency, offloads backend Only works if results are not personalized; harder invalidation

Recommended: a Redis result cache keyed by the normalized query (terms sorted, lowercased) with a short TTL, plus a CDN cache for the first page of the most popular queries since posts are public in our scope. A 60-second TTL is acceptable because our freshness requirement is about 1 minute anyway.

def cache_key(terms, sort, cursor):
    return f"search:{sort}:{'+'.join(sorted(terms))}:{cursor or 'p0'}"

def search(q, sort, cursor):
    terms = tokenize(q)
    key = cache_key(terms, sort, cursor)
    if (hit := redis.get(key)) is not None:
        return json.loads(hit)
    res = run_search(terms, sort, cursor)
    redis.setex(key, 60, json.dumps(res))
    return res

To avoid a thundering herd (many requests missing the cache at the same moment and all hitting the index), use request coalescing: the first miss takes a short lock and computes; others wait briefly for the result.

How do we keep storage affordable with hot and cold index tiers?

The problem: 10 years of index is petabytes. Keeping it all in RAM would cost tens of millions of dollars per year. But most searches care about recent posts, and very old posts are searched rarely.

Tier Data Storage Latency Cost
Hot Last ~7-30 days RAM (Redis or in-memory index) ~10 ms Highest
Warm Last 1 year SSD-backed index (Lucene segments) ~50-100 ms Medium
Cold Older than 1 year Compressed index files on S3, loaded on demand Seconds Lowest

Recommended: tier the index by time, since doc partitioning plus Snowflake ids makes time ranges natural.

  1. Recency queries read the hot tier first. If it returns at least K results, stop. Otherwise continue into warm, then cold. Most queries stop in the hot tier.
  2. Likes queries read a small, separate “all-time top” likes index per term (capped at 1,000 entries) that lives in the hot tier, plus the hot tier’s own likes lists. Old viral posts stay findable without scanning cold data.
  3. A nightly job rolls a day of hot data into warm segments, and old warm segments into cold files on S3. Cold segments are immutable, which makes them cheap and easy to compress.
 query "pizza" sort=recent
   |
   v
 [hot: 30 days, RAM] --enough? yes--> return
   | no
   v
 [warm: 1 year, SSD] --enough? yes--> return
   | no
   v
 [cold: S3 segments, lazy load + local cache] --> return (slower)

Rough cost picture: hot tier for 30 days at ~480 GB/day raw, compressed 4x, is ~3.6 TB per index type, about 7 TB with both, which fits on a few dozen memory-heavy hosts with replicas. The remaining petabytes live on SSD and S3 at a small fraction of the price.

What happens when things fail?

  • An index shard dies: each shard has 2-3 replicas; the aggregator routes to a healthy replica. If all replicas of a shard are down, return partial results with a flag.
  • The Indexer falls behind: Kafka buffers events (retain 7 days). Freshness degrades but nothing is lost. Autoscale indexer consumers by Kafka lag.
  • A shard’s in-memory index is lost: rebuild it by replaying Kafka from the last snapshot offset. Snapshots of each shard are written to S3 every hour, so replay is at most an hour of events.
  • Full rebuild (for example, a tokenizer change): run a batch job over the Posts DB to produce new segments offline, then swap aliases. The Posts DB, not the index, is the source of truth.

9. Common mistakes and interviewer follow-ups

  • Saying “just use a LIKE query on the posts table.” LIKE '%pizza%' scans every row; at billions of posts it never returns. Say: build an inverted index from term to posts.
  • Updating every term’s likes list on every like. That is millions of writes per second. Say: batch, only push score changes at power-of-2 milestones, and re-rank the final candidates with exact counts.
  • Sharding by term without addressing hot terms. A trending hashtag pins one shard. Say: shard by document, intersect locally, and scatter-gather with timeouts.
  • Keeping 10 years of index in RAM. It is petabytes and wildly expensive. Say: hot, warm, and cold tiers by time, with a capped all-time likes index.
  • Forgetting that the index is derived data. If you lose it, can you rebuild? Say: the Posts DB and Kafka are the source of truth; shards snapshot to S3 and replay Kafka.
  • Treating pagination as offset and limit. Deep offsets across shards are slow and unstable as new posts arrive. Say: cursor-based pagination that encodes the last seen score and post id per shard.
  • Follow-up: “How would you add privacy?” Answer: index author ids alongside posts and filter candidates against the viewer’s friend set (or pre-filter by visibility class), accepting some extra cost at query time.
  • Follow-up: “How would you support phrase search?” Answer: store term positions in postings so you can check that words appear next to each other.

10. One-page cheat sheet

Topic Key point
Scale 12k posts/s, 115k likes/s, 12k searches/s (3x at peak)
Latency / freshness Search p99 < 500 ms; new posts searchable < 1 min
Core structure Inverted index: term -> posting list of post ids
Two sort orders Per term: recency list (by Snowflake id) and likes list (by count)
Sharding By document, scatter-gather, merge top K, timeout -> partial results
Like writes 30 s batches, index update only at 2^n counts, re-rank top 2K exact
Likes index Capped to top 1,000 per term per shard
Caching Redis result cache 60 s TTL, CDN for top queries, request coalescing
Tiers Hot RAM (30 days), warm SSD (1 year), cold S3 (older)
Compression Delta + varint encoding on sorted ids, 3-5x
Recovery Posts DB + Kafka are truth; hourly shard snapshots to S3
CAP AP for search; eventual consistency of counts

28. Payment System (Hard)

A payment system like Stripe lets online businesses (merchants) accept card payments without building their own card processing. The customer types card details into a checkout form, the payment system sends the charge to a payment service provider (PSP, the company that actually talks to the card networks and banks, such as Adyen or a card acquirer), and the merchant learns whether the payment succeeded. The interviewer is really testing correctness under failure: how you make sure a customer is never charged twice, how you keep a ledger that always balances, how you handle a PSP that times out or answers late, and how you shrink the security burden of handling raw card numbers.

1. Functional requirements

Core (must have):

  1. Merchants can create a payment (a “payment intent”: an amount, a currency, and an order reference) for a customer.
  2. Customers can pay with a card through a hosted checkout or embedded form; the system charges the card via a PSP.
  3. Merchants can query a payment’s status (pending, succeeded, failed, refunded).
  4. Merchants receive notifications (webhooks) when a payment’s status changes.
  5. Merchants can refund a payment, fully or partly.

Below the line (out of scope, and why):

  • Payouts to merchant bank accounts. Important, but it is a second money-movement flow with the same ledger ideas.
  • Fraud scoring with machine learning. We note where it plugs in.
  • Multi-currency conversion and FX. Adds pricing logic, not new architecture.
  • Disputes and chargebacks. Mentioned in reconciliation only.
  • Subscriptions and invoicing. Built on top of single payments.

2. Non-functional requirements

  1. Correctness: never charge a customer twice for one payment, and never lose a successful charge. This is the top requirement, above latency.
  2. Consistency: strong consistency for payment state and the ledger (a payment must not appear succeeded in one place and failed in another). CAP choice: consistency over availability for the money path. If we cannot be sure, we return “pending” rather than guess.
  3. Durability: every state change and ledger entry is stored durably and replicated across zones before we acknowledge it.
  4. Latency: p99 under 2 seconds for a card charge end to end (PSP calls dominate), p99 under 200 ms for status reads.
  5. Availability: 99.99% for accepting payments.
  6. Scale: 10,000 payment attempts per second at peak (big sales events), ~100 million payments per day at peak days.
  7. Security and compliance: PCI DSS (the card industry’s security standard). Keep the set of systems that see raw card numbers as small as possible. Full audit trail of every change.

3. Back-of-the-envelope estimates

Assumption Number
Payments per day (average) 30 million
Peak payments per second 10,000
Status reads per payment ~5 (merchant polls, dashboard)
Ledger entries per payment ~4 (two per movement, auth + capture)
Payment row size ~1 KB
Ledger entry size ~200 bytes
Webhooks per payment ~2 
Writes
  Avg payments/s   = 30e6 / 86,400      = ~350/s
  Peak payments/s  = 10,000/s
  Ledger writes/s  = 10,000 * 4         = 40,000/s at peak
  Webhooks/s       = 10,000 * 2         = 20,000/s at peak

Reads
  Status reads/s   = 10,000 * 5         = 50,000/s at peak

Storage per year
  Payments: 30e6 * 365 * 1 KB          = ~11 TB/year
  Ledger:   30e6 * 365 * 4 * 200 B     = ~9 TB/year
  Keep 7+ years for audit              = ~140 TB total

The numbers are modest for modern databases. What makes this hard is not volume, it is that every write must be exact, and the PSP is a slow, unreliable external dependency.

4. Core entities

  • Merchant: the business. Fields: merchant_id, api_key_hash, webhook_url, webhook_secret.
  • Payment (payment intent): one attempt to collect money. Fields: payment_id, merchant_id, amount, currency, status, idempotency_key, psp_reference, created_at.
  • Payment method token: a stand-in for a card. Fields: token, card_fingerprint, last4, brand, expiry. The real card number lives only in the vault.
  • Transaction (PSP attempt): one call to a PSP for a payment. Fields: txn_id, payment_id, type (authorize, capture, refund), status, psp_request_id.
  • Ledger entry: one side of a money movement. Fields: entry_id, account_id, payment_id, direction (debit/credit), amount.
  • Refund: money returned. Fields: refund_id, payment_id, amount, status.
  • Webhook event: a notification to a merchant. Fields: event_id, merchant_id, type, payload, attempts, next_retry_at.
CREATE TABLE payments (
  payment_id       UUID PRIMARY KEY,
  merchant_id      UUID NOT NULL,
  idempotency_key  TEXT NOT NULL,
  amount_minor     BIGINT NOT NULL,      -- cents, never floats
  currency         CHAR(3) NOT NULL,
  status           TEXT NOT NULL,        -- see state machine
  psp_reference    TEXT,
  version          INT NOT NULL DEFAULT 0,
  created_at       TIMESTAMPTZ NOT NULL DEFAULT now(),
  UNIQUE (merchant_id, idempotency_key)
);

CREATE TABLE ledger_entries (
  entry_id      BIGSERIAL PRIMARY KEY,
  journal_id    UUID NOT NULL,           -- groups the debit and credit
  account_id    TEXT NOT NULL,           -- e.g. customer_funds, merchant_balance
  payment_id    UUID NOT NULL,
  direction     CHAR(1) NOT NULL CHECK (direction IN ('D','C')),
  amount_minor  BIGINT NOT NULL CHECK (amount_minor > 0),
  created_at    TIMESTAMPTZ NOT NULL DEFAULT now()
);
-- ledger rows are append-only: no UPDATE, no DELETE

5. API design

POST /v1/payments – create a payment intent. Header Idempotency-Key: <uuid> is required.

// request
{"amount": 4999, "currency": "USD", "order_id": "ord_881", "capture": "automatic"}
// response 201
{"payment_id": "pay_3f9a", "status": "requires_payment_method", "client_secret": "pay_3f9a_secret_x"}

POST /v1/payments/{payment_id}/confirm – attach a tokenized card and charge it. Called from the checkout page (using the client secret) or by the merchant server. Also needs Idempotency-Key.

// request
{"payment_method": "tok_visa_8812"}
// response 200
{"payment_id": "pay_3f9a", "status": "succeeded"}
// or 202 if the PSP has not answered in time
{"payment_id": "pay_3f9a", "status": "processing"}

GET /v1/payments/{payment_id} – get status. Response 200 with the payment object, 404 if not found.

POST /v1/payments/{payment_id}/refunds – refund. With Idempotency-Key.

// request
{"amount": 1000}
// response 201
{"refund_id": "re_71", "status": "pending"}

POST /v1/tokens – the card form posts raw card data here (directly from the browser to the vault domain) and gets a token back.

// request (sent from the browser iframe, never touches the merchant)
{"number": "4242424242424242", "exp_month": 12, "exp_year": 2028, "cvc": "123"}
// response 201
{"token": "tok_visa_8812", "last4": "4242", "brand": "visa"}

Webhook (outbound): POST {merchant webhook_url} with body {"id": "evt_1", "type": "payment.succeeded", "data": {...}} and header Signature: t=...,v1=<hmac>.

Status codes across the API: 200/201/202, 400 (validation), 401 (bad API key), 402 (card declined), 409 (idempotency key reused with a different body), 429 (rate limited). Auth: merchant secret API key on server calls; a publishable key plus client secret from the browser.

How will merchants create a payment?

  1. The merchant server calls POST /v1/payments with an Idempotency-Key.
  2. The API Gateway authenticates the API key and rate limits.
  3. The Payment Service inserts a row with status requires_payment_method, guarded by the unique (merchant_id, idempotency_key) constraint.
  4. It returns the payment id and a client secret the checkout page will use.
sequenceDiagram
    participant M as Merchant server
    participant G as API Gateway
    participant P as Payment Service
    participant D as Payments DB
    M->>G: POST payments with Idempotency Key
    G->>G: Authenticate API key and rate limit
    G->>P: Create payment intent
    P->>D: Insert row requires payment method
    D-->>P: ok or unique key conflict
    P-->>G: payment id and client secret
    G-->>M: 201 Created

How will customers pay with a card?

  1. The checkout page loads a card form in an iframe served from our vault domain. The customer types the card number there, so the merchant page never sees it.
  2. The iframe posts the card to POST /v1/tokens. The Token Vault encrypts and stores it and returns a token like tok_visa_8812.
  3. The page calls POST /v1/payments/{id}/confirm with the token.
  4. The Payment Service moves the payment to processing, records a transaction attempt, and calls the PSP Adapter.
  5. The PSP Adapter asks the vault to send the real card to the PSP (the vault, not the Payment Service, holds the card number), with our own idempotency key for this attempt.
  6. The PSP returns authorized or declined. The Payment Service, in one database transaction, updates status to succeeded or failed, writes ledger entries, and writes an outbox event.
  7. It returns the result to the page. If the PSP did not answer within the timeout, it returns processing and finishes later.

How will merchants check status and get notified?

  1. GET /v1/payments/{id} reads the payments table (from a replica for low latency, or primary if the merchant asks for strong reads).
  2. On each state change, an outbox row is written in the same transaction. A relay publishes it to Kafka. The Webhook Service delivers it to the merchant, signs it with HMAC, and retries with backoff until the merchant returns 2xx.

How will merchants refund?

  1. POST /v1/payments/{id}/refunds checks the payment is succeeded and that total refunds do not exceed the amount (done with a row lock or a version check).
  2. It creates a refund in pending, calls the PSP refund API with an idempotency key, and on success writes reversing ledger entries and emits refund.succeeded.

7. Deep dives

How do we make sure a customer is never charged twice?

The problem: networks fail. A merchant sends “confirm,” our response is lost, and the merchant retries. Or our service calls the PSP, the PSP charges the card, and the response times out, so we retry. Without protection, either retry can double-charge.

An idempotency key is a unique id the caller attaches to a request so that sending it again has no extra effect. We need them at two boundaries: merchant to us, and us to the PSP.

Option How Pros Cons
No keys, rely on clients Hope clients do not retry Simple Double charges
Idempotency table in the DB Store key, request hash, and response; replay on retry Exact, durable, transactional with the payment One more write per request
Idempotency in Redis only SETNX the key Fast Lost on Redis failover, not transactional with the payment

Recommended: a durable idempotency table in the same database as payments, written in the same transaction, plus a per-attempt idempotency key passed to the PSP.

def handle_confirm(merchant_id, idem_key, body):
    req_hash = sha256(canonical_json(body))
    with db.transaction():
        row = db.query_one("""
            INSERT INTO idempotency (merchant_id, key, req_hash, status)
            VALUES (%s, %s, %s, 'in_progress')
            ON CONFLICT (merchant_id, key) DO NOTHING
            RETURNING *""", merchant_id, idem_key, req_hash)
        if row is None:                                   # seen before
            prev = db.query_one("SELECT * FROM idempotency WHERE merchant_id=%s AND key=%s",
                                merchant_id, idem_key)
            if prev.req_hash != req_hash:
                return 409, {"error": "key reused with different body"}
            if prev.status == "in_progress":
                return 409, {"error": "request in progress, retry later"}
            return prev.response_code, prev.response_body  # replay
    resp_code, resp_body = do_confirm(body)               # PSP call, see below
    db.execute("""UPDATE idempotency SET status='done', response_code=%s,
                  response_body=%s WHERE merchant_id=%s AND key=%s""",
               resp_code, json.dumps(resp_body), merchant_id, idem_key)
    return resp_code, resp_body

End to end, the chain looks like this:

merchant --Idempotency-Key K--> Payment Svc
  idempotency(K) row ensures one confirm per K
Payment Svc --attempt id A (derived from payment_id + attempt #)--> PSP
  PSP dedups on A, so a retried call returns the same charge
DB unique (payment_id) on succeeded charges
  last line of defense: a payment can succeed only once

Also keep a client-side safeguard: the checkout button disables after the first click, and the payment intent itself is single-use (once succeeded, a second confirm returns the same result).

How do we track a payment’s lifecycle safely?

The problem: a payment moves through many states, and events can arrive out of order (a webhook from the PSP can beat our own synchronous response, or arrive twice). If any code path can set any status, bugs will move a refunded payment back to succeeded.

A state machine lists the allowed states and the only allowed moves between them.

 requires_payment_method
          | confirm
          v
     processing ---------------> failed
          |   \  timeout
          |    +--> unknown --(reconcile)--> succeeded / failed
          v
     authorized --(capture)--> succeeded --(refund)--> partially_refunded
          |                        |                         |
          +--(void)--> canceled     +--(full refund)--> refunded
Approach How Risk
Free-form status updates UPDATE ... SET status = ? Illegal moves, lost updates
State machine in code + optimistic locking Check allowed transition; WHERE version = ? Safe; retry on conflict
Event-sourced payment Store events, derive state Great audit, more complex

Recommended: an explicit transition table enforced in code, with optimistic concurrency (a version column) so two concurrent updates cannot both win. Keep every transition in an append-only payment_events table for audit.

ALLOWED = {
    "requires_payment_method": {"processing", "canceled"},
    "processing": {"authorized", "succeeded", "failed", "unknown"},
    "unknown": {"succeeded", "failed"},
    "authorized": {"succeeded", "canceled"},
    "succeeded": {"partially_refunded", "refunded"},
    "partially_refunded": {"partially_refunded", "refunded"},
}

def transition(payment_id, from_state, to_state, version):
    if to_state not in ALLOWED.get(from_state, set()):
        raise IllegalTransition(from_state, to_state)
    n = db.execute("""UPDATE payments SET status=%s, version=version+1
                      WHERE payment_id=%s AND status=%s AND version=%s""",
                   to_state, payment_id, from_state, version)
    if n == 0:
        raise ConcurrentUpdate()   # reload and re-evaluate

How do we keep the books correct with a double-entry ledger?

The problem: we need to know at any moment how much money we owe each merchant, how much is in flight, and how much we collected, and these numbers must add up exactly. Updating a single balance column is fragile: one bug and money appears or disappears with no trace.

Double-entry bookkeeping means every movement of money is recorded as two (or more) entries, a debit in one account and an equal credit in another. The sum of all debits always equals the sum of all credits. If it does not, there is a bug, and you can find it.

Option How Pros Cons
Mutable balance column UPDATE balance = balance + x Simple No history, silent errors, lost updates
Single-entry log Append one row per event History Cannot detect imbalance
Double-entry, append-only Every journal has debits = credits Self-checking, auditable, immutable More rows, need a balance cache

Recommended: append-only double-entry ledger in the same relational database as payments, written in the same transaction as the state change. Balances are computed from entries (or kept in a cached balance table that is updated in the same transaction and periodically verified).

A $49.99 card payment with a $1.75 fee:

Journal Account Debit Credit
capture psp_receivable 4999
capture merchant_balance 4824
capture fee_revenue 175
settle (later, PSP pays us) cash 4999
settle psp_receivable 4999 
-- Invariant check, run continuously
SELECT journal_id
FROM ledger_entries
GROUP BY journal_id
HAVING SUM(CASE WHEN direction='D' THEN amount_minor ELSE 0 END)
    <> SUM(CASE WHEN direction='C' THEN amount_minor ELSE 0 END);
-- must return zero rows

Refunds never delete or edit entries; they add new reversing entries. Money is always stored in integer minor units (cents), never floating point, because 0.1 + 0.2 is not exactly 0.3 in floats.

What happens when the PSP times out or answers late?

The problem: we called the PSP, and after 10 seconds there is no answer. The card might have been charged or might not. If we mark the payment failed and the customer retries, they may be charged twice. If we mark it succeeded, we may ship goods for free. “Exactly once” across a network boundary is impossible in general; we get “effectively once” by combining at-least-once retries with idempotent receivers.

Option How Pros Cons
Treat timeout as failure Mark failed, let customer retry Simple Double charges
Retry blindly Call PSP again Might succeed Double charges unless PSP dedups
Retry with the same PSP idempotency key, then reconcile Mark unknown, retry with same key, query PSP status, fall back to webhook and daily report Correct More states and background jobs

Recommended: on timeout, mark the payment unknown (shown to merchants as processing), and let a recovery worker resolve it.

def resolve_unknown(payment):
    attempt_key = f"{payment.payment_id}:{payment.attempt}"
    for delay in [1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32]:            # exponential backoff
        try:
            r = psp.get_payment(idempotency_key=attempt_key)  # status lookup
            if r.status in ("authorized", "captured"):
                return finalize(payment, "succeeded", r)
            if r.status in ("declined", "not_found"):
                return finalize(payment, "failed", r)
        except PspUnavailable:
            pass
        sleep(delay + random.random())            # jitter
    alert_ops(payment)                            # still unknown, daily recon will settle it

Important rules: retries reuse the same PSP idempotency key so the PSP returns the original charge rather than creating a new one; the customer cannot start a second attempt on the same payment intent while it is unknown; and if the PSP has no lookup API, we “void if unsure” (cancel any authorization the PSP later reports) rather than leaving the customer charged for a payment we marked failed.

Also put a circuit breaker in front of each PSP: if error rates spike, stop sending to it and fail over to a secondary PSP for new payments only (never for a payment already in flight with the first PSP).

How do we handle PSP webhooks and reconcile with the PSP?

The problem: PSPs tell us about final outcomes, disputes, and settlements by calling our webhook endpoint. Those calls can arrive late, twice, or out of order. And no matter how careful we are, our records and the PSP’s records can drift.

Inbound webhook handling:

  1. Verify the PSP signature. Reject unsigned or stale requests.
  2. Store the raw event with a unique constraint on the PSP’s event id (dedup). Return 200 fast.
  3. A worker processes stored events and applies them through the same state machine. An illegal or older transition is ignored, which makes out-of-order delivery harmless.
INSERT INTO psp_events (psp_event_id, payload, received_at)
VALUES ($1, $2, now())
ON CONFLICT (psp_event_id) DO NOTHING;   -- duplicates are no-ops

Reconciliation (checking our books against the outside world):

Check Frequency What it catches
Unknown payments resolver Every minute Timeouts not yet resolved
PSP settlement file vs ledger Daily Missing or extra charges, wrong amounts, fees
Bank statement vs cash account Daily Settlement money that never arrived
Ledger invariant (debits = credits) Continuous Code bugs 
  PSP daily settlement file (SFTP / API)
              |
              v
     +-------------------+      match by psp_reference
     | Reconciliation job|<---- our payments + ledger
     +-------------------+
        |        |       |
     matched  missing  mismatched
        |     in ours   amount
        v        |       |
      done       +---+---+
                     v
              exceptions queue --> auto-fix (e.g. mark succeeded,
                                   add ledger entries) or ops review

Outbound webhooks to merchants follow the same reliability pattern in reverse: the transactional outbox (write the event in the same DB transaction as the state change, then a relay publishes it) guarantees no event is lost, and we retry delivery with exponential backoff for up to 3 days. Each event has an id so merchants can dedup.

How do we reduce PCI scope with tokenization?

The problem: any system that stores, processes, or transmits raw card numbers falls under PCI DSS, with strict audits, network isolation, and key management. If the card number flows through the Payment Service, its databases, logs, and Kafka, all of it is in scope.

Option Who sees card numbers PCI scope
Merchant collects card, sends to us Merchant + all our services Huge for both
Our services handle cards directly All our services Huge for us
Hosted iframe + token vault Only the vault Small, isolated

Recommended: the browser posts card data directly to a small, isolated Token Vault from an iframe on our domain. The vault encrypts the card number with a key held in an HSM (hardware security module, tamper-resistant hardware that keeps keys) and returns a random token. Everything else (Payment Service, ledger, logs, Kafka) handles only tokens, last4, and brand. When a charge is needed, the vault forwards the card to the PSP itself (a “detokenizing proxy”), so even the PSP Adapter never sees the number.

 Browser iframe --card--> [ Vault (PCI) ] --card--> PSP
                               |
                          token only
                               v
         Payment Svc, DB, Kafka, logs (out of PCI scope)

Extra rules: never log request bodies on the vault path; store the CVC never (PCI forbids storing it after authorization); and compute a card fingerprint (a keyed hash of the number) so we can detect the same card across tokens for fraud checks without storing the number elsewhere.

How do we keep wallet balances, the ledger, and the PSP consistent?

The problem: a payment touches three places, our payment row, our ledger, and the PSP. The PSP is external, so we cannot put it in one database transaction with our tables. And if we added a stored-value wallet, it is a fourth balance to keep in sync.

Approach How Pros Cons
Two-phase commit across services Distributed transaction Atomic in theory PSPs do not support it; blocks on failure
Saga with compensation Sequence of local steps; undo on failure (void, refund) Works with external systems Must design every compensation
Single DB for payment + ledger + wallet, saga only for the PSP Local ACID for our data, saga for the external step Simple and strong locally Needs one DB that scales (shard by merchant)

Recommended: keep payment state, ledger entries, wallet balances, idempotency records, and the outbox in one relational database (Postgres or a distributed SQL database like CockroachDB/Spanner), sharded by merchant_id, so every local change is one ACID transaction. Treat the PSP call as a saga step: record intent first (processing), call the PSP, then record the outcome. If anything goes wrong after the PSP charged, compensate (void or refund) and record that too. Reconciliation is the final safety net.

 T1 (local tx): payment -> processing, attempt row, outbox "attempt_started"
 Step: call PSP with attempt key
 T2 (local tx): payment -> succeeded, ledger entries, wallet update, outbox
 On failure after PSP success: T3 (local tx) record compensation; call PSP void/refund

Scaling note: 40,000 ledger rows per second at peak is fine when sharded by merchant across, say, 16-32 database shards with synchronous replicas in other availability zones. Very large merchants can get their own shard.

9. Common mistakes and interviewer follow-ups

  • Treating a PSP timeout as a failure. The card may have been charged, so the customer retries and pays twice. Say: mark it unknown, retry with the same PSP idempotency key, query status, and reconcile.
  • Using an in-memory or Redis-only idempotency store. Failover loses keys and allows duplicates. Say: durable idempotency table in the same transaction as the payment.
  • Storing balances as a mutable column with floats. Rounding errors and silent drift. Say: integer minor units, append-only double-entry ledger, invariant checks.
  • Letting card numbers flow through the main services. That puts everything in PCI scope. Say: hosted iframe, token vault with HSM, detokenizing proxy to the PSP.
  • Publishing events after the DB commit with a separate call. A crash between the two loses the webhook. Say: transactional outbox.
  • Claiming exactly-once delivery across the network. Interviewers will push back. Say: at-least-once delivery plus idempotent receivers gives effectively-once outcomes.
  • Skipping reconciliation. Every real payment company runs it daily. Say: match PSP settlement files and bank statements to the ledger, with an exceptions queue.
  • Follow-up: “How do you fail over between PSPs?” Answer: only for new attempts, never mid-attempt; route by health, cost, and card type; each attempt has its own idempotency key and is reconciled with the PSP that handled it.

10. One-page cheat sheet

Topic Key point
Scale 10k payments/s peak, 40k ledger writes/s, 50k status reads/s
Priorities Correctness > availability > latency; CP for the money path
Idempotency Merchant key in a DB table (same tx), attempt key to PSP, unique constraint on success
State machine requires_pm -> processing -> (authorized) -> succeeded -> refunded; unknown on timeout
Concurrency Optimistic locking with a version column
Ledger Append-only double entry, integer cents, debits = credits check
PSP failure Mark unknown, backoff retries with same key, status lookup, circuit breaker
Events Transactional outbox -> Kafka -> signed webhooks, retry 3 days
Inbound webhooks Verify signature, dedup by event id, apply via state machine
Reconciliation Daily vs PSP settlement and bank files; exceptions queue
PCI Iframe + token vault + HSM; only the vault sees card numbers
Consistency One sharded SQL DB for local ACID; saga for the PSP step

29. Metrics Monitoring and Alerting (Hard)

A metrics monitoring system like Datadog or Prometheus collects numbers from servers and applications every few seconds (CPU usage, request count, error rate, latency), stores them as time series, shows them on dashboards, and sends alerts when something looks wrong. A time series is just a sequence of (timestamp, value) points for one named metric with a fixed set of labels. The interviewer is really testing whether you can design a write-heavy pipeline that ingests millions of tiny data points per second, store them cheaply with compression and downsampling, keep label cardinality under control, answer dashboard queries fast, and evaluate alert rules reliably without spamming people.

1. Functional requirements

Core (must have):

  1. Collect metrics from many hosts and services (system metrics like CPU and memory, plus application metrics like request counts and latencies).
  2. Store metrics as time series with labels (also called tags), for example http_requests_total{service="checkout", region="us-east-1", status="500"}.
  3. Query metrics over a time range with aggregation (sum, average, percentiles, rate) and grouping by labels, to power dashboards.
  4. Define alert rules (for example “error rate above 5% for 5 minutes”) and notify on-call engineers via email, Slack, or PagerDuty.

Below the line (out of scope, and why):

  • Logs and distributed traces. Related “observability” signals, but different storage and query patterns.
  • Anomaly detection with machine learning. A layer on top of the query engine.
  • Building the dashboard UI itself. We provide the query API it uses.
  • Billing and multi-tenant quotas in depth. We mention per-tenant limits for cardinality.

2. Non-functional requirements

  1. Scale: 10 million active time series per large tenant cluster, 100 million series overall; ingest about 10 million data points per second.
  2. Ingest latency: a data point is queryable within 10 seconds of being sent.
  3. Query latency: p99 under 1 second for typical dashboard queries over the last 1-24 hours; under 5 seconds for 30-day queries.
  4. Alerting latency: an alert fires within 1 minute of the condition becoming true.
  5. Availability: 99.9% for queries, 99.99% for ingest and alerting. The monitoring system must be more reliable than what it monitors, and it must keep working during the outages it is meant to detect.
  6. Retention: raw 10-second resolution for 15 days, 1-minute for 90 days, 1-hour for 2 years.
  7. Durability and consistency: losing a few seconds of points during a failure is acceptable; losing hours is not. Eventual consistency is fine. CAP choice: availability over consistency (AP). A dashboard missing the last 10 seconds is better than a monitoring outage.

3. Back-of-the-envelope estimates

Assumption Number
Hosts 1 million
Metrics per host (series) 100
Active series 100 million
Scrape / push interval 10 seconds
Raw point size uncompressed 16 bytes (8 B timestamp + 8 B float)
Compressed point size (Gorilla) ~1.4 bytes
Dashboard query QPS ~5,000
Alert rules ~1 million, evaluated every 30-60 s 
Ingest
  points/s = 100e6 series / 10 s          = 10 million points/s
  raw bytes/s = 10e6 * 16 B               = 160 MB/s uncompressed
  compressed  = 10e6 * 1.4 B              = 14 MB/s

Raw storage (10 s resolution, 15 days)
  per day  = 10e6 * 86,400 * 1.4 B        = ~1.2 TB/day
  15 days                                 = ~18 TB (x3 replicas = ~54 TB)

1-minute rollups, 90 days (6x fewer points, but store min/max/sum/count)
  ~1.2 TB / 6 * 4 values * 90 days        = ~72 TB (x3)  -> object storage

1-hour rollups, 2 years
  ~1.2 TB / 360 * 4 * 730                 = ~10 TB

Alert evaluation
  1e6 rules / 30 s                        = ~33,000 rule queries/s

Two lessons. Compression gives roughly 10x savings and is essential. And alert evaluation is itself a large, steady query load, roughly as big as dashboards, so it needs its own capacity.

4. Core entities

  • Metric: a named measurement, like cpu_usage or http_requests_total. Has a type: counter (only goes up), gauge (goes up and down), or histogram (bucketed distribution for percentiles).
  • Labels (tags): key-value pairs that identify one series of a metric, such as host, service, region.
  • Time series: one metric plus one unique label set. Identified by a series id (a hash of the metric name and sorted labels).
  • Data point (sample): one (timestamp, value) for a series.
  • Alert rule: a query, a condition, a duration, and routing info.
  • Alert (incident): a firing instance of a rule for a specific label set, with state (pending, firing, resolved).
  • Notification channel: where alerts go (Slack, email, PagerDuty).
{
  "metric": "http_requests_total",
  "labels": {"service": "checkout", "region": "us-east-1", "status": "500"},
  "series_id": "a91f3c...",
  "samples": [[1762369200, 18342], [1762369210, 18410]]
}
# Alert rule (Prometheus-style)
- alert: CheckoutHighErrorRate
  expr: |
    sum(rate(http_requests_total{service="checkout",status=~"5.."}[5m]))
      / sum(rate(http_requests_total{service="checkout"}[5m])) > 0.05
  for: 5m
  labels: {severity: page, team: payments}
  annotations:
    summary: "Checkout 5xx rate above 5% for 5 minutes"

5. API design

POST /v1/metrics – push a batch of samples (used by agents).

// request (often protobuf + snappy compression in practice)
{
  "series": [
    {"metric": "cpu_usage", "labels": {"host": "web-17", "region": "us-east-1"},
     "samples": [[1762369200, 0.62], [1762369210, 0.65]]}
  ]
}
// response 202 Accepted
{"accepted": 2}

Status codes: 202, 400 (malformed), 401 (bad API key), 413 (batch too large), 429 (tenant over rate or cardinality limit). Auth: per-tenant API key.

GET /v1/query?q=<expr>&start=...&end=...&step=60s – range query for dashboards.

// response 200
{
  "result": [
    {"labels": {"service": "checkout"},
     "values": [[1762369200, 0.031], [1762369260, 0.029]]}
  ]
}

POST /v1/alert-rules – create a rule. Body is the rule in JSON or YAML. Response 201 {"rule_id": "r_44"}.

GET /v1/alerts?state=firing – list current alerts.

POST /v1/silences – mute alerts matching labels for a time window (for planned maintenance).

{"matchers": {"service": "checkout"}, "starts_at": "...", "ends_at": "...", "comment": "deploy"}

Auth on all read and config endpoints: user tokens with per-team permissions.
