How will metrics be collected from hosts and services?

  1. Each host runs an agent that reads system metrics (CPU, memory, disk) and receives application metrics from client libraries.
  2. The agent batches samples for 10 seconds, compresses them, and sends them to the ingest gateway (push), or exposes them on a /metrics HTTP endpoint for scrapers (pull). See the push vs pull deep dive.
  3. The ingest gateway authenticates the tenant, validates, enforces rate and cardinality limits, and writes the batch to Kafka partitioned by series id.
sequenceDiagram
    participant A as Host agent
    participant G as Ingest gateway
    participant K as Kafka
    participant W as TSDB write node
    A->>A: Batch samples for 10 seconds
    A->>G: Push compressed batch
    G->>G: Authenticate tenant and validate
    G->>G: Check rate and cardinality limits
    G->>K: Write batch by series id
    K-->>G: ack
    G-->>A: 200 accepted
    K->>W: Consume partition
    W->>W: Append to WAL and head block

How will metrics be stored?

  1. TSDB (time-series database) write nodes consume their Kafka partitions. Each series is owned by one node (plus replicas).
  2. A node appends incoming points to a write-ahead log (WAL, an append-only file on disk used to recover after a crash) and to an in-memory “head block” with compressed chunks per series.
  3. Every 2 hours, the head block is cut into an immutable block (chunks plus an index from labels to series) and uploaded to object storage like S3.
  4. Background compaction merges small blocks into bigger ones and builds downsampled versions.

How will users query metrics for dashboards?

  1. The dashboard sends a query such as sum by (region) (rate(http_requests_total[5m])) for the last 6 hours.
  2. The query engine parses it, uses the label index to find matching series ids, and fetches chunks from the write nodes (recent data) and from object storage (older data), choosing the coarsest resolution that fits the requested step.
  3. It decompresses, applies functions (rate, sum, percentile), groups by labels, and returns the result.

How will alerts be defined and delivered?

  1. A user creates a rule. Rules are stored in a config DB and assigned to rule evaluator shards by hashing rule id.
  2. Every 30 seconds, each evaluator runs its rules as queries against the query engine.
  3. If a condition is true, the alert becomes “pending.” If it stays true for the for duration, it becomes “firing” and is sent to Alertmanager.
  4. Alertmanager dedups, groups related alerts, applies silences, and routes notifications to the right channels.

7. Deep dives

Should agents push metrics, or should the system pull them?

The problem: there are two common collection models, and each has trade-offs at scale.

Aspect Pull (Prometheus scrape) Push (Datadog agent, StatsD, OTLP)
Who starts the connection Server scrapes /metrics on each target Agent sends to an endpoint
Health detection Failed scrape means the target is down (free “up” metric) Need heartbeats to tell “down” from “quiet”
Short-lived jobs Can be missed between scrapes Natural fit
Network / firewalls Server must reach every target Targets only need outbound access
Service discovery Server needs a list of targets (Kubernetes, Consul) Agents just know one address
Load control Server controls rate Clients can flood; need rate limits
Multi-tenant SaaS Hard (cannot reach customer networks) Standard

Recommended: support both, but normalize at the edge. For a SaaS product (Datadog-like), push from agents is the main path because we cannot reach into customer networks. Inside a company’s own Kubernetes clusters, pull with local Prometheus-style scrapers that then forward (“remote write”) to the central system works well. Either way, everything lands in the same Kafka topics.

# Local scraper forwarding upstream (Prometheus remote_write style)
scrape_configs:
  - job_name: checkout
    scrape_interval: 10s
    kubernetes_sd_configs: [{role: pod}]
remote_write:
  - url: https://ingest.metrics.example.com/api/v1/push
    queue_config: {max_samples_per_send: 5000, capacity: 100000}

How do we store billions of points cheaply? (time-series storage and Gorilla compression)

The problem: 10 million points per second at 16 bytes is 160 MB/s, about 14 TB per day before replication. A general database with one row per point adds even more overhead and cannot keep up.

Option How Pros Cons
Relational DB, one row per point INSERT (series, ts, value) Familiar Huge index overhead, slow at this rate
Wide-column store (Cassandra) Row key = series + day, columns = timestamps Scales writes Weak compression, no native rate/percentile
Purpose-built TSDB with per-series compressed chunks Append to in-memory chunks, compress with Gorilla, flush immutable blocks ~1.4 B/point, fast scans Must build or adopt (Prometheus TSDB, M3, VictoriaMetrics)

Recommended: a purpose-built TSDB with Gorilla compression. Gorilla is a compression scheme from Facebook built on two observations:

  1. Timestamps arrive at regular intervals, so the “delta of deltas” is usually zero. If points come every 10 s, deltas are 10, 10, 10, and the delta-of-delta is 0, which can be stored in a single bit.
  2. Consecutive values are often equal or close. XOR the new float with the previous one: if equal, the XOR is 0 (one bit). If close, the XOR has many leading and trailing zeros, so only the middle “meaningful bits” are stored.
def encode_timestamps(ts):
    out = [("raw", ts[0])]
    prev, prev_delta = ts[0], 0
    for t in ts[1:]:
        delta = t - prev
        dod = delta - prev_delta          # delta of delta
        if dod == 0:
            out.append(("bit", 0))        # 1 bit
        elif -63 <= dod <= 64:
            out.append(("7bit", dod))     # '10' + 7 bits
        else:
            out.append(("big", dod))      # longer encodings
        prev, prev_delta = t, delta
    return out

def encode_values(vals):
    prev = float_bits(vals[0])
    out = [("raw", prev)]
    for v in vals[1:]:
        x = float_bits(v) ^ prev
        if x == 0:
            out.append(("bit", 0))        # same value: 1 bit
        else:
            lz, tz = leading_zeros(x), trailing_zeros(x)
            out.append(("xor", lz, tz, x >> tz))   # only meaningful bits
        prev = float_bits(v)
    return out

In Facebook’s data this averaged about 1.37 bytes per point, a 12x saving. Each series keeps a chunk of ~120 points (20 minutes at 10 s) in memory; full chunks are sealed and written into 2-hour blocks.

 Block (2 hours, immutable, on S3)
 +-----------------------------------------------+
 | chunks/  series 1: [gorilla bytes][gorilla..] |
 |          series 2: [...]                      |
 | index    label -> postings (series ids)       |
 |          series id -> chunk offsets           |
 | meta.json {min_time, max_time, resolution}    |
 +-----------------------------------------------+

How do we keep years of data without huge cost? (downsampling and retention tiers)

The problem: nobody needs 10-second points from 18 months ago, and a 1-year dashboard over raw data would scan 3 million points per series.

Downsampling means replacing many fine points with fewer coarse ones. Averaging alone loses information (a short spike disappears), so store several aggregates per bucket: min, max, sum, and count. From these, you can rebuild average (sum/count), peaks, and totals.

Tier Resolution Retention Storage Used for
Hot 10 s raw 15 days Memory + local SSD + S3 Incidents, last-day dashboards
Warm 1 minute (min/max/sum/count) 90 days S3 Weekly and monthly trends
Cold 1 hour (min/max/sum/count) 2 years S3 (infrequent access) Capacity planning, year-over-year

Recommended: a compactor service that, after blocks age past each boundary, produces downsampled blocks and deletes the finer ones when their retention expires. The query engine picks the tier automatically from the query’s step: a step of 1 hour reads hourly blocks.

def downsample(points, bucket_s):
    out = {}
    for ts, v in points:
        b = ts - ts % bucket_s
        agg = out.setdefault(b, {"min": v, "max": v, "sum": 0.0, "count": 0})
        agg["min"] = min(agg["min"], v)
        agg["max"] = max(agg["max"], v)
        agg["sum"] += v
        agg["count"] += 1
    return out

def pick_resolution(step_s):
    if step_s >= 3600: return "1h"
    if step_s >= 60:   return "1m"
    return "raw"

Counters need care: when you downsample a counter, store the last value of each bucket too (and handle resets when a process restarts and the counter drops to zero), so rate() stays correct.

How do we stop cardinality from exploding?

The problem: cardinality is the number of unique series. Every unique label combination is a new series with its own memory, index entries, and chunks. A developer who adds user_id or request_id as a label turns one metric into millions of series. This is the most common way real monitoring systems fall over: memory spikes on write nodes, the index bloats, and queries slow to a crawl.

http_requests_total with labels service(50) x endpoint(200) x status(10)
  = 100,000 series      fine
... add user_id (10 million users)
  = 1,000,000,000,000 potential series   not fine
Defense How Trade-off
Per-tenant and per-metric series limits Ingest gateway tracks active series per tenant/metric (with HyperLogLog sketches for cheap counting) and rejects new series beyond the limit with 429 Some data dropped, but the system survives
Label allowlists / denylists Drop known-bad labels (user_id, request_id, raw URLs) at the agent or gateway Needs configuration
Relabeling / normalization Replace /users/12345 with /users/:id Loses detail, keeps usefulness
Usage visibility Show teams their top series counts Social pressure, not enforcement
Send high-cardinality data elsewhere Use logs or traces for per-request detail Different tool

Recommended: all of the above, with hard limits enforced at the ingest gateway as the safety net.

def admit(tenant, series_id, metric):
    key = f"card:{tenant}:{metric}"
    if not active_series.contains(key, series_id):        # bloom/hash set
        if active_series.estimate(key) >= limits.per_metric(tenant, metric):
            metrics.inc("rejected_new_series", tenant=tenant, metric=metric)
            return False                                    # 429 for this series
        active_series.add(key, series_id)
    return True

Existing series keep flowing even when the limit is hit; only new series are rejected. That way a cardinality bomb in one service does not blind every other dashboard.

How do we make dashboard queries fast?

The problem: a query like sum by (region) (rate(http_requests_total{service="checkout"}[5m])) over 24 hours might touch thousands of series and millions of points, and 5,000 of these run per second.

The query engine has three main steps:

  1. Series lookup: use the inverted index (label value to series ids) to find matching series. For service="checkout" and __name__="http_requests_total", intersect two sorted posting lists, like a search engine.
  2. Data fetch: read chunks for those series in the time range, from write nodes (last ~2 hours) and object storage (older), using the right resolution tier.
  3. Evaluation: decompress and compute functions, then aggregate.
Speed-up What it does
Query splitting by time Split a 7-day query into 24-hour pieces, run in parallel, cache each piece
Results cache Cache finished, older time slices (they never change); only recompute the latest slice
Recording rules Precompute expensive expressions (e.g. per-service error rate) every minute and store them as new series
Pushdown Do partial aggregation on storage nodes, send only partial sums to the query frontend
Limits Max series per query, max points, query timeouts, per-tenant concurrency 
# Recording rule: precompute once, read cheaply on every dashboard load
- record: service:http_error_ratio:rate5m
  expr: |
    sum by (service) (rate(http_requests_total{status=~"5.."}[5m]))
      / sum by (service) (rate(http_requests_total[5m]))
 Dashboard --> Query frontend --(split by day, cache hits)--> Queriers
                                                                |
                                     +--------------------------+------+
                                     v                                 v
                           Write nodes (last 2 h)            Store gateway (S3)
                           partial aggregates                partial aggregates

How are alert rules evaluated reliably, without duplicate pages, even when parts fail?

The problem: about a million rules run every 30-60 seconds. The evaluator must not miss alerts if a node dies, must not page twice if two evaluators run the same rule, must not flap (fire and resolve repeatedly), and must still work when the thing being monitored (maybe even part of our own infrastructure) is broken.

Option How Pros Cons
Query-based polling Evaluators run rule queries on a schedule against the query engine Uses the same query language, simple Load on query engine; latency = interval
Stream-based evaluation Evaluate simple threshold rules on the ingest stream (Flink) Sub-second, no query load Hard for complex expressions across many series
Hybrid Stream for simple thresholds on hot metrics, polling for the rest Best of both Two systems

Recommended: query-based polling as the main path, with rules sharded across evaluators by consistent hashing on rule id, and each shard run by two replicas for high availability. Duplicates from the two replicas are harmless because Alertmanager dedups.

The alert lifecycle with for duration prevents flapping on a single bad sample:

  condition false             condition true
 [inactive] ---------------> [pending] --- true for 5m ---> [firing]
     ^                           | false                       | false
     +---------------------------+                             v
     +------------------- resolve notification --------- [resolved]

Alertmanager handles the rest:

  • Dedup: alerts are identified by a fingerprint (hash of rule name plus label set). Two evaluator replicas sending the same alert produce one notification. Alertmanager itself runs as a small cluster that gossips its notification log, so a failover does not re-send.
  • Grouping: 300 hosts failing for the same reason become one page (“HighLatency, 300 instances, region=us-east-1”), using group_by labels and a short group_wait.
  • Inhibition: if “datacenter down” is firing, suppress the thousands of downstream alerts it causes.
  • Silences: users mute alerts for maintenance.
  • Repeat interval: re-notify an unacknowledged firing alert every few hours, not every 30 seconds.
route:
  group_by: [alertname, service, region]
  group_wait: 30s
  group_interval: 5m
  repeat_interval: 4h
  receiver: default-slack
  routes:
    - matchers: [severity="page"]
      receiver: pagerduty-oncall
inhibit_rules:
  - source_matchers: [alertname="RegionDown"]
    target_matchers: [severity="page"]
    equal: [region]

Failure handling for alerting itself:

  • Missing data: a rule like up == 0 or “no data for 10 minutes” (absent()) detects silent failures, where a dead host stops sending anything.
  • Meta-monitoring: a separate, minimal monitoring stack (in another region or provider) watches the main one, and a “dead man’s switch” alert that always fires must keep arriving at PagerDuty; if it stops, PagerDuty pages us because the alert pipeline itself is broken.
  • Isolation: the alerting path has reserved query capacity so a dashboard storm during an incident cannot starve alert evaluation.

Failure handling for ingest and storage, so alerts have data to evaluate:

  • Ingest gateway dies: stateless; agents retry to another instance. Agents buffer points locally (for a few minutes) when the gateway is unreachable.
  • Kafka buffers: if write nodes fall behind or restart, Kafka holds the data (retain 24 hours) and nodes catch up.
  • Write node dies: each series is replicated to 3 nodes (replication factor 3). Queries read from any healthy replica and dedup samples by timestamp. A replacement node replays its WAL or its Kafka partitions to rebuild the head block.
  • Object storage outage: recent data is still served from write nodes; older queries fail or return partial results with a warning.
  • Region outage: run independent monitoring stacks per region; global views federate across them.

9. Common mistakes and interviewer follow-ups

  • Storing each point as a row in a general-purpose database. It cannot keep up with 10 million writes per second and costs 10x more. Say: purpose-built TSDB with per-series Gorilla-compressed chunks.
  • Ignoring cardinality. One bad label can take down the whole cluster. Say: per-tenant and per-metric series limits at ingest, label denylists, and relabeling.
  • Downsampling with averages only. Spikes vanish and alerts on old data mislead. Say: keep min, max, sum, and count per bucket.
  • Paging on a single sample. Noise and flapping burn out on-call. Say: for duration, grouping, inhibition, and repeat intervals.
  • Running alerting on the same capacity as dashboards. An incident creates a dashboard stampede that delays alerts. Say: reserved capacity or separate query paths for rule evaluation.
  • Forgetting “who monitors the monitor.” Say: meta-monitoring in another region plus a dead man’s switch.
  • Not handling missing data. A dead host sends nothing, so threshold rules never fire. Say: up == 0 and absent() style rules.
  • Follow-up: “Push or pull?” Answer: pull is great inside your own network for health detection and control; push is necessary for SaaS and short-lived jobs; support both and converge at the gateway.

10. One-page cheat sheet

Topic Key point
Scale 100M series, 10s interval, 10M points/s, ~33k alert queries/s
Latency Queryable in 10 s, dashboards p99 < 1 s, alerts within 1 min
CAP AP: prefer availability; losing seconds OK, hours not OK
Collection Push for SaaS and short jobs, pull for in-cluster; converge at gateway
Buffer Kafka partitioned by series id
Storage WAL + in-memory head, 2 h immutable blocks to S3
Compression Gorilla: delta-of-delta timestamps, XOR floats, ~1.4 B/point
Retention Raw 15 d, 1 min 90 d, 1 h 2 y; store min/max/sum/count
Cardinality Per-tenant/metric series limits, label denylist, relabel
Queries Label inverted index, split by time, results cache, recording rules
Alerting Sharded evaluators x2, pending -> firing with for, Alertmanager dedup/group/inhibit
Reliability RF=3 write nodes, agent buffering, meta-monitoring, dead man’s switch

30. Online Chess (Hard)

An online chess platform like Chess.com or Lichess lets two players anywhere in the world find an opponent of similar skill, play a game in real time with a ticking clock, and review the game afterward. Moves must show up on the other player’s screen almost instantly, the server must be the referee (no illegal moves, no cheating the clock), and a dropped connection must not lose the game. The interviewer is really testing real-time communication with WebSockets, keeping each game’s state on one authoritative server, rating-based matchmaking, careful time handling, durable game storage, and at least an outline of cheat detection.

1. Functional requirements

Core (must have):

  1. Players can request a game with a time control (for example 5+3: 5 minutes each plus 3 seconds added per move) and get matched with an opponent of similar rating.
  2. Players can make moves in real time; the opponent sees each move within a fraction of a second.
  3. The server validates every move and enforces chess rules, including check, checkmate, stalemate, and draws.
  4. The server runs each player’s clock; a player who runs out of time loses.
  5. Players can resign, offer a draw, and reconnect to an in-progress game after a disconnect.
  6. Finished games are stored and can be replayed move by move; ratings are updated after each game.

Below the line (out of scope, and why):

  • Spectators and live broadcast of top games. Same fan-out idea as live comments; we mention it briefly.
  • Chat between players. A small add-on.
  • Puzzles, lessons, and engine analysis UI. Separate products.
  • Tournaments. Built on matchmaking plus scheduling.

2. Non-functional requirements

  1. Move latency: p99 under 200 ms from one player’s move to the opponent’s screen within the same region; under 300 ms cross-continent.
  2. Correctness: the server is authoritative. No illegal move is ever accepted, and clocks are enforced fairly regardless of client tricks.
  3. Consistency: strong consistency within a game (both players see the same sequence of moves, in the same order). Each game has a single writer, its game server. CAP choice: for a single game we choose consistency; if the game server is unreachable, the game pauses or recovers rather than letting two servers diverge. The rest of the platform (profiles, history) can be eventually consistent and highly available.
  4. Durability: an in-progress game survives a game server crash with no lost moves.
  5. Matchmaking: most players matched within 5 seconds at popular ratings and time controls.
  6. Scale: 10 million daily active users, 1 million concurrent games at peak.
  7. Availability: 99.95% for starting and playing games.

3. Back-of-the-envelope estimates

Assumption Number
Daily active users 10 million
Games per user per day 5
Peak concurrent games 1 million (2 million connected players)
Average moves per game 80 half-moves (40 each)
Average game length 10 minutes
Move message size ~100 bytes
Stored game size (PGN text + metadata) ~2 KB 
Games per day
  10e6 users * 5 / 2 players          = 25 million games/day

Moves
  Peak moves/s = 1e6 games * 80 / 600 s = ~133,000 moves/s
  Each move: in from mover + out to opponent (+ spectators)
  Messages/s ~ 2 * 133k                 = ~270,000 msgs/s

WebSocket connections
  2 million concurrent; at ~50k connections per server = ~40 servers
  (plan ~100 for headroom and per-region spread)

Storage
  25e6 games * 2 KB                     = 50 GB/day
  per year                              = ~18 TB/year

Bandwidth
  270k msgs/s * 100 B                   = ~27 MB/s  (small)

The data volume is small. The hard parts are latency, keeping state for each game in exactly one place, and handling time fairly.

4. Core entities

  • Player: a user. Fields: player_id, username, ratings per time control (bullet, blitz, rapid), rating deviation.
  • Game: one match. Fields: game_id, white_id, black_id, time_control, status (active, finished), result, termination reason, created_at.
  • Move: one half-move. Fields: game_id, ply (move number in half-moves), uci (like e2e4), san (like e4), clock_ms_after, server_ts.
  • Clock state: remaining time for each side plus whose turn and when that turn started.
  • Match request (seek): a player waiting for an opponent. Fields: player_id, rating, time_control, enqueued_at.
  • Rating history: rating before and after each game.
CREATE TABLE games (
  game_id       UUID PRIMARY KEY,
  white_id      BIGINT NOT NULL,
  black_id      BIGINT NOT NULL,
  time_control  TEXT NOT NULL,        -- '300+3'
  status        TEXT NOT NULL,        -- 'active', 'finished'
  result        TEXT,                 -- '1-0', '0-1', '1/2-1/2'
  termination   TEXT,                 -- 'checkmate', 'timeout', 'resign', ...
  pgn           TEXT,                 -- full move list when finished
  started_at    TIMESTAMPTZ,
  ended_at      TIMESTAMPTZ
);

CREATE TABLE moves (
  game_id        UUID,
  ply            INT,
  uci            TEXT,
  clock_ms_after INT,
  server_ts      TIMESTAMPTZ,
  PRIMARY KEY (game_id, ply)
);
// In-memory game state on the game server
{
  "game_id": "g_81f2",
  "fen": "rnbqkbnr/pppp1ppp/8/4p3/4P3/8/PPPP1PPP/RNBQKBNR w KQkq e6 0 2",
  "ply": 2,
  "turn": "white",
  "clock_ms": {"white": 297400, "black": 298900},
  "turn_started_at": 1762369212345,
  "increment_ms": 3000
}

FEN (Forsyth-Edwards Notation) is a one-line text format that fully describes a chess position.

5. API design

REST for setup and history, WebSocket for live play.

POST /v1/matchmaking/seeks – ask to be matched.

// request
{"time_control": "300+3", "rated": true}
// response 202
{"seek_id": "s_19", "status": "searching"}

DELETE /v1/matchmaking/seeks/{seek_id} – cancel search. Response 204.

GET /v1/games/{game_id} – game metadata and full move list (for replay or reconnect). Response 200 with game object.

GET /v1/players/{player_id}/games?cursor=... – game history.

WS /v1/play – persistent connection. Messages are JSON:

// server -> client: match found
{"type": "game_start", "game_id": "g_81f2", "color": "white",
 "opponent": {"id": 77, "rating": 1512}, "time_control": "300+3",
 "game_server": "gs-use1-12"}

// client -> server: make a move
{"type": "move", "game_id": "g_81f2", "ply": 3, "uci": "g1f3", "client_ts": 1762369215000}

// server -> both clients: move accepted
{"type": "move_ack", "game_id": "g_81f2", "ply": 3, "uci": "g1f3",
 "clock_ms": {"white": 296100, "black": 298900}}

// server -> mover: rejected
{"type": "move_rejected", "ply": 3, "reason": "illegal_move"}

// other client messages
{"type": "resign", "game_id": "g_81f2"}
{"type": "offer_draw", "game_id": "g_81f2"}
{"type": "resync", "game_id": "g_81f2", "last_ply": 2}

// server -> both: game over
{"type": "game_over", "result": "1-0", "termination": "timeout",
 "rating_change": {"white": 8, "black": -8}}

Auth: session token on REST calls and on the WebSocket handshake. Every WebSocket message is checked against the player’s identity (you can only move your own pieces in your own game). Errors on REST use 400, 401, 404, 409 (already in a game), 429.

How will players find an opponent?

  1. The player calls POST /v1/matchmaking/seeks with a time control.
  2. The API service adds the seek to the Matchmaker’s pool for that time control, keyed by rating.
  3. The Matchmaker repeatedly pairs the oldest waiting player with the closest rating within an allowed range (the range widens the longer they wait).
  4. When a pair is found, it picks a game server (the least-loaded in the players’ region), creates the game there, registers game_id -> game server, and writes a games row with status active.
  5. It notifies both players over their WebSockets with a game_start message.
sequenceDiagram
    participant P as Player
    participant A as API service
    participant M as Matchmaker
    participant G as Game server
    participant D as Games DB
    P->>A: POST seeks with time control
    A->>M: Add seek to pool by rating
    A-->>P: 202 searching
    M->>M: Pair closest rating within range
    M->>G: Create game on least loaded server
    G-->>M: game created
    M->>D: Insert game row status active
    M-->>P: game start over WebSocket

How will players make moves and see the opponent’s moves?

  1. The client sends {"type": "move", ...} over its WebSocket.
  2. The gateway looks up which game server owns the game (cached registry) and forwards the message.
  3. The game server, which holds the game state in memory, checks it is the player’s turn, validates the move with a chess rules library, updates the clocks, and appends the move to a durable move log.
  4. It sends move_ack to both players, through their gateways.
  5. The opponent’s client draws the move and starts the opponent’s clock display.

How does the server enforce rules and the clock?

The game server owns the board (FEN) and both clocks. Clients only send intentions (“I move g1f3”). The server decides if it is legal and how much time was used. It also sets a timer for the current player’s remaining time; if the timer fires before a move arrives, the server ends the game on time.

How will players resign, draw, reconnect, and replay games?

  1. Resign and draw offers are WebSocket messages handled by the same game server, which changes game state and broadcasts game_over or a draw offer.
  2. On reconnect, the client opens a new WebSocket and sends resync with the last ply it knows; the server replies with any missed moves and current clocks.
  3. When a game ends, the game server writes the final PGN (Portable Game Notation, the standard text format for a chess game’s moves) and result to the Games DB, and emits a game_finished event for rating updates and anti-cheat.
  4. Replay is GET /v1/games/{id}, which returns the move list; the client steps through it locally.

7. Deep dives

How do we deliver moves in real time, and why does each game live on one server?

The problem: two players may be connected to different gateway machines. Moves must reach the opponent in well under 200 ms, and the game state must be updated by exactly one process to avoid two servers disagreeing about the board.

Transport How it works Pros Cons
HTTP polling Client asks “any new move?” every second Simple Slow and wasteful
Long polling Request stays open until a move arrives Works everywhere Reconnect per message, overhead
Server-Sent Events Server streams to client; client posts moves Simple, HTTP One direction; moves still need POSTs
WebSocket Full-duplex persistent connection Lowest latency, both directions Stateful connections to manage

Recommended: WebSockets. For state ownership:

Ownership model How Pros Cons
Stateless servers, state in Redis Any server loads state, updates with a transaction Easy scaling Extra round trip per move, race conditions between servers
Sticky game server (game affinity) Each game is owned by one game server; all messages for it are routed there In-memory speed, single writer, simple ordering Need routing and failover

Recommended: game affinity. Each game is assigned to one game server, which keeps the state in memory and is the only writer. Gateways terminate WebSockets (so game servers do not hold millions of sockets) and route messages by game_id using a registry.

 White --WS--> Gateway A --+                 +--> Gateway B --WS--> Black
                           |   gRPC stream   |
                           +--> Game server <+
                                gs-use1-12
                                (owns g_81f2)

Routing: the registry maps game_id -> game_server in Redis (or etcd), cached on gateways. Using consistent hashing of game_id over game servers is an alternative, but explicit assignment lets the matchmaker pick the least loaded server and keep both players’ region in mind.

To cut latency further, put both players’ game on a server in a region near both of them (for cross-continent games, pick the midpoint region or the one with lower combined round-trip time). A spectator fan-out, if added, goes through a pub/sub channel per game so the game server sends each move once.

How does the server validate moves and stay authoritative?

The problem: a client can be modified to send illegal moves, move twice, or claim a different clock time. If the client is trusted, cheating is trivial.

Option Who validates Risk
Client-side only Client Anyone can send any move
Both, server trusts client clocks Server validates rules, client reports time Clock manipulation
Server-authoritative Server validates rules and measures time Safe; client validation is only for UX

Recommended: server-authoritative. Clients validate locally only to give instant feedback and to draw legal-move hints. The server holds the true board and rejects anything wrong.

import chess   # python-chess rules library

class Game:
    def __init__(self, gid, white, black, base_ms, inc_ms):
        self.board = chess.Board()
        self.players = {chess.WHITE: white, chess.BLACK: black}
        self.clock = {chess.WHITE: base_ms, chess.BLACK: base_ms}
        self.inc = inc_ms
        self.turn_started = now_ms()
        self.ply = 0

    def on_move(self, player_id, ply, uci):
        color = self.board.turn
        if self.players[color] != player_id:
            return reject("not_your_turn")
        if ply != self.ply + 1:
            return reject("stale_or_duplicate")    # idempotency on retries
        move = chess.Move.from_uci(uci)
        if move not in self.board.legal_moves:
            return reject("illegal_move")

        elapsed = now_ms() - self.turn_started
        self.clock[color] -= elapsed
        if self.clock[color] <= 0:
            return self.finish(winner=not color, reason="timeout")
        self.clock[color] += self.inc

        move_log.append(self.gid, self.ply + 1, uci, self.clock[color])  # durable first
        self.board.push(move)
        self.ply += 1
        self.turn_started = now_ms()
        broadcast(self.gid, {"type": "move_ack", "ply": self.ply, "uci": uci,
                             "clock_ms": self.clock_view()})
        if self.board.is_game_over(claim_draw=True):
            self.finish_from_board()

The ply number makes moves idempotent: if a client resends a move after a timeout, the server sees the same ply and either returns the existing ack or rejects it as stale, never applying it twice.

How do we match players by rating quickly?

The problem: players should face opponents near their skill. If we only accept exact matches, people wait forever; if we accept anyone, games are lopsided. We also need to handle many time controls and regions.

Elo is a rating system where each player has a number (around 1200 for beginners, 2800 for world champions). After each game, points move from the loser to the winner, more points if the result was a surprise. Lichess uses Glicko-2, a refinement that also tracks how certain the rating is.

Option How Pros Cons
Single FIFO queue per time control Pair the first two Fastest Ignores skill
Rating buckets (e.g. 100-point wide) Queue per bucket; widen search to neighbor buckets over time Simple, fast lookups Edge effects at bucket borders
Sorted set by rating with expanding window Find nearest rating within +/- R, R grows with wait time Precise, flexible Needs a single owner per pool to avoid double matching

Recommended: a Redis sorted set per (time control, region) with score = rating, and an expanding search window. A single matchmaker worker owns each pool (sharded by time control and region), so two workers never match the same player. Every 100-200 ms it scans waiting players oldest first.

def window(wait_s):
    return min(50 + 25 * wait_s, 400)        # +/-50 at start, up to +/-400

def match_loop(pool):                        # pool = "seeks:300+3:use1"
    for player_id, rating, enq_ts in oldest_first(pool):
        r = window(now() - enq_ts)
        cands = redis.zrangebyscore(pool, rating - r, rating + r)
        cands = [c for c in cands if c != player_id and not recently_played(player_id, c)]
        if not cands:
            continue
        opp = min(cands, key=lambda c: abs(rating_of(c) - rating))
        # atomically remove both; if either is gone, someone else matched them
        if redis.zrem(pool, player_id, opp) == 2:
            create_game(player_id, opp)

The Elo update after a game:

def elo_update(ra, rb, score_a, k=20):
    expected_a = 1 / (1 + 10 ** ((rb - ra) / 400))
    new_a = ra + k * (score_a - expected_a)      # score_a: 1 win, 0.5 draw, 0 loss
    new_b = rb + k * ((1 - score_a) - (1 - expected_a))
    return round(new_a), round(new_b)

Rating updates happen asynchronously from the game_finished event, in a transaction that also writes the rating history row.

How do we handle clocks, lag, and disconnects fairly?

The problem: chess clocks are part of the rules. Network lag means the time between “player clicked” and “server received” is not the player’s thinking time, and players on slow connections feel cheated. Players also lose connections mid-game.

Clock approach How Pros Cons
Trust client clocks Client reports time used Fair for lag Easy to cheat
Server measures time only Time from previous ack sent to move received Cheat-proof Penalizes high-latency players
Server time with lag compensation Server time minus estimated one-way latency, capped Fair and safe Slightly more logic

Recommended: the server is the clock, with capped lag compensation. Each connection measures round-trip time with periodic pings. When a move arrives, the server credits back an estimate of the network delay (for example half the median RTT), up to a cap such as 500 ms per move, so lag cannot be abused for free time. Lichess uses a similar idea.

def charged_time(elapsed_ms, conn):
    lag = min(conn.median_rtt_ms / 2, 500)
    return max(elapsed_ms - lag, 0)

Clients display a local countdown between server updates, but every move_ack carries the server’s authoritative clock values, so displays snap back to the truth.

Timeouts: the game server keeps a timer per game set to the moving side’s remaining time. When it fires, the server ends the game. Many game timers on one server are stored in a hashed timer wheel or a min-heap keyed by deadline, so a million games across a fleet costs little.

Disconnects:

  1. When a player’s WebSocket drops, the gateway tells the game server. The player’s clock keeps running (otherwise disconnecting would be a way to pause).
  2. The opponent sees “opponent disconnected” and, after a grace period (for example 30 seconds or when the clock runs out, whichever is first), can claim victory or a draw.
  3. The client reconnects automatically with exponential backoff, sends resync with its last ply, and gets missing moves plus current clocks.
 t=0   Black disconnects        clocks keep running for Black
 t=3s  Black reconnects -> resync(last_ply=41) -> server sends ply 42, clocks
 or
 t=30s still gone  -> White offered "claim win"
 Black clock hits 0 -> server ends game: 1-0 timeout

How do we persist games and survive a game server crash?

The problem: games live in memory on one server. If that server dies mid-game, we must not lose moves or let the game silently vanish. Finished games must be stored for replay and history.

Option How Pros Cons
Write only at game end Store PGN when finished Cheapest Crash loses the whole game
Write every move to the DB synchronously INSERT per move before ack Durable ~133k writes/s on the DB, adds latency
Append each move to a replicated log, write DB at end Redis Stream with replication (or Kafka) per move; final PGN to DB Durable and fast; log replays state Needs a recovery process

Recommended: append every accepted move to a durable, replicated move log before acking it (Redis Streams with AOF and replicas, or Kafka keyed by game_id). The log is the in-game source of truth. When the game ends, write the final PGN and result to the Games DB, and keep the per-move table (with clock times) for analysis.

Recovery when a game server dies:

  1. A health checker notices the server is gone (missed heartbeats in the registry).
  2. Its games are reassigned to other game servers (the registry entries are updated with a fencing token, a number that increases on each reassignment so a zombie old server’s writes are rejected).
  3. The new owner rebuilds each game by replaying its moves from the log on top of the start position, restores clocks from the last logged clock values (minus time elapsed since, or paused for the outage, by policy), and tells gateways to route there.
  4. Clients reconnect and resync. Players see a short pause of a few seconds at most.
 gs-12 dies
    |
 registry: g_81f2 -> gs-12 (epoch 7)   ==>   g_81f2 -> gs-19 (epoch 8)
    |
 gs-19: replay move log g_81f2 [ply 1..41] -> board + clocks restored
    |
 gateways route g_81f2 -> gs-19; clients resync

Storage for history: games by player are read via an index (player_id, ended_at DESC). At 18 TB per year, a sharded Postgres or Cassandra keyed by game_id with a secondary table keyed by player works; old games can move to cheaper storage since they are rarely opened.

How would we detect cheating?

The problem: the most common cheat is using a chess engine during a game. Moves are legal, so the rules engine cannot catch it. Server authority stops illegal moves and clock tricks, but not engine assistance.

Signal What it measures Notes
Engine match rate How often the player’s move equals the engine’s top choice Strong players also match often; compare against rating peers
Average centipawn loss (ACPL) How much worse each move is than the best move, in hundredths of a pawn Very low ACPL sustained over many games is suspicious
Move-time patterns Time per move vs position complexity Engines users often take the same time on easy and hard moves
Client signals Tab switches, focus loss, paste events Weak signals, easy to fake, useful in combination
Rating jumps Sudden large improvements Triggers deeper review

Recommended outline:

  1. After each game, publish game_finished to Kafka.
  2. A cheap first pass flags games with unusual stats for the player’s rating (for example, top-engine match rate far above peers, or ACPL far below).
  3. Flagged games go to an engine analysis queue: worker machines run Stockfish on each position at fixed depth and compute ACPL and match rates.
  4. A model combines per-game and per-player history into a suspicion score. High scores go to human moderators; confirmed cheaters are banned and their opponents’ ratings are refunded.
 game_finished --> Kafka --> quick stats filter --(flag ~2%)--> analysis queue
                                                                   |
                                                    Stockfish workers (GPU/CPU)
                                                                   |
                                                    per-player model -> score
                                                                   |
                                               moderator review / auto-action

Analyzing every game with a deep engine is expensive (25 million games per day), which is why the cheap filter comes first.

9. Common mistakes and interviewer follow-ups

  • Trusting the client for move legality or time. Anyone can modify a client. Say: server-authoritative rules and clocks; client checks are only for UX.
  • Letting any server update any game from a shared store. Races and double-applied moves follow. Say: one owner game server per game, routed by game_id, with ply numbers for idempotency.
  • Pausing the clock on disconnect. Players will disconnect to think. Say: the clock keeps running; grace period, then the opponent can claim the win.
  • Ignoring lag. High-latency players lose on time unfairly. Say: server clock with capped lag compensation based on measured RTT.
  • Persisting only at game end. A server crash loses the game. Say: append each move to a replicated log before acking, rebuild by replay with fencing on failover.
  • Matchmaking with two workers on the same pool. They can pair one player twice. Say: one owner per pool, atomic removal of both players.
  • Analyzing every game with a deep engine. It costs too much. Say: cheap statistical filter first, deep analysis only for flagged games.
  • Follow-up: “How would you add spectators?” Answer: a pub/sub channel per game (Redis pub/sub or a fan-out service); the game server publishes each move once, and gateways push to spectators, with an optional delay to stop live cheating help.

Transport WebSockets via gateways; REST for setup and history

Authority Server validates with a rules library and owns clocks
Idempotency Ply number on every move message
Clocks Server time, capped lag credit (~RTT/2, max 500 ms), timer wheel
Disconnects Clock keeps running, auto reconnect + resync, claim after grace
Matchmaking Redis ZSET per time control and region, window grows with wait
Ratings Elo or Glicko-2, async on game_finished

31. ChatGPT (Hard)

ChatGPT is a chat product on top of a large language model (LLM, a neural network that predicts the next piece of text, one token at a time). A user types a message, and the reply appears word by word as the model generates it. Conversations are saved so users can come back, and they can be long. Behind the scenes, every reply needs expensive GPU time. The interviewer is really testing whether you can design around a slow, costly, stateful backend: streaming tokens to the client, storing conversations and fitting them into a limited context window, serving models efficiently on GPUs with batching and KV caches, enforcing rate limits and quotas, and routing between models with failover when capacity runs out.

1. Functional requirements

Core (must have):

  1. Users can start a conversation and send a message; the assistant’s reply streams back token by token.
  2. Users can continue a conversation; the model sees earlier turns as context.
  3. Users can list, open, rename, and delete past conversations.
  4. Users can pick a model (for example a fast small model or a slower, smarter large model), subject to their plan.
  5. Users can stop a reply mid-generation and regenerate a reply.

Below the line (out of scope, and why):

  • Training and fine-tuning models. A completely separate offline system.
  • Tool use, browsing, file uploads, and image generation. Each adds a subsystem; the core streaming and serving path is the same.
  • Safety classifiers in depth. We show where moderation plugs in.
  • Voice mode. Different transport, same backend.

2. Non-functional requirements

  1. Time to first token (TTFT): p50 under 500 ms and p99 under 2 seconds for the default model. This is what makes the product feel fast.
  2. Streaming speed: at least 30 tokens per second per response for the default model (faster than people read).
  3. Scale: 100 million daily active users, ~1 billion messages per day, peak ~30,000 new messages per second.
  4. Availability: 99.9% for chat. When GPU capacity is short, degrade gracefully (queue, route to a smaller model, or return a clear “at capacity” message) instead of failing silently.
  5. Durability: never lose a saved message; conversations persist indefinitely until the user deletes them.
  6. Consistency: a user’s own conversation must read their latest messages (read-your-writes). Conversation lists can be eventually consistent across devices within seconds. CAP choice: availability for the chat path, with per-conversation ordering guaranteed by a single writer.
  7. Cost efficiency: maximize GPU utilization (tokens per second per GPU), since GPUs dominate cost.
  8. Fairness: per-user rate limits and plan quotas so heavy users cannot starve others.

3. Back-of-the-envelope estimates

Assumption Number
Daily active users 100 million
Messages per user per day 10
Average prompt context sent to the model 2,000 tokens (history + new message)
Average reply length 400 tokens
Peak to average ratio 2.5x
Stored text per message ~2 KB (user + assistant text, metadata)
Decode throughput per GPU (with batching, mid-size model) ~2,000 output tokens/s
Prefill throughput per GPU ~20,000 input tokens/s 
Messages
  1e8 users * 10            = 1e9 messages/day
  avg msgs/s = 1e9 / 86,400 = ~11,600/s
  peak                      = ~30,000/s

Output tokens (decode)
  avg = 11,600 * 400        = ~4.6 million tokens/s
  peak                      = ~12 million tokens/s
  GPUs for decode at peak   = 12e6 / 2,000 = ~6,000 GPUs

Input tokens (prefill)
  peak = 30,000 * 2,000     = 60 million tokens/s
  GPUs for prefill          = 60e6 / 20,000 = ~3,000 GPUs
  (prefix caching can cut this a lot for long conversations)

Total: roughly 10,000 GPUs at peak for the default model alone.

Concurrent streams
  each reply ~400 tokens at 40 tok/s = ~10 s
  open streams at peak = 30,000/s * 10 s = ~300,000 SSE connections

Storage
  1e9 * 2 KB                = 2 TB/day
  per year                  = ~730 TB/year

The math shows two things. GPUs, not databases, are the expensive and scarce resource, so serving efficiency drives the design. And there are hundreds of thousands of long-lived streaming connections at any moment.

4. Core entities

  • User: account, plan (free, plus, enterprise), quotas. Fields: user_id, plan, created_at.
  • Conversation: a chat thread. Fields: conversation_id, user_id, title, model, created_at, updated_at, summary (optional).
  • Message: one turn. Fields: message_id, conversation_id, parent_id, role (user, assistant, system), content, model, token_count, status (streaming, complete, stopped, failed), created_at.
  • Model: a deployable LLM. Fields: model_id, context_window (max tokens), cost tier, endpoints.
  • Generation request: one inference job. Fields: request_id, message_id, model_id, prompt_tokens, max_tokens, priority.
  • Usage record: tokens used per user per window, for quotas and billing.

parent_id lets messages form a tree, so “regenerate” or “edit and resend” creates a sibling branch rather than overwriting history.

CREATE TABLE conversations (
  conversation_id UUID PRIMARY KEY,
  user_id         BIGINT NOT NULL,
  title           TEXT,
  model_id        TEXT,
  summary         TEXT,              -- rolling summary of old turns
  summary_upto    UUID,              -- last message covered by summary
  updated_at      TIMESTAMPTZ NOT NULL
);
CREATE INDEX ON conversations (user_id, updated_at DESC);

CREATE TABLE messages (
  conversation_id UUID,
  message_id      UUID,              -- time-ordered (UUIDv7)
  parent_id       UUID,
  role            TEXT,
  content         TEXT,
  token_count     INT,
  status          TEXT,
  created_at      TIMESTAMPTZ,
  PRIMARY KEY (conversation_id, message_id)
);

5. API design

POST /v1/conversations – create a conversation. Response 201 {"conversation_id": "c_42"}.

POST /v1/conversations/{id}/messages – send a message and stream the reply. The response is text/event-stream (Server-Sent Events).

// request
{"content": "Explain KV caching in one paragraph", "model": "gpt-default",
 "parent_id": "m_17", "client_message_id": "8c1f..."}
// response: 200, Content-Type: text/event-stream
event: message_start
data: {"message_id":"m_19","model":"gpt-default"}

event: delta
data: {"text":"A KV cache"}

event: delta
data: {"text":" stores the attention"}

event: message_end
data: {"finish_reason":"stop","usage":{"prompt_tokens":2140,"completion_tokens":388}}

POST /v1/messages/{message_id}/stop – stop generation. Response 202.

POST /v1/messages/{message_id}/regenerate – new sibling reply, streamed like above.

GET /v1/conversations?cursor=... – list conversations (title, updated_at), newest first.

GET /v1/conversations/{id} – full conversation with messages (current branch).

PATCH /v1/conversations/{id} – rename. DELETE /v1/conversations/{id} – delete (soft delete, purge later).

Status codes: 200, 201, 202, 400, 401, 404, 409 (duplicate client_message_id), 429 (rate limit or quota, with Retry-After), 503 (model at capacity). Auth: bearer session token; every call checks the conversation belongs to the user. client_message_id is an idempotency key so a retried send does not create a duplicate turn.

How will users send a message and see the reply stream in?

  1. The client calls POST /v1/conversations/{id}/messages and keeps the connection open for SSE.
  2. The gateway authenticates and the rate limiter checks request and token quotas.
  3. The Chat Service saves the user message (status complete), creates an assistant message row with status streaming, and builds the prompt: system instructions, relevant history, and the new message (see the context deep dive).
  4. It runs a quick moderation check on the input.
  5. It asks the Model Router for a target, which picks a GPU pool for the chosen model.
  6. The inference server streams tokens back over gRPC. The Chat Service forwards each chunk to the client as an SSE delta event and appends it to a buffer.
  7. When generation finishes, it writes the full assistant text, token counts, and status complete, and records usage.
sequenceDiagram
    participant C as Client
    participant G as Gateway
    participant S as Chat service
    participant D as Conversation store
    participant R as Model router
    participant I as Inference server
    C->>G: POST message and open SSE
    G->>G: Auth and check token quota
    G->>S: Forward message
    S->>D: Save user message and streaming reply row
    S->>S: Build prompt and run moderation
    S->>R: Pick GPU pool for model
    R-->>S: Target cluster
    S->>I: Generate with prompt
    loop each token chunk
        I-->>S: Token chunk
        S-->>C: SSE delta event
    end
    S->>D: Save full reply status complete
    S-->>C: SSE message end with usage

How will users continue a conversation?

  1. The client sends the next message with parent_id set to the last assistant message.
  2. The Chat Service loads the conversation branch (the chain of parent links) from the store or a cache of recent conversations.
  3. It assembles context within the model’s window (recent turns verbatim, older turns summarized) and proceeds as above.

How will users browse and manage past conversations?

  1. GET /v1/conversations reads the (user_id, updated_at DESC) index with a cursor.
  2. Titles are generated by a cheap small model after the first exchange, asynchronously.
  3. Rename updates one row. Delete marks the conversation deleted; a background job purges messages later.

How will users choose a model and stop or regenerate?

  1. The selected model id travels with each message. The router checks the user’s plan allows it.
  2. Stop sends POST /stop; the Chat Service cancels the inference request (freeing GPU capacity immediately), saves what was generated with status stopped, and ends the SSE stream.
  3. Regenerate creates a new assistant message with the same parent and streams a fresh reply.

7. Deep dives

How do we stream tokens to the client reliably?

The problem: replies take 5 to 30 seconds to generate. Making the user wait for the whole thing feels broken. We need to push small chunks as they are produced, across proxies and mobile networks, to ~300,000 concurrent streams.

Option Direction Pros Cons
Polling Client pulls Simple Laggy, wasteful
WebSocket Both ways Low latency, full duplex Stateful, more infra, needs its own auth and reconnect logic
Server-Sent Events (SSE) Server to client over HTTP Plain HTTP, works with standard proxies and load balancers, built-in event framing One direction (fine: the user only sends once per turn)

Recommended: SSE. The request is a normal HTTP POST, and the response is a long-lived text/event-stream body. It fits the pattern exactly: one request, many small server pushes.

Details that matter at scale:

  • Disable proxy buffering (for example X-Accel-Buffering: no on Nginx) or tokens arrive in bursts.
  • Send heartbeat comments (: ping) every 15 seconds so idle connections are not killed by load balancers during a slow first token.
  • Chunk coalescing: send every token or every ~20-50 ms, whichever comes later, to cut per-event overhead.
  • Resume on disconnect: the Chat Service writes deltas to a short-lived buffer (Redis Stream keyed by message_id). If the client reconnects, it sends the last event id it saw, and the server replays from there and continues. If the user simply reloads later, the saved message is shown.
  • Decouple generation from the connection: generation continues even if the client briefly drops, so the answer is complete when they return. Explicit stop is the only way to cancel.
async def stream_reply(req, conv, user_msg, model):
    asst = await store.create_message(conv.id, role="assistant", status="streaming",
                                      parent_id=user_msg.id)
    yield sse("message_start", {"message_id": asst.id, "model": model})
    buf, last_flush = [], time.monotonic()
    async for tok in inference.generate(build_prompt(conv, user_msg), model, req_id=asst.id):
        buf.append(tok)
        await redis.xadd(f"stream:{asst.id}", {"t": tok}, maxlen=5000)  # resume buffer
        if time.monotonic() - last_flush > 0.03:
            yield sse("delta", {"text": "".join(buf)}); buf.clear()
            last_flush = time.monotonic()
    if buf:
        yield sse("delta", {"text": "".join(buf)})
    await store.complete_message(asst.id)
    yield sse("message_end", {"finish_reason": "stop"})

How do we store conversations and fit them into the context window?

The problem: models have a fixed context window (for example 128,000 tokens), and every token sent costs prefill compute. A long conversation can exceed the window, and even when it fits, sending everything every time is slow and expensive. We also need durable storage for ~730 TB per year of messages.

Storage options:

Store Fit Notes
Postgres (sharded by user_id) Good: relational, indexes for listing Shard to handle 30k writes/s and hundreds of TB
Cassandra / DynamoDB, partition by conversation_id Very good for append-heavy, read-by-conversation Listing by user needs a second table
Object storage for old conversations Cheap archive Slower to open old chats

Recommended: a wide-column store (Cassandra or DynamoDB) with messages partitioned by conversation_id and clustered by time-ordered message_id, plus a conversations_by_user table for listing. Cache recently active conversations (last N messages) in Redis, since most messages continue a conversation used minutes ago.

Context building options:

Strategy How Pros Cons
Send everything Full history Best recall Hits the window, high cost
Sliding window Last N tokens of turns Simple, cheap Forgets early facts
Summary + recent turns Rolling summary of older turns plus recent turns verbatim Bounded cost, keeps key facts Summary may drop details
Retrieval Embed old turns, pull the most relevant ones Precise for specific recalls Extra infra and latency

Recommended: summary plus recent turns, with retrieval as an add-on for very long conversations. Count tokens with the model’s tokenizer and fill a budget in priority order: system prompt, the new message, as many recent turns as fit, then the summary, leaving room for the reply.

def build_prompt(conv, new_msg, model):
    budget = model.context_window - model.max_output_tokens   # leave room to answer
    parts = [system_prompt(model)]
    used = ntok(parts[0]) + ntok(new_msg.content)
    recent = []
    for m in reversed(conv.branch_messages()):               # newest first
        t = m.token_count
        if used + t > budget * 0.8:                          # keep 20% for summary
            break
        recent.append(m); used += t
    if conv.summary and len(recent) < len(conv.branch_messages()):
        parts.append({"role": "system", "content": "Earlier summary: " + conv.summary})
    parts += [as_msg(m) for m in reversed(recent)]
    parts.append(as_msg(new_msg))
    return parts

How do we serve the model efficiently on GPUs?

The problem: an LLM reply has two phases. Prefill processes the whole prompt in parallel (compute heavy, fast per token). Decode generates one token at a time, and each step reads the entire model weights from GPU memory (memory-bandwidth bound). Serving one request at a time leaves the GPU mostly idle. We need ~10,000 GPUs at peak, so every percent of utilization matters.

Key ideas:

  • Batching: run many users’ requests through the model together in each decode step. The cost of reading weights is shared across the batch, so throughput rises nearly linearly until compute or memory runs out.
  • Continuous (in-flight) batching: instead of waiting for a whole batch to finish, the scheduler adds new requests and removes finished ones at every decode step. Short replies do not wait for long ones.
  • KV cache: during generation, the model computes “key” and “value” vectors for every token in the attention layers. Caching them means each new token only does work for itself instead of reprocessing the whole sequence. The KV cache lives in GPU memory and is the main limit on how many requests fit in a batch.
  • Paged attention: store the KV cache in fixed-size blocks (like virtual memory pages) to avoid fragmentation, which can double usable batch size (the idea behind vLLM).
  • Prefix caching: many requests share the same system prompt, and a follow-up message shares the whole previous conversation. Keep KV blocks for common prefixes and reuse them, skipping most of prefill.
Approach Throughput Latency Notes
One request per GPU Very low Low TTFT Wasteful
Static batching Medium Poor: waits for slowest Simple
Continuous batching + paged KV cache High Good Standard today (vLLM, TensorRT-LLM, TGI)
Plus disaggregated prefill/decode pools Higher at scale Better TTFT control Must move KV cache between GPUs

Recommended: continuous batching with paged KV cache and prefix caching. At large scale, split prefill and decode onto separate GPU pools so long prompts do not stall token generation for others. Route follow-up messages of a conversation to the same model replica when possible (session affinity) so its prefix cache is warm.

 Scheduler (per model replica group)
   waiting queue (by priority, plan)
        |
        v
 every decode step:
   + admit new requests if KV blocks free  (prefill chunk)
   - evict finished / stopped requests      (free KV blocks)
   run one forward pass for all active requests
        |
        v
 GPU memory: [ model weights | KV cache blocks: req1 req2 ... reqN ]

KV cache memory, worked example for a mid-size model:

KV bytes per token = 2 (K and V) * layers * kv_heads * head_dim * bytes
                   = 2 * 32 * 8 * 128 * 2 B = 131 KB per token
A 4,000-token conversation        = ~0.5 GB
GPU with 80 GB, weights 16 GB     -> ~64 GB for KV -> ~120 such requests

Very large models are split across several GPUs (tensor parallelism inside a node, pipeline parallelism across nodes), and a replica is the group of GPUs that serves one copy of the model.

How do we enforce rate limits and quotas?

The problem: GPU capacity is fixed in the short term. Without limits, a few heavy users or scripts can fill the queues, and free-tier load can crowd out paying users during spikes. Requests also vary hugely in cost: a 100-token question and a 100,000-token document summary are not equal.

Limit type Measures Why
Requests per minute Messages sent Stops floods and scripts
Tokens per minute Prompt + estimated output tokens Reflects real GPU cost
Daily or rolling quota per plan and model Messages or tokens on expensive models Business plans, cost control
Concurrency Active streams per user Stops parallel abuse

Recommended: token-bucket limiters in Redis, checked at the gateway, keyed by user, plan, and model. Charge prompt tokens up front plus an estimate for output, then correct with the actual usage at the end. Add priority classes in the inference scheduler (paid traffic ahead of free) so overload degrades free users first.

LUA_TOKEN_BUCKET = """
local key, rate, cap, now, cost = KEYS[1], tonumber(ARGV[1]), tonumber(ARGV[2]),
                                  tonumber(ARGV[3]), tonumber(ARGV[4])
local b = redis.call('HMGET', key, 'tokens', 'ts')
local tokens = tonumber(b[1]) or cap
local ts = tonumber(b[2]) or now
tokens = math.min(cap, tokens + (now - ts) * rate)
if tokens < cost then return 0 end
redis.call('HMSET', key, 'tokens', tokens - cost, 'ts', now)
redis.call('EXPIRE', key, 3600)
return 1
"""

def allow(user, model, prompt_tokens):
    cost = prompt_tokens + model.expected_output_tokens
    lim = limits_for(user.plan, model.id)          # e.g. 40k tokens/min for plus
    return redis.eval(LUA_TOKEN_BUCKET, 1, f"tpm:{user.id}:{model.id}",
                      lim.rate_per_s, lim.capacity, time.time(), cost) == 1

When a user hits the limit, return 429 with Retry-After and a clear message (“You have reached your limit for this model, try again at 3:40 PM or switch to the faster model”), which is far better than a vague error.

How do we handle very long conversations?

The problem: some users keep one conversation going for weeks. Even with a 128k window, sending all of it each turn is slow (prefill grows with length), expensive, and eventually impossible. Research also shows models use the middle of very long contexts less reliably.

Option How Pros Cons
Truncate oldest turns Drop from the front Trivial Forgets important early facts
Rolling summarization Periodically summarize older turns into a compact note Bounded tokens, keeps key facts Lossy; extra model calls
Retrieval over history Embed each turn; fetch top-k relevant old turns per new message Recalls specific details Vector index, extra latency
Long-term memory Store durable user facts separately Personalization across chats Privacy and correctness concerns

Recommended: rolling summarization, triggered asynchronously when the un-summarized part of a conversation passes a threshold (for example 8,000 tokens), using a cheap small model. Store the summary and the id of the last covered message on the conversation row. For long chats, also index turns in a vector store and pull the top 3-5 relevant older turns into context.

 turns: [1 ... 120][121 ... 160]  new message
         \_______/   \________/
          summary     recent turns verbatim
         (~800 tok)   (~6,000 tok)
   + retrieved: turns 14, 37 (relevant to the new question)
async def maybe_summarize(conv):
    unsummarized = conv.tokens_after(conv.summary_upto)
    if unsummarized < 8000:
        return
    old = conv.messages_between(conv.summary_upto, keep_recent_tokens=4000)
    prompt = [{"role": "system", "content":
               "Update this summary with the new turns. Keep names, numbers, "
               "decisions, and user preferences. Max 300 words."},
              {"role": "user", "content": f"Summary so far:\n{conv.summary}\n\nNew turns:\n{render(old)}"}]
    new_summary = await inference.complete(prompt, model="small-fast")
    await store.update_summary(conv.id, new_summary, upto=old[-1].id)

Prefix caching on the inference side also helps: if the beginning of the prompt (system prompt plus summary plus early turns) is unchanged since the last message, the KV cache for it can be reused, so only the new tokens need prefill.

How do we route between models and fail over when capacity runs out?

The problem: there are several models (small, large, specialized), each deployed in many GPU clusters across regions. Some clusters fill up, some fail, and a new model version rolls out gradually. Users should rarely see an error.

Routing concern Approach
Which model User choice within plan; optional auto-routing sends simple prompts to a smaller model
Which cluster Least-loaded healthy cluster in or near the user’s region, weighted by queue depth and KV cache headroom
Affinity Prefer the replica that served the conversation’s previous turn (warm prefix cache)
Rollouts Canary a new model version to 1%, then 10%, compare quality and error metrics
Overload Admission control: queue briefly, then shed lowest priority, then fall back
Failure Health checks, circuit breakers, retry on another cluster before the first token

Recommended: a Model Router service that keeps a live view of every cluster (queue length, active batch size, free KV blocks, error rate) and picks a target per request. Failover rules:

  1. If a cluster fails before any token is sent, retry transparently on another cluster or region.
  2. If it fails mid-stream, do not silently restart (the user would see repeated text). Send an error event, keep the partial message with status failed, and offer a one-click retry.
  3. If every cluster for the chosen model is at capacity, queue for up to a few seconds with a “high demand” indicator, then fall back to a smaller model if the plan allows and tell the user, or return 503 with Retry-After.
def route(req):
    candidates = [c for c in clusters[req.model] if c.healthy and not c.breaker_open]
    if req.prev_replica in candidates and candidates_load(req.prev_replica) < 0.85:
        return req.prev_replica                     # warm prefix cache
    candidates.sort(key=lambda c: (c.region_distance(req.region),
                                   c.queue_depth / c.capacity))
    for c in candidates:
        if c.admit(req.priority, req.est_tokens):   # checks KV headroom
            return c
    if req.allow_fallback and (fb := fallback_model(req.model)):
        req.model, req.notice = fb, "Using a faster model due to high demand"
        return route(req)
    raise AtCapacity(retry_after=10)
            +------------------ Model Router ------------------+
 request -> | plan check -> affinity? -> least-loaded healthy   |
            | cluster -> admit? -> else fallback model -> 503   |
            +---------------------------------------------------+
               |                 |                    |
          large-model       large-model          small-model
          us-east (80%)     us-west (95% full)   us-east

Other failure handling:

  • Chat Service crash mid-stream: the assistant message stays streaming; a sweeper marks stale ones failed after a timeout. The client’s reconnect replays from the Redis resume buffer if generation is still running elsewhere.
  • Conversation store slow: buffer completed messages to a durable queue and write behind; the reply still streams.
  • Moderation service down: fail closed for high-risk categories (block with a message) or fail open with post-hoc review, by policy.

9. Common mistakes and interviewer follow-ups

  • Returning the whole reply at once. Users stare at a spinner for 20 seconds. Say: stream tokens with SSE, measure time to first token.
  • Treating inference like a normal stateless web call. GPU batching, KV cache memory, and prefill vs decode are the real bottlenecks. Say: continuous batching, paged KV cache, prefix caching, and capacity math in GPUs.
  • Sending the full history every turn. It breaks at the context window and wastes prefill compute. Say: token budget with recent turns, rolling summary, and optional retrieval.
  • Rate limiting by request count only. One giant prompt costs 1,000 small ones. Say: tokens-per-minute buckets plus plan quotas and priority classes.
  • Restarting a failed generation silently mid-stream. The user sees duplicated or inconsistent text. Say: retry only before the first token; after that, mark failed and offer retry.
  • Tying generation to the HTTP connection. A flaky mobile network cancels expensive work. Say: decouple generation, buffer deltas for resume, cancel only on explicit stop.
  • Overwriting messages on regenerate. History and branches are lost. Say: message tree with parent ids.
  • Follow-up: “How would you cut GPU cost?” Answer: route easy prompts to smaller models, quantize models (store weights in fewer bits), raise batch sizes with paged attention, use prefix caching, and use speculative decoding (a small model drafts tokens that the large model verifies in one pass).

10. One-page cheat sheet

Topic Key point
Scale 1B msgs/day, 30k/s peak, ~12M output tokens/s, ~10k GPUs, 300k open streams
Latency TTFT p50 < 500 ms, p99 < 2 s; >= 30 tokens/s
Streaming SSE, no proxy buffering, heartbeats, Redis Streams resume buffer
Storage Messages by conversation_id (Cassandra/DynamoDB), list by user, Redis hot cache
Branches Message tree with parent_id for regenerate and edits
Context Token budget: system + recent turns + rolling summary + retrieval
Serving Continuous batching, paged KV cache, prefix caching, prefill/decode split
KV math ~131 KB/token for a mid-size model; KV memory caps batch size
Limits Redis token buckets on tokens/min, requests/min, concurrency; plan quotas
Priority Paid ahead of free in the scheduler; shed free load first
Routing Plan check, conversation affinity, least-loaded healthy cluster
Failover Retry before first token; mark failed after; fallback model or 503
CAP Availability for chat; single writer per conversation for ordering

32. Flash Sale (Hard)

A flash sale sells a tiny amount of stock (say 1,000 discounted phones) to a huge crowd (say 1,000,000 shoppers) who all show up at the same second, for example at 12:00:00 noon. The product itself is simple: show the item, let people click Buy, take payment, confirm the order. What the interviewer is really testing is whether you can survive a traffic spike that is 100x to 1000x normal load, never sell item number 1,001 (no overselling), stay fair to real humans, and not let a few seconds of madness take down the rest of the shop. It is a focused problem: you design one hard corner of an e-commerce system, not the whole store.

1. Functional requirements

Core (must have):

  1. Users can view a flash sale page: product, price, start time, and a rough “items left” indicator.
  2. When the sale opens, users can try to reserve (claim) one unit of the item.
  3. A user who wins a reservation can pay within a time window (for example 10 minutes) to turn it into an order.
  4. If the user does not pay in time, the unit goes back into stock for someone else.
  5. Each user can buy at most N units (usually 1) per sale.
  6. Users get a clear answer: “you got one, pay now”, “you are in the queue”, or “sold out”.

Below the line (out of scope):

  • Product catalog management, search, and recommendations. These already exist in the normal store.
  • Shipping, returns, and warehouse fulfilment. They happen hours later and are not under spike load.
  • Building a payment processor. We call an existing one (Stripe, Adyen, an internal payments service).
  • Dynamic pricing. The price is fixed for the sale.

2. Non-functional requirements

  1. Correctness (no overselling): the number of confirmed orders must never exceed stock. This needs strong consistency for the inventory counter. Zero tolerance.
  2. Spike tolerance: handle about 1,000,000 users arriving within roughly 10 seconds, which peaks near 200,000 to 500,000 requests per second at the edge.
  3. Low latency for the decision: p99 time to tell a user “won / lost / waiting” under 500 ms once they reach the buy step.
  4. Availability: the sale page and waiting room should stay up (99.99%). If a backend part is struggling, shed load gracefully with a “please wait” instead of errors.
  5. Isolation: the flash sale must not hurt the rest of the store. Normal checkout keeps its normal latency.
  6. Fairness: roughly first come, first served among real users. Bots and scripts should not win most of the stock.
  7. Idempotency: a user double-clicking or a client retrying must never create two orders or two charges.
  8. CAP choice: for the inventory counter we choose consistency over availability (CP). If we cannot be sure a unit is free, we say “try again” rather than risk selling it twice. For the product page and “items left” display we choose availability (AP) and accept a number that is a second or two stale.

3. Back-of-the-envelope estimates

Assumption Number
Units of stock 1,000
Users who show up 1,000,000
Arrival window for most users 10 seconds
Page refreshes and retries per user in first minute about 5
Reservation window to pay 10 minutes
Size of one order record about 1 KB
Flash sales per day (whole company) about 20
Product page size (HTML + JSON, images on CDN) about 50 KB 
Edge traffic at peak:
  1,000,000 users * 5 requests / 10 s = 500,000 req/s  (mostly page loads,
  polling, retries; must be served by CDN and waiting room, not the backend)

Buy attempts reaching the inventory service (after the waiting room):
  We only need ~1,000 winners. Let in, say, 10,000 users per second.
  -> 10,000 write attempts/s at the counter, easy for one Redis node
     (a single Redis node handles ~100k simple ops/s)

Successful writes (orders):
  1,000 orders per sale * 20 sales/day = 20,000 orders/day
  -> tiny for a database; the hard part is the burst, not the volume

Storage per year:
  20,000 orders/day * 365 * 1 KB = ~7.3 GB/year of orders
  Plus reservation and audit logs, maybe 10x -> ~73 GB/year. Small.

Bandwidth at peak (page loads served from CDN):
  500,000 req/s * 50 KB = 25 GB/s  -> this is why the page must be static
  and cached at the CDN edge. Our origin servers must not see this.

The key insight from the math: the total amount of work is small, but it all arrives at once. 99.9% of the users will lose. Our job is to say “no” to them cheaply and say “yes” to 1,000 of them correctly.

4. Core entities

  • Sale: one flash sale event. Fields: sale_id, product_id, price, total_stock, start_at, end_at, per_user_limit, status.
  • Product: the item being sold. Fields: product_id, title, images, description (already exists in the catalog).
  • InventoryCounter: the live number of units left for a sale. Lives in Redis as the fast source of truth during the sale, backed by the database.
  • Reservation: a temporary hold on one unit for one user. Fields: reservation_id, sale_id, user_id, status (HELD, PAID, EXPIRED), expires_at.
  • Order: the final purchase after payment. Fields: order_id, reservation_id, user_id, amount, payment_id, status.
  • QueueTicket: a user’s place in the virtual waiting room. Fields: ticket_id, user_id, sale_id, position, signed token.
  • IdempotencyKey: a client-generated key that makes a request safe to retry. Fields: key, user_id, response, created_at.
CREATE TABLE sales (
  sale_id        BIGINT PRIMARY KEY,
  product_id     BIGINT NOT NULL,
  price_cents    INT NOT NULL,
  total_stock    INT NOT NULL,
  per_user_limit INT NOT NULL DEFAULT 1,
  start_at       TIMESTAMP NOT NULL,
  end_at         TIMESTAMP NOT NULL,
  status         VARCHAR(16) NOT NULL  -- SCHEDULED, LIVE, ENDED
);

CREATE TABLE reservations (
  reservation_id UUID PRIMARY KEY,
  sale_id        BIGINT NOT NULL,
  user_id        BIGINT NOT NULL,
  status         VARCHAR(16) NOT NULL, -- HELD, PAID, EXPIRED
  expires_at     TIMESTAMP NOT NULL,
  created_at     TIMESTAMP NOT NULL,
  UNIQUE (sale_id, user_id)            -- one active claim per user
);

CREATE TABLE orders (
  order_id        UUID PRIMARY KEY,
  reservation_id  UUID NOT NULL UNIQUE,  -- one order per reservation
  user_id         BIGINT NOT NULL,
  amount_cents    INT NOT NULL,
  payment_id      VARCHAR(64),
  status          VARCHAR(16) NOT NULL   -- PENDING, CONFIRMED, FAILED
);

The UNIQUE constraints are a safety net. Even if the fast path had a bug, the database refuses a second reservation for the same user or a second order for the same reservation.

5. API design

All write endpoints need a logged-in user (session cookie or JWT). Buy endpoints also need a valid waiting-room token.

GET /sales/{saleId} – get sale details (cacheable at CDN).

// response 200
{ "saleId": 77, "product": {"id": 9, "title": "Phone X"},
  "priceCents": 19900, "startAt": "2026-11-11T12:00:00Z",
  "status": "SCHEDULED", "stockHint": "AVAILABLE" }

POST /sales/{saleId}/queue – join the waiting room, get a ticket.

// response 202
{ "ticketId": "t_8f2", "position": 48210, "pollAfterMs": 2000 }

GET /sales/{saleId}/queue/{ticketId} – poll your status in the waiting room.

// response 200, still waiting
{ "state": "WAITING", "position": 3120, "pollAfterMs": 2000 }
// response 200, your turn
{ "state": "ADMITTED", "accessToken": "eyJhbGciOi...", "expiresInSec": 60 }
// response 200, sale over
{ "state": "SOLD_OUT" }

POST /sales/{saleId}/reservations – try to claim one unit. Headers: Authorization, X-Access-Token (from the waiting room), Idempotency-Key.

// request
{ "quantity": 1 }
// response 201
{ "reservationId": "r_51a", "expiresAt": "2026-11-11T12:10:04Z" }

Status codes: 201 won, 409 already have a reservation (returns the existing one), 410 sold out, 403 bad or expired access token, 429 slow down.

POST /reservations/{reservationId}/orders – pay and confirm. Headers: Idempotency-Key.

// request
{ "paymentMethodId": "pm_123" }
// response 202 (payment is processed async)
{ "orderId": "o_9c1", "status": "PENDING" }

GET /orders/{orderId} – check order status (PENDING, CONFIRMED, FAILED).
