How will users view the sale page?

  1. The client loads /sales/77. The HTML, JS and images are static and served by the CDN. No origin hit.
  2. The page fetches GET /sales/77 JSON. This is also cached at the CDN with a short TTL (1 to 5 seconds).
  3. A countdown runs in the browser using server time from a response header, so users with wrong clocks do not hit Buy early.
  4. The “items left” hint is a coarse value (AVAILABLE, FEW_LEFT, SOLD_OUT) refreshed every couple of seconds from Redis by the Sale Info Service. It is fine for this to be slightly stale.

        C-->>B: Cached sale details
    else cache miss
        C->>S: Fetch sale details
        S->>R: Read coarse stock hint
        R-->>S: AVAILABLE
        S-->>C: Sale JSON with server time
        C-->>B: Sale details
    end
    B->>B: Run countdown using server time

How will users get a fair chance to buy?

  1. At 12:00:00 the Buy button turns into “Join queue”. The client calls POST /sales/77/queue.
  2. The Waiting Room Service gives the user a ticket with a position. Positions come from INCR on a Redis key, so arrival order is preserved.
  3. The client polls with the pollAfterMs the server suggests. The server can raise this number to slow down polling when it is busy.
  4. A releaser lets in, say, 2,000 users per second. Admitted users get a short-lived signed access token.
  5. Once stock hits zero, every remaining ticket gets “SOLD_OUT” right away, so the crowd leaves quickly.

How will users reserve a unit?

  1. The admitted client calls POST /sales/77/reservations with the access token and an Idempotency-Key.
  2. The Reservation Service checks the token signature (no DB call, just crypto).
  3. It runs one Lua script in Redis that atomically checks the per-user limit and decrements stock (see deep dive).
  4. If the script says “won”, the service writes the reservation to Redis with a TTL and publishes a ReservationCreated event to Kafka.
  5. It returns 201 with a reservation id. This all takes a few milliseconds.

How will users pay and get an order?

  1. The client calls POST /reservations/r_51a/orders with a payment method and a new Idempotency-Key.
  2. The Order Service checks the reservation is still HELD and not expired, inserts an order as PENDING, and asks the Payment Service to charge.
  3. The Payment Service calls the provider with the same idempotency key, so a retry never double-charges.
  4. When the provider confirms (often by webhook), the order becomes CONFIRMED and the reservation PAID.
  5. The client polls GET /orders/o_9c1 or gets a push notification.

What happens if someone does not pay?

  1. Every reservation has expires_at. An Expiry Worker scans for HELD reservations past their time.
  2. It marks them EXPIRED and runs INCR on the stock counter so the unit is free again.
  3. The waiting room releases a few more users to take those units.

7. Deep dives

How do we make sure we never sell more units than we have?

The classic bug is read-then-write. Two servers both read “stock = 1”, both think there is one left, both sell it. We need the check and the decrement to happen as one atomic step.

Option How it works Pros Cons
DB row lock (SELECT ... FOR UPDATE) Lock the inventory row, check, update, commit Simple, strongly consistent, durable One hot row; maybe 500 to 2,000 updates/s before lock waits pile up
DB conditional update UPDATE ... SET stock = stock - 1 WHERE stock > 0 No explicit lock, atomic in one statement Still one hot row, same throughput ceiling
Redis DECR alone Decrement, if result < 0 then INCR back Very fast Brief negative values; per-user limit needs a second call, so not atomic
Redis Lua script Check user limit + stock + decrement in one script Atomic, about 100k ops/s on one node, handles limits Redis is in memory, so we need persistence and a reconcile step

Recommended: Redis Lua script as the gate, database as the record. Redis runs a Lua script as one uninterruptible unit, so no other command sneaks in between the check and the decrement.

-- KEYS[1] = stock:{77}        (integer units left)
-- KEYS[2] = buyers:{77}       (hash user_id -> units bought)
-- ARGV[1] = user_id, ARGV[2] = qty, ARGV[3] = per_user_limit
local stock = tonumber(redis.call('GET', KEYS[1]) or '0')
local qty   = tonumber(ARGV[2])
local had   = tonumber(redis.call('HGET', KEYS[2], ARGV[1]) or '0')

if had + qty > tonumber(ARGV[3]) then
  return -2              -- over the per-user limit
end
if stock < qty then
  return -1              -- sold out
end
redis.call('DECRBY', KEYS[1], qty)
redis.call('HINCRBY', KEYS[2], ARGV[1], qty)
return stock - qty       -- units left after this claim

The {77} in the key names is a Redis Cluster hash tag. It forces both keys onto the same shard, which Lua scripts need.

def reserve(sale_id: int, user_id: int, qty: int = 1) -> str:
    left = redis.evalsha(RESERVE_SHA, 2,
                         f"stock:{{{sale_id}}}", f"buyers:{{{sale_id}}}",
                         user_id, qty, PER_USER_LIMIT)
    if left == -1:
        raise SoldOut()
    if left == -2:
        raise LimitReached()
    rid = new_uuid()
    redis.set(f"resv:{rid}", user_id, ex=600)        # 10 min hold
    kafka.send("reservations", {"rid": rid, "sale": sale_id,
                                "user": user_id, "qty": qty})
    return rid

If the 1,000 units are the only thing that matters, you could even skip Redis and use the database conditional update, because the waiting room limits traffic to a few thousand attempts per second. Say this in the interview: “With a waiting room in front, a single Postgres row with a conditional update can work. I pick Redis because it gives me headroom and keeps the hot row off the main DB.”

A second safety net: the UNIQUE (sale_id, user_id) constraint in the reservations table, and a periodic reconcile job that checks total_stock = redis_stock + held + paid.

How do we stop 1,000,000 users from crushing the backend?

Only 1,000 can win. Letting 1,000,000 requests hit the Reservation Service wastes capacity and creates a thundering herd (everyone retrying at once).

Option Idea Pros Cons
Rate limit only Return 429 above N req/s Easy Users hammer refresh; unfair; random who wins
Virtual waiting room Give everyone a queue position, admit at a fixed rate Fair, smooth load, clear UX More moving parts, users must wait
Lottery / pre-registration Users register before; random draw picks buyers Calmest load, very bot resistant Changes the product; not first come first served
Load shedding at the edge Once sold out, CDN serves a static “sold out” page Kills traffic instantly Only helps after stock is gone

Recommended: waiting room plus edge shedding, with rate limits as a backstop.

 users --> CDN --> Waiting Room --(N/sec)--> Reservation Svc --> Redis
               \                                    |
                \--- "SOLD OUT" static page <-------+ (flag flips at stock 0)

The waiting room is cheap because it only does INCR for a position and returns small JSON. The admission rule can be simple:

# runs every 100 ms
def release_batch(sale_id):
    if int(redis.get(f"stock:{{{sale_id}}}") or 0) <= 0:
        redis.set(f"soldout:{sale_id}", 1)   # CDN and APIs read this
        return
    admitted = int(redis.get(f"admitted:{sale_id}") or 0)
    # admit a bit more than remaining stock to cover drop-outs
    target = admitted + RELEASE_PER_TICK     # e.g. 200 per 100 ms
    redis.set(f"admitted:{sale_id}", target)
    # tickets with position <= target are now ADMITTED

When a user polls, the service compares their position with admitted. If position is lower, it signs an access token:

token = jwt.encode({"sub": user_id, "sale": sale_id,
                    "exp": now() + 60}, SECRET, algorithm="HS256")

The Reservation Service only checks the signature. No database call, so it stays fast.

Polling control: the server returns pollAfterMs. Under heavy load it raises the number from 2,000 to 5,000 ms. This alone can cut polling traffic in half. Add random jitter so clients do not poll in lockstep.

How do we make order placement safe to retry?

Networks fail. A user taps Pay, the phone loses signal, the app retries. Without care, we charge twice or create two orders.

Option How Pros Cons
Idempotency key table Client sends a UUID; server stores key -> response Exact replay of the first answer Extra table and lookup
Natural unique key UNIQUE(reservation_id) on orders Simple, enforced by DB Does not cover the payment call itself
Both Key for the API, unique constraint as a net, same key passed to payment provider End-to-end safe Slightly more code

Recommended: both.

def create_order(resv_id, payment_method, idem_key, user_id):
    cached = db.fetch_one(
        "SELECT response FROM idempotency_keys WHERE key=%s AND user_id=%s",
        (idem_key, user_id))
    if cached:
        return cached["response"]                 # replay, no new work

    with db.transaction():
        resv = db.fetch_one("SELECT * FROM reservations "
                            "WHERE reservation_id=%s FOR UPDATE", (resv_id,))
        if resv["status"] != "HELD" or resv["expires_at"] < now():
            raise ReservationExpired()
        order_id = new_uuid()
        db.execute("INSERT INTO orders (order_id, reservation_id, user_id, "
                   "amount_cents, status) VALUES (%s,%s,%s,%s,'PENDING') "
                   "ON CONFLICT (reservation_id) DO NOTHING",
                   (order_id, resv_id, user_id, PRICE))
        resp = {"orderId": order_id, "status": "PENDING"}
        db.execute("INSERT INTO idempotency_keys VALUES (%s,%s,%s,now())",
                   (idem_key, user_id, json.dumps(resp)))

    payments.charge(order_id, payment_method, PRICE,
                    idempotency_key=f"order-{order_id}")   # async
    return resp

Payment providers like Stripe accept an idempotency key header. Passing order-{order_id} means a retry of the charge returns the same result instead of charging again.

How do we keep it fair and stop bots?

Bots can open thousands of sessions, poll faster than humans, and grab most of the stock to resell.

Defense What it stops Cost
Login required, account age check Throwaway accounts Some friction
Per-user and per-device limits (1 unit, 1 queue ticket) One bot with many tabs Needs device fingerprint
CAPTCHA or proof-of-work before joining queue Cheap scripted requests Slight UX cost
Pre-registration window Last-second bot floods Product change
Randomize queue order for arrivals in the first second Bots racing to be first by milliseconds Less strict FIFO
Post-sale audit, cancel suspicious orders Bots that got through Refund handling

Recommended: login plus per-user limit (enforced in the Lua script), a CAPTCHA or proof-of-work at queue join, and randomizing order within the first few seconds. Being 3 ms faster than a human should not matter.

def join_queue(user_id, sale_id):
    if not captcha_ok(request): raise Forbidden()
    if not redis.set(f"qticket:{sale_id}:{user_id}", 1, nx=True, ex=3600):
        return existing_ticket(user_id, sale_id)    # one ticket per user
    if now() < SALE_START + 5:                     # early burst window
        pos = random_slot_in_first_bucket()        # shuffled
    else:
        pos = redis.incr(f"qpos:{sale_id}") + EARLY_BUCKET_SIZE
    return pos

How do we prepare the system before the spike?

A cold system fails on the first second: empty caches, small autoscaling groups, cold DB connection pools.

Pre-warm step Why
Push sale page and JSON to CDN 10 minutes before Edge serves 25 GB/s without origin
Load stock counter into Redis (SET stock:{77} 1000) Gate is ready, no lazy load
Scale out waiting room and API pods to peak size in advance Autoscaling takes minutes, the spike takes seconds
Open DB connection pools, warm the Lua script with SCRIPT LOAD Avoid first-request latency
Load test with a replay of last sale’s traffic Find bottlenecks before customers do
Set a feature flag to turn flash sale paths off Fast kill switch if things go wrong 
# T-10 minutes runbook
redis-cli SET "stock:{77}" 1000
redis-cli SCRIPT LOAD "$(cat reserve.lua)"
kubectl scale deploy waiting-room --replicas=200
kubectl scale deploy reservation-svc --replicas=60
curl -X POST https://cdn.example.com/purge-and-prefetch -d '{"path":"/sales/77"}'

How do we decouple reservation from order creation, and handle failures?

If the reservation call also wrote to the database and called the payment provider in the same request, the slowest part (payment, often 1 to 3 seconds) would set the speed for everyone.

Option How Pros Cons
Synchronous all-in-one Reserve + order + charge in one request Simple code Slow, payment outages block reservations
Async via queue Reserve fast in Redis, publish event, workers write DB and charge Fast answers, absorbs bursts, retryable Eventually consistent order status

Recommended: async via Kafka (or SQS). The user gets “you got one” in milliseconds. Workers persist the reservation to Postgres at whatever rate the DB can take.

Failure cases and what we do:

Failure Effect Handling
Redis primary dies mid-sale Counter could be lost or stale on replica Use Redis with AOF appendfsync always for this key, or fail over and rebuild from DB + Kafka; pause sale briefly (CP choice)
Kafka publish fails after Redis decrement Unit is “taken” but no reservation record Retry publish; if it keeps failing, INCR stock back (compensation)
Order worker crashes Event not processed Kafka redelivers; DB unique keys make the replay safe
Payment provider down Orders stay PENDING Retry with backoff; extend hold window; if still failing, expire and release stock
User never pays Unit stuck Expiry worker returns it after 10 minutes

Rebuild after a Redis loss:

-- true remaining stock
SELECT s.total_stock
     - COUNT(*) FILTER (WHERE r.status IN ('HELD','PAID')) AS remaining
FROM sales s LEFT JOIN reservations r ON r.sale_id = s.sale_id
WHERE s.sale_id = 77
GROUP BY s.total_stock;

Events still in Kafka but not yet in the DB must also be counted, so we pause the waiting room, let the consumer catch up, then compute and SET the counter.

The CDN and gateway absorb the crowd at the edge, so only admitted users reach the Lua gate on Redis in the data subnet, and only the payment worker talks to the payment provider.

9. Common mistakes and interviewer follow-ups

  • Mistake: read stock, then write stock in two steps. It oversells under concurrency. Say instead: “The check and the decrement happen atomically, in a Lua script or a conditional UPDATE ... WHERE stock > 0.”
  • Mistake: sending all 1M users to the database. The DB melts and the rest of the store goes down with it. Say instead: “The CDN and waiting room absorb the crowd; only a controlled rate reaches the counter.”
  • Mistake: calling the payment provider inside the reservation request. Slow, and a provider outage blocks everything. Say instead: “Reserve fast, pay async, with a hold timer.”
  • Mistake: no plan for unpaid reservations. Stock leaks and the sale ends with unsold units. Say instead: “Holds expire after 10 minutes and an expiry worker returns units.”
  • Mistake: forgetting idempotency. Double clicks create double charges, which is the worst customer experience. Say instead: “Idempotency keys on the API and on the payment call, plus unique constraints.”
  • Mistake: trusting Redis alone forever. A failover can lose a few writes. Say instead: “Redis is the gate, Postgres is the record, and a reconcile job checks they agree.”
  • Follow-up: “What if there are 100 different products in one sale?” Each product gets its own counter key and hash tag, so they spread across Redis shards naturally.
  • Follow-up: “What if one product has 1,000,000 units?” Split the stock into buckets (10 keys of 100,000) and pick a random bucket per request; when a bucket is empty try another. This avoids one hot key.

10. One-page cheat sheet

Topic Key point
Scale 1M users, 1,000 units, 500k req/s at edge, ~10k/s at the counter
Core trick Say “no” cheaply to 99.9%, say “yes” correctly to 0.1%
Inventory gate Redis Lua: check per-user limit + stock + decrement atomically
Fallback gate Postgres UPDATE ... SET stock = stock - 1 WHERE stock > 0
Load control CDN static page, virtual waiting room, admit N/s, signed token
Sold out Flip a flag; CDN serves static sold-out page
Reservations 10-minute hold with TTL, expiry worker releases stock
Orders Async via Kafka; Order + Payment workers
Idempotency Idempotency-Key header, key table, unique(reservation_id), provider idem key
Fairness Login, 1 per user, CAPTCHA, shuffle first-second arrivals
Pre-warm Load counter, scale pods, prefetch CDN, SCRIPT LOAD, kill switch
CAP CP for stock counter, AP for page and stock hint
Safety nets DB unique constraints, reconcile job, compensation on publish failure

33. Food Review App (Medium)

A food review app lets people find restaurants near them, read what others thought, and post their own review with a star rating and photos. Think of a slimmer Yelp or Zomato focused on food. The interviewer wants to see three things: that you can store reviews and large photos without pushing image bytes through your own servers, that you can keep a restaurant’s average rating correct while many reviews arrive at once, and that you can answer “good ramen within 2 km of me” quickly using a geo index. Moderation and the “one review per user per restaurant” rule are classic correctness follow-ups.

1. Functional requirements

Core (must have):

  1. Users can search for restaurants near a location, filtered by cuisine and sorted by distance or rating.
  2. Users can view a restaurant page: details, average rating, review count, photos, and reviews.
  3. Users can post a review with a 1 to 5 star rating, text, and up to 10 photos.
  4. Each user can have at most one review per restaurant (they can edit it).
  5. Users can see a feed of recent reviews (near them, or from people they follow).
  6. Reviews and photos are moderated (spam, offensive content, fake reviews) before or shortly after they go live.

Below the line (out of scope):

  • Table booking and food delivery. Separate products with their own hard problems (payments, real-time tracking).
  • Restaurant owner dashboards and ads. Business features, not core to reviews.
  • Personalized recommendations with machine learning. We mention ranking but do not design the model.
  • Direct messaging between users.

2. Non-functional requirements

  1. Read-heavy: reads outnumber writes about 100:1. Optimize the read path with caching.
  2. Search latency: p99 under 300 ms for a nearby search.
  3. Restaurant page latency: p99 under 200 ms (cached).
  4. Review post latency: under 1 s to accept the review. Photos upload directly to object storage, so they do not count against this.
  5. Availability: 99.9% for writes, 99.99% for reads. Users browsing are more common than users posting.
  6. Consistency: eventual consistency for search results, feeds, and average ratings (a few seconds of lag is fine). Strong consistency for the “one review per user per restaurant” rule, which must never be broken.
  7. Durability: photos and reviews must never be lost (object storage with 11 nines durability, replicated DB).
  8. CAP choice: for browsing and search we choose availability (AP), since a slightly stale rating does not hurt anyone. The uniqueness rule is enforced inside one database partition, so it stays strongly consistent.

3. Back-of-the-envelope estimates

Assumption Number
Restaurants 10 million
Daily active users (DAU) 20 million
Searches per DAU per day 5
Restaurant page views per DAU per day 10
New reviews per day 1 million
Photos per review (average) 2
Average photo size (after compression) 2 MB original, 200 KB for display sizes
Average review text 1 KB 
Read QPS:
  searches:   20M * 5  / 86,400 s = ~1,150/s   (peak x3 = ~3,500/s)
  page views: 20M * 10 / 86,400 s = ~2,300/s   (peak x3 = ~7,000/s)

Write QPS:
  reviews:    1M / 86,400 s       = ~12/s      (peak ~40/s)
  photos:     2M / 86,400 s       = ~23/s

Storage per year:
  review text: 1M/day * 1 KB * 365       = ~365 GB/year
  photos:      2M/day * (2 MB + 0.6 MB)  = ~5.2 TB/day
               5.2 TB * 365               = ~1.9 PB/year  (object storage)
  restaurants: 10M * 2 KB                 = ~20 GB (fits in one DB + index)

Bandwidth (photo reads dominate):
  page views 7,000/s * 10 thumbnails * 30 KB = ~2.1 GB/s at peak
  -> must be served by a CDN, not by our servers

Takeaways: writes are tiny, reads are moderate, photos are huge. That points at a CDN in front of object storage, presigned uploads, and caching for restaurant pages.

4. Core entities

  • User: someone who browses and writes reviews. Fields: user_id, name, avatar_url, created_at, trust_score.
  • Restaurant: a place that serves food. Fields: restaurant_id, name, lat, lng, geohash, cuisine, price_level, avg_rating, review_count.
  • Review: one user’s opinion of one restaurant. Fields: review_id, restaurant_id, user_id, rating, text, status, created_at.
  • Photo: an image attached to a review. Fields: photo_id, review_id, s3_key, status (PENDING, READY, REJECTED), width, height.
  • RatingAggregate: running totals per restaurant. Fields: restaurant_id, rating_sum, rating_count, histogram (count per star).
  • Follow: user A follows user B, used for the feed.
  • ModerationCase: a review or photo flagged for checking. Fields: case_id, target_id, reason, decision.
CREATE TABLE restaurants (
  restaurant_id BIGINT PRIMARY KEY,
  name          TEXT NOT NULL,
  lat           DOUBLE PRECISION NOT NULL,
  lng           DOUBLE PRECISION NOT NULL,
  location      GEOGRAPHY(POINT) NOT NULL,   -- PostGIS
  cuisine       TEXT,
  price_level   SMALLINT,
  rating_sum    BIGINT NOT NULL DEFAULT 0,
  rating_count  INT NOT NULL DEFAULT 0
);
CREATE INDEX idx_rest_loc ON restaurants USING GIST (location);

CREATE TABLE reviews (
  review_id     BIGINT PRIMARY KEY,
  restaurant_id BIGINT NOT NULL REFERENCES restaurants,
  user_id       BIGINT NOT NULL,
  rating        SMALLINT NOT NULL CHECK (rating BETWEEN 1 AND 5),
  body          TEXT,
  status        VARCHAR(16) NOT NULL DEFAULT 'PENDING',
  created_at    TIMESTAMP NOT NULL DEFAULT now(),
  updated_at    TIMESTAMP NOT NULL DEFAULT now(),
  UNIQUE (restaurant_id, user_id)          -- one review per user per place
);
CREATE INDEX idx_reviews_rest_time ON reviews (restaurant_id, created_at DESC);

CREATE TABLE photos (
  photo_id   BIGINT PRIMARY KEY,
  review_id  BIGINT NOT NULL REFERENCES reviews,
  s3_key     TEXT NOT NULL,
  status     VARCHAR(16) NOT NULL DEFAULT 'PENDING'
);

Storing rating_sum and rating_count (not the average itself) is deliberate. You can always compute the average as sum / count, and adding or removing a review is just a plus or minus on two numbers.

5. API design

All write endpoints require a logged-in user (bearer token). Read endpoints are public.

GET /restaurants/search?lat=..&lng=..&radiusKm=2&cuisine=ramen&sort=rating&cursor=.. – find nearby restaurants.

// response 200
{ "results": [
    { "id": 81, "name": "Ichiran", "distanceM": 420,
      "avgRating": 4.6, "reviewCount": 1832, "thumbUrl": "https://cdn/.../t.jpg" }
  ],
  "nextCursor": "eyJvZmZzZXQiOjIwfQ" }

GET /restaurants/{id} – restaurant details plus rating summary.

{ "id": 81, "name": "Ichiran", "cuisine": "ramen",
  "avgRating": 4.6, "reviewCount": 1832,
  "histogram": {"5": 1200, "4": 400, "3": 150, "2": 50, "1": 32} }

GET /restaurants/{id}/reviews?sort=recent&cursor=.. – paginated reviews.

POST /uploads/photos – get presigned URLs for photo upload.

// request
{ "count": 2, "contentTypes": ["image/jpeg", "image/jpeg"] }
// response 200
{ "uploads": [
    { "photoId": 9001, "url": "https://s3/...&X-Amz-Signature=...", "expiresInSec": 900 },
    { "photoId": 9002, "url": "https://s3/...", "expiresInSec": 900 } ] }

POST /restaurants/{id}/reviews – create a review. Header Idempotency-Key.

// request
{ "rating": 5, "text": "Rich broth, fast service.", "photoIds": [9001, 9002] }
// response 201
{ "reviewId": 5551, "status": "PENDING" }

Status codes: 201 created, 409 you already reviewed this restaurant (response includes your existing review id), 400 bad rating, 401 not logged in.

PUT /reviews/{reviewId} – edit your own review (owner only, 403 otherwise).

DELETE /reviews/{reviewId} – delete your own review.

GET /feed?lat=..&lng=..&cursor=.. – recent reviews near you or from people you follow.

POST /reviews/{reviewId}/reports – report a review for moderation.

How will users find restaurants near them?

  1. The client sends GET /restaurants/search with its latitude, longitude, radius and filters.
  2. The Search Service runs a geo query on the geo index (Elasticsearch geo_distance, or PostGIS ST_DWithin).
  3. It applies filters (cuisine, price) and sorts by distance or by a mix of rating and distance.
  4. Results include the cached avgRating and reviewCount, so no join to the reviews table is needed.
  5. Popular searches (for example “downtown, pizza”) are cached in Redis for 60 seconds.
sequenceDiagram
    participant C as Client
    participant G as API Gateway
    participant S as Search Service
    participant R as Redis
    participant E as Geo index
    C->>G: GET search with lat lng radius filters
    G->>S: Forward search
    S->>R: Check cached popular search
    alt cache hit
        R-->>S: Cached results
    else cache miss
        S->>E: Geo distance query with filters
        E-->>S: Nearby restaurants sorted
        S->>R: Cache results for 60 seconds
    end
    S-->>G: Results with avg rating and count
    G-->>C: 200 results and next cursor

How will users view a restaurant and its reviews?

  1. The client calls GET /restaurants/81. The Review Service checks Redis first (restaurant:81, TTL 5 min).
  2. On a miss it reads the restaurant row (with rating_sum, rating_count, histogram) and caches it.
  3. GET /restaurants/81/reviews?sort=recent reads from the (restaurant_id, created_at DESC) index, 20 at a time with a cursor.
  4. Photo URLs point to the CDN, so images load straight from the edge.

How will users post a review with photos?

  1. The client asks POST /uploads/photos for 2 presigned URLs. The server creates PENDING photo rows and returns signed S3 URLs.
  2. The client uploads each photo straight to S3 with an HTTP PUT. Our servers never touch the bytes.
  3. The client sends POST /restaurants/81/reviews with rating, text, and the photo ids.
  4. The Review Service inserts the review. The unique constraint (restaurant_id, user_id) rejects a second review.
  5. It publishes a ReviewCreated event to Kafka.
  6. Consumers update the rating aggregate, run moderation, and push the review into feeds.

How will users see a feed of recent reviews?

  1. The client calls GET /feed. The Feed Service reads a precomputed list of review ids from Redis for the user’s area (geohash cell) and from people they follow.
  2. It hydrates the ids into full reviews from a cache, then returns them newest first.

7. Deep dives

How do we handle photo uploads without overloading our servers?

At 2 MB per photo and 2 million photos per day, piping uploads through our API servers would waste bandwidth and tie up threads for seconds per request on slow mobile networks.

Option How Pros Cons
Upload through API server Client sends bytes to us, we forward to S3 Simple, full control Servers become a bandwidth bottleneck, slow uploads hold connections
Presigned URL direct to S3 Server signs a short-lived URL, client PUTs to S3 No bytes through our servers, scales with S3 Need a callback to know upload finished
Multipart presigned upload Same, but file split into parts Resumable for huge files Overkill for 2 MB photos

Recommended: presigned PUT URLs, then process asynchronously.

import boto3, uuid
s3 = boto3.client("s3")

def create_photo_uploads(user_id: int, count: int):
    uploads = []
    for _ in range(min(count, 10)):
        photo_id = id_gen.next()
        key = f"raw/{user_id}/{photo_id}.jpg"
        url = s3.generate_presigned_url(
            "put_object",
            Params={"Bucket": "food-photos", "Key": key,
                    "ContentType": "image/jpeg"},
            ExpiresIn=900)                       # 15 minutes
        db.execute("INSERT INTO photos (photo_id, review_id, s3_key, status) "
                   "VALUES (%s, NULL, %s, 'PENDING')", (photo_id, key))
        uploads.append({"photoId": photo_id, "url": url})
    return uploads

After the upload, S3 sends an event (ObjectCreated) to a queue. An image processor worker:

  1. Checks the file is really an image and under the size limit (10 MB).
  2. Strips EXIF metadata (it can contain the uploader’s home GPS location).
  3. Creates thumbnail (150 px), medium (600 px) and large (1200 px) versions.
  4. Runs an image moderation model (nudity, violence).
  5. Marks the photo READY or REJECTED.

Orphan cleanup: photos still PENDING after 24 hours with no review attached are deleted by a nightly job.

How do we keep the average rating correct and fast to read?

Restaurant pages show “4.6 stars from 1,832 reviews”. Computing AVG(rating) over all reviews on every page view is too slow for popular places. But a naive “read average, compute new average, write back” loses updates when two reviews arrive at the same moment.

Option How Pros Cons
Compute on read SELECT AVG(rating) FROM reviews WHERE restaurant_id=? Always exact Slow for big restaurants, heavy on DB
Read-modify-write the average Read avg, recompute, write Simple Race conditions lose updates
Atomic increment of sum and count UPDATE ... SET sum = sum + r, count = count + 1 Exact, fast, no race Hot row for very popular places
Async aggregation via events Consumer batches events and applies deltas Absorbs bursts, decoupled Seconds of lag (fine here)

Recommended: async consumer applying atomic deltas. Each event carries the change, so creates, edits, and deletes are all handled the same way.

def on_review_event(evt):
    # evt: {"type": "CREATED"|"UPDATED"|"DELETED", "restaurantId": 81,
    #       "old": 3 or None, "new": 5 or None, "eventId": "..."}
    if already_processed(evt["eventId"]):        # dedupe, Kafka is at-least-once
        return
    d_sum   = (evt["new"] or 0) - (evt["old"] or 0)
    d_count = (1 if evt["new"] else 0) - (1 if evt["old"] else 0)
    db.execute("""
        UPDATE restaurants
           SET rating_sum   = rating_sum + %s,
               rating_count = rating_count + %s
         WHERE restaurant_id = %s""",
        (d_sum, d_count, evt["restaurantId"]))
    redis.delete(f"restaurant:{evt['restaurantId']}")   # invalidate cache
    mark_processed(evt["eventId"])

Example edit: a user changes 3 stars to 5 stars. The delta is sum + 2, count + 0. A delete of a 4-star review is sum - 4, count - 1.

A nightly job recomputes SUM and COUNT from the reviews table and fixes any drift. Only approved reviews count, so moderation decisions also emit events.

Bonus: raw average favors places with 2 five-star reviews. For sorting, use a Bayesian average that pulls small samples toward the global mean:

def bayesian_avg(sum_, count, global_mean=3.8, prior_weight=20):
    return (sum_ + global_mean * prior_weight) / (count + prior_weight)

How do we find nearby restaurants quickly?

A plain SQL WHERE lat BETWEEN .. AND lng BETWEEN .. with two separate B-tree indexes is slow, because the database can only use one index well at a time.

Option How Pros Cons
Geohash prefix Encode lat/lng into a string; nearby places share prefixes Works on any key-value store, easy to shard Edge effects at cell borders, need to query 9 neighbor cells
Quadtree Split the map into cells until each has under N places Adapts to density (cities vs deserts) Custom in-memory structure to maintain
PostGIS (R-tree / GiST index) Native spatial index in Postgres Exact distance, SQL filters, easy One DB can become a bottleneck for very high QPS
Elasticsearch geo queries geo_distance filter + text and filters Combines geo, text search, ranking Another system to run, eventually consistent

Recommended: Elasticsearch (or OpenSearch) for search, because users also type text (“spicy ramen”) and filter by cuisine. 10 million restaurants is small for Elasticsearch. Postgres stays the source of truth, and changes stream into Elasticsearch through change data capture (CDC).

POST /restaurants/_search
{
  "query": {
    "bool": {
      "must":   [{ "match": { "cuisine": "ramen" } }],
      "filter": [{ "geo_distance": {
                     "distance": "2km",
                     "location": { "lat": 37.776, "lon": -122.417 } } }]
    }
  },
  "sort": [
    { "_geo_distance": { "location": { "lat": 37.776, "lon": -122.417 },
                          "order": "asc", "unit": "m" } }
  ],
  "size": 20
}

If the interviewer pushes for no Elasticsearch, explain geohash: precision 6 gives cells of about 1.2 km by 0.6 km. Compute the user’s cell plus its 8 neighbors and look up all restaurants in those 9 cells, then filter by exact distance.

import pygeohash as pgh
cell = pgh.encode(37.776, -122.417, precision=6)   # e.g. '9q8yyk'
cells = [cell] + neighbors(cell)                     # 9 cells total
candidates = db.query("SELECT * FROM restaurants WHERE geohash6 = ANY(%s)", (cells,))

How do we build a feed of recent reviews?

Two flavors: “recent reviews near me” and “reviews from people I follow”. A review is written about 12 times a second, so writes are rare and reads are frequent.

Option How Pros Cons
Pull (fan-out on read) At read time, query reviews by followed users / nearby cells No extra storage, always fresh Slow for users who follow many people
Push (fan-out on write) On new review, append id to each follower’s feed list Very fast reads Heavy writes for users with millions of followers
Hybrid Push for normal users, pull for “celebrity” food critics Balanced More logic

Recommended: hybrid, plus a per-geohash list for “nearby”.

def on_review_approved(review):
    # nearby feed: one capped list per geohash-5 cell (~5 km)
    cell = review.restaurant_geohash[:5]
    redis.lpush(f"feed:geo:{cell}", review.id)
    redis.ltrim(f"feed:geo:{cell}", 0, 499)       # keep latest 500

    author = users.get(review.user_id)
    if author.follower_count < 10_000:             # push for normal users
        for follower_id in followers_of(author.id):
            redis.lpush(f"feed:user:{follower_id}", review.id)
            redis.ltrim(f"feed:user:{follower_id}", 0, 499)
    # big critics: their reviews are merged in at read time (pull)

Only approved reviews enter feeds, so moderation must finish first (usually a second or two for automatic checks).

How do we enforce one review per user and moderate content?

Two correctness problems. First, a user double-taps Post, or two devices post at once, and we end up with two reviews. Second, spam, fake reviews, and offensive photos.

For uniqueness:

Option How Pros Cons
Check then insert in app code SELECT exists, then INSERT Simple Race: two requests both see “no review”
DB unique constraint UNIQUE (restaurant_id, user_id) Bulletproof, atomic Need to handle the error nicely
Distributed lock Lock on user:restaurant key Works across stores More moving parts, locks can leak

Recommended: unique constraint, and map the error to 409 with the existing review id so the client can switch to edit mode.

INSERT INTO reviews (review_id, restaurant_id, user_id, rating, body)
VALUES ($1, $2, $3, $4, $5)
ON CONFLICT (restaurant_id, user_id) DO NOTHING
RETURNING review_id;
-- no row returned -> 409 Conflict

If reviews are sharded, shard by restaurant_id so the constraint lives on one shard.

For moderation, use a layered pipeline:

 ReviewCreated --> [1. rules: banned words, links, rate limits]
               --> [2. ML: spam, toxicity, fake-review score]
               --> score < 0.3 : APPROVED (live)
                   score > 0.8 : REJECTED
                   otherwise   : human review queue

Signals for fake reviews: brand-new account, many 5-star reviews in a short time, reviews from far away from the user’s usual area, many reviews from the same device or IP. Rate limit posting to, say, 10 reviews per user per day. Only APPROVED reviews count toward the rating aggregate and appear in feeds.

How does it scale and survive failures?

  • Reads: cache restaurant pages and review first pages in Redis (hit rate around 90%). Add Postgres read replicas.
  • Writes: 40 writes per second at peak fits one Postgres primary easily. Shard by restaurant_id only if growth requires it.
  • Photos: S3 plus CDN scales on its own.
  • Kafka consumer down: events wait in Kafka; ratings and feeds catch up when it returns. The nightly recompute fixes drift.
  • Elasticsearch down: fall back to a PostGIS query with a smaller page size.
  • Region outage: replicate Postgres to a second region and serve reads from there; writes pause or fail over.

9. Common mistakes and interviewer follow-ups

  • Mistake: uploading photos through the API server. It wastes bandwidth and slows everyone. Say instead: “Presigned URLs, direct to S3, async processing.”
  • Mistake: storing only the average rating. You cannot update it correctly on edits or deletes. Say instead: “Store sum and count, apply deltas atomically.”
  • Mistake: computing AVG() on every page view. It does not scale for popular restaurants. Say instead: “Precomputed aggregate, cached, refreshed by events.”
  • Mistake: checking for an existing review in code, then inserting. Race conditions create duplicates. Say instead: “A unique constraint on (restaurant_id, user_id) is the real guard.”
  • Mistake: using two plain lat/lng indexes for nearby search. Slow scans. Say instead: “A real geo index: geohash, quadtree, PostGIS GiST, or Elasticsearch.”
  • Mistake: forgetting EXIF data. Photos can leak a user’s home location. Say instead: “Strip metadata during processing.”
  • Follow-up: “How do you rank reviews on a restaurant page?” Mix recency, helpful votes, reviewer trust score, and whether it has photos. Precompute a score per review.
  • Follow-up: “How do you handle a restaurant that gets 10,000 reviews in an hour after going viral?” The async aggregator batches deltas per restaurant, so it is one update per batch instead of 10,000 row updates.

10. One-page cheat sheet

Topic Key point
Scale 20M DAU, ~7k reads/s peak, ~40 review writes/s, ~2 PB photos/year
Photos Presigned PUT to S3, async resize + EXIF strip + scan, served via CDN
Rating Store rating_sum and rating_count; atomic deltas from Kafka events
Ranking Bayesian average to avoid “2 reviews, 5 stars” winning
Geo search Elasticsearch geo_distance; geohash-6 + 9 cells as a fallback
Uniqueness UNIQUE (restaurant_id, user_id), return 409 with existing id
Feed Hybrid fan-out; per-geohash capped Redis lists for “nearby”
Moderation Rules -> ML score -> human queue; only approved reviews count
Caching Restaurant page + first review page in Redis, invalidate on event
CAP AP for browsing and ratings, strong for uniqueness

34. Game Leaderboard (Medium)

A game leaderboard shows players ranked by score. Players want to see the top 10 in the world, their own rank (“you are #48,213”), the players just above and below them, and how they compare with friends. Boards usually come in daily, weekly and all-time versions. This question has been asked at Google. The interviewer is testing whether you know the right data structure (a sorted set, usually Redis), whether you can explain why a SQL ORDER BY with COUNT(*) does not work at scale, how you shard when one sorted set gets too big, how you handle ties and time windows, and how you recover if the in-memory store is lost.

1. Functional requirements

Core (must have):

  1. A game server can submit a player’s score after a match.
  2. Players can see the top N players (for example top 100) of a board.
  3. Players can see their own rank and score.
  4. Players can see the players around them (5 above and 5 below).
  5. There are daily, weekly and all-time boards.
  6. Players can see a leaderboard of just their friends.

Below the line (out of scope):

  • Anti-cheat and score validation logic. We assume the game server is trusted and already validated the match. We mention it but do not design it.
  • Matchmaking and the game itself.
  • Regional boards per country. Same design with a different key, so we only note it.
  • Rewards and prizes at the end of a season.

2. Non-functional requirements

  1. Scale: 50 million total players, 10 million daily active users (DAU).
  2. Fresh: a submitted score shows up on the board within 1 to 2 seconds.
  3. Low latency: p99 under 50 ms for “top 100” and “my rank”.
  4. Write throughput: handle at least 5,000 score updates per second at peak.
  5. Availability: 99.99% for reads. If the leaderboard is down the game still works, but players notice.
  6. Durability: no score is lost. Redis is fast but in memory, so we need a durable record somewhere.
  7. Consistency: eventual consistency is fine for ranks (a rank that is 1 second old is OK). The stored score per player must be correct (no lost updates).
  8. CAP choice: availability (AP). Showing a slightly stale rank is far better than showing an error.

3. Back-of-the-envelope estimates

Assumption Number
Total players 50 million
DAU 10 million
Matches per DAU per day 10
Leaderboard views per DAU per day 10
Peak to average ratio 5x
Bytes per sorted set entry (member + score + overhead) about 100 bytes
Boards kept in memory all-time, current week, current day (plus a few old ones) 
Writes (score submissions):
  10M * 10 matches / 86,400 s = ~1,160/s average
  peak 5x                      = ~5,800/s
  each submission updates 3 boards (daily, weekly, all-time) -> ~17,400 ZADDs/s

Reads (leaderboard views):
  10M * 10 / 86,400 s          = ~1,160/s average
  peak 5x                      = ~5,800/s
  each view = top-N + my-rank  -> ~12,000 Redis ops/s

Memory:
  all-time board: 50M entries * 100 B = 5 GB
  weekly board:   ~20M players  * 100 B = 2 GB
  daily board:    10M players   * 100 B = 1 GB
  total hot data                        = ~8 GB  (fits on one large Redis node,
                                                  plus a replica)

Durable storage (score history):
  10M * 10 matches * 50 B per row = 5 GB/day -> ~1.8 TB/year

One Redis node can do around 100,000 simple ops per second, and ZADD on a 50 million entry set is O(log N), about 26 steps. So for this size a single primary with replicas is enough. Sharding becomes necessary at roughly 10x this size, or for a game with hundreds of millions of players.

4. Core entities

  • Player: a user of the game. Fields: player_id, display_name, avatar_url, country.
  • Match: one finished game. Fields: match_id, player_id, score, played_at.
  • Leaderboard: a named board with a time window. Fields: board_id, game_id, window (DAILY, WEEKLY, ALL_TIME), period key (for example 2026-11-05 or 2026-W45).
  • LeaderboardEntry: a player’s score on one board. Lives in Redis as a member of a sorted set. Fields: player_id, score.
  • Friendship: player A is friends with player B.
  • ScoreEvent: the durable log of every submitted score, used to rebuild boards.
CREATE TABLE score_events (
  event_id    UUID PRIMARY KEY,          -- idempotency, one row per match
  player_id   BIGINT NOT NULL,
  game_id     INT NOT NULL,
  score       BIGINT NOT NULL,
  played_at   TIMESTAMP NOT NULL
);
CREATE INDEX idx_score_events_time ON score_events (game_id, played_at);

CREATE TABLE player_best (
  game_id     INT NOT NULL,
  player_id   BIGINT NOT NULL,
  best_score  BIGINT NOT NULL,
  achieved_at TIMESTAMP NOT NULL,
  PRIMARY KEY (game_id, player_id)
);
Redis keys:
  lb:{game}:all                -> sorted set  member=player_id score=best
  lb:{game}:week:2026-W45      -> sorted set  (TTL 30 days)
  lb:{game}:day:2026-11-05     -> sorted set  (TTL 7 days)
  player:{id}                  -> hash  name, avatar  (kept out of the set)

5. API design

Score submission is called by trusted game servers (service-to-service auth like mTLS or a signed token), never directly by the client, so players cannot post fake scores.

POST /games/{gameId}/scores – submit the result of a match.

// request
{ "matchId": "m_7f3a", "playerId": 1234, "score": 98200,
  "playedAt": "2026-11-05T18:02:11Z" }
// response 202
{ "accepted": true }

Status codes: 202 accepted, 200 duplicate match id (already processed), 400 invalid, 401 caller is not a game server.

GET /games/{gameId}/leaderboards/{window}?limit=100&offset=0 – top N of a board. window is daily, weekly or alltime.

// response 200
{ "window": "weekly", "period": "2026-W45",
  "entries": [
    { "rank": 1, "playerId": 88, "name": "Kai", "score": 151000 },
    { "rank": 2, "playerId": 12, "name": "Mira", "score": 149800 } ] }

GET /games/{gameId}/leaderboards/{window}/players/{playerId} – one player’s rank.

{ "rank": 48213, "score": 98200, "percentile": 99.03 }

GET /games/{gameId}/leaderboards/{window}/players/{playerId}/around?count=5 – players around you.

GET /games/{gameId}/leaderboards/{window}/friends?playerId=1234 – friends-only board.

Read endpoints need a logged-in player. Public “top 100” can be cached at a CDN for a few seconds.

How will a score get onto the board?

  1. The game server sends POST /scores with a unique matchId.
  2. The Score Ingest Service writes the event to Kafka (durable log) first.
  3. A consumer stores the event in the database (the source of truth) and updates Redis.
  4. For each board (daily, weekly, all-time) it runs ZADD with the GT flag, so the stored score only goes up if the new one is higher (for “best score” games).
  5. Within about a second, the new score is visible.
sequenceDiagram
    participant G as Game server
    participant S as Score Ingest
    participant K as Kafka
    participant C as Consumer
    participant D as Database
    participant R as Redis
    G->>S: POST scores with match id
    S->>K: Write score event
    K-->>S: ack
    S-->>G: 202 accepted
    K->>C: Deliver event
    C->>D: Insert score event by match id
    C->>R: ZADD GT daily board
    C->>R: ZADD GT weekly board
    C->>R: ZADD GT all time board
    R-->>C: ok

How will players see the top 100?

  1. The client calls GET /leaderboards/weekly?limit=100.
  2. The Read Service runs ZREVRANGE lb:{g}:week:2026-W45 0 99 WITHSCORES on a Redis replica.
  3. It looks up names and avatars for those 100 ids with one pipelined HMGET batch (or a local cache).
  4. The response is cached for 2 to 5 seconds, because thousands of players ask for the same top 100.

How will a player see their own rank?

  1. The client calls GET /leaderboards/weekly/players/1234.
  2. The Read Service runs ZREVRANK (0-based rank from the top) and ZSCORE.
  3. It adds 1 to the rank and returns it. Both calls are O(log N), well under a millisecond.

How will a player see the players around them?

  1. Get the player’s rank r with ZREVRANK.
  2. Run ZREVRANGE key max(0, r-5) r+5 WITHSCORES.
  3. Hydrate names and return 11 rows with the player in the middle.

How will a player see their friends’ board?

  1. Load the friend list (say 200 ids) from the social service.
  2. Fetch each friend’s score with ZMSCORE in one call, sort in the service, return. Details in the deep dive.

7. Deep dives

Why a sorted set, and what does the code look like?

The naive SQL design is one scores table and:

-- top 100: fine with an index on score
SELECT player_id, score FROM scores ORDER BY score DESC LIMIT 100;

-- my rank: this is the problem
SELECT COUNT(*) + 1 FROM scores WHERE score > (SELECT score FROM scores
                                               WHERE player_id = 1234);

The rank query has to count every row above you. For a player in the middle of 50 million rows, that is 25 million index entries scanned per request. At thousands of requests per second the DB collapses.

Option Top N My rank Updates Notes
SQL table + index Fast O(N) count, slow Fast Fine under ~1M players
Redis sorted set O(log N + M) O(log N) O(log N) Skip list + hash map, in memory
Precomputed ranks (batch job) Fast Fast Stale by minutes Good for huge boards, not live

Recommended: Redis sorted set. It is a skip list (a sorted linked list with “express lanes” so you can jump ahead) plus a hash map from member to score. Each skip list node also stores span counts, which is why Redis can tell you a rank without counting every member.

import redis
r = redis.Redis(host="lb-redis", decode_responses=True)

def board_keys(game, ts):
    day  = ts.strftime("%Y-%m-%d")
    week = ts.strftime("%G-W%V")              # ISO week, e.g. 2026-W45
    return [f"lb:{game}:all", f"lb:{game}:week:{week}", f"lb:{game}:day:{day}"]

def submit_score(game, player_id, score, ts):
    pipe = r.pipeline()
    for key in board_keys(game, ts):
        pipe.zadd(key, {player_id: score}, gt=True)   # keep the best score
    pipe.expire(board_keys(game, ts)[1], 60 * 86400)  # weekly TTL
    pipe.expire(board_keys(game, ts)[2], 8 * 86400)   # daily TTL
    pipe.execute()

def top_n(key, n=100):
    return r.zrevrange(key, 0, n - 1, withscores=True)

def my_rank(key, player_id):
    rank = r.zrevrank(key, player_id)          # 0-based, None if absent
    if rank is None:
        return None
    return {"rank": rank + 1, "score": r.zscore(key, player_id)}

def around_me(key, player_id, k=5):
    rank = r.zrevrank(key, player_id)
    start = max(0, rank - k)
    return r.zrevrange(key, start, rank + k, withscores=True)

If the game sums points instead of keeping the best score, use ZINCRBY key points player_id. Both are atomic in Redis, so two concurrent updates never lose each other.

How do we break ties?

Two players with 98,200 points. Redis sorts equal scores by member name (lexicographic), which is not fair. Most games say “whoever reached the score first ranks higher”.

Option How Pros Cons
Accept Redis default Ties ordered by player id string Nothing to do Arbitrary, players complain
Share the rank Both are #5, next is #7 Fair, simple to explain Need extra query (ZCOUNT of higher scores)
Encode time into the score score * 2^k + (MAX_TS - ts) First to reach wins, one sorted set Must fit in 53 bits of a double

Recommended: encode the time into the score. Redis scores are 64-bit floats, which hold integers exactly up to 2^53 (about 9 * 10^15).

MAX_TS = 2_000_000_000            # seconds, year 2033

def encode(score: int, ts_sec: int) -> int:
    # score up to ~4.5 million fits: 4.5e6 * 2e9 = 9e15 < 2^53
    return score * MAX_TS + (MAX_TS - ts_sec)   # earlier ts -> bigger tail

def decode(packed: int) -> int:
    return packed // MAX_TS

If scores are too large for this trick, use “shared rank”: rank = ZCOUNT(key, "(" + score, "+inf") + 1, which counts players with a strictly higher score.

How do we shard when one sorted set is too big?

A single sorted set lives on one Redis node. If the game has 500 million players (50 GB) or 200,000 writes per second, one node is not enough.

Option How Top N My rank Cons
Shard by player id (hash) Player goes to shard hash(id) % K Merge top N from all K shards Sum of ranks across all K shards Rank needs K queries
Shard by score range Shard 1: 0 to 1k, shard 2: 1k to 10k, … Read from top shard only Rank in own shard + sizes of higher shards Uneven shards, players move between shards
Exact top, approximate rank Keep a small exact top 10k set; estimate others from a histogram Exact “Top 3%” Not exact for most players

Recommended for most games: hash by player id with scatter-gather, plus the approximate trick for players far from the top.

SHARDS = [redis.Redis(host=f"lb-{i}") for i in range(16)]

def shard_for(player_id):
    return SHARDS[hash(player_id) % len(SHARDS)]

def global_top_n(key, n=100):
    # each shard returns its own top n; merge and keep the best n
    pipes = [s.zrevrange(key, 0, n - 1, withscores=True) for s in SHARDS]
    merged = sorted((e for part in pipes for e in part),
                    key=lambda x: x[1], reverse=True)
    return merged[:n]

def global_rank(key, player_id):
    score = shard_for(player_id).zscore(key, player_id)
    if score is None:
        return None
    higher = sum(s.zcount(key, f"({score}", "+inf") for s in SHARDS)
    return higher + 1

Each ZCOUNT is O(log N), and the 16 calls run in parallel, so rank lookup is still a few milliseconds. Cache the global top 100 for a couple of seconds so the merge does not run for every request.

The approximate trick: most players do not care whether they are #4,812,331 or #4,812,330. Keep a histogram of score buckets (for example count of players per 100-point bucket) and answer “you are in the top 9.6%”. Only the top 10,000 get an exact number.

How do we handle daily, weekly and all-time boards?

Option How Pros Cons
One set per period key lb:g:day:2026-11-05, TTL to expire Simple, reset is automatic (new key) 3 writes per score
One set + filter by time Store timestamps, filter at read One write Sorted set cannot filter by time; needs rebuild
Rebuild with ZUNIONSTORE Weekly = union of 7 daily sets with AGGREGATE MAX Fewer writes Union of big sets is slow, must be run on schedule

Recommended: one sorted set per period, written in the same pipeline. A new day simply means a new key name, so there is no “reset” job and no race at midnight. TTLs clean up old boards. Before a key expires, a job copies the final top 1,000 into the database as a permanent record (“last week’s winners”).

Time zones: pick one (UTC) for global boards and say so. Regional boards can use local time with a region in the key: lb:g:day:IN:2026-11-05.

How do we build a friends leaderboard?

A player has maybe 50 to 500 friends. Keeping a separate sorted set per player would mean every score update writes to every friend’s set (fan-out on write), which is expensive for players with many friends.

Option How Pros Cons
Fan-out on write Update every friend’s personal sorted set Fast read Write amplification, 500x writes
Fan-out on read with ZMSCORE Fetch friends’ scores from the global set, sort in app No extra storage, always fresh 1 call per read, fine for 500 friends
ZINTERSTORE with friend set Intersect global board with a set of friend ids Pure Redis Creates temp keys, slower on big sets

Recommended: fan-out on read with ZMSCORE. One round trip, 500 lookups at O(1) each.

def friends_board(key, player_id, friend_ids):
    ids = list(friend_ids) + [player_id]
    scores = r.zmscore(key, ids)                 # list, None if no score
    rows = [(pid, s) for pid, s in zip(ids, scores) if s is not None]
    rows.sort(key=lambda x: x[1], reverse=True)
    return [{"rank": i + 1, "playerId": pid, "score": s}
            for i, (pid, s) in enumerate(rows)]

Cache the result for 10 seconds per player.

How do we persist and recover if Redis is lost?

Redis is the fast view, not the source of truth. If a node dies and data is lost, we must rebuild.

Option How Pros Cons
Redis persistence only (RDB snapshots + AOF) Redis writes to disk Simple Can lose last second; corrupted file means total loss
Durable event log + rebuild Every score in Kafka and DB; replay to rebuild Full recovery, audit trail Rebuild of 50M entries takes minutes
Replicas + failover Redis Sentinel or Cluster promotes a replica Seconds of downtime Async replication can lose a few writes

Recommended: all three. Replicas for fast failover, AOF with appendfsync everysec to limit loss, and the database player_best table as the true record.

-- rebuild all-time board from the source of truth
SELECT player_id, best_score, achieved_at
FROM player_best
WHERE game_id = 7;
def rebuild(game):
    tmp = f"lb:{game}:all:rebuild"
    for batch in db.stream("SELECT player_id, best_score FROM player_best "
                           "WHERE game_id=%s", (game,), batch_size=10_000):
        r.zadd(tmp, {row.player_id: row.best_score for row in batch})
    r.rename(tmp, f"lb:{game}:all")       # atomic swap, readers never see half

At 10,000 entries per pipelined batch and about 500,000 entries per second, 50 million rows take under 2 minutes. During that time the replica serves reads. Kafka consumers then replay any events newer than the snapshot. Because ZADD GT is idempotent (the same score twice does nothing), replay is safe.

Idempotency on ingest: the matchId is the primary key of score_events, so a retried submission is a no-op in the DB, and ZADD GT with the same score changes nothing in Redis.

9. Common mistakes and interviewer follow-ups

  • Mistake: COUNT(*) in SQL for rank. It scans millions of rows per request. Say instead: “A sorted set gives rank in O(log N).”
  • Mistake: letting the client submit its own score. Easy to cheat. Say instead: “Only the trusted game server submits, after validating the match.”
  • Mistake: a nightly reset job for the daily board. Race conditions at midnight and a window where the board is empty. Say instead: “A new key per period, old keys expire with a TTL.”
  • Mistake: treating Redis as the only copy. One bad failover loses everything. Say instead: “Kafka and a database are the truth; Redis can be rebuilt.”
  • Mistake: ignoring ties. Players notice and complain. Say instead: “Encode the timestamp in the score so whoever got there first ranks higher.”
  • Mistake: sharding too early. 50 million players is about 5 GB, which fits on one node. Say instead: “Start with one primary and replicas; shard by player id with scatter-gather when memory or write rate requires it.”
  • Follow-up: “How would you show a percentile?” rank / ZCARD(key). With shards, sum ZCARD from each shard.
  • Follow-up: “What if 1 million players finish a tournament at the same second?” Kafka absorbs the burst, the Redis updater batches ZADD calls with pipelining, and ranks catch up within seconds.

10. One-page cheat sheet

Topic Key point
Scale 50M players, ~6k score submits/s peak, ~17k ZADD/s, ~8 GB in Redis
Data structure Redis sorted set (skip list + hash), O(log N) for update and rank
Commands ZADD GT, ZINCRBY, ZREVRANGE, ZREVRANK, ZSCORE, ZMSCORE, ZCOUNT
Time windows One key per period (day:2026-11-05, week:2026-W45), TTL cleanup
Ties Pack score and (MAX_TS - ts) into one 53-bit number
Sharding Hash by player id; top N = merge of shard tops; rank = sum of ZCOUNT
Huge boards Exact top 10k, approximate percentile for the rest
Friends Fan-out on read with ZMSCORE, sort in app, cache 10 s
Durability Kafka + DB as truth, Redis replicas + AOF, rebuild with atomic RENAME
Security Scores only from game servers (mTLS), dedupe by match id
CAP AP, stale-by-a-second ranks are fine

35. Donations Website (Hard)

A donations website lets viewers of a charity livestream give money to pre-selected charities while the show is on. The page shows a big running total (“$1,284,330 raised”), a goal bar, and a live list of top donors, and the host reads out donations on air. This was asked at Whatnot, a live shopping company, so the “live” part matters. The interviewer is testing four things: that you handle real money correctly (payment provider integration, idempotency, no double charges, no lost donations), that you can keep a running total accurate under thousands of donations per second during a spike, that the number on screen matches the money actually collected (and handles refunds and chargebacks), and that the system survives the moment a celebrity says “donate now”.

1. Functional requirements

Core (must have):

  1. Users can donate an amount to one of the charities in an event using a card or wallet (Apple Pay, Google Pay).
  2. Users see a confirmation once their payment succeeds.
  3. Everyone watching sees a real-time running total for the event (and per charity).
  4. Everyone sees a live top donors leaderboard and a feed of recent donations (with an optional name and message).
  5. Donors can choose to be anonymous.
  6. Admins can see reconciled totals and handle refunds and chargebacks.

Below the line (out of scope):

  • The video streaming itself. We assume the livestream already exists and we embed a widget next to it.
  • Paying out money to charities (settlement to bank accounts). Done after the event, low volume, offline.
  • Recurring donations and tax receipts by mail. Nice to have, not core to the live event.
  • Building our own card processing. We use a payment provider (Stripe, Adyen, Braintree).

2. Non-functional requirements

  1. Correctness of money: a donor must never be charged twice for one click, and a successful charge must never be lost. This needs strong consistency in the payment ledger.
  2. Spike tolerance: normal rate maybe 50 donations per second, but a shout-out on stream can cause 5,000 to 10,000 donations per second for a minute.
  3. Freshness of the total: the displayed total updates within 1 to 2 seconds of a payment succeeding.
  4. Fan-out: 2 million concurrent viewers all watching the same total and feed.
  5. Latency: donate button to “thank you” in under 3 seconds p99 (most of that is the payment provider).
  6. Availability: 99.99% during the event window (24 to 48 hours). Losing donations during a peak is the worst failure.
  7. Accuracy of the display: the displayed total can lag, but must converge to the ledger total. It must never show money that was not collected for more than a few seconds, and refunds must eventually be subtracted.
  8. Security: PCI DSS scope kept minimal (card numbers never touch our servers), fraud checks for stolen cards.
  9. CAP choice: the payment ledger is CP (correct or nothing). The live total and leaderboard are AP: always show something, accept a short lag.

3. Back-of-the-envelope estimates

Assumption Number
Event length 48 hours
Total donations in the event 5 million
Average donation $25
Peak donation rate (after a shout-out) 10,000 per second for 60 s
Concurrent viewers at peak 2 million
Donation record size 1 KB
Total update push to viewers 1 per second (batched)
Feed messages shown per second 20 (sampled at peak) 
Average write rate:
  5,000,000 / (48 * 3,600 s) = ~29 donations/s

Peak write rate:
  10,000 donations/s  (300x average)
  -> payment provider calls at 10,000/s; check provider rate limits!
  -> ledger inserts at 10,000/s; fine for a sharded DB or DynamoDB,
     tight for one Postgres primary

Money:
  5M * $25 = $125M total for the event

Storage:
  5M * 1 KB = 5 GB for donations + ~3x for payment events and audit
  -> ~20 GB total. Tiny.

Fan-out to viewers:
  2M viewers * 1 total update/s           = 2M messages/s
  2M viewers * 20 feed items/s (peak)     = 40M messages/s if naive
  -> batch: one message/s per viewer with total + last N items
  -> 2M messages/s, each ~500 bytes = ~1 GB/s outbound across the fleet
  -> with ~50k connections per WebSocket server: 40 servers at peak

The math says: the write rate is spiky but manageable, the money must be exact, and the read side (2 million watchers) is a broadcast problem, not a database problem.

4. Core entities

  • Event: a fundraising livestream. Fields: event_id, title, start_at, end_at, goal_cents, status.
  • Charity: an organization in the event. Fields: charity_id, event_id, name, logo_url.
  • Donor: a user, possibly a guest. Fields: donor_id, email, display_name.
  • Donation: one gift intent. Fields: donation_id, event_id, charity_id, donor_id, amount_cents, currency, status (CREATED, AUTHORIZED, SUCCEEDED, FAILED, REFUNDED, DISPUTED), is_anonymous, message, idempotency_key.
  • PaymentAttempt: one call to the provider for a donation. Fields: attempt_id, donation_id, provider, provider_payment_id, status, raw_response.
  • LedgerEntry: an append-only money record (credit on success, debit on refund or chargeback). Fields: entry_id, donation_id, amount_cents (positive or negative), type, created_at.
  • TotalCounter: the live running total, sharded in Redis, rebuilt from the ledger.
CREATE TABLE donations (
  donation_id     UUID PRIMARY KEY,
  event_id        BIGINT NOT NULL,
  charity_id      BIGINT NOT NULL,
  donor_id        BIGINT,
  amount_cents    BIGINT NOT NULL CHECK (amount_cents > 0),
  currency        CHAR(3) NOT NULL,
  status          VARCHAR(16) NOT NULL,
  is_anonymous    BOOLEAN NOT NULL DEFAULT false,
  message         VARCHAR(280),
  idempotency_key VARCHAR(64) NOT NULL,
  created_at      TIMESTAMP NOT NULL DEFAULT now(),
  UNIQUE (donor_id, idempotency_key)
);

CREATE TABLE ledger_entries (
  entry_id      UUID PRIMARY KEY,
  donation_id   UUID NOT NULL REFERENCES donations,
  event_id      BIGINT NOT NULL,
  charity_id    BIGINT NOT NULL,
  amount_cents  BIGINT NOT NULL,         -- +credit, -refund/chargeback
  type          VARCHAR(16) NOT NULL,    -- CAPTURE, REFUND, CHARGEBACK
  provider_ref  VARCHAR(64) NOT NULL,
  created_at    TIMESTAMP NOT NULL DEFAULT now(),
  UNIQUE (provider_ref, type)            -- a provider event applies once
);

Money is always stored as integer cents, never floats. 0.1 + 0.2 in floating point is not 0.3, and auditors notice.

5. API design

Donating requires either a logged-in user or a guest session with email. Admin endpoints require an admin role.

GET /events/{eventId} – event info, charities, goal (CDN-cacheable).

POST /events/{eventId}/donations – create a donation intent. Header Idempotency-Key (UUID created by the client when the form opens).

// request
{ "charityId": 3, "amountCents": 2500, "currency": "USD",
  "isAnonymous": false, "displayName": "Sam", "message": "Go team!" }
// response 201
{ "donationId": "d_71c", "status": "CREATED",
  "clientSecret": "pi_3Nx..._secret_abc" }

The clientSecret lets the browser confirm the payment directly with the provider’s SDK (Stripe Elements, for example), so card numbers never reach us.

GET /donations/{donationId} – poll status (CREATED, SUCCEEDED, FAILED).

{ "donationId": "d_71c", "status": "SUCCEEDED", "amountCents": 2500 }

POST /webhooks/payments – the provider calls this with payment results. Verified by signature header, not by user auth.

{ "id": "evt_1PQ", "type": "payment_intent.succeeded",
  "data": { "object": { "id": "pi_3Nx", "amount": 2500,
            "metadata": { "donationId": "d_71c" } } } }

Responds 200 quickly (even for duplicates), 400 for bad signature.

GET /events/{eventId}/live – WebSocket or Server-Sent Events (SSE) stream of totals, top donors and recent donations.

{ "type": "tick", "totalCents": 128433000, "byCharity": {"3": 51200000},
  "topDonors": [{"name": "Ana", "cents": 1000000}],
  "recent": [{"name": "Sam", "cents": 2500, "msg": "Go team!"}] }

GET /events/{eventId}/leaderboard?limit=50 – top donors (REST fallback).

POST /admin/donations/{donationId}/refund – admin refund (admin role, audited).
